papers.2: Paper 2 AS Data Response and Essays
papers.4: Paper 4 A Level Data Response and Essays

topics.name: The price system and the microeconomy (A Level)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which condition holds for a firm in long-run equilibrium in perfect competition?
A price = marginal cost = minimum average cost
B price > marginal cost and the firm earns supernormal profit
C marginal revenue = marginal cost at an output below minimum average cost
D price = average variable cost
parts.answer: A price = marginal cost = minimum average cost
parts.working: Free entry and exit remove supernormal profit, so P = AR = MR = MC = minimum AC and the firm earns normal profit. C describes monopolistic competition in the long run (excess capacity).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the kinked demand curve model of oligopoly, explaining the assumptions about how rival firms react.
parts.answer: Rivals match price cuts but do not follow price rises, so demand is elastic above the current price and inelastic below it, producing a kink.
parts.working: 1 mark: assumption that rivals do not follow a price rise – demand above the kink is price elastic (firm loses many customers). 1 mark: rivals follow a price cut – demand below the kink is price inelastic (little gain in sales). 1 mark: kink at the current price. 1 mark: MR curve has a vertical discontinuity (gap) below the kink.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the model predicts that prices in oligopoly will be stable even when costs change.
parts.answer: Because MC can shift up or down within the gap in the MR curve without changing the profit-maximising output and price.
parts.working: 1 mark: profit maximisation where MR = MC. 1 mark: the discontinuity in MR means MC can rise or fall within the gap. 1 mark: output and price stay the same – price rigidity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one limitation of the kinked demand curve model.
parts.answer: It does not explain how the initial price was set (or: evidence shows oligopoly prices do change; ignores non-price competition and collusion).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two conditions that make collusion between firms in an oligopoly more likely.
parts.answer: Few firms, so agreements are easy to make and monitor; similar costs and products, so firms can agree on one price; also high barriers to entry, stable demand, and weak competition law enforcement.
parts.working: For each of two conditions: 1 for the condition, 1 for why it helps collusion. Conditions: small number of firms; similar costs/homogeneous products; barriers to entry stop new firms undercutting; easy to observe rivals' prices (cheating detected); stable market demand; weak competition authority; a dominant firm that can act as price leader.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each member of a cartel has an incentive to cheat on the agreement.
parts.answer: The cartel price is above each member's marginal cost, so a firm that secretly sells more at, or slightly below, the agreed price raises its own profit, at the expense of the other members; if all do this the price falls.
parts.working: 1: cartel restricts output to raise price above MC; 1: one firm can raise its own profit by selling extra units/undercutting; 1: gain to cheater comes at the expense of others, so the agreement is unstable (prisoners' dilemma).

practice.stem: A company holds the only government licence to build and operate mobile phone towers in a country (invented).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three barriers to entry that could allow a monopoly to keep earning supernormal profit in the long run.
parts.answer: Legal barriers such as licences or patents; economies of scale that give the incumbent much lower average cost; high sunk costs (e.g. network infrastructure) that new firms cannot recover; also control of essential inputs, brand loyalty, or anti-competitive pricing.
parts.working: For each of three barriers: 1 mark for the barrier, 1 mark for explaining how it keeps rivals out. Barriers: legal (licence, patent, franchise); economies of scale/natural monopoly; sunk costs; control of raw materials or distribution; strong brand loyalty/advertising; limit or predatory pricing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why supernormal profit would be competed away in the long run if there were no barriers to entry.
parts.answer: Supernormal profit attracts new firms; supply rises and price falls until only normal profit is earned.
parts.working: 1: profit signals entry of new firms; 1: increased supply lowers price/each firm's demand until P = AC (normal profit).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A monopolist faces the following prices and total costs.
Output (units): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Price ($): 50, 45, 40, 35, 30, 25
Total cost ($): 30, 48, 62, 80, 105, 138
Which output maximises profit?
A 3 units
B 4 units
C 5 units
D 6 units
parts.answer: B 4 units
parts.working: TR = 50, 90, 120, 140, 150, 150 and profit = TR − TC = 20, 42, 58, 60, 45, 12, so profit is greatest at 4 units. Check with marginal values: the 4th unit has MR = 20 and MC = 18 (worth producing), but the 5th unit has MR = 10 and MC = 25 (not worth producing). C and D are wrong: total revenue is highest at 5–6 units, but profit falls there.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a perfectly contestable market.
parts.answer: A market where entry and exit are free and costless, with no sunk costs, so incumbents face the threat of entry whatever the number of firms.
parts.working: 1 mark: no barriers to entry or exit. 1 mark: no sunk costs, so firms can leave without loss. 1 mark: entrants have access to the same technology / incumbents cannot react instantly; number of firms may be small.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the threat of 'hit-and-run' entry affects the behaviour of a firm in such a market.
parts.answer: Supernormal profits would attract entrants who take profits and leave, so incumbents keep prices near average cost.
parts.working: 1 mark: hit-and-run entry described. 1 mark: incumbents therefore limit price to earn only normal profit. 1 mark: they also have an incentive to minimise costs – outcome may be close to productive/allocative efficiency even with few firms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of a sunk cost that might make the market for domestic air travel less contestable.
parts.answer: Advertising to build a brand / training of crew / landing slot fees that cannot be recovered.
parts.working: B1 (aircraft themselves can be leased or resold, so are not mainly sunk).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that monopoly is always against the interests of consumers.
parts.answer: Not always: monopoly can bring higher prices and lower output, but economies of scale, dynamic efficiency and regulation may benefit consumers.
parts.working: Knowledge and understanding / analysis (up to 14): diagram comparing monopoly with perfect competition – monopoly sets MR = MC, higher price, lower output, P > MC (allocative inefficiency), possibly not at minimum AC (productive inefficiency), deadweight loss, transfer of consumer surplus to producer; X-inefficiency without competition; less choice. Counter-arguments: natural monopoly and economies of scale may give lower costs and prices than many small firms; supernormal profit funds research and development (dynamic efficiency, new products); contestable markets restrain prices; price discrimination can allow some consumers to be served who otherwise would not; regulation (price caps) and competition policy. Evaluation (up to 6): depends on barriers to entry, the industry (utilities vs consumer goods), whether profits are reinvested, government regulation; reasoned conclusion on 'always'. Level 4 (15–20) requires a well-supported judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes a firm in monopolistic competition in long-run equilibrium?
A It earns normal profit and produces an output at which its average cost is still falling.
B It earns normal profit and produces at the lowest point of its average cost curve.
C It earns supernormal profit because its product is differentiated.
D It sets its price equal to marginal cost.
parts.answer: A It earns normal profit and produces an output at which its average cost is still falling.
parts.working: Free entry removes supernormal profit, so the demand (AR) curve is tangent to AC. Because AR slopes downwards, the tangency is on the falling part of AC: the firm has excess capacity. B describes perfect competition; C applies only in the short run; D does not hold because P > MR = MC.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether firms in oligopoly are more likely to compete through non-price competition than through price.
parts.answer: Interdependence makes price competition risky (price wars, kinked demand), so oligopolists often prefer branding, advertising, quality and loyalty schemes; but price competition does occur when firms have cost advantages, products are homogeneous, a firm wants market share, or collusion breaks down.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: features of oligopoly (few firms, interdependence, barriers); kinked demand curve: rivals match price cuts but not rises → price rigidity; game theory: price cutting leads to a worse outcome for all (prisoners' dilemma); non-price competition builds brand loyalty, makes demand less price elastic, and is harder to copy quickly. Evaluation: homogeneous products (cement, fuel) leave little room for non-price competition; a firm with lower costs may start a price war to drive out rivals; new entrants often compete on price (budget airlines); collusion/price leadership may replace both; consumer search tools increase price competition; conclusion depends on the type of product and market.

practice.stem: A rail company sells peak-time and off-peak tickets on one route (invented data). Peak demand is P = 100 − 2Q and off-peak demand is P = 60 − Q, where P is the fare in dollars and Q is thousands of tickets per week. Marginal cost is constant at $20 per ticket in both markets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit-maximising quantity and price in each market.
parts.answer: Peak: Q = 20 thousand, P = $60; off-peak: Q = 20 thousand, P = $40

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand (as a positive number) in each market at these prices, and explain how this relates to the prices charged.
parts.answer: Peak 1.5; off-peak 2.0; the higher price is charged where demand is less price elastic.
parts.working: For P = a − bQ, PED = P ÷ (a − P). Peak: 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5 (B1). Off-peak: 40 ÷ 20 = 2.0 (B1). The firm charges more in the market with lower PED (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the firm's total profit from the two markets, ignoring fixed costs.
parts.answer: $1200 thousand

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two conditions that make it possible for the company to practise this price discrimination.
parts.answer: Some monopoly power; markets can be separated (ticket valid only at that time) with no resale; different PEDs in the two markets.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
Two airlines, Alpha and Beta, are the only carriers on a route. Each must choose a high fare or a low fare. The table shows annual profits in $ million (Alpha's profit first, Beta's second) (invented data).
Alpha high, Beta high: 60, 60
Alpha high, Beta low: 20, 80
Alpha low, Beta high: 80, 20
Alpha low, Beta low: 35, 35

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify each airline's dominant strategy, if it has one. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Both airlines have a dominant strategy of a low fare.
parts.working: If Beta sets High, Alpha earns 80 with Low > 60 with High (1). If Beta sets Low, Alpha earns 35 with Low > 20 with High (1). So Low is dominant for Alpha; by symmetry also for Beta (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the Nash equilibrium and explain why the airlines may be tempted to collude.
parts.answer: Nash equilibrium: both set low fares ($35 million each). If both colluded on high fares they would each earn $60 million.
parts.working: 1 mark: Nash equilibrium (Low, Low). 1 mark: joint profit at (High, High) is 120 > 70. 1 mark: this is a prisoners' dilemma – collusion raises profit but each has an incentive to cheat (80 > 60), so agreements are unstable without trust or enforcement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether price discrimination by firms such as airlines and electricity suppliers benefits consumers.
parts.answer: Some consumers gain (lower prices, access to services), others lose (higher prices, loss of consumer surplus); overall benefit depends on output effects and use of profit.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): definition and conditions (market power, separation of markets, different PED, no resale); third-degree price discrimination diagram with two markets, higher price in the inelastic market; first-degree discrimination converts all consumer surplus to producer surplus. Benefits: lower prices for students, off-peak users or low-income groups; total output may rise; a service may only be viable with discrimination (covering high fixed costs); off-peak pricing spreads demand and uses capacity better; profits may fund investment. Costs: consumers in the inelastic market pay more; loss of consumer surplus; perceived unfairness; may be used to drive out rivals (predatory). Evaluation (up to 6): judge which consumers, whether output increases, whether profits are reinvested and whether regulation protects captive users; reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm in a perfectly competitive market sells at the market price of $17. At its profit-maximising output of 500 units, its average variable cost is $15 and its average total cost is $21. What should the firm do?
A Shut down immediately, because it is making a loss of $3 000.
B Continue producing in the short run, making a loss of $2 000, but leave the industry in the long run if the price stays at $17.
C Continue producing in the long run, because the price is above average variable cost.
D Continue producing, because it earns $1 000 above its variable costs and so covers all its costs.
parts.answer: B Continue producing in the short run, making a loss of $2 000, but leave the industry in the long run if the price stays at $17.
parts.working: Loss if it produces = (17 − 21) × 500 = −$2 000. Fixed cost = (21 − 15) × 500 = $3 000, which would be the loss if it shut down. Since P > AVC, producing reduces the loss, so it stays in the short run; in the long run all costs must be covered, so it leaves if P < ATC. A gives the shutdown loss, not the loss from producing; D confuses contribution to fixed costs with covering all costs.

practice.stem: A regional water company is the only supplier in its area (invented data). Its total cost is TC = 60 + 4Q and its demand curve is P = 40 − 2Q, where Q is millions of cubic metres a year, P is dollars per cubic metre and TC is in $ million. So MC = 4, AC = 60/Q + 4 and MR = 40 − 4Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit-maximising output, price and profit.
parts.answer: Q = 9 million m³, P = $22 per m³, profit = $102 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The regulator requires the company to set price equal to marginal cost. Calculate the output and the profit or loss.
parts.answer: Q = 18 million m³ at P = $4; loss of $60 million.
parts.working: 40 − 2Q = 4 → Q = 18 (1); TR = 72, TC = 60 + 72 = 132, loss = 60 (equal to the fixed cost) (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The regulator instead requires price to equal average cost. Calculate the output and price, each to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Q = 16.14 million m³, P = $7.72.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why this firm is a natural monopoly and why marginal-cost pricing is difficult to sustain.
parts.answer: Average cost falls over the whole range of demand because the large fixed cost of pipes and treatment works is spread over more output, so one firm can supply the market more cheaply than two. Because AC > MC, a price equal to MC always makes a loss, which needs a subsidy.
parts.working: 1: very high fixed/sunk costs; 1: AC falls over the whole range of market output, so one firm has lowest cost; 1: MC < AC so P = MC gives a loss (here the whole fixed cost) and needs a subsidy, or the firm will not invest.

practice.stem: A cinema is the only one in a small town. Demand for tickets to a screening is P = 50 − Q, where P is the ticket price in dollars and Q is the number of tickets. Marginal cost is constant at $10 per ticket and there are no fixed costs (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: If the cinema charges a single price, calculate its output, price, profit and the consumer surplus.
parts.answer: Q = 20 tickets, P = $30, profit = $400, consumer surplus = $200.

parts.label: b
parts.text: If the cinema could practise first-degree (perfect) price discrimination, calculate its output, profit and the consumer surplus.
parts.answer: Q = 40 tickets, profit = $800, consumer surplus = $0.
parts.working: Each ticket sold at the buyer's maximum price, so MR = demand; sell until P = MC: 50 − Q = 10 → Q = 40 (1); profit = ½ × 40 × (50 − 10) = 800 (1); consumer surplus = 0 (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why output under perfect price discrimination is allocatively efficient even though consumers are worse off.
parts.answer: Output rises to where price of the last unit equals marginal cost, so there is no deadweight loss; but all the surplus goes to the producer instead of consumers.
parts.working: 1: last unit sold at P = MC (output 40 = competitive output), so no deadweight welfare loss; 1: the whole surplus is transferred to the producer, so it is efficient but not equitable.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Households that install solar panels reduce air pollution for their neighbours. Assuming no government intervention, what is true of the market for solar panels?
A marginal social benefit is less than marginal private benefit, so too many are installed
B marginal social benefit exceeds marginal private benefit, so too few are installed
C marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost, so too many are installed
D marginal social cost equals marginal social benefit at the market output
parts.answer: B marginal social benefit exceeds marginal private benefit, so too few are installed
parts.working: There is a positive externality (external benefit), so MSB > MPB and the market output, where MPB = MPC, is below the socially optimal output where MSB = MSC. C describes a negative production externality.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a cost-benefit analysis of a new public park, when would a shadow price be used?
A to value benefits such as lower stress and better health of residents, which are not bought and sold in a market
B to convert costs and benefits that occur in future years into present values
C to estimate the entrance fee that a private firm would charge visitors
D to record the actual prices paid for land and building materials
parts.answer: A to value benefits such as lower stress and better health of residents, which are not bought and sold in a market
parts.working: A shadow price is an estimated money value for a cost or benefit that has no market price. B describes discounting, the main distractor; D uses market prices, so no shadow price is needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a negative production externality and a negative consumption externality, giving an example of each.
parts.answer: A negative production externality is a cost to third parties arising from producing a good (e.g. smoke from a cement factory); a negative consumption externality is a cost to third parties arising from consuming a good (e.g. second-hand smoke from cigarettes).
parts.working: 1 mark each for the two definitions (cost imposed on third parties from production / from consumption, not paid for); 1 mark each for a suitable example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why marginal social cost is greater than marginal private cost when there is a negative production externality.
parts.answer: MSC = MPC + marginal external cost; the external cost is positive, so MSC lies above MPC.
parts.working: 1: MSC = MPC + MEC; 1: producer ignores the cost to third parties, so MEC > 0 and MSC > MPC.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a cost-benefit analysis of a public project includes external costs and benefits, whereas a private firm's investment decision usually does not.
parts.answer: A government aims to maximise the welfare of society, so it counts all social costs and benefits; a private firm aims at profit, so it counts only its own revenues and costs, which are private.
parts.working: 1: CBA considers social costs and benefits (private + external); 1: government objective is social welfare; 1: private firm considers only private costs/revenues to maximise profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the main stages of a cost-benefit analysis.
parts.answer: Identify all private and external costs and benefits; place money values on them, using shadow prices where there is no market price; discount future values to present values and calculate net social benefit (or a benefit-cost ratio); decide, accepting projects with positive net social benefit, and test the result for sensitivity to the assumptions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four stages: identify costs and benefits (including externalities); value them (shadow pricing); allow for time (discounting/present values) and compute net social benefit; decision rule and sensitivity analysis/allowing for risk.

practice.stem: In an invented fruit-growing district, beekeepers sell honey. Their bees also pollinate nearby orchards. For honey production, MPB = MSB = 80 − Q and MPC = 20 + 2Q. Each hive also gives orchards an external benefit worth $6, so the marginal social cost of keeping hives is $6 less than the marginal private cost. Q is the number of hives in hundreds and values are $ per hive per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a positive production externality, using this example.
parts.answer: A benefit to third parties from producing a good: the beekeepers' bees pollinate nearby orchards, raising fruit yields, but the beekeepers are not paid for this.
parts.working: 1: benefit to a third party arising from production, not paid for; 1: applied to bees pollinating orchards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of hives kept in the free market and the socially optimal number of hives.
parts.answer: Free market: 2 000 hives; social optimum: 2 200 hives.

practice.stem:
A city government is considering a new metro line. Estimated values over its life, in present-value terms ($ million, invented data):
private costs (construction and operation): 900
private benefits (fare revenue): 600
external benefits (time saved by road users, less pollution, fewer accidents): 520
external costs (noise and disruption during construction): 80

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net private benefit and the net social benefit of the project.
parts.answer: Net private benefit −$300 million (a loss of $300 million); net social benefit +$140 million
parts.working: Net private = 600 − 900 = −300 (B1). Social benefit = 600 + 520 = 1120; social cost = 900 + 80 = 980 (M1); NSB = 140 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why the project would not be built by a private firm but might be undertaken by the government.
parts.answer: A private firm only counts private costs and benefits, which give a loss; the government includes externalities, which make social benefits exceed social costs.
parts.working: 1 mark: private firm makes a loss of $300 million. 1 mark: external benefits (time saved, cleaner air, fewer accidents) are not paid for by users, so they are ignored by the market. 1 mark: social benefits exceed social costs, so CBA supports public provision or a subsidy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two difficulties in valuing the external benefits of the project.
parts.answer: Placing money values on time saved and lives saved; predicting future usage; choosing a discount rate; deciding which third parties to include.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained difficulties (identify 1, explain 1).

practice.stem: In an invented country, the monthly market for a childhood vaccine has marginal private benefit MPB = 60 − Q and marginal private cost MPC = MSC = 12 + Q. Each dose also gives a constant marginal external benefit of $12, so MSB = 72 − Q. Q is in thousand doses and values are in $ per dose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the free-market output and price.
parts.answer: 24 thousand doses at $36 per dose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the socially optimal output.
parts.answer: 30 thousand doses.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the deadweight welfare loss at the free-market output, in dollars.
parts.answer: $36 000 per month.
parts.working: Triangle between MSB and MSC from Q = 24 to 30: height at Q = 24 is MSB − MSC = 48 − 36 = 12 (1); ½ × 6 × 12 = 36 thousand dollars (1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the free market under-consumes vaccinations.
parts.answer: Consumers base decisions on their private benefit only and ignore the benefit to others of lower infection, so MSB > MPB and demand is too low.
parts.working: 1: consumers consider only MPB; 1: external benefit (reduced spread to others) ignored, so MSB > MPB and output < social optimum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why loud music played late at night at outdoor wedding events is an example of a negative consumption externality, referring to marginal private benefit and marginal social benefit.
parts.answer: The families holding the event gain private benefit, but neighbours lose sleep, an external cost not considered by the consumers; so marginal social benefit is below marginal private benefit (MSB = MPB − marginal external cost).
parts.working: 1: consumption by the event holders; 1: cost to third parties (neighbours) not paid for; 1: MSB < MPB.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the free market leads to too much of this activity and a welfare loss.
parts.answer: Consumers choose the level where MPB = MPC, which is beyond the level where MSB = MSC; for the extra units, the social cost exceeds the social benefit, giving a deadweight loss.
parts.working: 1: market equilibrium where MPB = MPC; 1: social optimum where MSB = MSC at lower output; 1: over-consumption → units where MSC > MSB → deadweight welfare loss / allocative inefficiency.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): About 8 000 brick kilns surround a large city. In winter, smoke from the kilns adds to a smog that causes breathing illnesses. Converting a kiln to a cleaner design costs about Rs 3 million and cuts its smoke emissions by about 40 %, and it saves the owner about Rs 0.5 million a year in fuel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of converting all the kilns, in Rs billion.
parts.answer: Rs 24 billion
parts.working: 8 000 × Rs 3 million = Rs 24 000 million = Rs 24 billion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many years it takes for the fuel savings to repay the conversion cost of one kiln.
parts.answer: 6 years
parts.working: Rs 3 million ÷ Rs 0.5 million a year = 6 years.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why kiln owners may not convert their kilns without government intervention, even though society would gain.
parts.answer: Owners compare only private costs and benefits: a Rs 3 million cost repaid only after 6 years may not be worth it to them, especially if they lack finance; the health benefits of less smog go to other people and are ignored, so the private return understates the social return.
parts.working: 1: owners consider private costs/benefits only; 1: private payback is slow / high upfront cost / lack of credit; 1: external benefit of cleaner air (lower health costs) not received by the owner, so social benefit > private benefit.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Consider one difficulty in measuring the external cost of smoke from the kilns.
parts.answer: Smog comes from many sources (vehicles, crop burning, industry), so the share caused by kilns is hard to separate; valuing illness and early death needs shadow prices that are disputed; effects may be long-term and spread across a wide area.
parts.working: 1: identifies a difficulty; 1: explains it; 1: judgement on why it matters, e.g. leads to a tax or regulation at the wrong level.

practice.stem: In a cement market, the marginal private benefit is MPB = 100 − Q and the marginal private cost is MPC = 20 + Q, where Q is output in thousand tonnes and values are in dollars per tonne. Production causes air pollution with a constant external cost of $20 per tonne. There are no external benefits (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the free-market output and the socially optimal output.
parts.answer: Free market 40 thousand tonnes; social optimum 30 thousand tonnes
parts.working: Market: MPB = MPC: 100 − Q = 20 + Q so Q = 40 (B1). MSC = MPC + 20 = 40 + Q (M1); with no external benefit MSB = MPB, so 100 − Q = 40 + Q gives Q = 30 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the deadweight welfare loss caused by the externality.
parts.answer: $100 thousand
parts.working: Triangle between MSC and MSB from Q = 30 to 40: at Q = 40, MSC − MSB = 80 − 60 = 20 (M1); ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the free market overproduces cement in this case.
parts.answer: Producers ignore the external cost of pollution, so they produce where MPB = MPC, beyond the output where MSB = MSC.
parts.working: 1 mark: external cost not included in private costs. 1 mark: so MPC < MSC and the market output (40) exceeds the social optimum (30), where the extra units cost society more than they are worth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether cost-benefit analysis is a reliable method for deciding whether a government should build a large dam for irrigation and electricity.
parts.answer: CBA provides a systematic framework including externalities, but valuations, forecasts, discount rates and distributional issues make results uncertain.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): stages of CBA – identify private and external costs and benefits (irrigation, electricity, flood control vs construction, displacement of communities, loss of farmland, ecological damage, downstream effects); place money values (shadow pricing, willingness to pay); discount future values to present value; compare social benefits with social costs. Strengths: considers third parties, makes assumptions transparent, allows comparison of projects. Weaknesses: valuing intangibles (lives, cultural sites, biodiversity); forecasting over 50+ years; choice of discount rate can reverse the decision; who gains and who loses (distribution) is not shown by net figures; political bias in estimates; risks such as earthquakes. Evaluation (up to 6): CBA is better than ignoring external effects but should be combined with sensitivity analysis and consultation; reasoned conclusion.

practice.stem:
A provincial government can afford only one of two projects. Estimated values over each project's life, in present-value terms, $ million (invented data):
Flood barrier: private costs 400; private benefits (fees) 320; external benefits 250; external costs 90
Ring road: private costs 650; private benefits (tolls) 600; external benefits 180; external costs 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net social benefit of each project.
parts.answer: Flood barrier: $80 million; ring road: $90 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of total social benefits to total social costs for each project, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Flood barrier: 1.16; ring road: 1.13.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answers, discuss which project the government should choose.
parts.answer: The ring road gives the larger net social benefit ($90 m vs $80 m), but the flood barrier gives more benefit per dollar of social cost and needs $250 m less spending, which could fund other projects; the choice also depends on the reliability of the estimates, who gains and loses, and risks such as flood damage to the poor.
parts.working: Up to 2 for using both measures: ring road highest NSB; flood barrier higher benefit/cost ratio and lower cost, so if the remaining funds can be used for another project with positive NSB the barrier may give more in total. Up to 2 for evaluation: estimates of external benefits (lives saved, time saved) are uncertain/shadow priced; distribution of benefits (equity); time period and discount rate; political factors; justified choice.

practice.stem: In the market for steel in an invented country, MPB = MSB = 100 − Q and MPC = 10 + Q. Production also causes pollution with a marginal external cost MEC = 0.5Q, which rises with output. Q is in thousand tonnes and values are in $ per tonne.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the free-market output.
parts.answer: 45 thousand tonnes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the socially optimal output, and the tax per tonne that would achieve it if the tax were set equal to the marginal external cost at that output.
parts.answer: 36 thousand tonnes; tax of $18 per tonne.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the deadweight welfare loss at the free-market output.
parts.answer: $101 250 (101.25 thousand dollars).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the marginal external cost of pollution may rise as output rises.
parts.answer: The environment can absorb small amounts of pollution with little harm, but as output and emissions grow, concentrations exceed safe levels, causing increasingly serious damage to health and ecosystems.
parts.working: 1: natural absorption capacity at low levels; 1: damage per extra tonne increases as concentration rises / more people affected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether the existence of external costs means that a free market will always allocate resources inefficiently.
parts.answer: External costs usually cause over-production because MSC > MPC, giving a deadweight loss; but if the externality is small, if property rights are clear and bargaining is cheap (Coase), or if social norms and private agreements deal with it, the market outcome may be close to efficient; intervention may also fail.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: diagram MSC above MPC, market output where MPB = MPC above optimum where MSB = MSC; deadweight loss triangle; allocative inefficiency (P < MSC). Evaluation: Coase theorem — with clear property rights and low transaction costs, bargaining can reach the efficient output; very small or local externalities may not matter; reputation, corporate social responsibility and consumer pressure may cut pollution; if marginal external cost is zero at the market output, no loss; but with many affected people, transaction costs are high and bargaining fails; measurement problems; government failure may make intervention worse; conclusion: 'always' is too strong but the presumption of inefficiency is strong for large, diffuse externalities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that a government should aim to eliminate all negative externalities.
parts.answer: The efficient level of a negative externality is usually not zero: it is where the marginal benefit of the activity equals its marginal social cost; eliminating all pollution would mean giving up valuable output. But some externalities (toxic, irreversible) should be eliminated, and equity or sustainability may justify stricter limits.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: externality diagram: the social optimum still has some output and therefore some external cost; the cost of reducing pollution rises as more is cut (marginal abatement cost) while the benefit of further cuts falls; zero externality would require banning many useful activities (transport, electricity). Evaluation: where harm is severe or irreversible (lead, toxic waste), a ban may be justified; uncertainty and the precautionary principle; distribution of harm on poor communities; future generations and climate change; government failure and enforcement costs; conclusion: aim for the socially optimal level, not zero, except for the most harmful externalities.

practice.stem: A consumer has an income of $1200 to spend on two goods, X and Y. The price of X is $40 and the price of Y is $30 (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum quantity of each good the consumer could buy, and the slope of the budget line (Y on the vertical axis).
parts.answer: X intercept 30; Y intercept 40; slope −4/3 (−1.33)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The price of X falls to $30. Describe how the budget line changes.
parts.answer: It pivots outwards from the Y intercept (40): the X intercept rises to 40 and the slope becomes −1.
parts.working: 1 mark pivot about the Y intercept. 1 mark new X intercept 40 / slope −1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the condition for the consumer's optimum choice in terms of indifference curves and the budget line.
parts.answer: Where the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve (MRS = Px/Py).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define an indifference curve.
parts.answer: A curve showing all combinations of two goods that give a consumer the same level of satisfaction (utility).
parts.working: 1: combinations of two goods; 1: equal satisfaction/utility, so the consumer is indifferent between them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why indifference curves are normally convex to the origin.
parts.answer: Because of a diminishing marginal rate of substitution: as a consumer has more X and less Y, she is willing to give up less and less Y for each extra unit of X, so the curve becomes flatter.
parts.working: 1: slope = MRS; 1: MRS diminishes as more X is consumed; 1: because each extra X adds less satisfaction while Y becomes relatively more valued → curve flattens.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why two indifference curves for the same consumer cannot cross.
parts.answer: If they crossed, the crossing point would give the same utility as two bundles on different curves, one of which contains more of both goods; this contradicts the assumptions that more is preferred and that preferences are consistent (transitive).
parts.working: 1: crossing implies one bundle is equal in utility to two bundles of different utility; 1: contradicts non-satiation/transitivity.

practice.stem: A student spends her monthly allowance on mobile data (X), which costs $15 per GB, and snacks (Y), which cost $10 per packet. Her allowance rises from $600 to $900 while prices do not change (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum quantity of mobile data (X) and of snacks (Y) she could buy before and after the rise in her allowance.
parts.answer: Before: 40 GB or 60 packets; after: 60 GB or 90 packets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the budget line changes and state its slope (Y on the vertical axis).
parts.answer: It shifts outwards parallel to the original line; the slope stays at −1.5.
parts.working: 1: parallel outward shift; 1: slope = −Px/Py = −15/10 = −1.5, unchanged.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Mobile data is an inferior good for this student. State what happens to the quantity of data she buys.
parts.answer: It falls.
parts.working: For an inferior good the income effect is negative: a rise in income lowers quantity demanded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what a budget line shows and what determines its slope.
parts.answer: It shows all combinations of two goods that a consumer can buy when spending all of a given income at given prices; its slope is the ratio of the prices (−Px/Py with Y on the vertical axis).
parts.working: 1: combinations affordable with all income spent; 1: depends on income and prices; 1: slope = −Px/Py (relative prices / opportunity cost of X in terms of Y).

parts.label: b
parts.text: With Y on the vertical axis, explain how the budget line changes when only the price of Y rises.
parts.answer: It pivots inwards around its intercept on the X axis; the Y intercept falls and the line becomes flatter.
parts.working: 1: pivots inward on the Y axis, X intercept unchanged; 1: flatter slope because Px/Py falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For a Giffen good, which describes the effects of a rise in its price?
A the substitution effect and the income effect both reduce quantity demanded
B the substitution effect reduces quantity demanded and the income effect increases it by a larger amount
C the substitution effect increases quantity demanded and the income effect reduces it
D the substitution effect reduces quantity demanded and the income effect increases it by a smaller amount
parts.answer: B the substitution effect reduces quantity demanded and the income effect increases it by a larger amount
parts.working: A Giffen good is a strongly inferior good: a price rise lowers real income, which raises quantity demanded by more than the substitution effect reduces it, so quantity rises. D describes an ordinary inferior good.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the usefulness of indifference curve analysis in explaining why demand curves usually slope downwards.
parts.answer: It separates income and substitution effects, explains normal, inferior and Giffen goods without measuring utility, but rests on unrealistic assumptions.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): indifference curves (convex, MRS diminishing), budget lines, optimum at tangency; price fall pivots budget line; derive demand curve from successive tangencies (price-consumption curve); separation into substitution effect (always negative) and income effect (positive for normal, negative for inferior goods); explains why most demand curves slope down and the Giffen exception; uses ordinal not cardinal utility, an advance on marginal utility theory. Limitations: assumes rational, consistent, fully informed consumers; only two goods; preferences fixed; behavioural economics (habits, bounded rationality, framing) challenges it; hard to test. Evaluation (up to 6): a reasoned judgement on usefulness – strong theoretical insight, weaker predictive power; conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A consumer maximises her utility when buying goods X and Y. The price of X is $6 and the price of Y is $2. With Y on the vertical axis, what is her marginal rate of substitution of Y for X (units of Y she is willing to give up for one more unit of X) at the optimum?
A 1/3
B 2
C 3
D 12
parts.answer: C 3
parts.working: At the optimum the indifference curve is tangent to the budget line, so MRS = Px/Py = 6/2 = 3. A is Py/Px (the inverted ratio), the main distractor.

practice.stem:
A consumer has $120 to spend on goods X (price $4) and Y (price $6). Points on three of her indifference curves are given as (units of X, units of Y) (invented data):
IC1: (4, 15), (10, 10), (16, 7)
IC2: (3, 24), (6, 18), (12, 12), (20, 9), (30, 7)
IC3: (8, 18), (12, 15), (18, 12)
IC3 gives the highest satisfaction and IC1 the lowest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each indifference curve, state which of the listed combinations the consumer can afford.
parts.working: Costs: IC1 = $106, $100, $106 (all ≤ $120); IC2 = $156, $132, $120, $134, $162 (only (12,12) affordable); IC3 = $140, $138, $144 (none). 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for two curves correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the combination that maximises the consumer's utility and explain why.
parts.answer: 12 units of X and 12 units of Y, on IC2.
parts.working: 1: (12,12); 1: it is on the highest indifference curve the consumer can reach, IC3 being unaffordable and IC1 lower; 1: at this point the budget line just touches (is tangent to) IC2, so MRS = Px/Py = 4/6 and all income ($120) is spent.

practice.stem: A household spends an income of Rs 2 000 a week on two goods: X at Rs 50 per unit and Y at Rs 20 per unit. Next year its income rises by 10 % and both prices also rise by 10 % (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum quantities of X and of Y the household can buy this year and next year.
parts.answer: Both years: 40 units of X or 100 units of Y.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what happens to the budget line and to the household's optimum combination.
parts.answer: The budget line does not move, because money income and prices change in the same proportion, so real income and relative prices are unchanged; the optimum stays the same.
parts.working: 1: same intercepts → same budget line; 1: real income and relative prices unchanged, so same tangency/optimum (no money illusion).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what would happen to the budget line if income rose by 10 % but both prices rose by 15 %.
parts.answer: Real income falls, so the budget line shifts inwards parallel to the original (max X about 38.3, max Y about 95.7); the slope is unchanged because relative prices are the same.
parts.working: 1: parallel inward shift (2 200/57.5 = 38.3; 2 200/23 = 95.7); 1: relative prices unchanged so slope same; lower real income.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using indifference curves and budget lines, described in words, explain how a rise in income affects the quantity demanded of (i) a normal good and (ii) an inferior good.
parts.answer: A rise in income shifts the budget line outward parallel; the consumer moves to a tangency with a higher indifference curve. For a normal good the new tangency has more of the good; for an inferior good the new tangency has less of it (and more of the other good). Joining tangencies gives the income-consumption curve.
parts.working: 1: rise in income → parallel outward shift (prices unchanged); 1: new optimum where new budget line is tangent to a higher IC; 1: utility rises; 1: normal good — new tangency to the right (more X); 1: inferior good — tangency to the left (less X), income-consumption curve bends back; 1: link to positive/negative income elasticity or an example (e.g. cheaper staple food).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether indifference curve analysis is more useful than marginal utility theory in explaining how consumers respond to a change in price.
parts.answer: Indifference curve analysis needs only ordinal ranking and separates the substitution and income effects, so it explains inferior and Giffen goods; marginal utility theory explains downward-sloping demand simply but needs measurable utility and constant marginal utility of money. Both assume rational, well-informed consumers, which behavioural economics questions.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: MU theory: equi-marginal principle MUx/Px = MUy/Py; a rise in Px → buy less X → downward-sloping demand; assumes cardinal utility and constant MU of money. IC analysis: budget line pivots; decomposition into substitution and income effects (diagram); normal, inferior and Giffen goods; derivation of demand curve. Evaluation: IC analysis is more general and realistic in its ordinal assumption, but harder to apply to many goods and still relies on rationality; MU theory is simpler and useful for teaching consumer surplus; behavioural factors (habits, framing, bounded rationality) limit both; conclusion with justified judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using indifference curves and budget lines described in words, explain the income and substitution effects of a fall in the price of an inferior good that is not a Giffen good.
parts.answer: Substitution effect increases quantity; income effect reduces it; the substitution effect is larger, so quantity demanded rises overall.
parts.working: 1 mark: budget line pivots outwards; new tangency on a higher indifference curve. 1 mark: hypothetical (compensated) budget line parallel to the new one, tangent to the original indifference curve, separates the effects. 1 mark: substitution effect – movement along original curve; always increases quantity of the cheaper good. 1 mark: income effect – parallel shift; for an inferior good, higher real income reduces quantity. 1 mark: substitution effect outweighs income effect. 1 mark: net result – quantity demanded rises, so the demand curve slopes downwards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the result would differ for a Giffen good.
parts.answer: The negative income effect is larger than the substitution effect, so quantity demanded falls when price falls (upward-sloping demand).
parts.working: 1 mark income effect outweighs substitution effect. 1 mark quantity falls when price falls.

practice.stem:
A consumer buys goods X and Y. When the price of X falls, her optimum moves from point A to point C. Point B is on her original indifference curve where it is tangent to a line with the new price ratio (the income effect has been removed). The quantities of X at each point in three different cases are (invented data):
Case 1: A = 10, B = 13, C = 16
Case 2: A = 10, B = 13, C = 11
Case 3: A = 10, B = 13, C = 8

parts.label: a
parts.text: For Case 1, calculate the substitution effect and the income effect on the quantity of X, and state what type of good X is.
parts.answer: Substitution effect +3; income effect +3; X is a normal good.
parts.working: A → B: 13 − 10 = +3; B → C: 16 − 13 = +3 (1); income effect positive → normal good (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: For Case 2, calculate the two effects and state what type of good X is.
parts.answer: Substitution effect +3; income effect −2; X is an inferior good but not a Giffen good.
parts.working: SE = +3 and IE = 11 − 13 = −2 (1); the negative income effect is smaller than the substitution effect, so quantity still rises overall (10 → 11): X is inferior but not a Giffen good (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: For Case 3, calculate the two effects and state what type of good X is.
parts.answer: Substitution effect +3; income effect −5; X is a Giffen good.
parts.working: SE = +3, IE = 8 − 13 = −5 (1); negative IE larger than SE, so quantity falls when price falls → Giffen good (1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the substitution effect of a fall in the price of a good always increases the quantity bought.
parts.answer: Holding utility constant, the good is now relatively cheaper, so the consumer moves along the same convex indifference curve to a point with more of it, where the flatter/steeper budget slope is tangent.
parts.working: 1: SE measured along the original indifference curve with the new relative prices; 1: because indifference curves are convex, a lower relative price always gives a tangency with more of the cheaper good.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate, using indifference curve analysis, whether giving low-income households a cash transfer is better for them than a food subsidy that costs the government the same amount.
parts.answer: A cash transfer shifts the budget line out parallel, while a food subsidy pivots it; for the same cost, the cash budget line passes through the bundle chosen under the subsidy, so the household can reach at least as high an indifference curve with cash, and usually higher. But if the aim is better nutrition, or if households are not rational, a food subsidy may be preferred.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: two goods (food, other goods); subsidy lowers food price → budget line pivots out; equal-cost cash transfer → parallel shift passing through the subsidy optimum; consumer can choose that same bundle or a better one → cash gives equal or higher utility; subsidy distorts relative prices (substitution effect towards food). Evaluation: if preferences give a corner/near-identical result, the difference is small; merit good argument — government may value nutrition more than the household; information failure, addiction or intra-household control of cash; administration and leakages (subsidy reaches rich as well as poor if universal); inflationary or market effects; conclusion depends on the objective (welfare vs nutrition).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shape of the indifference curves for two goods that are perfect complements, such as left and right shoes.
parts.answer: L-shaped (right-angled) curves with the corner on a ray where the goods are in fixed proportion (1:1 for shoes).
parts.working: 1: L-shaped/right angle; 1: corners lie on a line showing the fixed proportion; extra units of one good alone add no utility.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why there is no substitution effect when the price of one of two perfect complements falls.
parts.answer: With L-shaped curves, the optimum is always at the corner; a change in relative prices with utility held constant leaves the consumer at the same corner, so the quantity does not change. The whole change in demand is an income effect.
parts.working: 1: optimum at the corner of an L-shaped curve; 1: compensated price change → tangency at the same corner → no change in quantity; 1: all change in quantity is the income effect (real income rises, so more of both bought).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the shape of the indifference curves for two perfect substitutes, and state where the consumer's optimum is likely to be.
parts.answer: Straight lines with a constant MRS; the consumer usually buys only the good that is relatively cheaper (a corner solution).
parts.working: 1: straight, downward-sloping lines (constant MRS); 1: corner solution — all income on the cheaper good per unit of satisfaction.

practice.stem:
A bakery has a fixed number of ovens. The table shows total product (loaves per hour) for different numbers of workers (invented data).
Workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Total product: 10, 26, 45, 60, 70, 75

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the marginal product and the average product of labour for each number of workers.
parts.working: MP = change in TP for each extra worker (B1 all correct); AP = TP ÷ workers (B1 all correct); accuracy (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State after which worker diminishing marginal returns set in, and explain why they occur.
parts.answer: After the 3rd worker (MP falls from 19 to 15 with the 4th worker).
parts.working: B1 identification. Explanation (2): in the short run at least one factor (the bakery's ovens/space) is fixed; adding more variable labour to the fixed factor eventually gives each worker less capital to work with, so the extra output falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is meant by the minimum efficient scale of production?
A the output at which marginal cost is at its lowest
B the lowest output at which long-run average cost is minimised
C the output at which a firm first makes normal profit
D the highest output a firm can produce before diseconomies of scale stop
parts.answer: B the lowest output at which long-run average cost is minimised
parts.working: Minimum efficient scale is the smallest output at which the long-run average cost curve reaches its minimum, i.e. where economies of scale are exhausted. A refers to marginal cost, which reaches its minimum before average cost does.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between the short run and the long run in production.
parts.answer: In the short run at least one factor of production is fixed (e.g. factory size); in the long run all factors are variable.
parts.working: 1 for each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two internal economies of scale that a large car manufacturer might gain.
parts.answer: Technical economies: it can use large, specialised machinery and assembly lines whose cost is spread over many cars; purchasing economies: it can buy steel and parts in bulk at lower prices per unit (also financial, managerial, marketing, risk-bearing).
parts.working: For each of two: 1 for naming an internal economy, 1 for explaining how it lowers long-run average cost for the car maker.

practice.stem:
A furniture workshop has total fixed cost of $200 a week. Its average variable cost (AVC) at different outputs is (invented data):
Output (chairs per week): 10, 20, 30, 40
AVC ($): 12, 10, 11, 14

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total variable cost and total cost at each level of output.
parts.working: TVC = AVC × Q (1); TC = TVC + 200 (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average total cost at each output, to two decimal places where necessary.
parts.working: ATC = TC/Q: 320/10, 400/20, 530/30, 760/40 (2 marks all correct; 1 mark for two or three).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the marginal cost per chair as output rises from 10 to 20, from 20 to 30 and from 30 to 40.
parts.answer: $8, $13, $23 per chair.
parts.working: ΔTC/ΔQ: 80/10, 130/10, 230/10 (2 marks all correct; 1 mark for two).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two causes of internal diseconomies of scale.
parts.answer: Coordination and communication problems: in a very large firm messages pass through many layers, so decisions are slow and mistakes more likely; worker motivation: employees feel remote from management and less valued, so productivity falls (also control problems, bureaucracy).
parts.working: For each of two causes: 1 for the cause, 1 for explaining why it raises cost per unit as the firm grows.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of diseconomies of scale on the long-run average cost curve.
parts.answer: LRAC rises as output increases (the upward-sloping part of the curve).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A perfectly competitive firm has the following total costs (invented data).
Output (units): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Total cost ($): 120, 180, 220, 252, 300, 370, 462

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average variable cost, average total cost and marginal cost for outputs of 1 to 6 units.
parts.working: FC = 120 (TC at zero output). AVC = (TC − 120) ÷ Q (B1); ATC = TC ÷ Q (B1); MC = change in TC (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the minimum price the firm needs in order to continue producing in the short run, and in the long run. Explain your answers.
parts.answer: Short run: $44 (minimum AVC); long run: $74 (minimum ATC)
parts.working: B1 $44: in the short run the firm stays open if price covers AVC, because fixed costs must be paid anyway (B1). B1 $74: in the long run all costs are variable, so price must cover ATC or the firm leaves the industry (B1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A factory raises its output from 400 to 500 units a week and its total cost rises from $6 000 to $7 000. Which statement is correct?
A Average cost falls from $15 to $14, and the marginal cost per extra unit is $10.
B Average cost rises from $14 to $15, and the marginal cost per extra unit is $10.
C Average cost falls from $15 to $14, and the marginal cost per extra unit is $14.
D Average cost falls from $15 to $14, and the marginal cost per extra unit is $1 000.
parts.answer: A Average cost falls from $15 to $14, and the marginal cost per extra unit is $10.
parts.working: AC = 6 000/400 = $15 and 7 000/500 = $14. MC = ΔTC/ΔQ = 1 000/100 = $10. Since MC < AC, AC falls. D gives the change in total cost, not the cost per unit; C confuses MC with the new AC.

practice.stem:
A bus company in a mountain region faces the following weekly demand for day trips (invented data). Its marginal cost is constant at $10 per trip.
Trips per week: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Price per trip ($): 30, 27, 24, 21, 18, 14

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate total revenue and marginal revenue for each number of trips.
parts.working: TR = P × Q (1); MR = change in TR (1); all correct (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the output that maximises profit and the output that maximises total revenue.
parts.answer: Profit: 4 trips; total revenue: 5 trips.
parts.working: Profit max where MR ≥ MC for the last trip: the 4th trip adds $12 revenue and $10 cost, the 5th adds only $6 revenue but $10 cost → 4 trips (profit $44 = 84 − 40) (1); TR max at 5 trips ($90), where MR changes from positive to negative (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a profit-maximising firm would not produce the output that maximises total revenue.
parts.answer: Beyond 4 trips each extra trip adds less to revenue than to cost (MR $6 < MC $10), so profit falls (from $44 to $40) even though revenue is still rising.
parts.working: 1: MR < MC for the 5th trip; 1: profit falls by $4 when output rises from 4 to 5 trips.

practice.stem: Hundreds of firms making surgical instruments and sports goods are located in and around one city in Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by external economies of scale, using two examples that could arise in an industrial cluster of this kind.
parts.answer: Falls in a firm's long-run average cost that result from the growth of the whole industry in an area, not from the firm's own size. Examples: a pool of skilled workers trained in the trade; local suppliers of specialised parts and services; shared transport links, testing labs or export agents; spread of ideas.
parts.working: 1: definition (cost savings from growth of the industry/location, outside the firm); 1: not due to the firm's own scale; 1 each for two relevant examples applied to the cluster (max 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how external economies of scale affect a firm's long-run average cost curve.
parts.answer: The whole LRAC curve shifts downwards, whereas internal economies are a movement along the LRAC curve.
parts.working: 1: downward shift of the LRAC curve; 1: contrast with internal economies (movement along LRAC as the firm grows).

practice.stem: A small food-processing firm sells jars of mango pickle at Rs 250 each. Its average variable cost is constant at Rs 150 per jar, and its fixed costs are Rs 400 000 a month (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even output per month.
parts.answer: 4 000 jars.
parts.working: Contribution per jar = 250 − 150 = Rs 100 (1); 400 000/100 = 4 000 jars (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the firm's profit when it sells 6 000 jars a month.

parts.label: c
parts.text: During a price war the firm can sell only 3 000 jars a month at Rs 180 each. Explain why it should continue to produce in the short run.
parts.answer: At Rs 180 each jar covers its variable cost (Rs 150) and contributes Rs 30 to fixed costs, so the loss is Rs 310 000 if it produces compared with Rs 400 000 (its fixed costs) if it shuts down.
parts.working: 1: price above AVC; 1: loss if producing = 3 000 × 30 − 400 000 = −Rs 310 000; 1: smaller than the shutdown loss of Rs 400 000.

practice.stem: A firm faces the demand curve P = 80 − 2Q, where P is the price in dollars and Q is the quantity per day (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output and price at which total revenue is maximised, and the value of total revenue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand (as a positive number) when the price is $60, and explain whether the firm should raise or cut its price from $60 to increase revenue.
parts.answer: PED = 3; demand is price elastic, so cut the price.
parts.working: At P = 60, Q = 10; dQ/dP = −½ (M1); PED = ½ × 60 ÷ 10 = 3 (A1). Elastic, so a price cut raises TR (MR > 0) (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the price elasticity of demand at the revenue-maximising output.
parts.answer: Unit elasticity (PED = 1)

practice.stem: A textile mill doubles all of its inputs — machines, workers, floor space and energy — and its weekly output rises from 500 to 1 150 metres of cloth (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in output and state what type of returns to scale the mill experiences.
parts.answer: +130 %; increasing returns to scale.
parts.working: (1 150 − 500)/500 × 100 = 130 % (1); output rises by a larger proportion (130 %) than inputs (100 %) → increasing returns to scale (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between returns to scale and the law of diminishing marginal returns.
parts.answer: Returns to scale are a long-run idea: all inputs change in the same proportion and we compare the proportional change in output. Diminishing marginal returns are a short-run idea: one input (e.g. labour) is added to a fixed factor, and eventually each extra unit adds less to output than the one before.
parts.working: Returns to scale: long run (1), all factors varied in proportion (1). Diminishing returns: short run with at least one fixed factor (1), marginal product of the variable factor eventually falls (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how increasing returns to scale affect the shape of the long-run average cost curve.
parts.answer: If output rises proportionately more than inputs (and input prices are constant), cost per unit falls as scale rises, so LRAC slopes downwards (economies of scale).
parts.working: 1: cost rises by less than output; 1: LRAC falls over this range (economies of scale).

practice.stem:
A car-wash business hires workers at $80 per day; ignore its other costs (invented data).
Workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Cars washed per day: 10, 26, 46, 62, 72, 77

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the marginal product of each worker.
parts.working: Change in total product for each extra worker (all correct for 1 mark).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the marginal cost of washing a car when the 5th worker is hired, and the average variable cost per car when 5 workers are employed (to two decimal places).
parts.answer: MC = $8.00 per car; AVC = $5.56 per car.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the relationship between the marginal product of labour and the marginal cost of output.
parts.answer: MC = wage ÷ MP when labour is the only variable cost; while MP rises (up to the 3rd worker) MC falls, and when diminishing marginal returns set in (from the 4th worker) MC rises. So the MC curve is the mirror image of the MP curve.
parts.working: 1: MC = W/MP; 1: rising MP → falling MC (e.g. $8 → $5 → $4); 1: diminishing returns → rising MC (e.g. $5, $8, $16), explaining the U-shape of the short-run MC curve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether large firms always have lower average costs than small firms.
parts.answer: Large firms often benefit from internal economies of scale (technical, purchasing, financial, managerial), so long-run average cost falls as they grow; but beyond the minimum efficient scale diseconomies of scale (coordination, communication, motivation) can raise costs, MES may be small in some industries, and small firms may gain from external economies, flexibility and lower overheads.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: LRAC curve; internal economies with examples; minimum efficient scale; diseconomies of scale; X-inefficiency in large protected firms. Evaluation: depends on the industry (MES large in steel, cars; small in hairdressing, consultancy); market size limits scale; small firms in clusters gain external economies; technology (e.g. digital tools) lowers small firms' costs; large firms may use market power rather than efficiency; 'always' is too strong; conclusion.

practice.stem: Ayesha runs her own clothing shop (invented data). In one year her sales revenue was Rs 9.6 million and her explicit costs (wages, rent, stock and other bills) were Rs 7.2 million. She could earn Rs 1.8 million a year as a manager in a department store, and the Rs 4 million of her own money invested in the shop could earn 12 % a year in a bank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Ayesha's accounting profit for the year.
parts.answer: Rs 2.4 million.
parts.working: 9.6 − 7.2 = Rs 2.4 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate her economic profit and state whether she earns supernormal profit.
parts.answer: Economic profit = Rs 0.12 million; she earns a small supernormal profit.
parts.working: Opportunity cost of her time = 1.8 m and of her capital = 12 % × 4 m = 0.48 m (1); economic profit = 2.4 − 1.8 − 0.48 = 0.12 m (1); positive → supernormal profit (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what is meant by normal profit and why economists treat it as a cost.
parts.answer: Normal profit is the minimum profit needed to keep the entrepreneur in the business — the return the resources could earn in their next best use; it is the opportunity cost of the owner's time and capital, so it is part of the cost of production.
parts.working: 1: minimum return to keep the firm in the industry; 1: equals the opportunity cost of the owner's own resources, so counted in costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A consumer buys two goods. Good X costs $2 and its marginal utility is 30 utils. Good Y costs $5 and its marginal utility is 50 utils. To maximise total utility with the same income, the consumer should
A buy more X and less Y
B buy more Y and less X
C make no change
D buy more of both goods
parts.answer: A buy more X and less Y
parts.working: MUx/Px = 15 utils per $ and MUy/Py = 10 utils per $. Each dollar moved from Y to X raises total utility until the ratios are equal. B compares total MU (50 > 30) without dividing by price.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between total utility and marginal utility.
parts.answer: Total utility is the total satisfaction from consuming a quantity of a good; marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from consuming one more unit.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the law of diminishing marginal utility.
parts.answer: As a consumer consumes more units of a good in a period, the additional utility from each extra unit eventually falls.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why total utility is at its maximum when marginal utility is zero.
parts.answer: While MU is positive, each extra unit adds to total utility; once MU becomes negative, extra units reduce total utility; so TU reaches its peak where MU = 0.
parts.working: 1: positive MU → TU rising; 1: negative MU → TU falling, so the peak is at MU = 0.

practice.stem:
A student's total utility from slices of pizza at one meal is (invented data):
Slices: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Total utility (utils): 30, 55, 72, 82, 85, 83

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the marginal utility of each slice.
parts.working: Change in TU for each slice (2 marks all correct; 1 mark for four correct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of slices at which total utility is greatest, and explain why a rational consumer would not eat the sixth slice even if it were free.
parts.answer: Five slices (85 utils). The sixth slice has negative marginal utility (−2), so it reduces total satisfaction.
parts.working: 1: five slices; 1: MU of 6th slice negative → TU falls from 85 to 83.

practice.stem: A student is willing to pay the following amounts for successive tickets to matches in a cricket series: 1st $50, 2nd $40, 3rd $30, 4th $20, 5th $10. Each ticket costs $20 (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how many tickets she buys.
parts.answer: 4 tickets.
parts.working: She buys while willingness to pay ≥ $20: 1st–4th (the 4th exactly equals the price).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate her consumer surplus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how diminishing marginal utility explains why her willingness to pay falls for each extra ticket.
parts.answer: Each extra match gives her less additional satisfaction than the previous one, and the amount she is willing to pay reflects the marginal utility of that ticket.
parts.working: 1: MU of each extra ticket falls; 1: willingness to pay is based on MU, so it falls.

practice.stem:
A consumer has Rs 900 to spend on goods X and Y. The price of X is Rs 100 and the price of Y is Rs 200. The table shows the marginal utility (utils) of each unit (invented data).
Unit: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
MU of X: 400, 300, 200, 150, 100
MU of Y: 1000, 800, 400, 300, 200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the combination of X and Y that maximises the consumer's total utility, and the total utility at that combination.
parts.answer: 3 units of X and 3 units of Y; total utility 3100 utils
parts.working: MU/P for X: 4, 3, 2, 1.5, 1; for Y: 5, 4, 2, 1.5, 1 (M1). Equi-marginal principle: MUx/Px = MUy/Py = 2 at 3X, 3Y (M1); spending 3 × 100 + 3 × 200 = 900 = income (A1). TU = 400 + 300 + 200 + 1000 + 800 + 400 = 3100 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the consumer would not choose 5 units of X and 2 units of Y, even though this also costs Rs 900.
parts.answer: At that combination MUx/Px (1) < MUy/Py (4), so switching spending from X to Y raises total utility (TU = 2950 < 3100).
parts.working: 1 mark: ratios unequal. 1 mark: transferring Rs 200 from 2 units of X to 1 unit of Y adds more utility than it loses; TU would be 1150 + 1800 = 2950.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that consumers rarely behave in the way that traditional utility theory predicts.
parts.answer: Traditional theory explains many broad patterns (downward-sloping demand), but behavioural evidence shows systematic departures; the importance depends on the decision.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): traditional theory – rational utility maximisers, diminishing MU, equi-marginal principle, derivation of demand. Behavioural evidence – bounded rationality and heuristics, anchoring (initial prices), framing ('90 % fat-free'), loss aversion, default choices (pension opt-out), herd behaviour, present bias (saving, unhealthy food), altruism. Governments use nudges based on these ideas. Counter-view: in aggregate, demand still falls when price rises; for repeated purchases consumers learn; some 'irrational' behaviour is rational given information costs. Evaluation (up to 6): weigh the extent – theory useful for predicting market-level responses, weaker for one-off, complex or emotional decisions (health, pensions); reasoned conclusion on 'rarely'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A consumer's total utility from cups of tea in a day is: 1 cup 20 utils, 2 cups 36, 3 cups 48, 4 cups 56, 5 cups 60. She values each util at Rs 1 and a cup costs Rs 10. How many cups does she buy, and what is her consumer surplus?
A 3 cups; consumer surplus Rs 18
B 4 cups; consumer surplus Rs 16
C 5 cups; consumer surplus Rs 10
D 3 cups; consumer surplus Rs 48
parts.answer: A 3 cups; consumer surplus Rs 18
parts.working: Marginal utilities are 20, 16, 12, 8, 4. She buys while MU ≥ price (Rs 10): 3 cups (the 4th gives only 8). Consumer surplus = total utility valued in rupees − spending = 48 − 30 = Rs 18. B buys a cup worth less than its price; D forgets to subtract the spending.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Water is essential for life but is usually cheap, while diamonds are not essential but are very expensive. Use the concepts of total utility and marginal utility to explain this.
parts.answer: Water gives very high total utility, but because it is plentiful people consume many units and the marginal utility of the last unit is low, so they are willing to pay little for it. Diamonds are scarce, so few are consumed and the marginal utility of the last one is high. Price reflects marginal, not total, utility.
parts.working: 1: distinguishes total and marginal utility; 1: water — abundant, high TU but low MU at the margin; 1: diamonds — scarce, MU of the last unit high; 1: willingness to pay/price is related to MU, not TU.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the price of water can become very high in a desert or during a severe drought.
parts.answer: When water is scarce, people consume fewer units, so the marginal utility of the last unit is very high and they are willing to pay a high price for it; supply is also low relative to demand.
parts.working: 1: scarcity → fewer units consumed → high MU; 1: high willingness to pay / low supply relative to demand raises price.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the cardinal measurement of utility, and why it is a weakness of marginal utility theory.
parts.answer: Cardinal measurement assumes that satisfaction can be given exact numbers (utils) so that differences and ratios have meaning; in reality satisfaction is subjective and cannot be measured or compared between people, so the theory rests on an unrealistic assumption.
parts.working: 1: utility measured in numbers/units (utils); 1: assumed that one can say how much more satisfaction one unit gives than another; 1: satisfaction is subjective/psychological, cannot be observed; 1: so predictions rely on an untestable assumption / interpersonal comparisons invalid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how indifference curve analysis avoids this problem.
parts.answer: It needs only ordinal utility: the consumer can rank bundles as preferred, less preferred or equal, without measuring by how much; combined with the budget line this still predicts choices and the response to price changes.
parts.working: 1: ordinal ranking only; 1: indifference curves show equal-preference combinations without numbers; 1: optimum where budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve, so demand can still be derived.

practice.stem: A consumer is in equilibrium buying goods X and Y. The marginal utility of the last unit of X is 60 utils and its price is $3. The marginal utility of the last unit of Y is 100 utils and its price is $5 (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the consumer is in equilibrium.
parts.working: Both ratios equal 20 utils per dollar.

parts.label: b
