parts.text: The price of X rises to $4. Calculate the new marginal utility per dollar for X and explain how the consumer will change her purchases.
parts.answer: 15 utils per dollar. Since 15 < 20, she buys less X and more Y until the ratios are equal again (MU of X rises as she buys less X and MU of Y falls as she buys more Y).
parts.working: 1: 60/4 = 15; 1: lower MU per dollar on X than on Y; 1: reallocate spending from X to Y until MUx/Px = MUy/Py.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how this result is linked to the law of demand.
parts.answer: A rise in the price of X led the consumer to buy less X, so quantity demanded falls as price rises: an inverse relationship giving a downward-sloping demand curve.
parts.working: 1: higher price → lower quantity demanded of X; 1: so the individual demand curve slopes downward.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the principle of diminishing marginal utility can be used to derive a downward-sloping demand curve for an individual consumer.
parts.answer: A consumer buys until MU/P is equal across goods; if price falls, MU/P rises, so the consumer buys more until MU falls enough to restore equality.
parts.working: 1 mark: diminishing MU – each extra unit adds less satisfaction. 1 mark: equi-marginal condition MUa/Pa = MUb/Pb. 1 mark: a fall in Pa makes MUa/Pa > MUb/Pb. 1 mark: consumer buys more A, MUa falls until equality is restored – lower price, higher quantity demanded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two limitations of the assumption that consumers behave rationally when making choices.
parts.answer: e.g. bounded rationality (limited information and time), habits, anchoring/framing, herd behaviour, inconsistent preferences over time.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained limitations drawn from behavioural economics: bounded rationality, rules of thumb (heuristics), anchoring, social norms and herd behaviour, present bias (choosing short-term pleasure), and difficulty measuring utility in cardinal units.

practice.stem: A consumer's marginal utility from successive units of good X in a week is 40, 32, 24, 16 and 8 utils. The marginal utility of money to this consumer is constant at 2 utils per dollar, so she buys a unit only if its marginal utility per dollar spent is at least 2 (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many units of X the consumer buys at prices of $16, $12, $8 and $4.
parts.answer: $16: 2 units; $12: 3 units; $8: 4 units; $4: 5 units.
parts.working: Buys a unit only if MU ≥ 2 × price (MU/P ≥ MU of money). At $16 needs MU ≥ 32 → 2; at $12 MU ≥ 24 → 3; at $8 MU ≥ 16 → 4; at $4 MU ≥ 8 → 5 (3 marks all four correct; 2 for three; 1 for two).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the consumer surplus when the price is $8.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how your answers to (a) show that diminishing marginal utility leads to a downward-sloping demand curve, and state one limitation of the assumption that the marginal utility of money is constant.
parts.answer: Because each extra unit gives less utility, the consumer will only buy more if the price falls, so price and quantity demanded are inversely related. Limitation: if the price change is large relative to income, the marginal utility of money changes (income effect), so the simple derivation may not hold.
parts.working: 1: falling MU means a lower price is needed for each extra unit; 1: points (16,2), (12,3), (8,4), (4,5) trace a downward-sloping demand curve; 1: valid limitation — MU of money varies with income/spending, utility not measurable in cardinal units.

practice.stem:
Invented experiment at a cinema:
Week 1: popcorn sold in two sizes, small at Rs 300 and large at Rs 700. Of 2 000 buyers, 400 chose large.
Week 2: a medium size at Rs 650, only slightly smaller than large, was added. Of 2 000 buyers, 1 100 chose large, 150 medium and 750 small.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of buyers who chose the large size in each week.
parts.answer: Week 1: 20 %; Week 2: 55 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why traditional utility theory predicts that adding the medium size should not increase the number of buyers choosing the large size.
parts.answer: A rational consumer has stable preferences and compares the utility per rupee of each option; adding an option that is not chosen does not change the utility or price of small and large, so anyone who preferred small before should still prefer it.
parts.working: 1: rational, utility-maximising consumers with fixed preferences; 1: choice between small and large depends only on their own MU and prices, which did not change; 1: an irrelevant extra option should not change the ranking (so the share choosing large should stay at 20 % or fall if some buy medium).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how ideas from behavioural economics could explain the result.
parts.answer: Consumers have bounded rationality and judge value relative to nearby options: the medium (Rs 650) acts as a decoy that makes the large (only Rs 50 more) look like good value, so many switch to large. People use rules of thumb rather than calculating utility per rupee.
parts.working: 1: bounded rationality / use of heuristics; 1: relative comparison or anchoring on the medium price (decoy effect); 1: applied to the data (large looks cheap compared with medium, share rises from 20 % to 55 %).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether marginal utility theory provides a strong case for a government to redistribute income from the rich to the poor.
parts.answer: If the marginal utility of income diminishes and people are alike, a rupee taken from a rich person reduces utility less than it adds for a poor person, so redistribution raises total welfare. But utility cannot be measured or compared between people, redistribution may reduce incentives and output, and equity is a normative judgement.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: diminishing marginal utility of income; transfer from high to low income raises total utility; implications for progressive taxation and transfers. Evaluation: interpersonal comparisons of utility are not possible (ordinal utility); people differ in how they gain from income; incentive effects of high taxes and benefits (labour supply, enterprise, tax avoidance, poverty trap) may shrink the total; Pareto efficiency criterion cannot justify making the rich worse off; other arguments for redistribution (equity, social cohesion, positive externalities of health/education); conclusion: the theory gives a supporting argument but not a strong proof.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a consumer who aims to maximise utility will always buy more of a good when its price falls.
parts.answer: Usually yes: the substitution effect always raises quantity and for normal goods the income effect adds to it (equi-marginal principle, diminishing MU). But for an inferior good the income effect works against it and for a Giffen good it is stronger; status (Veblen) goods, expectations of further price falls, and behavioural factors can also stop a price fall raising quantity bought.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: equi-marginal principle — a fall in Px raises MUx/Px, so the consumer buys more X until ratios equalise; substitution and income effects (indifference curve diagram); normal goods. Evaluation: inferior goods (smaller rise); Giffen goods (quantity falls — staple foods for very poor households); Veblen/status goods where a lower price reduces appeal; expectations of further price falls (delay purchase); quality signalled by price; habits and inattention; satiation (MU near zero); conclusion that 'always' does not hold, though it usually does.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define allocative efficiency and productive efficiency, stating the condition for each.
parts.answer: Allocative: resources produce the goods consumers value most, P = MC. Productive: output is produced at the lowest possible average cost, at minimum AC (MC = AC).
parts.working: 1 mark each definition, 1 mark each condition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by dynamic efficiency.
parts.answer: Efficiency over time through innovation and investment that lower costs or create better products.
parts.working: 1 mark: improvements over time. 1 mark: via research and development, new technology and new products, often financed from profits.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what is meant by Pareto optimality.
parts.answer: A position where no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.
parts.working: 1 mark definition; 1 mark link: it requires both allocative and productive efficiency in all markets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by market failure.
parts.answer: A situation in which the free market allocates resources inefficiently, so that output is not at the level where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost and society's welfare is not maximised.
parts.working: 1: free market leads to an inefficient allocation of resources; 1: e.g. MSB ≠ MSC / over- or under-production / welfare loss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify three different causes of market failure, giving an example of each.
parts.answer: Any three, e.g.: externalities (air pollution from factories); public goods (street lighting); information failure (patients and doctors); monopoly power (a single electricity supplier); factor immobility (unemployed miners).
parts.working: 1 mark for each cause with a relevant example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define X-inefficiency.
parts.answer: Producing at a higher average cost than is necessary for a given output, so the firm is above its lowest possible cost curve, due to lack of competitive pressure.
parts.working: 1: costs higher than the minimum possible for that output (above the cost curve); 1: caused by slack / lack of competitive pressure / poor management.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a monopoly that is protected from competition may be X-inefficient.
parts.answer: With no rivals and secure supernormal profit, managers face little pressure to control costs; they may over-staff, pay excessive salaries, use outdated methods, or pursue their own objectives, and the firm still survives.
parts.working: 1: lack of competitive pressure/threat of entry; 1: supernormal profit allows slack (overmanning, waste, perks); 1: firm survives even with high costs, so no incentive to cut them.

practice.stem:
A firm's total costs at different outputs are (invented data):
Output (units): 100, 200, 300, 400, 500
Total cost ($): 2 800, 4 400, 6 000, 8 400, 12 000
The market price is $24.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average cost at each output, and identify the productively efficient output.
parts.answer: AC: $28, $22, $20, $21, $24; productively efficient at 300 units.
parts.working: AC = TC/Q (1); lowest AC ($20) at 300 units (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the marginal cost per unit for each increase of 100 units, and identify the allocatively efficient output when the market price is $24.
parts.answer: MC: $16, $16, $24, $36 per unit; allocatively efficient at 400 units.
parts.working: MC = ΔTC/ΔQ (1); P = MC = $24 for the units from 300 to 400, so 400 units (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a Pareto improvement.
parts.answer: A change in the allocation of resources that makes at least one person better off without making anyone else worse off.
parts.working: 1: at least one person better off; 1: nobody worse off.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why breaking up a monopoly to create a competitive market may not be a Pareto improvement, even if it removes a deadweight loss.
parts.answer: Lower prices raise consumer surplus and remove the deadweight loss, but the former monopoly owners lose supernormal profit (producer surplus); since someone is worse off, it is not a Pareto improvement, although gainers could in principle compensate the losers.
parts.working: 1: consumers gain (lower price, higher output); 1: monopoly shareholders lose profit; 1: someone is made worse off, so not a Pareto improvement (gains exceed losses, so a potential improvement only if compensation is paid).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm sells its output at a price of $12. At its current output, its marginal cost is $9 and its average cost is $10. What can be concluded?
A the firm is allocatively efficient
B the firm is producing less than the allocatively efficient output
C the firm is producing more than the allocatively efficient output
D the firm is making a loss
parts.answer: B the firm is producing less than the allocatively efficient output
parts.working: P > MC means consumers value an extra unit ($12) more than it costs to produce ($9), so output is below the allocatively efficient level. D is wrong: P ($12) > AC ($10), so the firm makes supernormal profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm sells its output at $40. At its current output, its marginal cost is $40 and its average cost is $46. Which statement describes the firm at this output?
A It is allocatively efficient but not productively efficient.
B It is productively efficient but not allocatively efficient.
C It is both allocatively and productively efficient.
D It is neither allocatively nor productively efficient.
parts.answer: A It is allocatively efficient but not productively efficient.
parts.working: P = MC ($40), so the firm is allocatively efficient. Because MC < AC, average cost is still falling, so the firm is not at minimum AC and is not productively efficient. B reverses the two conditions.

practice.stem: An industry faces the demand curve P = 100 − 2Q, where P is in dollars and Q is in thousand units a year. Marginal cost and average cost are constant at $20 (invented data). Compare perfect competition with a monopoly that has the same costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output and price if the industry is perfectly competitive.
parts.answer: Q = 40 thousand units, P = $20.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the output and price if a single monopoly firm with the same costs supplies the market. Its marginal revenue is MR = 100 − 4Q.
parts.answer: Q = 20 thousand units, P = $60.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the deadweight welfare loss caused by the monopoly.
parts.answer: $400 000 (400 thousand dollars).
parts.working: Triangle between demand and MC from Q = 20 to 40: ½ × (40 − 20) × (60 − 20) (1) = 400 thousand dollars (1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the monopoly outcome is allocatively inefficient.
parts.answer: At Q = 20 the price ($60), which measures the value of the last unit to consumers, is above the marginal cost ($20); units between 20 and 40 are worth more to consumers than they cost to make but are not produced.
parts.working: 1: P > MC at the monopoly output; 1: under-production → loss of consumer and producer surplus not gained by anyone.

practice.stem: In a large city's market for used motorcycles, sellers know much more about the condition of each machine than buyers do.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how asymmetric information can lead to market failure in this market.
parts.answer: Buyers cannot tell good motorcycles from poor ones, so they offer only an average price; owners of good machines will not sell at that price and leave the market, so the average quality offered falls (adverse selection, 'market for lemons'); fewer mutually beneficial trades take place and resources are misallocated.
parts.working: 1: sellers know more than buyers; 1: buyers will pay only a price reflecting average/expected quality; 1: sellers of good-quality machines withdraw → quality falls (adverse selection); 1: market shrinks or collapses → under-consumption / welfare loss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which the problem might be reduced.
parts.answer: Any two: warranties or guarantees from dealers; independent inspection/certification; required disclosure of service and accident history; online review/reputation systems; government regulation of dealers.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between occupational and geographical immobility of labour.
parts.answer: Occupational immobility: workers cannot easily move between jobs because they lack the skills or qualifications; geographical immobility: workers cannot easily move between places because of housing costs, family ties or information.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how factor immobility can cause market failure, using the example of workers from closing textile mills and a shortage of software developers.
parts.answer: When textile mills close, their workers' skills do not suit software jobs and retraining takes time and money, so they stay unemployed while software firms cannot fill vacancies; resources are not reallocated in response to price signals, so output is below potential and wages for scarce skills are bid up.
parts.working: 1: price signals (high software wages) should attract labour; 1: lack of skills/retraining costs prevent movement (occupational immobility); 1: distance/housing may also prevent moving to tech hubs; 1: result — unemployment alongside vacancies, resources not fully or efficiently used (inside PPC) = market failure.

practice.stem: Invented data: a pharmaceutical company spent $1.2 billion over 12 years developing a new medicine. Only about 1 in 10 medicines that reach clinical trials are eventually approved. The new medicine is protected by a 20-year patent. Its marginal cost of production is about $30 per course of treatment, but it is sold for $900 per course.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a 20-year patent may reduce allocative efficiency.
parts.answer: It gives the firm monopoly power, so it sets price above marginal cost and restricts output.
parts.working: 1 mark: patent = legal barrier to entry. 1 mark: firm sets MR = MC. 1 mark: price ($900) far above marginal cost ($30). 1 mark: output below the level where P = MC; some patients who value the drug above its cost cannot afford it – deadweight loss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: With reference to the data, evaluate whether patents increase economic efficiency overall.
parts.answer: Patents trade static allocative efficiency for dynamic efficiency; the overall effect depends on how much innovation they cause and how high prices are.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 6): high R&D costs ($1.2 billion) and a low chance of success (1 in 10) mean firms would not invest without the chance of supernormal profit; without patents, rivals could copy at marginal cost; so patents promote dynamic efficiency (new medicines). Costs: price 30 times MC, large deadweight loss, low-income patients excluded; firms may make small changes to extend patents. After expiry, generic producers lower prices. Evaluation (up to 2): judgement – efficiency gains likely where innovation is costly and risky, but shorter patents, price regulation or tiered pricing for low-income countries could reduce the static losses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how adverse selection may arise in a private health insurance market.
parts.answer: Buyers know more about their own health than insurers; at an average premium, people with high health risks are most likely to buy cover, while healthy people find it poor value and drop out; claims and premiums rise, driving out more low-risk buyers, so the market may shrink or fail.
parts.working: 1: asymmetric information before the contract (buyers know their risk); 1: insurer sets premium on average risk; 1: high-risk people buy, low-risk people leave; 1: premiums rise in a spiral / under-provision of insurance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by moral hazard, and how it can lead to over-use of medical services.
parts.answer: Moral hazard is a change in behaviour after a contract is made because the person no longer bears the full cost of their actions. Insured patients pay little or nothing at the point of use, so they may visit doctors for minor problems or take fewer precautions; doctors may also over-treat because the insurer pays.
parts.working: 1: definition — behaviour changes after the contract; 1: hidden action/insurer cannot monitor; 1: zero or low price at point of use → demand where MPB is near zero, beyond MSC = MSB; 1: example — extra visits, tests, less care with health; over-use raises premiums.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether dynamic efficiency is more important than allocative and productive efficiency for raising living standards in the long run.
parts.answer: Dynamic efficiency — innovation and investment that lower costs and create new products over time — drives long-run growth, so it can outweigh static losses; but static inefficiency wastes resources now, and supernormal profit does not guarantee innovation; the best outcome combines competition with incentives to innovate.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: definitions and conditions (P = MC; minimum AC; investment in new products/processes over time); diagrams showing AC falling over time; Schumpeter's argument that firms with supernormal profit can fund R&D; patents trade static loss for dynamic gain. Evaluation: monopolies may become X-inefficient and not innovate; competition can also drive innovation; distribution of gains; static inefficiency harms the poor through higher prices now; in developing economies, adoption of existing technology may matter more; conclusion with justified weighting.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): A country has four mobile phone networks with market shares (by subscribers) of 34 %, 28 %, 22 % and 16 %. The third and fourth largest networks plan to merge. They say the merger will let them invest in faster 5G coverage across the country. The competition authority fears that prices will rise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the three-firm concentration ratio before and after the merger.
parts.answer: Before: 84 %; after: 100 %.
parts.working: 34 + 28 + 22 = 84 % (1); after merger shares are 38, 34 and 28, so CR3 = 100 % (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between static efficiency and dynamic efficiency, using this example.
parts.answer: Static efficiency is about resource use at a point in time (allocative and productive efficiency) — with fewer firms, prices may rise above MC. Dynamic efficiency is about improvements over time — the merged firm may use its larger profits and scale to invest in 5G, lowering future costs and improving service.
parts.working: 1: static efficiency definition; 1: dynamic efficiency definition; 1: applied to merger (higher prices now vs investment in 5G).

parts.label: c
parts.text: With reference to the data, evaluate whether the competition authority should allow the merger.
parts.answer: The merger would make the market much more concentrated (three firms with 100 %), raising the risk of higher prices and collusion; but a larger third firm (38 %) could compete better with the leaders and fund 5G investment. The authority could allow it with conditions (price caps, investment commitments, network sharing) if the efficiency gains are likely to be passed on.
parts.working: Up to 4 for analysis: reduced competition → higher prices, lower consumer surplus, allocative inefficiency; tacit collusion easier with three firms; but economies of scale (network costs are high fixed costs), stronger challenger to the two leaders, dynamic efficiency from 5G. Up to 2 for evaluation: whether claims are credible; contestability (entry barriers high); conditions/remedies; justified decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a perfectly competitive market will always be both allocatively and productively efficient.
parts.answer: In long-run equilibrium a perfectly competitive firm produces where P = MC (allocative) and P = minimum AC (productive). But in the short run firms may not be at minimum AC; externalities mean P = MC ≠ MSC; information failure, factor immobility and the lack of funds for innovation can also prevent efficiency; and the model's assumptions rarely hold.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: firm and industry diagrams; short-run supernormal profit/losses → entry/exit → long-run equilibrium at P = MC = minimum AC. Evaluation: short-run outcomes need not be productively efficient; allocative efficiency is only private — with externalities, MSC ≠ MPC; public goods not provided; unrealistic assumptions (perfect information, homogeneous products, no barriers); lack of dynamic efficiency (normal profit only, no funds for R&D); distribution of income not addressed; conclusion: efficient in theory in the long run under strict assumptions, but not 'always'.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define organic (internal) growth of a firm.
parts.answer: Growth by expanding the firm's own operations — e.g. selling more, opening new branches, investing in more capacity — rather than by merging with or taking over other firms.
parts.working: 1: expanding own output/capacity/sales; 1: not through mergers or takeovers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why many small firms survive alongside large firms.
parts.answer: Small markets or niche products where large firms cannot gain economies of scale; personal service and flexibility valued by customers; low minimum efficient scale; owners may accept low profits; external economies in clusters; subcontracting to large firms.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 for the reason, 1 for explaining why it lets the small firm survive.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each of the following as horizontal integration, backward vertical integration, forward vertical integration or conglomerate integration.
(i) A textile mill buys a cotton-ginning factory.
(ii) A dairy company buys a chain of milk shops.
(iii) Two cement manufacturers merge.
(iv) A sugar producer buys an insurance company.
parts.answer: (i) backward vertical; (ii) forward vertical; (iii) horizontal; (iv) conglomerate.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit of backward vertical integration for the textile mill.
parts.answer: It secures supplies of ginned cotton of the right quality and timing, and removes the supplier's profit margin, lowering its costs.
parts.working: 1: benefit (security/quality of supply, lower costs, control over inputs); 1: explanation linked to the mill.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms
practice.stem: A soap manufacturer's sales rose from Rs 450 million to Rs 540 million in a year, while total sales in the soap market rose from Rs 3 000 million to Rs 3 300 million (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the firm's market share in each year (to one decimal place) and the percentage growth of its sales.
parts.answer: Market share: 15.0 % then 16.4 %; sales growth 20 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a firm may aim to increase its market share.
parts.answer: A larger share can give it more market power to influence prices, more economies of scale, greater security against rivals, or more bargaining power with retailers.
parts.working: 1: reason; 1: explanation.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the condition for profit maximisation.
parts.answer: Marginal revenue = marginal cost (with MC rising through MR).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At its current output, a firm's marginal revenue is $18 and its marginal cost is $24. Explain what it should do to increase its profit.
parts.answer: Reduce output: the last unit adds $24 to cost but only $18 to revenue, so each unit cut raises profit by the difference until MR = MC.
parts.working: 1: reduce output; 1: MC > MR means last unit loses $6; 1: cut output until MR = MC.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a firm whose main objective in a recession is survival might set its price below the profit-maximising level.
parts.answer: In a recession demand falls; a lower price keeps sales and cash flow up, covers variable costs and keeps customers and market share, so the firm avoids closure even though short-run profit is lower.
parts.working: 1: survival requires cash flow/covering variable costs; 1: lower price maintains sales volume or market share; 1: accepts lower short-run profit to stay in business until demand recovers.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the principal-agent problem that can arise from the divorce of ownership and control in large public limited companies.
parts.answer: Shareholders (principals) want maximum profit, but managers (agents) may pursue their own goals such as high salaries, sales growth or status.
parts.working: 1 mark: divorce of ownership (shareholders) and control (managers). 1 mark: managers have more information than shareholders (asymmetric information). 1 mark: managers may pursue sales/revenue maximisation, growth or perks. 1 mark: result – profits lower than shareholders want.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which shareholders might reduce this problem.
parts.answer: Link managers' pay to profits or share price (share options, bonuses); vote out directors / threat of takeover; independent non-executive directors and audits.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained methods.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'satisficing'.
parts.answer: Aiming for a satisfactory level of profit that keeps shareholders content, while also meeting the goals of other stakeholders.
parts.working: 1 mark: satisfactory rather than maximum profit. 1 mark: balancing competing stakeholder objectives.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms
practice.stem: Farmers in a district own a dairy co-operative that buys their milk and sells processed milk. Its stated aim is to pay members a fair price for their milk and to keep milk affordable for local families (invented).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the co-operative's objective differs from profit maximisation.
parts.answer: A profit maximiser would pay farmers as little as possible for milk and charge consumers the price where MR = MC; the co-operative aims to benefit its members and the community, so it accepts lower profits, aiming at a target (e.g. break-even or satisficing) rather than maximum profit.
parts.working: 1: profit maximisation = MR = MC; 1: co-operative serves members/stakeholders; 1: accepts lower profit / break-even / satisficing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the co-operative's price and output might differ from those of a profit-maximising firm.
parts.answer: It is likely to charge a lower price and sell more milk, possibly up to where average revenue equals average cost, and to pay farmers a higher price; the result is closer to allocative efficiency but leaves less profit for investment.
parts.working: 1: lower price to consumers; 1: higher output (e.g. AR = AC rather than MR = MC); 1: higher price to farmer-members / less retained profit for investment.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms
practice.stem:
A firm's weekly total revenue (TR) and total cost (TC) are shown below (invented data), $ thousand.
Output (thousand units): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60
TR: 200, 360, 480, 560, 600, 598
TC: 150, 240, 325, 415, 505, 596

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the firm's profit at each output.
parts.working: Profit = TR − TC (2 marks all correct; 1 mark for four).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the output that (i) maximises profit, (ii) maximises total revenue, and (iii) maximises sales while still earning at least normal profit. Total cost includes normal profit.
parts.answer: (i) 30 000 units; (ii) 50 000 units; (iii) 60 000 units.
parts.working: 1 each: profit greatest $155 000 at 30 000; TR greatest $600 000 at 50 000; largest output with profit ≥ 0 is 60 000 (profit $2 000).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why managers might prefer to maximise sales rather than profit.
parts.answer: Managers' pay, status and job security may depend on the size of the firm or its sales rather than profit; a larger market share may also protect the firm from rivals.
parts.working: 1: divorce of ownership and control / managerial objectives; 1: explanation (salary linked to size, prestige, market share, survival).

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether growth through mergers and takeovers is more likely to benefit a firm's shareholders than its consumers.
parts.answer: Mergers can raise profits through economies of scale and market power, which benefit shareholders; consumers gain only if savings are passed on as lower prices or better products. Many mergers fail to raise shareholder value because of overpayment and diseconomies, so the answer depends on market structure, the type of merger and regulation.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: horizontal, vertical and conglomerate mergers; economies of scale lower AC; greater market power → higher price, lower output (monopoly diagram, deadweight loss) → higher profit for shareholders; managers' motives (sales or empire building, principal-agent problem). Evaluation: evidence that many takeovers reduce acquiring firm's share value; integration problems and diseconomies; consumers can benefit from lower costs, wider range, R&D (dynamic efficiency) if markets remain contestable; competition authority may block harmful mergers; conclusion depends on context.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three factors that may limit the growth of a firm.
parts.answer: Any three, e.g.: limited access to finance (banks unwilling to lend, high interest rates); small size of the market or niche demand; diseconomies of scale and management problems; competition authorities blocking mergers; owners' wish to keep control; shortage of skilled labour or inputs.
parts.working: For each of three factors: 1 for the factor, 1 for explaining why it constrains growth.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms
practice.stem: A firm faces the demand curve P = 120 − 2Q and has total cost TC = 400 + 20Q, where P is in dollars and Q in units per week. Total cost includes normal profit (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output, price and profit if the firm maximises profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the output, price and profit if the firm maximises total revenue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the largest output the firm can sell while still earning at least normal profit (sales maximisation). Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether the vertical integration of firms is likely to benefit consumers.
parts.answer: It may lower costs and secure supply, benefiting consumers through lower prices and reliability, but can increase market power and foreclose rivals.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): distinguish backward and forward vertical integration (with horizontal and conglomerate as contrast); motives – control of supplies and quality, removing intermediaries' profit margins, reducing transaction costs, securing retail outlets, economies of scale; benefits to consumers – lower costs passed on as lower prices, more reliable supply, better coordination and quality. Risks – market power increases; rivals may be denied access to inputs or outlets (foreclosure), raising barriers to entry; reduced competition leads to higher prices; diseconomies of scale and X-inefficiency in a large firm; managers may lack expertise in the new stage. Evaluation (up to 6): depends on market structure at each stage, competition policy, whether cost savings are passed on; reasoned conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms
practice.stem: Two bakeries in a city each produce 50 000 loaves a week. Bakery P has an average cost of $1.20 per loaf and Bakery R has an average cost of $1.40. After merging, the combined firm produces 100 000 loaves a week at an average cost of $1.15 (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the weekly saving in total cost from the merger, and the percentage fall in total cost (to one decimal place).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two possible sources of the cost saving.
parts.answer: Any two: closing the less efficient bakery's duplicate administration or distribution; buying flour in bulk at lower prices; using larger ovens at full capacity (technical economies); lower borrowing costs.
parts.working: 1 each for two relevant sources (rationalisation, purchasing, technical, managerial or financial economies).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether consumers in the city will benefit from the merger.
parts.answer: Lower costs could be passed on as lower bread prices or better quality, but the merger also removes a competitor; if the merged firm gains market power it may keep the savings as profit or even raise prices, so the benefit depends on remaining competition and regulation.
parts.working: Up to 3 for analysis: lower AC → scope for lower prices; but fewer competitors → market power → P above MC; possible loss of choice; job losses may reduce local incomes. Up to 1 for judgement: depends on number of other bakeries, ease of entry, competition authority.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms
practice.stem: An established fertiliser producer has an average cost of $8 per bag at its output of 200 000 bags a month. A potential entrant could produce only at a small scale, with an average cost of $10 per bag. The established firm sets its price at $9.50 per bag (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by limit pricing, using these figures.
parts.answer: The incumbent sets its price ($9.50) below the average cost of a potential entrant ($10) but above its own average cost ($8), so entry would be loss-making for the newcomer while the incumbent still earns supernormal profit.
parts.working: 1: price set to deter entry; 1: price below entrant's AC ($10), so entrant would make a loss; 1: above incumbent's AC ($8), so incumbent still profitable (uses its economies of scale).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the incumbent's supernormal profit per month at this price. Average cost includes normal profit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Distinguish between limit pricing and predatory pricing.
parts.answer: Limit pricing keeps price low enough to stop rivals entering while the incumbent remains profitable; predatory pricing sets price below the predator's own cost (often below AVC) for a time to force an existing rival out, then raises price. Predatory pricing is usually illegal.
parts.working: 1: limit pricing — deters entry, still profitable; 1: predatory — price below own cost to drive out existing rivals, with later price rises; 1: legal/competition policy difference or short-run losses accepted by predator.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that all firms aim to maximise profits.
parts.answer: Profit maximisation (MR = MC) is the standard assumption and is needed for survival in competitive markets, but many firms pursue other aims: revenue or sales maximisation, growth, satisficing, survival, social or environmental objectives, or public service in state-owned and non-profit organisations. Lack of information also makes exact profit maximisation unlikely.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: profit-maximising output where MR = MC; diagram comparing outputs for profit, revenue (MR = 0) and sales maximisation (AR = AC); divorce of ownership and control, principal-agent problem; behavioural theories (satisficing, multiple stakeholders). Evaluation: in perfect competition firms must maximise profit to survive; shareholders can discipline managers (takeover threat, bonuses); other objectives may be means to long-run profit; owners of small firms may value independence; social enterprises, co-operatives and state firms have different goals; firms lack information on MR and MC; conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms
practice.stem:
A conglomerate has two divisions. Their profits, $ million, were (invented data):
Year 1: textiles 120; food 60
Year 2: textiles −40; food 110
Year 3: textiles 90; food 70

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total profit of the conglomerate in each year, and the range of profits over the three years for the textile division and for the conglomerate as a whole.
parts.answer: Totals: $180 m, $70 m, $160 m. Range: textiles $160 m; whole firm $110 m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, explain how conglomerate integration can reduce risk.
parts.answer: The divisions face different markets whose profits do not move together; when textiles made a loss in Year 2, food profits rose, so total profit varied less (range $110 m instead of $160 m) and the firm stayed profitable.
parts.working: 1: diversification across unrelated markets; 1: reference to data (Year 2 loss offset; smaller range).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider two disadvantages of growth through conglomerate integration.
parts.answer: Managers may lack expertise in unrelated industries, causing poor decisions; the firm gains few economies of scale or synergies; a large, varied organisation can suffer diseconomies of scale; shareholders could diversify more cheaply themselves; but the size of these problems depends on how independently the divisions are run.
parts.working: For each of two disadvantages: 1 for identification, 1 for explanation/consideration.
