practice.stem: Invented data for a country in one year: GDP is $380 billion. Income earned in the country by foreign-owned firms and sent abroad is $20 billion. Income earned by the country's residents from assets they own abroad is $8 billion. The population is 240 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the country's gross national income (GNI).
parts.answer: $368 billion
parts.working: GNI = GDP + net primary income from abroad (M1) = 380 − 20 + 8 = $368 billion (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate GNI per head. Give your answer to the nearest dollar.
parts.working: 368,000 million ÷ 240 million = $1,533 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why GNI per head is a better indicator than GDP per head of the income available to the residents of this country.
parts.answer: GNI excludes income that flows abroad to foreign owners (e.g. repatriated profits) and includes residents' income from abroad.
parts.working: 1 mark: GDP measures output produced in the country, whoever owns it. 1 mark: $20 billion of income goes to foreign firms, so GDP overstates residents' income.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature is most typical of a low-income developing economy?
A a high proportion of the labour force employed in the primary sector
B a low birth rate and an ageing population
C a high level of capital per worker
D a small informal sector
parts.answer: A a high proportion of the labour force employed in the primary sector
parts.working: Low-income economies usually have a large share of employment in agriculture and other primary activities. B, C and D are features of high-income economies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why comparing GDP per head converted at market exchange rates may give a misleading view of relative living standards in two countries.
parts.answer: Market exchange rates do not reflect the cost of living (non-traded goods are cheaper in low-income countries), so PPP should be used; exchange rates fluctuate for financial reasons; and differing sizes of the informal sector or of non-market output make GDP less comparable.
parts.working: 1 reason + 1 explanation, twice.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a large informal economy affects measured GDP.
parts.answer: Informal output is not recorded, so measured GDP understates actual output and income.
parts.working: 1 not recorded; 1 understates GDP/living standards.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which indicator is NOT used in calculating the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)?
A years of schooling of household members
B child mortality in the household
C household income per person
D access to clean drinking water
parts.answer: C household income per person
parts.working: The MPI measures deprivation in health, education and living standards using non-income indicators (nutrition, child mortality, schooling, school attendance, cooking fuel, sanitation, water, electricity, housing, assets). Income is deliberately excluded. A, B and D are all MPI indicators.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the Measure of Economic Welfare (MEW) and why it might give a different view of living standards from real GDP per head.
parts.answer: MEW adjusts GDP by adding the value of non-market activities that raise welfare and subtracting activities that do not add to welfare.
parts.working: 1 mark: MEW starts from GDP/GNP. 1 mark: adds value of leisure, household production (unpaid work) and the informal economy. 1 mark: subtracts 'regrettables' such as defence and commuting, and environmental damage. 1 mark: so two countries with the same GDP per head can have very different MEW, e.g. if one has longer working hours or more pollution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difficulty in calculating the MEW.
parts.answer: Valuing non-market items (leisure, unpaid care, pollution) in money terms is subjective.
parts.working: 1 mark difficulty; 1 mark explanation (choice of values / data availability makes comparisons unreliable).

practice.stem: Invented population data for a low-income country: aged 0–14: 72 million; aged 15–64: 150 million; aged 65 and over: 9 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dependency ratio (dependants per 100 people of working age).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two economic characteristics, other than population structure, commonly found in low-income countries.
parts.answer: e.g. large share of employment in agriculture/primary sector; large informal sector; low savings and investment; low productivity; high dependence on primary exports.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained characteristics.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a fall in the birth rate could give this country a 'demographic dividend'.
parts.answer: The working-age share rises relative to dependants, raising output per head, savings and investment.
parts.working: 1 mark: dependency ratio falls as fewer children are born. 1 mark: more workers per dependant can raise income per head and savings, if jobs are available.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether HDI is a better measure of living standards than real GNI per head.
parts.answer: HDI is broader because it includes health and education, but it still omits inequality, freedom and the environment; the better measure depends on the purpose.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): real GNI per head – adjusts for inflation and population, PPP allows comparison, measures material living standards; limitations – ignores distribution, informal sector, non-market output, leisure, environmental damage, quality of goods, exchange-rate issues. HDI – geometric mean of life expectancy, education (mean and expected years of schooling) and GNI per head; reflects capabilities; shows countries with high income but poor health/education; limitations – only three dimensions, averages hide inequality (inequality-adjusted HDI exists), ignores freedom, security, environment; arbitrary weights and goalposts; slow to change. Other measures – MPI, MEW, happiness indices. Evaluation (up to 6): judgement – HDI generally a better indicator of overall living standards, but GNI still essential for income comparisons; use several indicators.

practice.stem:
Invented data for Country K:
Real GDP per head ($): 2015 2,400; 2025 3,600
Life expectancy (years): 2015 64.0; 2025 64.5
Mean years of schooling: 2015 4.1; 2025 4.3
Share of national income of richest 10%: 2015 30%; 2025 42%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in real GDP per head between 2015 and 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, explain why economic growth may not lead to economic development.
parts.answer: Real GDP per head rose 50% but life expectancy and schooling barely changed, and the top 10%'s share rose from 30% to 42%: the gains went mainly to the rich and were not used for health and education, so wider well-being improved little.
parts.working: 1 distinguish growth from development; 1 use of health/education data; 1 rising inequality; 1 explanation of why benefits did not spread.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one other indicator that would help judge whether development has taken place.
parts.answer: e.g. Multidimensional Poverty Index / share of population below the poverty line / access to clean water / infant mortality.
parts.working: 1 indicator; 1 reason it shows development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether improving the education of girls is the most effective way to raise living standards in a low-income country.
parts.answer: Education of girls raises productivity, earnings, lowers fertility and child mortality, improves HDI; but other constraints (infrastructure, health, jobs for graduates, governance, capital) may bind more; effectiveness depends on quality and labour-market access. Judgement.
parts.working: Knowledge, understanding and analysis (up to 14): human capital and productivity; effects on fertility, health and child schooling (intergenerational); links to HDI and MPI dimensions; comparison with other policies (infrastructure, health, credit, trade). Evaluation (up to 6): time lags; need for jobs and complementary investment; cultural and cost barriers; quality of schooling; reasoned conclusion on 'most effective'.

practice.stem:
The Human Development Index uses these formulas:
life expectancy index = (life expectancy − 20) ÷ (85 − 20)
education index = average of (mean years of schooling ÷ 15) and (expected years of schooling ÷ 18)
income index = (ln GNI per head − ln 100) ÷ (ln 75,000 − ln 100), with GNI per head in PPP$
Invented data for a country: life expectancy 67.5 years; mean years of schooling 8.0; expected years of schooling 11.0; GNI per head PPP$5,800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the life expectancy index, the education index and the income index. Give each to 3 decimal places.
parts.answer: Life expectancy index 0.731; education index 0.572; income index 0.613

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the country's HDI as the geometric mean of the three indices. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify which dimension contributes least to the country's HDI and suggest one policy that could raise it.
parts.answer: Education (index 0.572); e.g. increase spending on schools, teacher training or conditional cash transfers for school attendance.
parts.working: 1 mark education identified; 1 mark appropriate policy.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a year, a country's nominal GDP rises by 12 %, the general price level rises by 8 % and the population rises by 2 %. What is the approximate change in real GDP per head?
A a rise of about 1.7 %
B a rise of about 3.7 %
C a rise of about 6.0 %
D a rise of about 10.0 %
parts.answer: A a rise of about 1.7 %
parts.working: Real GDP growth = 1.12 ÷ 1.08 − 1 = 3.7 %; per head = 1.037 ÷ 1.02 − 1 ≈ 1.7 %. B ignores population growth; C adds population growth instead of subtracting it.

practice.stem:
Invented data for two countries.
Country P: GNI per head (PPP$) 14,000; HDI 0.70; life expectancy 68 years; mean years of schooling 6.5; Gini coefficient 0.52; oil is 60 % of exports
Country Q: GNI per head (PPP$) 9,000; HDI 0.76; life expectancy 74 years; mean years of schooling 10.0; Gini coefficient 0.34

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which Country P's GNI per head exceeds that of Country Q. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, explain why Country Q has a higher HDI than Country P despite its lower GNI per head.
parts.answer: Q has better health and education outcomes, which raise the other two dimensions of the HDI.
parts.working: 1 mark: HDI combines income, health and education. 1 mark: Q's life expectancy is 6 years higher. 1 mark: Q's mean years of schooling are 3.5 years higher. 1 mark: the higher health and education indices more than offset Q's lower income index; e.g. P's income may be concentrated in an oil sector with little spending on public services.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether HDI shows that living standards are higher in Country Q than in Country P.
parts.answer: Probably, but HDI omits inequality, freedom, environment and other factors; the MPI and inequality data could give a different picture.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 6): HDI is broader than GNI per head and captures capabilities; but it is an average – Gini data show P is much more unequal (0.52 vs 0.34), so typical households in P may be worse off than the GNI figure suggests, strengthening the view that Q is better off; HDI ignores political freedom, environmental quality, working hours, housing, security; equal weighting of the three dimensions is arbitrary; data quality. Evaluation (up to 2): judgement, e.g. evidence supports higher living standards in Q, especially given the lower inequality, but a fuller view needs MPI and other indicators.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that rapid population growth is the main obstacle to economic development in low-income countries.
parts.answer: Rapid population growth can hold back income per head and strain services, but it can also provide a labour force and markets; institutions, investment and human capital may matter more.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): Malthusian view – population outpaces food and resources; diluted capital per worker; high dependency ratio; pressure on schools, health, housing; unemployment and urban slums; lower savings. Counter-arguments – demographic transition and demographic dividend when the working-age share rises; larger domestic markets and economies of scale; young, adaptable labour force; technology raises food output. Other obstacles – low savings and investment, poor infrastructure, weak institutions and corruption, debt, dependence on primary exports, conflict, low human capital, inequality. Evaluation (up to 6): population growth is a consequence as well as a cause of poverty (birth rates fall as incomes, education of women and health improve); 'main' obstacle requires a comparison and a reasoned judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's GNI per head is Rs 1,200,000. The market exchange rate is Rs 280 = $1 and the purchasing power parity (PPP) rate is Rs 95 = $1. What is GNI per head in PPP dollars, to the nearest dollar?
A $4,286
B $12,632
C $8,459
D $1,454
parts.working: 1,200,000 ÷ 95 = $12,632. A converts at the market exchange rate (1,200,000 ÷ 280), which understates living standards where non-traded goods are cheap. C averages A and B; D adjusts the market-rate figure in the wrong direction (4,286 × 95 ÷ 280).

practice.stem:
Invented data for a South Asian country. Share of total employment (%):
1995: primary 62, secondary 14, tertiary 24
2025: primary 38, secondary 15, tertiary 47
Total employment: 20 million in 1995; 32 million in 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in the share of employment in each sector between 1995 and 2025, in percentage points.
parts.answer: Primary −24; secondary +1; tertiary +23
parts.working: M1 subtraction; A1 all three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of workers in the primary sector in 1995 and in 2025.
parts.answer: 12.4 million and 12.16 million

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a change in the structure of employment is linked to economic development.
parts.answer: As countries develop, labour moves from low-productivity agriculture to manufacturing and services where output per worker is higher; this raises incomes and is associated with urbanisation, education and better services.
parts.working: 1 productivity differences; 1 movement of labour; 1 higher incomes; 1 link to wider development.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate whether a country can achieve development by moving workers straight from agriculture into services, without a large manufacturing sector.
parts.answer: Modern services (IT, finance, tourism) can have high productivity and export earnings; but many service jobs are informal and low-productivity, manufacturing offers mass employment for less-skilled workers and learning effects; depends on education, infrastructure and global demand. Judgement.
parts.working: Analysis up to 5 (two-sided, using the data: tertiary share rose 23 points while manufacturing barely changed); evaluation up to 3 (conditions, type of services, conclusion).

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between bilateral aid and multilateral aid.
parts.answer: Bilateral aid is given directly by one government to another; multilateral aid is channelled through international organisations such as the World Bank or UN agencies.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why tied aid may bring fewer benefits to the receiving country than untied aid.
parts.answer: Tied aid must be spent on goods/services from the donor country, which may be more expensive or unsuitable, and does not support local producers.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition of tied aid. 1 mark: recipient cannot buy from the cheapest supplier, so less value is obtained. 1 mark: goods may not suit local needs or use inappropriate technology. 1 mark: money flows back to donor firms rather than local businesses/jobs.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an example of foreign direct investment (FDI) in Pakistan?
A a Pakistani worker in Dubai sends money home to his family
B a foreign pension fund buys a small number of shares in a Karachi-listed bank
C a foreign car maker builds and operates a new assembly plant near Lahore
D a foreign government gives a grant to build schools in Balochistan
parts.answer: C a foreign car maker builds and operates a new assembly plant near Lahore
parts.working: FDI involves a foreign firm acquiring a lasting controlling interest in productive assets, such as building its own factory. B is portfolio investment (no control); A is a remittance (a transfer); D is aid.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which remittances from workers abroad can help the economic development of the receiving country.
parts.answer: They raise household income and consumption (reducing poverty); they are spent on education, health and housing (human capital); they finance small businesses; they earn foreign currency that helps finance imports.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for each of two developed points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one possible disadvantage of relying on remittances.
parts.answer: e.g. loss of skilled workers (brain drain); remittances fall when host economies enter recession; may raise demand for imports or property prices rather than investment.
parts.working: 1 point; 1 explanation.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between foreign direct investment and portfolio investment.
parts.answer: FDI: buying or building a lasting controlling interest in productive assets abroad (e.g. a factory). Portfolio investment: buying shares or bonds without control, often for short-term financial return.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why large flows of short-term portfolio investment ('hot money') can be harmful to a developing economy.
parts.answer: Such flows can reverse quickly when interest rates or confidence change, causing sharp depreciation, a fall in asset prices, loss of reserves and a financial crisis; the central bank may have to raise interest rates sharply, harming growth.
parts.working: 1 volatile/quick to leave; 1 effect on exchange rate; 1 effect on reserves or asset prices; 1 policy response/harm to growth.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)
practice.stem: Invented data for a copper-exporting country in 2025: external debt service payments (interest and principal) were $9.6 billion and export earnings were $32 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the debt service ratio (debt service as a percentage of export earnings) in 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Export earnings are forecast to fall by 20 % in 2026 because of a fall in copper prices, while debt service payments stay the same. Calculate the new debt service ratio.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a rising debt service ratio may reduce the country's prospects for development.
parts.answer: More foreign currency goes on interest and repayments, leaving less for imports of capital goods and for spending on health and education.
parts.working: 1 mark: opportunity cost – foreign exchange and government revenue diverted to creditors. 1 mark: less investment, capital imports, social spending. 1 mark: risk of default, higher borrowing costs, IMF conditions, falling investor confidence.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two possible benefits to a low-income host country of a multinational company (MNC) setting up a factory there.
parts.answer: Jobs and incomes; transfer of technology and skills; tax revenue; exports and foreign currency; investment in infrastructure.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained benefits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by transfer pricing and why it can reduce the benefits to the host country.
parts.answer: MNCs set the prices of goods traded between their own subsidiaries so that profits are recorded in low-tax countries; the host country loses tax revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition – prices charged in trade between branches of the same MNC. 1 mark: overcharging the host-country subsidiary for inputs/fees, or undercharging for its output. 1 mark: profits appear in a low-tax country. 1 mark: host government loses corporate tax revenue.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether foreign direct investment by multinational companies is more beneficial to low-income countries than official development aid.
parts.answer: FDI brings capital, technology and jobs without debt, but is driven by profit and may concentrate in extractive sectors; aid can target poverty and public goods but has its own problems; they complement each other.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): FDI – capital inflow, jobs, technology and management skills, exports, tax revenue, multiplier effects; costs – profit repatriation, transfer pricing, enclave production with weak linkages, environmental damage, influence over government, footloose firms, goes to countries with resources or large markets, not the poorest. Aid – grants and concessional loans, can fund health, education and infrastructure (public goods) that attract FDI later; humanitarian relief; problems – tied aid, corruption, dependency, loans add to debt, donor priorities, Dutch-disease effects. Evaluation (up to 6): depends on the country's institutions, sector of FDI, type of aid (project vs budget support); FDI more beneficial for middle-income countries with infrastructure; aid more important for the poorest; reasoned judgement.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an example of a 'soft loan' to a low-income country?
A a loan from a commercial bank at the market rate of interest
B a loan at a below-market rate of interest with a long repayment period and a grace period
C a grant that never has to be repaid
D a purchase of government bonds by foreign investors
parts.answer: B a loan at a below-market rate of interest with a long repayment period and a grace period
parts.working: A soft (concessional) loan has better terms than the market: low interest, long repayment and often a grace period. C is a grant, not a loan; A and D are on market terms.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)
practice.stem: Invented data. A country owes $40 billion of external debt at an interest rate of 6% a year. Its export earnings are $30 billion a year. The exchange rate falls from Rs 280 = $1 to Rs 350 = $1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual interest payments in dollars and as a percentage of export earnings.
parts.answer: $2.4 billion; 8%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of the debt in rupees before and after the depreciation, and the percentage change.
parts.answer: Rs 11,200 billion → Rs 14,000 billion; +25%

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the debt as a percentage of GDP before and after the depreciation, assuming GDP in rupees is unchanged at Rs 44,800 billion.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why borrowing in a foreign currency is risky for a low-income country.
parts.answer: If the currency depreciates, the burden of interest and repayment rises in domestic currency, and more export earnings or tax revenue must be used to service the debt.
parts.working: 1 exchange-rate risk; 1 higher burden/less for development spending.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a multinational clothing company may choose to locate its factories in Bangladesh.
parts.answer: Low wage costs; large supply of labour; preferential access to rich-country markets under trade agreements; established supplier networks; government incentives such as export processing zones.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for each of two developed reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether the host government should offer tax holidays to attract such companies.
parts.answer: Tax holidays may attract FDI that brings jobs, exports and skills; but they lose tax revenue, may start a 'race to the bottom', and firms may leave when the holiday ends (footloose). Judgement depends on linkages with local firms.
parts.working: Up to 2 analysis; up to 2 evaluation and judgement.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)
practice.stem:
Invented data for a small mineral-exporting country in one year:
GDP: $50 billion
profits of foreign-owned MNCs sent abroad: $3.5 billion
income received by residents from assets abroad: $0.5 billion
MNC employment: 40,000 workers, total wages $1.2 billion
average wage in the rest of the economy: $8,000 per worker
MNC exports: $6 billion; corporate tax paid by MNCs: $0.9 billion

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the country's GNI and GNI as a percentage of GDP.
parts.answer: GNI $47 billion; 94 % of GDP

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average annual wage paid by the MNC per worker, in dollars.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate, using the data, whether the MNCs bring more benefits than costs to the country.
parts.answer: The MNCs create well-paid jobs, exports and tax revenue, but large profit outflows and possible environmental costs reduce the net gain.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 5): benefits – 40,000 jobs at wages ($30,000) far above the national average ($8,000); $6 billion exports earn foreign currency; $0.9 billion tax revenue; skills transfer. Costs – $3.5 billion profits repatriated reduces GNI (GNI is only 94 % of GDP); dependence on a few foreign firms; possible environmental damage and use of non-renewable resources; little linkage to local suppliers if inputs are imported; possible transfer pricing. Evaluation (up to 2): reasoned judgement, e.g. net benefits appear positive, but depend on reinvestment, linkages and government regulation.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether debt relief is the most effective way to promote economic development in heavily indebted low-income countries.
parts.answer: Debt relief frees resources for spending on development, but its effectiveness depends on governance and on what is done with the savings; trade access, FDI and institutional reform may be more important.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): burden of debt – high debt service ratio, diversion of foreign exchange and tax revenue, debt overhang deters investment, austerity cuts social spending; debt relief reduces payments, allows spending on health, education and infrastructure, improves credit rating. Problems – moral hazard (may encourage future over-borrowing), funds may be wasted through corruption, conditions attached may impose unpopular reforms, relief is a one-off and does not address causes (dependence on primary exports, low productivity, volatile commodity prices). Alternatives – fairer trade and market access, diversification, FDI, aid targeted at human capital, institutional reform, microfinance. Evaluation (up to 6): relief is a necessary condition in some cases but rarely sufficient; reasoned judgement on 'most effective'.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the main roles of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank in relation to low-income countries.
parts.answer: IMF: short- to medium-term loans for balance-of-payments problems, surveillance, technical advice. World Bank: long-term loans and grants for development projects (infrastructure, health, education) and poverty reduction.
parts.working: 2 marks each: IMF (1 role identified, 1 developed); World Bank (1 role identified, 1 developed).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss why the conditions attached to IMF loans are often controversial.
parts.answer: Conditions such as cutting budget deficits, removing subsidies, raising interest rates and privatisation can restore stability but may raise poverty and unemployment in the short run.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): conditions aim to correct the causes of the crisis and ensure repayment; but austerity reduces aggregate demand and social spending, removal of fuel/food subsidies hurts the poor, loss of policy independence, 'one-size-fits-all' criticisms. Judgement (1): e.g. conditions may be needed for credibility but should be phased and protect vulnerable groups.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)
practice.stem:
Invented data for three donor countries in one year:
Donor A: GNI $2,400 billion; ODA $9.6 billion
Donor B: GNI $600 billion; ODA $5.7 billion
Donor C: GNI $1,500 billion; ODA $7.5 billion

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate official development assistance (ODA) as a percentage of GNI for each donor, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much extra aid Donor A would need to give to reach the UN target of 0.7% of GNI.
parts.answer: $7.2 billion

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the amount of aid given may be a poor guide to how much it helps development.
parts.answer: Aid may be tied to donors' exports, spent on donor consultants, used for donors' strategic aims, lost to corruption, or crowd out local effort; the type (grants v loans, project v budget support) matters more than the amount.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for each of two developed points.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate whether low-income countries would gain more from donors opening their markets to their exports than from an increase in aid.
parts.answer: Trade gives lasting income, encourages efficient industries and avoids dependency; but low-income countries may lack the capacity to export, face non-tariff barriers, and need aid for health and infrastructure first. Judgement: complements rather than substitutes.
parts.working: Analysis up to 4 ('trade not aid' argument v aid's role); evaluation up to 3 (conditions and conclusion).

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether large infrastructure projects financed by foreign loans promote economic development in low-income countries.
parts.answer: Roads, ports and power plants raise productivity, attract FDI and reduce costs; but loans add to external debt and repayment burdens, projects may be poorly chosen or over-priced, use imported labour and inputs, and returns may be slow. Judgement depends on loan terms, project quality and governance.
parts.working: Knowledge, understanding and analysis (up to 14): infrastructure as public/merit goods and supply-side improvement; multiplier effects; debt servicing and the current account; opportunity cost; examples from transport and energy. Evaluation (up to 6): terms of the loans (soft v commercial, currency); whether projects earn foreign exchange; corruption and transparency; time horizon; reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a floating exchange rate, a fixed exchange rate and a managed float.
parts.answer: Floating: set by market demand and supply with no target. Fixed: the central bank holds the currency at an official rate. Managed float: mostly market-determined, but the central bank intervenes to influence it.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a central bank could prevent its currency from falling below a fixed exchange rate.
parts.answer: Buy its own currency using foreign exchange reserves; raise interest rates to attract capital inflows; (also capital controls or borrowing from the IMF).
parts.working: 2 marks each: method identified (1) and explained in terms of demand for the currency (1).

practice.stem: A Pakistani textile firm sells shirts for Rs 5,600 each. The exchange rate changes from Rs 280 = $1 to Rs 300 = $1 (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dollar price of the shirt before and after the change in the exchange rate, and the percentage change. Give the percentage to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Before $20.00; after $18.67; a fall of 6.7 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rupee cost of a $50 machine part before and after the change.
parts.answer: Rs 14,000 before; Rs 15,000 after

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the depreciation might not raise the textile exporter's profits as much as expected.
parts.answer: Its imported inputs (machinery, dyes, fuel) become more expensive, raising costs; foreign demand may be price inelastic.
parts.working: 1 mark point (dearer imported inputs / inelastic demand / competitors' currencies also falling); 1 mark development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two factors that would increase the demand for Pakistani rupees on the foreign exchange market.
parts.answer: e.g. a rise in foreign demand for Pakistani exports (rice, textiles); higher remittance inflows converted into rupees; foreign direct investment into Pakistan; higher Pakistani interest rates attracting financial inflows.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for each of two developed factors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one factor that would increase the supply of rupees on the foreign exchange market.
parts.answer: e.g. Pakistani firms buying more imported oil or machinery need foreign currency, so they sell rupees.
parts.working: 1 factor; 1 explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a depreciation and a devaluation of a currency.
parts.answer: Depreciation: a fall in the value of a floating currency caused by market forces. Devaluation: a deliberate reduction by the government/central bank in the fixed (pegged) value.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a depreciation of a country's currency affects the foreign-currency price of its exports and the domestic-currency price of its imports.
parts.answer: Each unit of foreign currency buys more domestic currency, so exports become cheaper in foreign currency; each unit of domestic currency buys less foreign currency, so imports cost more in domestic currency.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for exports; 1 + 1 for imports.

practice.stem: Invented data: a burger costs Rs 900 in Pakistan and $5.50 in the USA. The market exchange rate is Rs 280 = $1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the exchange rate implied by purchasing power parity (PPP) for the burger. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Rs 163.6 per $

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the rupee is undervalued against the dollar on this measure. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: At the market rate the burger costs 900 ÷ 280 = $3.21 in Pakistan; 3.21 ÷ 5.50 = 0.584 (M1); undervalued by 1 − 0.584 = 41.6 % (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why a single-product comparison may not give a reliable estimate of the PPP exchange rate.
parts.answer: The burger includes non-traded inputs (rent, wages) whose prices differ; local tastes, taxes and competition differ; one product does not represent the whole basket.
parts.working: 1 mark reason; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
According to the Marshall–Lerner condition, a depreciation of a currency will improve a country's current account balance if
A the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports is greater than one
B the price elasticity of demand for exports is less than one
C the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports is less than one
D the income elasticity of demand for imports is greater than one
parts.answer: A the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports is greater than one
parts.working: If the sum of PEDs (in absolute value) exceeds 1, export revenue rises and import spending falls by enough to improve the balance. C describes the case in which the balance worsens, as at the start of the J-curve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a fixed exchange rate system is better than a floating exchange rate system for a developing economy.
parts.answer: A fixed rate gives certainty and can control inflation, but needs large reserves and removes monetary policy independence; a floating rate adjusts automatically but can be volatile; the better choice depends on the economy.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): fixed – certainty for traders and investors, reduces speculation (if credible), imposes discipline and can anchor inflation; costs – need for large foreign currency reserves, loss of independent monetary policy (interest rates set to defend the peg), risk of speculative attack and forced devaluation, misalignment can harm competitiveness. Floating – automatic correction of current account imbalances, no need for reserves, monetary policy free to target domestic goals; costs – volatility and uncertainty, depreciation raises import prices (imported inflation, cost of fuel and food), raises the burden of foreign-currency debt, speculation. Managed float as a middle way. Evaluation (up to 6): depends on reserves, inflation history, openness, credibility of the central bank, size of foreign-currency debt, commodity dependence; reasoned judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change, other things equal, is most likely to cause a floating currency to appreciate?
A a rise in the country's interest rates relative to those abroad
B a higher rate of inflation than in its trading partners
C an increase in the country's demand for imports
D the central bank selling its own currency in exchange for foreign currency
parts.answer: A a rise in the country's interest rates relative to those abroad
parts.working: Higher relative interest rates attract financial inflows, raising demand for the currency. B and C raise the supply of the currency (depreciation); D increases supply of the currency on the market.

practice.stem: Invented data. Exchange rates at the start of a year: €1 = $1.10 and $1 = Rs 280. At the end of the year: €1 = $1.15 and $1 = Rs 300.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rupee price of €1 before and after the changes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the rupee cost of a German machine priced at €200,000, to one decimal place.
parts.answer: +12.0% (Rs 61.6 million → Rs 69.0 million)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how this change could affect a Pakistani textile firm that imports German machinery and exports to Europe.
parts.answer: Investment in machinery becomes more expensive, raising costs; but the rupee has fallen against the euro, so its exports are cheaper in euros and may sell more; net effect depends on the import content and PED of exports.
parts.working: 1 dearer machinery; 1 effect on costs/investment; 1 cheaper exports in euros; 1 net effect depends on elasticities/import content.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a central bank may prefer a managed float to a freely floating exchange rate.
parts.answer: e.g. it smooths large short-term swings that create uncertainty for exporters, importers and investors; it limits sharp depreciation that would raise import prices and inflation; it reduces overshooting caused by speculative hot-money flows; it can stop the currency rising so fast that exporters lose competitiveness.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for each of two developed reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider the costs to a developing country of holding large foreign currency reserves to manage its exchange rate.
parts.answer: Reserves earn low returns compared with domestic investment (opportunity cost); building them may require borrowing or running surpluses; but they reduce the risk of a currency crisis and reassure investors. Judgement.
parts.working: Up to 2 costs; up to 2 benefits/judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data. Interest rates on one-year deposits are 12% in Pakistan and 4% in the USA. The exchange rate at the start of the year is Rs 280 = $1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An investor converts $1,000 into rupees, earns 12% interest for one year, then converts back to dollars after the exchange rate has moved to Rs 308 = $1 (the rupee price of a dollar has risen by 10%). Calculate the final amount in dollars and the return as a percentage, to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare this return with that from leaving the money in the USA.
parts.answer: The US deposit gives 4% ($1,040), which is higher.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how expectations of depreciation can affect financial flows and the exchange rate.
parts.answer: If investors expect the rupee to fall, the expected return on rupee assets falls below foreign returns, so they move money out; this increases the supply of rupees, causing the depreciation to happen (self-fulfilling).
parts.working: 1 lower expected return; 1 outflows; 1 currency falls.

practice.stem:
Invented data: a country's currency depreciated by 15 % at the start of Quarter 1. Its current account balance ($ billion) was:
Quarter 0: −2.0
Quarter 1: −2.6
Quarter 2: −2.9
Quarter 3: −2.1
Quarter 4: −1.2
Quarter 5: −0.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the quarter in which the current account deficit was largest, and calculate the improvement from that quarter to Quarter 5.
parts.answer: Quarter 2 (−$2.9 billion); improvement of $2.5 billion
parts.working: B1 Quarter 2. −0.4 − (−2.9) = $2.5 billion (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the J-curve effect to explain the pattern in the data.
parts.answer: In the short run demand for exports and imports is price inelastic, so the deficit widens; over time demand becomes more elastic and the Marshall–Lerner condition is met, so the balance improves.
parts.working: 1 mark: depreciation makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home. 1 mark: in the short run contracts and habits mean quantities change little (PEDs sum < 1), so import spending rises and the deficit worsens (Q1–Q2). 1 mark: over time buyers switch, PEDs rise and the sum exceeds 1. 1 mark: the deficit narrows (Q3–Q5), giving the J shape.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason, other than the depreciation, why the current account might have improved.
parts.answer: A recession in the country reducing import demand / rise in world prices of its exports / faster growth in trading partners.

practice.stem: Invented data. A country's nominal exchange rate index (foreign currency per unit of domestic currency, start of year = 100) falls to 95 during the year. Over the same year domestic prices rise by 12% and prices in its trading partners rise by 3%. Real exchange rate index = nominal index × (domestic price index ÷ foreign price index).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the real exchange rate index at the end of the year, to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the country's currency has depreciated or appreciated in real terms, and by what percentage.
parts.answer: Appreciated by about 3.3% in real terms
parts.working: 1 appreciation; 1 3.3%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the competitiveness of the country's exports has fallen even though its currency depreciated in nominal terms.
parts.answer: Domestic inflation (12%) was much higher than foreign inflation (3%), so the rise in domestic prices more than offset the 5% fall in the nominal exchange rate; export prices in foreign currency rose relative to foreign goods.
parts.working: 1 inflation differential; 1 offsets nominal depreciation; 1 relative prices of exports rise.

practice.stem:
Invented estimates for a country whose currency has depreciated by 15%:
Price elasticity of demand for exports: short run 0.4, long run 0.9
Price elasticity of demand for imports: short run 0.3, long run 0.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports in the short run and in the long run.
parts.answer: Short run 0.7; long run 1.5
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the Marshall–Lerner condition to explain the likely effect of the depreciation on the current account in the short run and the long run.
parts.answer: Short run: sum 0.7 < 1, so volumes respond too little to offset the lower foreign-currency price of exports and higher domestic price of imports; the deficit worsens. Long run: sum 1.5 > 1, so the current account improves (J-curve).
parts.working: 1 statement of condition; 1 short-run worsening; 1 long-run improvement; 1 link to J-curve/time lags.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether the depreciation is likely to reduce the country's current account deficit.
parts.answer: Likely in the long run on these estimates, but: rising import prices cause inflation that erodes competitiveness; exports may be limited by capacity; trading partners' incomes matter; elasticities are estimates. Judgement.
parts.working: Analysis up to 4; evaluation up to 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that a floating exchange rate will automatically correct a current account deficit.
parts.answer: In theory a deficit means more supply of the currency, so it depreciates, making exports cheaper and imports dearer until the deficit closes; but financial flows dominate currency markets, the Marshall–Lerner condition may fail in the short run, depreciation causes cost-push inflation, and structural causes of deficits remain. Judgement.
parts.working: Knowledge, understanding and analysis (up to 14): demand and supply of currency; mechanism of depreciation; Marshall–Lerner and J-curve; role of capital flows and interest rates; inflation effects. Evaluation (up to 6): time lags; size of capital flows; import dependence; elasticities; need for supply-side policies; reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a free trade area, a customs union and a common market.
parts.answer: Free trade area: no tariffs between members, each sets its own external tariffs. Customs union: free trade area plus a common external tariff. Common market: customs union plus free movement of labour and capital.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one problem that can arise in a free trade area that does not arise in a customs union.
parts.answer: Trade deflection: imports enter through the member with the lowest external tariff and are moved to other members; rules of origin are needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: trade deflection. 1 mark: rules of origin/border checks needed, adding cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two causes of globalisation in recent decades.
parts.answer: e.g. falling transport costs (containerisation); cheaper communication and the internet; reduction of trade barriers through trade agreements; growth of MNCs; liberalisation of capital flows.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for each of two developed causes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one cost of globalisation for low-skilled workers in high-income countries.
parts.answer: Production moves to low-wage countries or imports replace domestic output, so these workers face unemployment or lower wages.
parts.working: 1 cost; 1 explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two functions of the World Trade Organization (WTO).
parts.answer: Provides a forum for negotiating reductions in trade barriers; settles trade disputes between members; monitors trade policies and enforces agreed rules.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for each of two functions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the 'most favoured nation' principle.
parts.answer: A member must offer any trade concession (e.g. a lower tariff) it gives to one WTO member to all other WTO members, so it does not discriminate between them.
parts.working: 1 concession to one = to all; 1 non-discrimination.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three features of globalisation.
parts.answer: e.g. growth of world trade relative to output; increased flows of capital/FDI; growth of MNCs and global supply chains; migration; spread of technology and culture.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how lower transport and communication costs have encouraged global supply chains.
parts.answer: Firms can split production into stages and locate each where it is cheapest, then ship parts between countries cheaply and coordinate production instantly across borders.
parts.working: 1 cheaper movement of parts; 1 cheaper coordination; 1 location by comparative cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a feature of a customs union but not of a free trade area?
A removal of tariffs on trade between member countries
B a common external tariff on imports from non-members
C free movement of labour between member countries
D a single currency used by all members
parts.answer: B a common external tariff on imports from non-members
parts.working: Both arrangements remove internal tariffs (A), but only a customs union adds a common external tariff. Free movement of labour (C) is a feature of a common market; a single currency (D) of a monetary union.

practice.stem:
Invented data for a country ($ billion):
2015: exports 12, imports 18, GDP 40
2025: exports 15, imports 20, GDP 50

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the trade openness ratio ((exports + imports) as a percentage of GDP) for 2015 and 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A newspaper said the data show the country 'became less involved in globalisation'. Explain why this conclusion may be wrong.
parts.answer: Trade grew in absolute terms (from $30 billion to $35 billion); the ratio fell only because GDP grew faster; other aspects of globalisation (FDI, migration, technology, capital flows) are not shown.
parts.working: 1 mark: exports and imports both rose in value. 1 mark: the ratio fell because GDP rose by 25 % while trade rose by about 17 %. 1 mark: globalisation also includes FDI, capital and labour flows not in the data. 1 mark: real vs nominal values / exchange-rate changes may distort figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature is found in an economic union but NOT in a common market?
A free movement of labour and capital between members
B a common external tariff
C removal of tariffs on trade between members
D harmonisation of economic policies, such as a single currency or common fiscal rules
parts.answer: D harmonisation of economic policies, such as a single currency or common fiscal rules
parts.working: A common market already has free trade, a common external tariff and free movement of factors (A, B, C). An economic union adds harmonised economic policies.

practice.stem: Invented data. Country X can produce a good at $15 per unit. Country W can supply it at $10 and Country P at $12. Country X charges a 60% tariff on all imports.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price to consumers in Country X of imports from Country W and from Country P, and explain where Country X obtains the good.
parts.answer: W: $16; P: $19.20. Domestic producers at $15 are cheapest, so the good is produced at home.
parts.working: 1 $16; 1 $19.20; 1 domestic production at $15.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Country X forms a free trade area with Country P but keeps the tariff on Country W. State where Country X now obtains the good and whether this is trade creation or trade diversion.
parts.answer: From Country P at $12; trade creation (a higher-cost domestic source is replaced by a lower-cost imported source).
parts.working: 1 Country P; 1 trade creation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the saving in resource cost per unit compared with domestic production, and the extra cost per unit compared with the world's lowest-cost producer.
parts.answer: Saving $3 per unit; still $2 per unit more than Country W

practice.stem:
Invented data for a country before and after joining a regional trading bloc:
Before: total exports $50 billion, of which $9 billion to bloc members
Five years after: total exports $60 billion, of which $20.4 billion to bloc members

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the share of the country's exports going to the bloc in each year, and the percentage change in exports to the rest of the world.
parts.answer: 18% and 34%; exports to the rest of the world fell by 3.4% (from $41 billion to $39.6 billion)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the data might show trade creation and trade diversion.
parts.answer: Exports to the bloc more than doubled, which may be trade creation if partners replaced high-cost domestic production with these exports; but exports to the rest of the world fell slightly, which may be trade diversion if partners switched away from cheaper non-member suppliers.
parts.working: 1 + 1 trade creation; 1 + 1 trade diversion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one other reason why exports to the bloc might have grown.
parts.answer: e.g. faster income growth in partner countries / exchange rate changes / new transport links.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how globalisation can spread new technology to developing countries.
parts.answer: Through FDI by MNCs bringing new machines and methods; through imports of capital goods; through supply-chain links where foreign buyers set standards; through migration and returning workers; through licensing.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for each of two developed channels.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether this means that incomes in developing countries will catch up with those in high-income countries.
parts.answer: Technology transfer can raise productivity and support convergence (as in parts of East Asia); but it requires absorptive capacity (education, infrastructure, institutions), and MNCs may keep high-value activities at home. Judgement.
parts.working: Up to 2 analysis; up to 2 evaluation.

practice.stem: Country A imports a good. It can buy the good from Country B at $10 per unit or from Country C at $8 per unit. Before joining a customs union, Country A charges a 50 % tariff on imports from all countries. Country A then forms a customs union with Country B, keeping a 50 % common external tariff on goods from Country C (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain from which country Country A imports the good before and after joining the customs union.
parts.answer: Before: from Country C ($8 + $4 tariff = $12, cheaper than B at $10 + $5 = $15). After: from Country B ($10, no tariff, cheaper than C at $12).
parts.working: 1 mark each, with prices shown.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether this is trade creation or trade diversion, and calculate the extra resource cost per unit to the world of buying from the new supplier.
parts.answer: Trade diversion; extra resource cost $2 per unit
parts.working: B1 trade diversion: imports switch from a more efficient non-member to a less efficient member. M1 cost per unit B $10 − C $8; A1 $2 per unit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why consumers in Country A may still gain even though the government of Country A loses.
parts.answer: Consumers pay $10 instead of $12, but the government loses the $4 per unit tariff revenue it used to collect.
parts.working: 1 mark consumers' price falls by $2. 1 mark government loses tariff revenue of $4 per unit, which is greater than consumers' gain per unit on existing imports.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that globalisation has reduced inequality between countries.
parts.answer: Globalisation has helped many emerging economies converge, but some low-income and commodity-dependent countries have fallen further behind; effects vary.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): features of globalisation – trade liberalisation, FDI and MNCs, capital flows, migration, technology transfer, global supply chains. Arguments for reduced inequality between countries – rapid growth in China, India, Vietnam and others through export-led manufacturing; technology and capital flows to lower-income countries; comparative advantage; remittances. Arguments against – benefits concentrated in countries with infrastructure, skills and stable institutions; least developed countries remain dependent on primary exports with volatile prices and declining terms of trade; capital flight and financial crises; brain drain; MNC profits repatriated; protection by high-income countries in agriculture. Distinguish inequality between countries vs within countries. Evaluation (up to 6): weighted judgement, e.g. average gap between countries has narrowed, largely because of a few large Asian economies, while some countries have been left behind; depends on policy and institutions.

practice.stem: Invented data. Country Y imports 1 million units a year of a good from the world's lowest-cost supplier at $20 per unit, plus a 25% tariff. It joins a customs union with Country Z, which can supply the good at $23 per unit with no tariff. The common external tariff keeps the world supplier's price above $23.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the consumer price before and after joining, and the tariff revenue the government loses.
parts.answer: $25 → $23; tariff revenue lost $5 million
parts.working: M1 20 × 1.25 = 25. A1 revenue 5 × 1 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gain in consumer surplus, given that imports rise from 1.0 million to 1.2 million units.
parts.answer: $2.2 million
parts.working: M1 2 × 1.0 million + ½ × 2 × 0.2 million. A1 2.2 million.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net welfare effect on Country Y, assuming it has no domestic producers.
parts.answer: A net loss of $2.8 million

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why joining the customs union reduced Country Y's welfare in this case.
parts.answer: Imports switch from the lowest-cost world supplier ($20) to a higher-cost partner ($23): trade diversion costs $3 per unit on 1 million units, which outweighs the small gain from extra consumption (trade creation of $0.2 million).
parts.working: 1 trade diversion; 1 resource cost of $3 per unit; 1 outweighs trade creation gain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether joining a regional trading bloc is better for a developing economy than reducing its trade barriers with all countries.
parts.answer: Regional blocs give secure market access, economies of scale and political cooperation, and are easier to negotiate; but they risk trade diversion, rules-of-origin costs and dependence on partners. Unilateral/multilateral liberalisation avoids diversion and gives access to the cheapest suppliers but exposes infant industries and gives no reciprocal access. Judgement.
parts.working: Knowledge, understanding and analysis (up to 14): types of trading blocs; trade creation and diversion; comparative advantage and gains from free trade; economies of scale; WTO and multilateral liberalisation. Evaluation (up to 6): size and nature of partners; whether partners are low-cost producers; external tariff level; stage of development; reasoned conclusion.

practice.stem: Invented data. A UK insurance company plans to move 400 customer-service jobs to Lahore. Average monthly wage cost per worker: UK £2,200; Pakistan £350. Extra costs of managing the overseas centre are £2 million a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Pakistani wage as a percentage of the UK wage, to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the annual saving in wage costs from moving 400 jobs, and the net annual saving after the extra costs.
parts.answer: £8.88 million; £6.88 million

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two benefits to Pakistan of attracting such outsourced service work.
parts.answer: Jobs for educated young people; foreign exchange earnings (service exports); skills and training; multiplier effects on local spending.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for each of two developed benefits.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate whether outsourcing of services is likely to benefit both the UK and Pakistan.
parts.answer: UK: lower costs, cheaper services, resources freed for higher-value work, but job losses and regional unemployment. Pakistan: jobs and exports, but low-value work, vulnerability to automation/AI and reversal, wage pressure. Mutual gains like comparative advantage, distribution matters. Judgement.
parts.working: Analysis up to 4 (both countries); evaluation up to 3.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which policy is an expenditure-reducing policy for correcting a current account deficit?
A a devaluation of the currency
B a tariff on imported cars
C an increase in income tax rates
D a subsidy to exporters
parts.answer: C an increase in income tax rates
parts.working: Higher income tax reduces disposable income and total spending, including spending on imports. A, B and D are expenditure-switching policies, because they change relative prices to move spending from imports to domestic goods.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a tariff on imported goods could reduce a current account deficit.
parts.answer: The tariff raises the domestic price of imports, so consumers switch to domestic substitutes (expenditure switching); import spending falls, reducing the deficit.
parts.working: 1 higher import price; 1 switch to domestic goods; 1 lower import spending.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the tariff might fail to reduce the deficit.
parts.answer: Trading partners may retaliate with their own tariffs, reducing exports; or imported inputs become dearer, raising export costs; or demand for imports is price inelastic.
parts.working: 1 reason; 2 explanation.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments
practice.stem: Invented current account data for a country in one year ($ billion): trade in goods −24; trade in services −3; primary income −6; secondary income +28. GDP is $350 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current account balance in $ billion and as a percentage of GDP, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: −$5 billion; −1.43% of GDP

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government aims to reduce the deficit to 1% of GDP. Calculate the reduction needed, assuming GDP is unchanged.
parts.answer: $1.5 billion

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the component that most offsets the trade deficit, and explain one risk of relying on it.
parts.answer: Secondary income (+$28 billion, mainly remittances); it can fall if conditions in the countries where migrants work worsen.
parts.working: 1 secondary income; 1 risk.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a rise in interest rates can reduce a current account deficit by reducing expenditure.
parts.answer: Higher interest rates raise borrowing costs and encourage saving, so consumption and investment fall; aggregate demand and national income fall; with a marginal propensity to import, spending on imports falls.
parts.working: 1 borrowing/saving effect; 1 lower C and I; 1 lower income; 1 lower imports.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the same rise in interest rates might make the current account worse.
parts.answer: Financial inflows raise demand for the currency, causing appreciation; exports become dearer abroad and imports cheaper (expenditure switching in the wrong direction).
parts.working: 1 appreciation; 1 effect on export/import prices.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a cyclical and a structural current account deficit.
parts.answer: Cyclical: caused by a temporary boom raising imports, disappears when the economy slows. Structural: caused by long-term weakness, e.g. lack of competitiveness or a narrow export base, which persists over the cycle.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a suitable type of policy for each type of deficit.
parts.answer: Cyclical: expenditure-reducing (or no action). Structural: supply-side policies (or expenditure-switching).
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why using the wrong type of policy can be costly.
parts.answer: e.g. cutting demand to fix a structural deficit causes a long recession without removing the cause; supply-side policies for a cyclical deficit take too long.
parts.working: 1 mismatch; 1 cost.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between expenditure-switching and expenditure-reducing policies for correcting a current account deficit, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: Switching policies change relative prices so that spending moves from imports to domestic output (e.g. devaluation, tariffs); reducing policies lower total demand so that imports fall (e.g. higher interest rates, tax rises, spending cuts).
parts.working: 1 mark each definition, 1 mark each example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether expenditure-reducing policies are a suitable way to correct a current account deficit in a country with high unemployment.
parts.answer: They reduce imports but at the cost of lower output and higher unemployment; supply-side or switching policies may be more appropriate.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): lower AD reduces imports according to the marginal propensity to import; may also lower inflation and improve competitiveness; but output and employment fall further, with multiplier effects; conflict between external balance and full employment; if the MPM is small, a large fall in income is needed for a small improvement. Evaluation (up to 2): judgement – unsuitable as the main policy in a recession; better to use expenditure-switching or supply-side policies, unless the deficit is caused by excess demand.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which policy is most likely to reduce a current account deficit in the long run without reducing real national income?
A supply-side policies that raise productivity in export industries
B a rise in income tax rates
C a rise in interest rates
D a cut in government spending
parts.answer: A supply-side policies that raise productivity in export industries
parts.working: Supply-side policies raise competitiveness and productive capacity, improving the current account while raising output. B, C and D are expenditure-reducing policies that work by lowering income.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments
practice.stem: Invented data. A country's marginal propensity to import is 0.25 and the multiplier is 2. The government wants to cut imports by $3 billion by reducing its own spending.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fall in national income needed to reduce imports by $3 billion.
parts.answer: $12 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cut in government spending needed to bring about this fall in national income.
parts.answer: $6 billion
parts.working: M1 12 ÷ 2. A1 $6 billion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why using this policy to correct the deficit has a high cost.
parts.answer: To save $3 billion of imports, national income must fall by $12 billion: output falls by four times the improvement, raising unemployment and reducing living standards.
parts.working: 1 large output loss relative to the gain; 1 unemployment; 1 other cost (lower tax revenue, lower investment).

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a government might want to reduce a large and persistent current account surplus.
parts.answer: A surplus means domestic consumption is lower than possible; it adds to inflationary pressure and upward pressure on the currency; it may provoke retaliation from trading partners; it may reflect weak domestic demand.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for each of two developed reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider which policies a country could use to reduce its surplus.
parts.answer: Expansionary fiscal policy to raise domestic demand and imports; allowing the currency to appreciate; lowering import barriers; but these may cause inflation or harm export industries. Judgement.
parts.working: Up to 2 policies explained; up to 2 evaluation.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how supply-side policies could reduce a current account deficit.
parts.answer: Education/training and infrastructure raise productivity and lower unit costs; firms become more competitive in export markets and against imports; export capacity grows; quality improves.
parts.working: 1 policy; 1 productivity/cost; 1 competitiveness; 1 effect on exports/imports.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider why supply-side policies may not be enough to deal with a current account crisis.
parts.answer: They take years to work, while a crisis needs action within months; costs require government spending that may worsen the deficit; results are uncertain; demand-side measures may be needed in the short run.
parts.working: Up to 2 analysis; up to 2 evaluation.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how import quotas and exchange controls can be used to reduce a current account deficit.
parts.answer: Quota: a limit on the quantity of a good imported, directly cutting import volumes. Exchange controls: limits on access to foreign currency, so importers cannot pay for as many imports and capital outflows are restricted.
parts.working: 2 for quotas; 2 for exchange controls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why many countries avoid these policies.
parts.answer: They break trade agreements/WTO rules and may provoke retaliation; they create black markets and inefficiency; they deter foreign investment.
parts.working: 1 reason; 1 explanation.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments
practice.stem: Invented data. A country with a fixed exchange rate devalues its currency by 10%. Before devaluation exports are $40 billion and imports $55 billion. The price elasticity of demand for its exports is 1.2 and for its imports 0.5. Assume export prices in domestic currency and import prices in dollars are unchanged, so that export prices in dollars fall by 10% and import prices in domestic currency rise by 10%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dollar value of exports and of imports after the devaluation.
parts.answer: Exports $40.32 billion; imports $52.25 billion
parts.working: M1 export dollar price −10%, volume +12%; A1 40 × 0.9 × 1.12 = 40.32; M1 import volume −5%; A1 55 × 0.95 = 52.25.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in the current account deficit.
parts.answer: Falls from $15 billion to $11.93 billion, an improvement of $3.07 billion

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why these results are consistent with the Marshall–Lerner condition.
parts.answer: The sum of the elasticities (1.2 + 0.5 = 1.7) is greater than 1, so a devaluation improves the trade balance.
parts.working: 1 sum; 1 > 1 → improvement.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a devaluation is more effective than import controls in reducing a persistent current account deficit.
parts.answer: Devaluation switches expenditure on both exports and imports, follows WTO rules, but needs Marshall–Lerner, causes inflation and J-curve delays. Import controls (tariffs, quotas) act quickly on specific goods but invite retaliation, protect inefficiency, breach trade agreements and raise costs. Judgement depends on the cause of the deficit and elasticities.
parts.working: Knowledge, understanding and analysis (up to 14): expenditure-switching; Marshall–Lerner and J-curve; tariffs and quotas with effects on prices and quantities; inflation and competitiveness. Evaluation (up to 6): elasticities; import dependence; retaliation; time scale; structural v cyclical causes; reasoned conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that a current account deficit should be corrected using supply-side policies rather than demand-side policies.
parts.answer: Supply-side policies address the root causes (low productivity, narrow export base) and avoid lost output, but take time and may cost money; expenditure-reducing policies work faster but reduce growth and raise unemployment; expenditure-switching may be needed in a crisis. Judgement: depends on urgency, cause and financing.
parts.working: Knowledge, understanding and analysis (up to 14): causes of deficits; expenditure-reducing (fiscal, monetary) and expenditure-switching policies; supply-side policies and competitiveness; AD/AS analysis. Evaluation (up to 6): time lags; size of the deficit and how it is financed; conflicts with other objectives; combination of policies; reasoned conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments
practice.stem:
Invented data for a country with a balance of payments crisis. Measures: central bank policy rate raised from 15% to 22%; currency devalued by 18%; higher import duties on cars and phones.
One year later: current account deficit fell from 4.7% to 0.9% of GDP; real GDP growth fell from 6.0% to −0.5%; inflation rose from 9% to 29%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in the current account balance and in real GDP growth, in percentage points.
parts.answer: Current account improved by 3.8 points; growth fell by 6.5 points

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify which of the measures are expenditure-switching and which are expenditure-reducing.
parts.answer: Switching: devaluation, higher import duties. Reducing: higher interest rate.
parts.working: 1 each group.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why inflation rose sharply after the measures were introduced.
parts.answer: The devaluation and import duties raised the domestic prices of imported fuel, food and inputs (cost-push); this fed into wages and expectations.
parts.working: 1 import prices; 1 cost-push; 1 second-round effects.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate whether the policies were successful.
parts.answer: The deficit was largely closed (target met), restoring confidence; but at a cost of recession and 29% inflation, which hurt the poor; part of the improvement may be from lower income (temporary) rather than competitiveness. Judgement depends on the alternative (a default) and longer-term outcomes.
parts.working: Analysis up to 5 using the data; evaluation up to 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm sells its product in a perfectly competitive market at $5 per unit and hires labour in a perfectly competitive labour market at a wage of $70 per day. Daily output for 1 to 5 workers is 20, 38, 54, 66 and 74 units. How many workers will a profit-maximising firm employ?
A 2
B 3
C 4
D 5
parts.answer: B 3
parts.working: Marginal products are 20, 18, 16, 12, 8, so MRP = 100, 90, 80, 60, 40. The firm hires while MRP ≥ wage: the 3rd worker adds $80 > $70, the 4th adds only $60 < $70. C assumes hiring continues until total output is high rather than comparing MRP with the wage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define marginal revenue product of labour.
parts.answer: The extra revenue a firm earns from employing one more worker: marginal physical product × marginal revenue (or price in perfect competition).
parts.working: 1 change in total revenue from one more worker; 1 MPP × MR.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a firm's demand curve for labour slopes downwards.
parts.answer: Diminishing marginal returns: as more workers are added to fixed capital, MPP and therefore MRP fall; the firm hires up to where MRP = wage, so at a lower wage it hires more workers; the MRP curve is the demand curve.
parts.working: 1 diminishing marginal returns/falling MPP in short run; 1 MRP falls as employment rises; 1 profit-maximising firm employs where wage = MRP, so a lower wage → more workers (MRP curve = demand curve).

practice.stem: A leading Pakistani cricketer earns Rs 80 million a year from playing and sponsorship. The best alternative job open to him is coaching, which would pay Rs 6 million a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cricketer's economic rent.
parts.answer: Rs 74 million a year
parts.working: 1 80 − 6 = Rs 74 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why economic rent forms a large part of the earnings of top sports players.
parts.answer: Their supply is highly inelastic because talent is rare and cannot be quickly trained; demand (from leagues, sponsors, broadcasters) is high, so the wage is far above transfer earnings.
parts.working: 1 rare natural talent → very inelastic supply; 1 high demand/MRP (TV and sponsorship revenue); 1 so earnings well above transfer earnings, most is economic rent.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two factors that affect the elasticity of supply of labour to an occupation.
parts.answer: Any two: length of training/qualifications required; skills needed; geographical and occupational mobility; time period; availability of workers in other occupations; non-monetary benefits.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the demand for labour is a derived demand.
parts.answer: Labour is demanded not for itself but for the goods and services it helps to produce; demand for workers depends on demand for the product.
parts.working: 1 demanded for what it produces; 1 changes in product demand change labour demand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two factors that affect the wage elasticity of demand for labour.
parts.answer: Any two: ease of substituting capital for labour; price elasticity of demand for the product; proportion of labour costs in total costs; time period.
parts.working: Up to 2 each: factor identified + direction explained (e.g. easy to replace workers with machines → elastic).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change is most likely to make the supply of labour to nursing more elastic with respect to the wage?
A a reduction in the length of training needed to qualify as a nurse
B a rise in the wage paid to nurses
C the introduction of a stricter licensing examination for nurses
D a fall in the demand for health care
parts.answer: A a reduction in the length of training needed to qualify as a nurse
parts.working: Elasticity of labour supply depends on how quickly people can enter the occupation; shorter training lets supply respond more to a wage rise. B causes a movement along the supply curve, not a change in its elasticity; C makes entry harder, so supply becomes less elastic.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The supply of labour to an occupation is L = 20W − 200, where W is the hourly wage in $ and L the number of workers. The market wage is $30 per hour. What is the total economic rent earned by the workers per hour?
A $4,000
B $6,000
C $8,000
D $12,000
parts.working: L = 400 at W = 30; supply starts at W = 10 when L = 0. Total earnings = 30 × 400 = $12,000. Transfer earnings = area under the supply curve = ½ × 400 × (10 + 30) = $8,000. Economic rent = area above supply, below the wage = ½ × 400 × 20 = $4,000. C is transfer earnings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why software engineers in Lahore usually earn more than food delivery riders.
