parts.answer: Higher MRP: engineers' productivity and the value of software output is high, so demand for them is high; supply is limited by long training and scarce skills (inelastic), whereas riders need few skills, so supply is large and elastic.
parts.working: Up to 2 for demand/MRP reason; up to 2 for supply reason (training, skills, barriers to entry); or other valid reasons such as international demand for engineers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a higher national minimum wage would reduce the wage differential between the two groups.
parts.answer: It would raise riders' pay (if the minimum is above their market wage and enforced) so the gap narrows, but riders may lose jobs or hours, many are self-employed gig workers outside the law, and engineers' pay is unaffected or rises further.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): minimum wage above equilibrium raises pay of low-paid; engineers paid well above minimum so differential falls; possible excess supply/unemployment among riders. Consideration (1+): enforcement in informal/gig work, platform responses, differentials may re-emerge; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, with the help of a diagram, how a trade union may raise the wage in a competitive labour market, and the effect on employment.
parts.answer: By collective bargaining the union sets a wage above equilibrium; the supply curve becomes horizontal at the union wage up to the original supply; firms move up the demand (MRP) curve so employment falls.
parts.working: 1 collective bargaining/threat of strike sets wage above equilibrium; 1 diagram: labour market with W and L axes, wage floor; 1 employment falls along MRP/demand curve; 1 excess supply of labour (or effect smaller if demand is wage inelastic / productivity agreements shift MRP).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether the effect of a trade union on employment would be different if the employer were a monopsonist.
parts.answer: Yes: a union facing a monopsonist acts as bilateral monopoly; a negotiated wage between the monopsony wage and the competitive level can raise both wage and employment. The outcome depends on bargaining strength and where the wage is set; above the competitive level employment falls.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): monopsony pays below MRP; union wage makes MCL flat; employment can rise. Consideration (1+): if wage set too high employment falls; firms may substitute capital; depends on relative bargaining power; judgement.

practice.stem: Invented article. A food delivery platform in Karachi used 15,000 riders. It cut the payment per delivery from Rs 120 to Rs 100. Three months later 14,100 riders were still working for it. Two smaller platforms also operate in the city.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wage elasticity of supply of riders. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the supply of riders might be wage inelastic.
parts.answer: Few alternative jobs for low-skilled workers in the city; riders have already bought motorcycles; many need income urgently and cannot afford to be unemployed; low occupational mobility.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for two reasons; 1 for development linking to small change in labour supplied.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the data suggest that the platform company has monopsony power.
parts.answer: Possibly: it could cut pay by 17% and still keep 94% of riders, suggesting few alternative employers; but riders may work for several platforms, the data cover a short period and other factors (unemployment rising) may explain it.
parts.working: 1 monopsony = dominant buyer of labour able to set wage; 1 evidence: large pay cut, small fall in riders; 1 consideration of other explanations/limitations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an individual's supply curve of labour may bend backwards at high wage rates.
parts.answer: A higher wage has a substitution effect (leisure becomes more expensive → work more) and an income effect (higher income → want more leisure, a normal good → work less). At high wages the income effect can outweigh the substitution effect, so hours offered fall.
parts.working: 1 substitution effect explained; 1 income effect explained; 1 at low wages substitution dominates (upward slope); 1 at high wages income effect dominates (backward bend).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider the implications of a backward-bending supply curve for a government that cuts income tax rates to increase hours worked.
parts.answer: A tax cut raises the net wage; for workers on the upward part hours rise, but for high earners on the backward-bending part hours may fall, so the policy may not raise labour supply; effect varies between groups and contracts often fix hours.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): tax cut = higher net wage; outcome depends on which effect dominates for each group; may reduce hours of high earners. Consideration (1+): many workers cannot choose hours; participation decisions (second earners) may respond more; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a competitive labour market, the demand for labour is L = 900 − 30W, where L is the number of workers and W is the hourly wage in dollars. The equilibrium wage is $15. A minimum wage of $20 per hour is introduced. What happens to employment and to the total hourly wage bill?
A Employment falls by 150 and the total wage bill falls by $750 per hour.
B Employment falls by 150 and the total wage bill rises by $750 per hour.
C Employment falls by 50 and the total wage bill rises by $1 250 per hour.
D Employment is unchanged and the total wage bill rises by $2 250 per hour.
parts.answer: A Employment falls by 150 and the total wage bill falls by $750 per hour.
parts.working: At $15: L = 900 − 450 = 450, wage bill = $6 750. At $20: L = 900 − 600 = 300 (employment is set by demand), wage bill = $6 000. So employment falls by 150 and the wage bill falls by $750: demand for labour is wage elastic over this range. B ignores that the fall in employment outweighs the higher wage; D assumes no fall in employment.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A monopsony employer faces the labour supply curve W = 4 + 0.5L, so its marginal cost of labour is MCL = 4 + L. The marginal revenue product of labour is MRP = 40 − 0.5L. (W in $ per hour, L in workers.) What wage will the monopsonist pay?
A $16
B $22
C $28
D $40
parts.working: The monopsonist hires where MCL = MRP: 4 + L = 40 − 0.5L → L = 24, then pays the wage on the supply curve: W = 4 + 0.5 × 24 = $16. B ($22) is the competitive outcome where supply = MRP; C ($28) is the MRP at 24 workers, the gap being the monopsony exploitation.

practice.stem: In the market for unskilled factory labour in an invented country, labour demand is Ld = 1000 − 20W and labour supply is Ls = −200 + 40W, where W is the daily wage in $ and L is in thousand workers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium wage and level of employment.
parts.answer: W = $20 per day; L = 600 thousand

parts.label: b
parts.text: A minimum wage of $24 per day is introduced. Calculate the change in employment and the excess supply of labour.
parts.answer: Employment falls by 80 thousand (to 520 thousand); excess supply = 240 thousand
parts.working: M1 Ld = 1000 − 480 = 520; M1 Ls = −200 + 960 = 760. A1 employment −80 thousand and excess supply 240 thousand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a minimum wage could raise both the wage and employment if the labour market were a monopsony.
parts.answer: A monopsonist restricts hiring to pay a low wage (MCL above supply). A minimum wage between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage makes MCL horizontal at the minimum wage up to the supply curve, so the firm hires more workers at a higher wage.
parts.working: 1 monopsonist hires where MCL = MRP and pays below MRP; 1 minimum wage removes the need to raise the wage for all workers when hiring one more, so MCL = minimum wage; 1 employment rises towards the competitive level if the minimum is set below the competitive wage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a national minimum wage is the best way to reduce poverty among low-paid workers.
parts.answer: A minimum wage raises pay for those who keep their jobs and can raise employment under monopsony, but it may cause unemployment in competitive markets, does not reach informal workers or the unemployed, and poverty depends on household circumstances. Alternatives (in-work benefits, negative income tax, training, progressive taxes) may target poverty better; a combination is usually best.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: competitive labour market diagram with minimum wage above equilibrium → higher wage, lower employment, excess supply; monopsony diagram → higher wage and employment; higher spending of low-paid workers; incentive to work. Evaluation: size of minimum relative to median wage; elasticity of demand for labour; informal sector and enforcement (large in low-income countries); poverty is household-based (number of earners, dependants); alternatives: transfer payments, tax credits, universal basic income, education/training to raise MRP, each with costs (funding, disincentives, time lags). Conclusion: 'best' must be judged against alternatives and context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether differences in labour productivity are the main reason why average wages in the information technology sector are much higher than average wages in agriculture.
parts.answer: Productivity (MRP) is a major reason, but supply-side factors (skills, training, barriers, mobility), product demand and prices, market power (unions, monopsony), discrimination, informal employment and government policy also matter.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: marginal productivity theory — wage = MRP in competitive markets; MRP = MPP × MR so both productivity and the value of output matter; diagram comparing two labour markets with different demand (MRP) and supply elasticities; supply of IT workers restricted by education and training; large, mobile supply of unskilled farm labour. Evaluation: MRP is hard to measure in services; product prices matter (agricultural prices low and volatile); monopsony landowners or agro-processors; seasonal and informal work; global demand for IT services; discrimination; government minimum support prices. Judgement on 'main reason'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A chemical factory's marginal private cost is MPC = 20 + 2Q and the marginal external cost of its pollution is a constant $10 per unit. Marginal social benefit equals marginal private benefit: MSB = 110 − 2Q. Which specific tax per unit would achieve the socially optimal output, and what is that output?
A $10 per unit; output 20 units
B $10 per unit; output 22.5 units
C $5 per unit; output 20 units
D $20 per unit; output 20 units
parts.answer: A $10 per unit; output 20 units
parts.working: Market output: 20 + 2Q = 110 − 2Q → Q = 22.5. MSC = 30 + 2Q; optimum 30 + 2Q = 110 − 2Q → Q = 20. A tax equal to the marginal external cost ($10) makes MPC + tax = MSC, so output falls to 20. B gives the output before the tax.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'nudge' in government policy.
parts.answer: A change to the way choices are presented that steers people towards a better decision without banning options or changing financial incentives much.
parts.working: 1 influences behaviour through choice architecture/framing; 1 freedom of choice kept (no ban, no large tax).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how automatic enrolment of employees into a workplace pension scheme is an example of a nudge.
parts.answer: Workers are placed in the scheme by default and must actively opt out; because of inertia and present bias most stay in, so saving rises while choice is preserved.
parts.working: 1 default option/opt-out; 1 uses inertia or present bias to raise saving.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one limitation of using nudges to correct market failure.
parts.answer: e.g. effects can be small or fade over time; people may still opt out; they do not raise revenue; seen as manipulative; hard to design for different groups.
parts.working: 1 limitation; 1 explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how extending property rights could reduce overfishing in a coastal fishery.
parts.answer: Open-access fish stocks are a common resource, so each boat overfishes. Giving communities or firms ownership/quotas of the stock makes them bear the cost of depletion, so they limit catches to protect future income.
parts.working: 1 overfishing arises because no one owns the stock (common resource/tragedy of the commons); 1 property rights/individual transferable quotas assign ownership; 1 owners internalise the cost and conserve stocks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two problems with using property rights to solve this problem.
parts.answer: Any two: hard to define and enforce rights at sea; monitoring costs; fish move across boundaries; poor fishers may lose access (equity); transaction costs of bargaining.
parts.working: 1 each.

practice.stem: The weekly market for plastic shopping bags in a city has demand Qd = 900 − 100P and supply Qs = −100 + 100P, where P is the price in Rs per bag and Q is in thousand bags. To reduce litter, the government puts a specific tax of Rs 2 per bag on sellers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the new price paid by consumers and the new quantity.
parts.answer: Rs 6; 300 thousand bags

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the government's weekly tax revenue.
parts.answer: Rs 600 thousand
parts.working: 1 2 × 300 thousand = Rs 600 thousand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how much of the tax per bag is paid by consumers and how much by producers.
parts.answer: Consumers Rs 1 per bag; producers Rs 1 per bag
parts.working: 1 original equilibrium P = Rs 5 (900 − 100P = −100 + 100P), so consumers pay 6 − 5 = Rs 1; 1 producers receive 6 − 2 = Rs 4, so they bear 5 − 4 = Rs 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two firms are in a tradable pollution permit scheme. Firm X can cut a tonne of emissions at a cost of $30 and Firm Y at a cost of $70. The permit price is $50 per tonne. What is likely to happen?
A X buys permits from Y and pollutes more.
B Y cuts its emissions and sells permits to X.
C X cuts its emissions and sells permits to Y.
D Neither firm trades because both costs differ from the permit price.
parts.answer: C X cuts its emissions and sells permits to Y.
parts.working: X can cut emissions for less than the permit price, so it abates and sells spare permits at $50; Y finds buying a permit at $50 cheaper than abating at $70. Emissions are cut where it is cheapest. A reverses the roles.

practice.stem: In the market for household solar water heaters in an invented country, MPB = 80 − Q, MSB = 100 − Q and MPC = MSC = 20 + Q, where prices are in $ and Q is in thousand heaters per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the free-market output and the socially optimal output.
parts.answer: Free market: 30 thousand; social optimum: 40 thousand

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government pays a subsidy of $20 per unit to producers. Calculate the total cost of the subsidy.
parts.answer: $800 thousand ($0.8 million)
parts.working: M1 with subsidy MPC falls to Q; 80 − Q = Q → Q = 40 thousand. A1 20 × 40 thousand = $800 thousand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the government may set the subsidy at the wrong level.
parts.answer: The external benefit is hard to measure in money (information failure), so the subsidy may be too high or too low; lobbying may also distort it.
parts.working: 1 difficulty valuing external benefits/imperfect information; 1 consequence: over- or under-provision.

practice.stem: Invented data. To reduce winter smog and congestion, a city government introduces a daily charge of Rs 500 for cars entering the central business area of Lahore. Car trips into the area fall from 400,000 to 340,000 a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in car trips and the daily revenue from the charge.
parts.answer: 15% fall; Rs 170 million a day

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a road-user charge can correct the negative externalities of car use.
parts.answer: Drivers ignore the costs they impose on others (congestion, smog). The charge raises the private cost of driving towards the social cost, so drivers with low benefit switch mode or time, reducing trips towards the social optimum.
parts.working: 1 external costs of congestion and pollution; 1 charge internalises the externality (MPC + charge ≈ MSC); 1 trips fall towards where MSC = MSB.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider one reason why the charge may not achieve the socially optimal number of trips.
parts.answer: The external cost is hard to measure, so the charge may be set too low or high; demand for car trips may be inelastic with poor public transport; traffic may divert to roads outside the zone.
parts.working: 1 reason; 1 explanation; 1 judgement/consideration (e.g. effect depends on using revenue to improve buses).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a large tax on cigarettes may not reduce smoking by very much.
parts.answer: Cigarettes are addictive with few substitutes, so demand is price inelastic: the tax raises price but quantity falls only slightly; smokers may also switch to cheaper illegal or untaxed products.
parts.working: 1 addictive/habit-forming, few substitutes; 1 price inelastic demand → small fall in quantity; 1 smuggling/illegal market or cheaper brands.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether such a tax is still worthwhile for the government.
parts.answer: Yes in some ways: it raises large revenue (inelastic demand) that can fund healthcare and anti-smoking campaigns, and may deter young people whose demand is more elastic; but it is regressive, may encourage smuggling, and does little to cut external costs if consumption barely falls.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): revenue, long-run elasticity higher, effect on new smokers, internalising external costs. Consideration (1+): regressive, illegal markets, enforcement; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a market with a positive consumption externality, MPB = 50 − Q, the marginal external benefit is a constant $10 per unit, and MPC = MSC = 10 + Q (P in $, Q in thousand units). The government pays a per-unit subsidy equal to the marginal external benefit. What is the total cost of the subsidy to the government?
A $250 000
B $200 000
C $300 000
D $125 000
parts.working: Free market: 50 − Q = 10 + Q → Q = 20. With a $10 subsidy, effective demand becomes MSB = 60 − Q, so 60 − Q = 10 + Q → Q = 25 thousand units. Cost = $10 × 25 000 = $250 000. B uses the free-market output (20 000) instead of the new output; C wrongly treats MSC as constant (output 30 000); D halves the cost as if it were a welfare triangle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether subsidies are the most effective way for a government to increase the use of public transport in large cities.
parts.answer: Subsidies lower fares and correct the under-consumption caused by positive externalities (less congestion and pollution), but demand for public transport may be price inelastic and depend more on speed, reliability, safety and coverage; road pricing, investment in new routes, regulation of private cars and information may be more effective, often in combination.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: positive externality diagram (MSB > MPB) and subsidy shifting supply/raising effective demand to the social optimum; lower fares → substitution away from cars; complementary effect on congestion (negative externality of car use). Evaluation: price elasticity of demand for bus/metro travel; quality (frequency, safety for women, last-mile links) matters; opportunity cost of subsidy and risk of X-inefficiency in subsidised operators; information problems in setting the right rate; congestion charges or fuel taxes raise the cost of the alternative and raise revenue; direct provision of new metro or bus lines; conclusion: subsidies help but are rarely enough on their own.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm producing fertiliser has marginal private cost MPC = 10 + Q. Its production causes a constant marginal external cost of $12 per unit. Marginal social benefit equals marginal private benefit: MSB = 100 − 2Q (P in $, Q in units). What is the deadweight welfare loss if output is left to the free market?
A $12
B $24
C $48
D $360
parts.working: Free market: 10 + Q = 100 − 2Q → Q = 30. MSC = 22 + Q; optimum: 22 + Q = 100 − 2Q → Q = 26. Welfare loss triangle between MSC and MSB from Q = 26 to 30, with height 12 at Q = 30: ½ × (30 − 26) × 12 = $24. C forgets the ½ (it is a triangle, not a rectangle); D is the total external cost of all 30 units, not the welfare loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether tradable pollution permits are more effective than direct regulation in reducing carbon emissions from power stations.
parts.answer: Permits fix the total quantity of emissions and let firms that can cut cheaply do so, so the target is reached at least cost and firms have an incentive to innovate; regulation is simpler, more certain for each plant and easier to enforce in some countries. Effectiveness depends on the cap, monitoring, permit allocation and market conditions.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: negative externality diagram (MSC > MPC); how a cap-and-trade scheme works and why it achieves the cut at lowest total abatement cost; permit price as incentive; regulation (emission limits, technology standards, bans) — certain outcome per plant, but same rule for all ignores different costs. Evaluation: setting the cap and allocating permits (free allocation, lobbying, too many permits → low price); monitoring and enforcement costs; price volatility; carbon leakage; regulation inflexible but suitable where few large plants or where hotspots matter; information failure in both. Conclusion on 'more effective' with conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that providing information and using nudges are better ways to reduce the consumption of sugary drinks than placing a tax on them.
parts.answer: Information and nudges tackle the root cause (information failure, present bias) cheaply and preserve choice, but effects are often small; a tax directly raises price, cuts consumption if demand is elastic enough, raises revenue and pushes firms to reformulate, but is regressive and may be weak if demand is inelastic. A combination is often most effective.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: demerit good/negative externality and information failure diagram (overconsumption where MPB > MSB); information campaigns and labels shift perceived MPB left; nudges (placement, default portion sizes); tax shifts supply left by the tax, price up, quantity down, revenue raised. Evaluation: PED of sugary drinks; regressive burden on low-income households; substitution to untaxed sugary products; evidence that nudges fade; cost and reach of campaigns; tax revenue can fund health programmes; judgement on 'better'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether privatisation is an effective way to correct market failure in the distribution of electricity in a developing economy.
parts.answer: Privatisation may improve efficiency through the profit motive (lower losses and theft, better billing, investment) but electricity distribution is a natural monopoly with externalities and equity issues; without strong regulation, private owners may raise prices and neglect poor areas. Effectiveness depends on regulation and competition.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: market failures in electricity (natural monopoly, positive externalities of access, information problems, government failure in state-owned firms: losses, overstaffing); privatisation → profit incentive → productive and dynamic efficiency; access to private capital. Evaluation: private monopoly may restrict output and raise price (monopoly diagram) — needs price-cap regulation; regulatory capture; rural areas unprofitable → subsidies needed; tariffs politically sensitive; evidence varies by country; alternatives such as reform of state firms, competitive tendering. Conclusion on effectiveness and conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Compared with a scheme of tradable pollution permits, what is an advantage of a tax on each tonne of carbon emitted?
A Firms know in advance the cost they will pay for each tonne they emit.
B The government knows exactly how many tonnes will be emitted in total.
C The government does not need to measure the emissions of each firm.
D Firms no longer have any incentive to emit less than their current level.
parts.answer: A Firms know in advance the cost they will pay for each tonne they emit.
parts.working: A carbon tax fixes the price per tonne, so firms can plan investment with certainty about costs; the quantity emitted is uncertain. B is the advantage of permits, which fix the total quantity but let the price vary. C is false for both schemes; D is false because a tax rewards every tonne cut.

practice.stem:
Invented income tax schedule:
First Rs 600,000 of annual income: 0%
Rs 600,001 to Rs 1,200,000: 10%
Above Rs 1,200,000: 20%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the income tax paid by a person with an annual taxable income of Rs 2,000,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate this person's average rate of tax.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this tax system is progressive.
parts.answer: The average rate of tax rises as income rises because higher slices of income are taxed at higher marginal rates (0% → 10% → 20%).
parts.working: 1 average tax rate rises with income; 1 marginal rate above average rate/higher bands.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a country, the poorest 20 % of households receive 6 % of total income and the richest 20 % receive 48 %. How many times greater is the average income of the richest fifth than the average income of the poorest fifth?
A 8
B 42
C 2.4
D 0.125
parts.answer: A 8
parts.working: Each group contains the same number of households, so the ratio of average incomes is 48/6 = 8. B is the difference in percentage points; C compares the richest fifth with the average of the whole population (48/20); D is the inverse ratio.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between horizontal equity and vertical equity.
parts.answer: Horizontal equity means treating people in the same circumstances in the same way (e.g. two people with equal incomes pay the same tax); vertical equity means treating people in different circumstances differently, e.g. people with higher incomes pay a larger share of their income in tax.
parts.working: 2 marks for each: definition (1) and example or explanation (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a tax designed to achieve vertical equity.
parts.answer: A progressive income tax (or a wealth/property tax with higher rates on larger holdings).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Invented data: the median household income in a country is Rs 60 000 a month. The government defines relative poverty as an income below 60 % of the median.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative poverty line.
parts.answer: Rs 36 000 a month.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A household earns Rs 33 000 a month. Calculate how far its income is below the poverty line, as a percentage of the line, to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Distinguish between absolute poverty and relative poverty.
parts.answer: Absolute poverty: income too low to buy basic needs such as food, shelter and clothing (often measured by a fixed daily income line); relative poverty: income well below the typical level in the country (e.g. below 60 % of median), so a household cannot take part in normal life. Relative poverty can rise even if absolute poverty falls.
parts.working: 2 marks each: definition and an example/measure, or the point that relative poverty depends on others' incomes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the distribution of wealth is usually more unequal than the distribution of income.
parts.answer: Wealth is a stock built up over time from saving and inheritance; high-income households can save more, and their assets earn further income and capital gains, while low-income households save little; inheritance passes wealth between generations.
parts.working: 1: wealth is a stock accumulated over time, income is a flow; 1: rich save a larger proportion and assets generate returns; 1: inheritance concentrates wealth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two causes of inequality of income within a country.
parts.answer: Differences in education and skills, giving different marginal revenue products and wages; ownership of wealth, which earns rent, interest and profit; also discrimination, regional differences, unemployment, and family size.
parts.working: For each of two causes: 1 for the cause, 1 for explaining how it leads to different incomes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On a Lorenz curve diagram, the area between the line of perfect equality and the Lorenz curve is 0.18, and the area below the Lorenz curve is 0.32. What is the Gini coefficient?
A 0.18
B 0.36
C 0.56
D 0.64
parts.working: Gini = A ÷ (A + B) = 0.18 ÷ (0.18 + 0.32) = 0.18 ÷ 0.5 = 0.36. C divides 0.18 by 0.32; A forgets to divide by the total area under the equality line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a universal basic income.
parts.answer: A regular, unconditional cash payment made by the state to every adult, whatever their income or employment status.
parts.working: 1 regular payment to all citizens/adults; 1 not means-tested or conditional on work.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a universal basic income would reduce inequality more effectively than means-tested benefits.
parts.answer: It avoids the poverty trap and stigma, has full take-up and low administration costs, so it reaches all the poor; but paying everyone is very expensive, so the amount may be too low to cut inequality unless financed by progressive taxes; means-tested benefits target money on the poorest.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): means-tested benefits are withdrawn as income rises → high effective marginal tax rates/poverty trap; low take-up, stigma, admin cost; UBI simple and keeps work incentives at the margin; distribution depends on how it is financed. Evaluation (up to 2): fiscal cost, possible inflation, may reduce labour supply (income effect), equal payment to rich and poor; judgement.

practice.stem: A worker receives a means-tested housing benefit. When her monthly earnings rise by Rs 10 000, she pays income tax of 20 % on the extra earnings and loses housing benefit equal to 55 % of the extra earnings (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how much of the Rs 10 000 rise in earnings she keeps, and her effective marginal tax rate.
parts.answer: She keeps Rs 2 500; effective marginal tax rate 75 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this situation creates a poverty trap.
parts.answer: Because she loses three-quarters of any extra earnings through tax and withdrawn benefit, the reward for working more hours or taking a better job is very small, so she may not try; her income stays close to the benefit level and she remains in poverty.
parts.working: 1: high effective marginal tax rate from tax + benefit withdrawal; 1: weak incentive to work more/seek promotion; 1: household remains on low income/dependent on benefits.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way the government could reduce the poverty trap.
parts.answer: Withdraw the benefit more slowly (taper), raise the tax-free allowance, or replace means-tested benefits with a negative income tax or universal benefit.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A government introduces a negative income tax (invented data). The threshold is Rs 40 000 a month and the rate is 50 %. People earning below the threshold receive a payment of 50 % of the difference between their earnings and the threshold; people earning above it pay tax of 50 % on earnings above the threshold.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the final monthly income of a person who earns Rs 20 000 and of a person who earns Rs 60 000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the final income of a person with no earnings.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one advantage of a negative income tax over a system of separate means-tested benefits.
parts.answer: It combines tax and benefits into one system, so every extra rupee earned raises final income by a known 50 paise; there is no sudden loss of benefits, which reduces the poverty trap; it is also simpler and cheaper to administer and has less stigma, so take-up is higher.
parts.working: 1: identifies advantage; 2: explains it (e.g. constant, known withdrawal rate → always better off working; lower administration costs; automatic, higher take-up).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why policies to redistribute income may reduce economic efficiency.
parts.answer: Higher marginal tax rates reduce the reward for extra work, saving, investment and enterprise, so labour supply and investment may fall; means-tested benefits create poverty and unemployment traps; high taxes encourage avoidance, evasion and movement of skilled people and capital abroad; administration has costs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four points: work incentives/substitution effect; investment/enterprise incentives; benefit traps; avoidance/evasion/brain drain; administrative costs; deadweight loss of taxation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether there is always a trade-off between equity and efficiency.
parts.answer: Not always: spending on education and health for poor families raises productivity and growth; reducing extreme inequality can improve social stability and use of talent; well-designed taxes (on land, pollution) can raise efficiency. But badly designed high taxes and benefits can reduce output, so the size of the trade-off depends on policy design.
parts.working: Up to 2 for analysis of cases where equity and efficiency are complementary (human capital, lower crime, positive externalities, higher aggregate demand from the poor's higher MPC). Up to 2 for evaluation: depends on design and level of taxes; evidence mixed; justified judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether greater equality in the distribution of income is always desirable for an economy.
parts.answer: Greater equality can raise total welfare (diminishing marginal utility of income), reduce poverty, improve health and education and social cohesion, and support demand. But some inequality provides incentives for effort, skills and enterprise, and policies to reduce it can harm efficiency; fairness is a normative judgement, and equity is not the same as equality.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: Lorenz curve/Gini; benefits of equality — poverty reduction, higher MPC of poor raises AD, human capital, lower crime, political stability; costs of inequality — unequal opportunity, persistent poverty. Evaluation: incentive role of wage differentials (MRP, compensation for training and risk); redistribution policies may reduce labour supply, investment and raise avoidance; equality vs equity (horizontal/vertical); depends on the starting level of inequality and the means used; conclusion: 'always' too strong, but reducing extreme inequality is usually desirable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether progressive income taxes are the most effective way to reduce inequality of income and wealth in a developing economy.
parts.answer: Progressive taxes narrow post-tax income gaps, but in many developing economies few people pay income tax, the informal sector is large and evasion is common; wealth inequality needs wealth, property or inheritance taxes. Spending on education and health, transfers, minimum wages and land reform may be more effective; a mix is needed.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: Lorenz curve/Gini; how progressive taxes raise the average rate with income and fund transfers; effect on disposable income. Evaluation: narrow tax base, informal economy, evasion and avoidance; disincentives to work and invest; capital flight; income taxes do little for wealth inequality (land and property); regressive indirect taxes may dominate the tax system; alternatives — cash transfers (e.g. targeted programmes for poor households), universal education and health, property taxes, minimum wage, microfinance — with their limitations. Conclusion on 'most effective'.

practice.stem:
Shares of total household income received by each fifth (quintile) of households, from poorest to richest, in an invented country (%):
Before taxes and transfers: 5, 9, 14, 22, 50
After taxes and transfers: 7, 11, 16, 22, 44

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cumulative share of income for each quintile before taxes and transfers.
parts.working: Running totals of 5, 9, 14, 22 and 50.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Treating the Lorenz curve as straight lines between the quintile points, calculate the Gini coefficient before and after taxes and transfers, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Before: 0.41; after: 0.34.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the change shows, and one limitation of a Gini coefficient calculated from quintile data.
parts.answer: Taxes and transfers reduce inequality: the Lorenz curve moves closer to the line of equality and the Gini falls from 0.41 to 0.34, mainly because the richest fifth's share falls from 50 % to 44 % and the poorest three fifths gain. Limitation: grouping hides inequality within each fifth, so the true Gini is understated; it also does not show where in the distribution changes happen or include wealth or in-kind benefits.
parts.working: 1: inequality reduced, with data; 1: identifies shift of income from top quintile to bottom three; 1: valid limitation (within-group inequality ignored/understated, same Gini for different shapes, excludes wealth/public services).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a tax on the ownership of land and property would be an effective way to reduce inequality of wealth in a developing economy.
parts.answer: Land and property make up most wealth and are owned mainly by the rich, and they cannot easily be moved abroad, so a property tax can be progressive, raise revenue for spending on the poor and discourage speculative holding of land. But valuation and records are often poor, the rich have political influence and may avoid the tax, asset-rich but cash-poor owners may struggle to pay, and the tax may be passed on in rents.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: distribution of wealth more unequal than income; wealth generates income (rent, capital gains) so inequality persists across generations; tax on immobile assets hard to evade; progressive rates/exemptions for small holdings; revenue for transfers, health and education (vertical equity); efficiency gains from bringing idle land into use. Evaluation: weak land registries and outdated valuations; corruption and political opposition from large landowners; incidence — landlords may pass tax on to tenants; liquidity problems for small farmers; administrative cost; capital flight into other assets; compare with income tax, inheritance tax, spending on education; conclusion depending on administration and design.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): A government spends Rs 600 billion a year keeping petrol and diesel prices below world prices. A study finds that 70 % of this subsidy benefits the richest 40 % of households, who own most of the cars. The government plans to replace the subsidy with an annual cash transfer of Rs 30 000 to each of 9 million low-income households.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of the fuel subsidy that goes to the richest 40 % of households.
parts.answer: Rs 420 billion.
parts.working: 70 % × 600 = Rs 420 billion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the annual cost of the planned cash transfers and the net saving to the government budget.
parts.answer: Cost Rs 270 billion; saving Rs 330 billion.
parts.working: 30 000 × 9 million = Rs 270 billion (1); 600 − 270 = Rs 330 billion (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the fuel subsidy is a poorly targeted way to help low-income households.
parts.answer: The benefit rises with the amount of fuel used, and richer households own more cars and use more fuel, so most of the subsidy (70 %) goes to them; poor households gain only indirectly through cheaper transport, and the subsidy also encourages over-use of fuel, adding to pollution.
parts.working: 1: benefit proportional to consumption; 1: richer households consume more (data: 70 % to richest 40 %); 1: leakage/opportunity cost or encourages over-consumption with negative externalities.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate whether replacing the subsidy with cash transfers would improve equity.
parts.answer: It is likely to: the transfers go directly to 9 million low-income households and cost less, freeing Rs 330 billion for other spending; but fuel prices will rise, raising transport and food costs for all, including poor households not covered; targeting errors, delays and corruption may stop payments reaching the right people; the effect depends on whether the transfer is enough to offset higher prices and on how the savings are used.
parts.working: Up to 5 for analysis: vertical equity improves as benefits shift from rich to poor; cash allows households to choose; removal of price distortion; savings used for health/education; but higher fuel prices → cost-push inflation, hurting the poor (food, buses); households just above the eligibility line lose. Up to 3 for evaluation: accuracy of targeting (exclusion and inclusion errors), real value of Rs 30 000 against price rises, political resistance, phasing/timing, use of savings; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define government failure.
parts.answer: When government intervention in a market leads to a less efficient allocation of resources (a greater net welfare loss) than would have occurred without it.
parts.working: 1: government intervention; 1: makes the allocation of resources worse / creates a net welfare loss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three causes of government failure.
parts.answer: Any three: lack of information (setting taxes or subsidies at the wrong level); unintended consequences; administrative and enforcement costs; regulatory capture; political self-interest or short-termism; distortion of incentives (moral hazard); conflicting objectives.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A city bans thin plastic shopping bags. Afterwards, sales of thicker plastic bin bags rise sharply, and some shops pay small fines rather than stop giving out thin bags (invented).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an unintended consequence of government intervention, using this example.
parts.answer: An effect of a policy that the government did not plan for and that may work against its aim: the ban was meant to reduce plastic waste, but people now buy thicker bin bags instead of reusing shopping bags, so the amount of plastic may not fall, or may even rise.
parts.working: 1: outcome not intended by policymakers; 1: people change behaviour in response to the policy; 1: applied — substitution to thicker bin bags offsets the aim.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one other reason why the ban may fail to reduce plastic litter.
parts.answer: Weak enforcement: fines are small compared with the cost of switching, so shops ignore the ban and pay the fines (or bags are smuggled in from other areas).
parts.working: 1: reason (enforcement/penalty too low, illegal supply, no affordable substitutes); 1: explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by regulatory capture.
parts.answer: When a regulator comes to act in the interests of the firms it regulates rather than the public interest.
parts.working: 1: regulator acts for the regulated industry; 1: rather than consumers/public interest (e.g. through lobbying, close links, staff moving between them).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how regulatory capture of an electricity regulator might lead to government failure.
parts.answer: The regulator may allow high tariffs, accept inflated cost claims, or fail to penalise poor service, so consumers pay more than necessary and the firms have little incentive to cut costs; the outcome may be worse than with no regulator because consumers believe they are protected.
parts.working: 1: regulator allows higher prices/profits than efficient; 1: weak incentive for efficiency (X-inefficiency), poor service; 1: welfare loss to consumers → allocation worse than intended (government failure).

practice.stem: A city council spends Rs 800 million a year enforcing a ban on street vending in a crowded market area. It estimates the benefit of reduced congestion at Rs 650 million a year (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net benefit of the ban per year.
parts.answer: −Rs 150 million (a net cost).
parts.working: 650 − 800 = −Rs 150 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how administrative and enforcement costs can cause government failure, using the data.
parts.answer: The resources used to enforce the ban (Rs 800 million) have an opportunity cost; because they exceed the benefits (Rs 650 million), society is worse off by Rs 150 million than without the policy, even though the policy may achieve its aim of less congestion.
parts.working: 1: enforcement uses scarce resources with an opportunity cost; 1: costs exceed benefits (data); 1: net welfare loss → government failure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one further cost of the ban that is not included in the council's figures.
parts.answer: Street vendors lose their income and customers lose access to cheap goods; vendors may move to other streets and create congestion there.
parts.working: 1: identifies a cost (lost incomes of vendors, higher prices for consumers, displacement); 1: explains why it adds to the net cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by government failure in microeconomic intervention.
parts.answer: When government intervention to correct a market failure leads to a less efficient allocation of resources than before (a net welfare loss).
parts.working: 1 intervention in a market; 1 results in a worse/less efficient outcome than without it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the example of a maximum price set below the equilibrium price for wheat flour, consider how such intervention may lead to government failure.
parts.answer: The price ceiling causes excess demand: shortages, queues, rationing by waiting, black markets, hoarding and smuggling; farmers and millers have less incentive to supply, so output falls. But the policy may protect the poor if combined with subsidies or a buffer stock, so failure depends on design and enforcement.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): diagram with max price below equilibrium; Qd > Qs; shortages, illegal markets at higher prices, lower quality; reduced supply incentive; administrative costs; unintended consequences. Evaluation (up to 2): information problems vs benefits to low-income consumers; can be avoided with release of government stocks, targeted subsidies; judgement on whether the outcome is worse than the free market.

practice.stem: A government pays a subsidy of Rs 25 per kg on a fertiliser. It expected subsidised sales of 2.0 million tonnes a year, but sales reached 2.6 million tonnes, and investigators estimate that 15 % of the subsidised fertiliser was smuggled to neighbouring countries (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected cost and the actual cost of the subsidy in a year, in Rs billion.
parts.answer: Expected Rs 50 billion; actual Rs 65 billion.
parts.working: 2.0 million tonnes = 2 000 million kg × Rs 25 = Rs 50 billion (1); 2.6 million tonnes × 1 000 × 25 = Rs 65 billion (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of the subsidy paid on fertiliser that was smuggled abroad.
parts.answer: Rs 9.75 billion.
parts.working: 15 % × 65 = Rs 9.75 billion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this outcome is an example of government failure.
parts.answer: The subsidy was meant to raise domestic use of fertiliser and farm output, but the government lacked information and could not control where the fertiliser went; the cost rose by 30 %, and almost Rs 10 billion of taxpayers' money benefited foreign farmers and smugglers, so the opportunity cost of the policy rose while its benefit to the country was less than planned.
parts.working: 1: intended aim; 1: information failure/unintended consequence (smuggling because domestic price is below foreign price); 1: higher cost/opportunity cost of public funds; 1: net welfare lower than intended → government failure.

practice.stem: In the market for rented flats in a large city (invented data), demand is Qd = 120 − 2R and supply is Qs = 20 + 3R, where R is the monthly rent in Rs thousand and Q is in thousand flats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium rent and number of flats rented.
parts.answer: Rent Rs 20 000 a month; 80 000 flats.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government sets a maximum rent of Rs 15 000 a month. Calculate the shortage of flats.
parts.answer: 25 000 flats.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which this rent control could lead to government failure.
parts.answer: Fewer flats are offered (65 000 instead of 80 000), so some households who would pay the market rent cannot find homes; landlords may cut maintenance, ask for illegal 'key money' or switch flats to short-term or commercial use; flats go to those with connections rather than greatest need; long-term building of new rental housing falls.
parts.working: For each of two ways: 1 for the point, 1 for explaining how it worsens the allocation (shortage/queues, black market, lower quality, reduced supply over time, misallocation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why it is difficult for a government to measure the marginal external cost of pollution accurately.
parts.answer: External costs fall on many people over a wide area and a long time; health damage, lost crops and harm to ecosystems have no market price and need shadow prices; pollution comes from many sources, so the share caused by each firm is hard to separate; scientific evidence is uncertain and costs rise as pollution builds up.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four points: many third parties/diffuse; no market price/shadow pricing; multiple sources; long-term and uncertain effects; MEC varies with output and location.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether tradable pollution permits avoid this problem.
parts.answer: Permits let the government set the total quantity of pollution, and the market sets the price, so it does not need to know each firm's abatement costs; but it still needs to know the socially optimal level of emissions, which depends on the external cost, and to measure each firm's emissions; if too many permits are issued the price collapses.
parts.working: Up to 2 for analysis: cap fixes quantity; firms with low abatement costs cut most; price discovered by market. Up to 2 for evaluation: setting the right cap still needs MEC information; monitoring and enforcement; risk of over-allocation, lobbying; judgement.

practice.stem: In an invented country, households pay an average of Rs 40 per unit of electricity, while the cost of supplying it is Rs 52 per unit. Households use 120 billion units a year. The government has kept the price unchanged for two years before an election.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual cost of keeping the household price below the cost of supply, in Rs billion.
parts.answer: Rs 1 440 billion.
parts.working: Subsidy per unit = 52 − 40 = Rs 12 (1); 12 × 120 billion = Rs 1 440 billion (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how political self-interest can lead to government failure, using this example.
parts.answer: Politicians may keep electricity prices low before elections to win votes, even though the price is below the cost of supply; this encourages over-use of electricity, leaves suppliers short of money to maintain the network, and uses tax revenue that has a high opportunity cost, so resources are misallocated.
parts.working: 1: politicians act to maximise votes/short-term popularity (public choice); 1: price below cost → overconsumption (P < MC); 1: losses/debts for suppliers → under-investment, power cuts; 1: high opportunity cost of public funds/benefits go mainly to large users.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a government's promise to rescue state-owned banks if they get into difficulty may create moral hazard.
parts.answer: Because the banks expect to be rescued, they do not bear the full cost of failure, so their managers take bigger risks (e.g. lending to unprofitable or politically connected borrowers); if the risks go wrong, taxpayers pay.
parts.working: 1: guarantee protects the bank from consequences; 1: incentive to take excessive risks; 1: losses shifted to taxpayers / resources misallocated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one other way in which government intervention may distort incentives.
parts.answer: E.g. means-tested benefits withdrawn as income rises reduce the incentive to work more (poverty trap); guaranteed crop prices encourage farmers to over-produce one crop; free services with no price can lead to over-use.
parts.working: 1: identifies intervention; 1: incentive affected; 1: resulting misallocation.

practice.stem: In an invented market, MPB = MSB = 110 − Q and MPC = 20 + Q. Production causes a constant marginal external cost of $10 per unit. Q is in thousand units and values are in $ per unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the free-market output.
parts.answer: 45 thousand units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the socially optimal output and the correct tax per unit.
parts.answer: 40 thousand units; $10 per unit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The government overestimates the external cost and sets a tax of $30 per unit. Calculate the new output.
parts.answer: 30 thousand units.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the welfare loss with the $30 tax and the welfare loss in the free market, and explain what your answers show.
parts.answer: Loss with the tax: $100 000; free-market loss: $25 000. The badly set tax causes a larger welfare loss than doing nothing — government failure.
parts.working: With tax: at Q = 30, MSB − MSC = 80 − 60 = 20; loss = ½ × (40 − 30) × 20 = 100 thousand (1). Free market: at Q = 45, MSC − MSB = 75 − 65 = 10; loss = ½ × 5 × 10 = 25 thousand (1). Intervention made allocation worse (1) because of imperfect information about the size of the externality (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether the risk of government failure is a stronger argument against intervention in markets than market failure is an argument for it.
parts.answer: Market failure (externalities, public goods, information failure, monopoly) creates a case for intervention, but governments face information gaps, political pressures, capture and enforcement costs, so intervention can make things worse. The balance depends on the size of the market failure, the type of policy and the quality of institutions.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: market failure diagrams (externality, under-provision of public/merit goods) and the welfare gain from correct intervention; causes of government failure with examples (wrong tax level, price controls creating shortages, subsidies captured by rich, state enterprises' X-inefficiency). Evaluation: where market failure is large (pure public goods, severe pollution), intervention is clearly needed; choose policies that need less information (permits, nudges); independent regulators and transparency reduce failure; in countries with weak institutions the risk of failure is higher; compare likely net gains; conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether state-owned enterprises, such as national airlines and railways, are more likely to suffer from government failure than privately owned firms.
parts.answer: State-owned enterprises often have soft budget constraints, political interference, conflicting objectives and weak incentives, causing X-inefficiency and losses; but they may provide socially valuable services that private firms would not, and private firms can also be inefficient or abuse market power. Performance depends on governance, competition and regulation rather than ownership alone.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: government failure in SOEs — political appointments, overstaffing, prices kept low for political reasons, losses covered by taxpayers (moral hazard), lack of profit motive → X-inefficiency, low dynamic efficiency. Evaluation: SOEs can internalise positive externalities (rail reduces congestion, connects remote regions), avoid monopoly pricing in natural monopolies; private firms may also fail (monopoly power, cutting safety); examples of well-run state firms with independent boards; privatisation may simply create a private monopoly needing regulation (which can also fail); conclusion.

practice.stem: In the market for a grain crop in an invented country, demand is Qd = 30 − 0.05P and supply is Qs = −6 + 0.04P, where P is in $ per tonne and Q is in million tonnes a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity without intervention.
parts.answer: $400 per tonne; 10 million tonnes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government sets a guaranteed minimum price of $500 per tonne and buys any surplus. Calculate the surplus and the cost of buying it.
parts.answer: Surplus 9 million tonnes; cost $4.5 billion.
parts.working: Qd = 30 − 25 = 5; Qs = −6 + 20 = 14; surplus = 9 million tonnes (1); 9 million × $500 = $4 500 million (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Storage costs $25 per tonne a year. Calculate the annual cost of storing the surplus.
parts.answer: $225 million.
parts.working: 9 million × $25 = $225 million.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Consider whether this support price is an example of government failure.
parts.answer: Farmers gain a higher, stable income and food security may improve, but consumers pay more (and buy less: 5 instead of 10 million tonnes), taxpayers pay $4.5 billion plus storage, and resources are drawn into over-producing a crop that partly goes to waste; unless the surplus is used (exports, food aid, buffer stock) the net welfare loss suggests government failure.
parts.working: Up to 2 for analysis: allocative inefficiency (overproduction, Qs > Qd), higher consumer price, cost to taxpayers, storage losses/waste; benefits to farmers, income stability. Up to 2 for evaluation: depends on whether the surplus is sold later or exported, the objective (food security, rural poverty), and alternatives (direct income support); judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data: legal cigarette sales in a country were 4.0 billion packs a year, with a tax of Rs 100 per pack; illicit (smuggled or untaxed) packs were estimated at 15 % of total consumption. The tax was raised to Rs 160 per pack. Legal sales fell to 2.8 billion packs and the illicit share rose to 30 % of total consumption.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the tax revenue from legal sales before and after the tax rise, in Rs billion.
parts.answer: Before Rs 400 billion; after Rs 448 billion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate total consumption (legal plus illicit) before and after the tax rise, in billion packs to two decimal places, and the percentage change in total consumption to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Before 4.71 billion packs; after 4.00 billion packs; a fall of 15.0 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the tax rise should be judged a success or an example of government failure.
parts.answer: Partly a success: revenue rose by 12 % and total smoking fell by 15 %, reducing health costs. But legal sales fell 30 % while illicit packs rose from about 0.71 to 1.20 billion, so much of the effect was a switch to untaxed, unregulated cigarettes, which may be more harmful and fund crime; the outcome depends on enforcement against smuggling.
parts.working: Up to 2 for analysis using the data: revenue +48 bn; total consumption −15 %; illicit packs 0.71 → 1.20 bn (smuggling as unintended consequence). Up to 2 for evaluation: objective (health vs revenue), enforcement costs, quality risks of illicit products, justified judgement.

topics.name: The price system and the microeconomy

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Printers and ink cartridges are complements. The price of printers falls sharply. What is most likely to happen in the market for ink cartridges?
A price falls and quantity bought rises
B price rises and quantity bought rises
C price rises and quantity bought falls
D price and quantity bought are unchanged
parts.answer: B price rises and quantity bought rises
parts.working: Cheaper printers → more printers bought → demand for cartridges shifts right → higher equilibrium price and quantity. A is wrong: it describes an increase in supply, not demand. D ignores the link between complements.

practice.stem:
The daily market for tomatoes in Karachi is described by:
Qd = 240 − 4P
Qs = −30 + 5P
where P is the price in Rs per kg and Q is in thousand kg per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.answer: P = Rs 30 per kg, Q = 120 thousand kg per day

parts.label: b
parts.text: The city government fixes the price at Rs 24 per kg. Calculate the excess demand at this price.
parts.answer: Excess demand = 54 thousand kg per day
parts.working: M1 Qd = 240 − 96 = 144; Qs = −30 + 120 = 90. A1 excess demand = 54 thousand kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how, without price control, the price mechanism would remove a shortage in this market.
parts.answer: Buyers compete and bid the price up; higher price contracts quantity demanded and extends quantity supplied until the market clears at Rs 30.
parts.working: 1 mark each: shortage leads buyers/sellers to raise price (signal); higher price gives incentive to sellers → extension of supply (movement along supply); higher price rations → contraction of demand; process continues until Qd = Qs at equilibrium.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Demand for new houses in Islamabad rises sharply. Bricks are used only in building. Other things equal, what is most likely to happen in the market for bricks?
A price rises and quantity traded rises
B price rises and quantity traded falls
C price falls and quantity traded rises
D price and quantity traded are unchanged because bricks are not bought by households
parts.answer: A price rises and quantity traded rises
parts.working: Demand for bricks is derived from the demand for houses, so the demand curve for bricks shifts right: price and quantity both rise. D ignores derived demand: firms, not households, buy bricks.

practice.stem: The weekly market for bicycles in Hanoi is described by Qd = 900 − 3P and Qs = 100 + 5P, where P is the price in US$ and Q is the number of bicycles (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.answer: P = $100, Q = 600 bicycles per week

parts.label: b
parts.text: A new duty on imported bicycle parts changes supply to Qs = 20 + 5P. Calculate the new equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.answer: P = $110, Q = 570 bicycles per week

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate total spending on bicycles before and after the change, and explain why spending rose even though fewer bicycles were sold.
parts.answer: $60,000 → $62,700 a week (a rise of $2,700). The price rose by 10% but quantity fell by only 5%, so demand is price inelastic over this range.
parts.working: 1 both totals (600 × 100 and 570 × 110); 1 percentage price rise larger than percentage fall in quantity (inelastic demand).

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by derived demand?
parts.answer: Demand for a good or factor that comes from the demand for another good it helps to produce.
parts.working: 1 demand that arises from demand for something else; 1 example, e.g. demand for fertiliser derived from demand for wheat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The price of fertiliser rises sharply. Explain the likely effect on the market for wheat and then on the market for wheat flour (atta).
parts.answer: Fertiliser is a cost of growing wheat, so the supply of wheat shifts left: the wheat price rises and less is traded. Wheat is the main input into atta, so the supply of atta also shifts left and its price rises.
parts.working: 1 higher input cost; 1 wheat supply shifts left, price up, quantity down; 1 wheat is an input to atta; 1 atta supply shifts left, price up.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Beef and leather are in joint supply. Demand for beef from restaurants in Lahore rises. Other things equal, what happens in the leather market?
A Supply of leather falls and its price rises
B Demand for leather rises and its price rises
C Supply of leather rises and its price falls
D Demand for leather falls and its price falls
parts.answer: C Supply of leather rises and its price falls
parts.working: More cattle are slaughtered to meet beef demand, so more hides are produced as a by-product: the supply curve of leather shifts right, price falls and quantity rises. B confuses joint supply with joint demand; the demand for leather has not changed.

practice.stem: Invented data. In 2025 floods cut a South Asian country's cotton crop by 28%. The world price of raw cotton rose from 78 US cents per pound in 2024 to 96 US cents per pound in 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the world price of cotton between 2024 and 2025. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, with the help of a demand and supply diagram, the likely effect of the rise in the cotton price on the market for polyester fibre.
parts.answer: Polyester is a substitute: demand for polyester shifts right, raising its equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.working: 1 polyester and cotton are substitutes (competitive demand); 1 demand curve for polyester shifts right (diagram with labelled axes P, Q and D1→D2); 1 equilibrium price and quantity both rise.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Cottonseed oil is produced from the seeds left after cotton is ginned. Consider the effect of the smaller cotton crop on the market for cottonseed oil.
parts.answer: Joint supply: a smaller crop reduces supply of cottonseed, so supply of oil shifts left, price rises and quantity falls; the size depends on stocks, imports and PED.
parts.working: 1 joint supply identified; 1 supply of cottonseed oil shifts left → price up, quantity down; 1 consideration, e.g. effect smaller if stocks held or imports of other edible oils available, or if demand for the oil is price elastic as other cooking oils substitute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the market for a good is linked to the markets for its complements and for goods produced in joint supply with it, and consider whether a fall in the price of a good will always change the equilibrium in a related market.
parts.answer: Complements: lower price of good A raises demand for complement B (P and Q of B rise). Joint supply: changes in output of A change supply of its by-product. A related market changes only if the price fall causes a change in quantity of A and the link is strong.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: definitions of complements (joint demand), joint supply, a related market. Analysis: price of A falls → extension of demand for A → demand for complement shifts right (diagram); if price of A falls because of lower demand, output of A falls → supply of joint product shifts left → its price rises (diagram). Evaluation: effect depends on how strong the link is (cross elasticity), on the PED of A (if inelastic, little extra quantity), on whether the fall in price is caused by demand or supply, and on time; a weakly related good will hardly change. Judgement: not always, and the size varies.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the weeks before Ramadan, demand for dates rises in Pakistan. At the same time, a poor harvest reduces the supply of dates. What is the effect on the equilibrium price and quantity of dates?
A price rises; quantity rises
B price rises; the change in quantity cannot be predicted
C the change in price cannot be predicted; quantity falls
D price falls; quantity falls
parts.answer: B price rises; the change in quantity cannot be predicted
parts.working: Demand shifts right (price up, quantity up) and supply shifts left (price up, quantity down). Both raise price; the effects on quantity work in opposite directions, so the net change depends on the sizes of the shifts. A assumes the demand shift is larger.

practice.stem: Invented data. A government rule requires petrol to contain 10% ethanol, which is made from molasses. Molasses is a by-product of crushing sugar cane to make white sugar. In one year the price of molasses rose from Rs 18,000 to Rs 27,000 per tonne.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the price of molasses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Molasses and white sugar are in joint supply. Explain the likely effect of the higher price of molasses on the market for white sugar.
parts.answer: Mills earn more from each tonne of cane crushed, so they buy and crush more cane; this increases the supply of white sugar (supply shifts right), lowering the price of sugar and raising the quantity traded.
parts.working: 1 joint supply: both come from crushing cane; 1 higher molasses price makes crushing more profitable; 1 supply of sugar shifts right; 1 sugar price falls, quantity rises.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether households in Pakistan will gain from the ethanol-blending rule.
parts.answer: Possibly: cheaper sugar via joint supply, but the size depends on how much extra cane can be grown (PES of cane), the PED for sugar, possible higher fuel costs, and whether cane land replaces food crops. Judgement needed.
parts.working: Up to 4 for analysis: lower sugar price; extra cane raises demand for land/inputs; cane price may rise; fuel price effect of ethanol blend. Up to 2 for evaluation: depends on supply response of cane in the short run, share of sugar in household budgets; reasoned conclusion.

practice.stem: Fresh milk is used by households for drinking and by firms to make yoghurt and cheese.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by composite demand?
parts.answer: Demand for a good that has more than one use, so that the different uses compete for the same supply.
parts.working: 1 good with several uses; 1 an increase in one use reduces the amount available for the others.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Cheese factories in Punjab increase their demand for fresh milk. Explain the likely effect on the price and output of yoghurt.
parts.answer: Milk is in composite demand: the higher demand from cheese makers raises the price of milk; this raises the cost of making yoghurt, so the supply of yoghurt shifts left, its price rises and output falls.
parts.working: 1 demand for milk rises → milk price rises; 1 milk is a cost of yoghurt; 1 supply of yoghurt shifts left; 1 higher price, lower quantity of yoghurt.

practice.stem: The Punjab government is considering a subsidy for each electric motorcycle sold in Lahore. Most motorcycles in the city currently run on petrol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the relationship between electric motorcycles and electricity, and between electric motorcycles and petrol motorcycles.
parts.answer: Electric motorcycles and electricity: complements (joint demand). Electric and petrol motorcycles: substitutes (competitive demand).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct relationship.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether a government subsidy for electric motorcycles in Lahore will reduce the price of petrol.
parts.answer: Possibly a small fall in petrol demand, but the effect on the petrol price is likely to be small: Pakistan's petrol price depends on world oil prices, the exchange rate, taxes and government pricing, and motorcycles are only part of petrol demand.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): subsidy lowers price of e-motorcycles → more bought → fewer petrol motorcycles bought (substitutes) → demand for petrol falls → leftward shift of petrol demand → lower equilibrium price, other things equal; also demand for electricity rises (complement). Evaluation (up to 2): petrol price is largely set by world crude price and government levy, not local demand; motorcycles are a small share of total fuel use; existing petrol bikes last years so effect is slow; supply of petrol may be elastic (imports) so price change is small; judgement needed.

practice.stem: The market for fitness bands in Dubai is described by Qd = 500 − 10P and Qs = 50 + 5P, where P is the price in US$ and Q is in thousands per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the original equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.answer: P = $30, Q = 200 thousand per month

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rising incomes change demand to Qd = 560 − 10P and a fall in component costs changes supply to Qs = 80 + 5P. Calculate the new equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.answer: P = $32, Q = 240 thousand per month

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why, when demand and supply both increase, the direction of the change in equilibrium price cannot be predicted without knowing the size of each shift.
parts.answer: Both shifts raise quantity, but an increase in demand raises price while an increase in supply lowers it, so the net price change depends on which shift is larger.
parts.working: 1 increase in demand alone → higher price and quantity; 1 increase in supply alone → lower price, higher quantity; 1 so quantity definitely rises but price rises only if the demand shift is larger (here demand rose by 60 thousand at each price, supply by 30 thousand, so price rose).

practice.stem: Invented data. The market for good X is described by Qd = 200 − 4Px + 2Py and Qs = −40 + 6Px, where Px and Py are the prices of goods X and Y in $ and Q is in thousand units per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the relationship between goods X and Y and explain how the demand equation shows it.
parts.answer: Substitutes: the coefficient on Py is positive, so a rise in the price of Y increases the demand for X.
parts.working: 1 substitutes; 1 positive coefficient on Py.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When Py = 30, calculate the equilibrium price and quantity of X.
parts.answer: Px = 30, Qx = 140 thousand units

parts.label: c
parts.text: The price of Y rises to 45. Calculate the new equilibrium price and quantity of X.
parts.answer: Px = 33, Qx = 158 thousand units

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the change in the price of Y causes a shift of the demand curve for X but a movement along the supply curve of X.
