parts.answer: Py is a non-price determinant of demand for X, so the demand curve shifts; supply of X does not depend on Py, so the higher Px is met by an extension along the existing supply curve.
parts.working: 1 shift of demand (condition of demand changes); 1 extension of supply in response to the higher Px.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a sharp rise in the world price of crude oil will raise the prices of all goods that are related to oil, such as natural gas, plastic packaging, electric cars and bicycles.
parts.answer: Not all: prices of substitutes in demand (gas, electric cars, bicycles) are likely to rise as demand shifts right, and of goods using oil as an input (plastic) as supply shifts left; but complements of oil (petrol cars) fall in price, and the size of each effect depends on XED, PES and time period.
parts.working: AO1/AO2 (up to 8): oil price rise → demand for substitutes rises (gas, electric cars, bicycles) → their prices rise; plastic: derived/cost link → supply shifts left → price rises; complements such as large petrol cars: demand falls → price falls; joint supply (e.g. by-products of refining) may change. AO3 (up to 4): size depends on cross elasticity and PES of each related good; short v long run (electric car supply may expand, lowering price later); other factors (subsidies, technology); reasoned conclusion that the claim is not true for all related goods.

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A household's monthly income rises from Rs 40,000 to Rs 46,000. The number of restaurant meals it buys in a year rises from 200 to 236. What is its income elasticity of demand for restaurant meals, and what kind of good are they?
A 0.83, a normal good that is a necessity
B 1.2, a normal good that is income elastic
C −1.2, an inferior good
D 1.2, an inferior good
parts.answer: B 1.2, a normal good that is income elastic
parts.working: %ΔQ = 36/200 = 18%; %ΔY = 6,000/40,000 = 15%; YED = 18 ÷ 15 = +1.2. Positive and greater than 1 → normal, income elastic (luxury). A inverts the formula (15 ÷ 18).

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand
practice.stem: A supermarket in Islamabad raises the price of loose tea from Rs 1,200 to Rs 1,380 per kg. Over the next month its sales of instant coffee rise from 5,000 to 5,450 jars.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cross elasticity of demand for instant coffee with respect to the price of tea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the sign of your answer shows about the two goods.
parts.answer: Positive: they are substitutes.
parts.working: 1 positive XED → substitutes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one way the supermarket could use this information.
parts.answer: e.g. when tea prices rise, stock more coffee / raise coffee price slightly, as demand for coffee will increase.
parts.working: 1 use identified (stocking, pricing, promotion); 1 linked to the positive but low XED (coffee demand rises only modestly, by 0.6% per 1% rise in tea price).

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The cross elasticity of demand for good X with respect to the price of good Y is +0.4. What does this show?
A X and Y are complements and demand for X is very responsive to the price of Y
B X and Y are weak substitutes
C X and Y are close substitutes
D X is an inferior good
parts.answer: B X and Y are weak substitutes
parts.working: A positive XED means a rise in the price of Y raises demand for X, so they are substitutes; a value well below 1 means demand for X responds only a little, so they are weak substitutes. C would need a large positive value. D confuses XED with YED.

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand
practice.stem: Invented data. A household in Karachi has a monthly income that rises from Rs 150,000 to Rs 180,000. The number of domestic flights it takes in a year rises from 4 to 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the income elasticity of demand for domestic flights.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what type of good domestic flights are for this household.
parts.answer: A normal luxury good (YED > 1).
parts.working: 1 luxury / income elastic normal good.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one way an airline could use this information.
parts.answer: e.g. expand capacity when incomes are forecast to rise, or cut routes/prices in a recession, because demand changes more than in proportion to income.
parts.working: 1 use (planning capacity, marketing to high-income groups); 1 link to YED > 1.

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand
practice.stem: Invented data. A shop in Dubai cuts the price of its tablets from $250 to $200. Monthly sales of tablet styluses rise from 12,000 to 13,800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cross elasticity of demand for styluses with respect to the price of tablets.
parts.working: M1 %ΔQ styluses = +15%, %ΔP tablets = −20%. A1 15 ÷ (−20) = −0.75.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the sign and size of your answer show.
parts.answer: Negative: the goods are complements. Less than 1 in absolute value: demand for styluses responds less than proportionately to tablet prices (weak complements).
parts.working: 1 negative → complements; 1 inelastic/weak relationship.

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand
practice.stem:
Invented estimates of income elasticity of demand (YED) for goods bought by households in Pakistan:
Wheat flour: 0.2
Motorcycles: 1.8
Second-hand clothing: −0.4
Private tuition: 1.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the inferior good in the table and explain how you know.
parts.answer: Second-hand clothing: its YED is negative (−0.4).
parts.working: 1 second-hand clothing; 1 negative YED means demand falls as income rises.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Real household incomes are forecast to fall by 5%. Calculate the percentage change in demand for motorcycles and for second-hand clothing.
parts.answer: Motorcycles: -9%; second-hand clothing: +2%
parts.working: 1 motorcycles 1.8 × (−5) = −9%; 1 second-hand clothing −0.4 × (−5) = +2%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a motorcycle manufacturer could use the YED estimate when planning production.
parts.answer: With YED 1.8, sales are very sensitive to income: cut planned output/stocks and staff hiring when incomes are expected to fall, expand when growth is expected; consider cheaper models.
parts.working: 1 income elastic, so demand changes more than proportionately with income; 1 plan output, stock or capacity in line with forecast income (e.g. reduce output about 9% if incomes fall 5%); 1 further use, e.g. diversify into lower-priced models or export markets with rising incomes.

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand
practice.stem: A games company estimates that the cross elasticity of demand between its consoles and its games is −2.5. It sells 40,000 games a month and plans to cut the price of its consoles by 8%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected percentage change in sales of games and the new monthly sales.
parts.answer: +20%; 48,000 games a month

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether cutting the price of its consoles is likely to increase the firm's total profit.
parts.answer: Probably, if the extra profit on games (strong complements, XED −2.5) outweighs lower revenue per console; it depends on console PED, margins on games and competitors' reactions.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): strong complements → large rise in game sales; games often have higher profit margins than consoles; extra console buyers also buy games for years. Consideration (1+): lower revenue per console may cause losses on hardware; XED is an estimate and may change; rivals may also cut prices; judgement.

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand
practice.stem: Invented estimates of income elasticity of demand in Malaysia: fresh fish +0.6; instant noodles −0.4; foreign holidays +2.2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Real household income is forecast to rise by 4%. Calculate the expected percentage change in demand for each product.
parts.answer: Fresh fish +2.4%; instant noodles −1.6%; foreign holidays +8.8%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Instead, real income falls by 3%. Calculate the change in demand for foreign holidays.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain which of the three firms is most at risk from a recession, and why one of them might gain.
parts.answer: The holiday firm: YED 2.2 means demand falls by more than income. The noodle maker may gain because noodles are inferior (negative YED), so demand rises when income falls.
parts.working: 1 holiday firm most at risk; 1 YED > 1 explanation; 1 noodles inferior; 1 demand rises as households switch to cheaper food.

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand
practice.stem: Invented data. A ride-hailing company in Lahore plans to raise its fares by 15%. The cross elasticity of demand for journeys on the city's metro bus with respect to ride-hailing fares is estimated at +0.4. The metro bus currently carries 50,000 passengers a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected number of daily metro bus journeys after the fare rise.
parts.answer: 53,000 journeys a day (+6%)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the cross elasticity is positive but low.
parts.answer: Positive: they are substitutes for travel. Low: they are not close substitutes (comfort, speed, door-to-door service), so few riders switch.
parts.working: 1 substitutes; 1 reason for weak substitution.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the bus company should raise its own fares after the ride-hailing fare rise.
parts.answer: It could: demand for buses has shifted right and passengers have fewer cheap alternatives, so a moderate rise may raise revenue. But it depends on the PED for bus journeys, whether ride-hailing fares fall back, and the loss of goodwill/public-service aims.
parts.working: Up to 2 analysis (higher demand allows higher price; revenue effect depends on PED); up to 2 evaluation (temporary rise, competition from rickshaws, regulation of fares, judgement).

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the income elasticity of demand for motorcycles may be higher in a low-income country than in a high-income country.
parts.answer: In a low-income country many households are just able to afford a first motorcycle, so a rise in income brings many new buyers (YED > 1); in a rich country most households already own a car and motorcycles may be a necessity or even inferior, so YED is low or negative.
parts.working: 1 YED depends on income level/stage of development; 1 in LIC motorcycle is a step up (luxury); 1 in HIC car replaces it; 1 so YED low/negative.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider how a motorcycle maker in Pakistan could use income elasticity estimates.
parts.answer: To forecast sales as incomes grow, plan capacity and stock, and target new models at income groups; but estimates may be out of date, differ by region and ignore price and credit conditions.
parts.working: Up to 2 uses; up to 2 limitations/judgement.

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether income elasticity of demand is more useful than cross elasticity of demand to a firm planning its production for the next five years.
parts.answer: A balanced judgement: YED is usually more useful for long-term planning because incomes change predictably over five years, but XED matters more in markets with close rivals or complements.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides with a diagram where relevant and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. YED points: measures response to income; normal/inferior/luxury; over five years real income growth forecasts allow capacity, product range and market choice (e.g. a firm with YED > 1 expands as the economy grows; inferior-good producers plan for decline). XED points: substitutes and complements; helps predict effect of rivals' price changes and pricing of complementary products; useful for bundling and competition strategy. Evaluation: estimates are based on past data and may change; income forecasts are uncertain; XED changes as new substitutes appear; usefulness depends on market structure and type of product; PED and PES may also matter; both are needed. Judgement must answer 'more useful'.

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A household's monthly income rises from Rs 60,000 to Rs 64,800. Its monthly purchases of a cheap brand of cooking oil fall from 250 to 240 units. Using the original values as the base, what is the income elasticity of demand and what type of good is it?
A −0.5, an inferior good
B −2.0, an inferior good
C +0.5, a normal necessity
D −0.5, a normal necessity
parts.answer: A −0.5, an inferior good
parts.working: %ΔQ = −10 ÷ 250 = −4%; %ΔY = 4,800 ÷ 60,000 = +8%; YED = −4 ÷ 8 = −0.5. A negative YED means demand falls as income rises: an inferior good. B inverts the formula (8 ÷ −4); C ignores the sign; D gets the value right but a normal good has a positive YED.

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand
practice.stem: Invented data. A firm sells 20,000 tins of its powdered milk a month. Its income elasticity of demand is +1.5. The cross elasticity of demand for its milk with respect to the price of a rival brand is +0.8. Next month consumers' incomes rise by 4% and the rival cuts its price by 5%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected percentage change in monthly sales and the new monthly sales.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two assumptions made in your calculation.
parts.answer: e.g. other things (own price, tastes) unchanged; the elasticities stay constant and the two effects can simply be added.
parts.working: 1 each for any two reasonable assumptions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the firm might be more concerned about its rival's price cut than about the rise in income.
parts.answer: The rival's action is a deliberate strategy that may be repeated or extended, and the firm can respond (e.g. match price); the income rise is outside anyone's control and is already in its favour; the cross effect nearly cancels the income gain.
parts.working: 1 each for up to three relevant points.

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the sign and size of income elasticity of demand and cross elasticity of demand are used to classify goods, and consider whether a product's classification is likely to stay the same over time.
parts.answer: YED: negative = inferior, 0–1 = normal necessity, >1 = luxury. XED: positive = substitutes, negative = complements, zero = unrelated; size shows closeness. Classifications change as incomes, tastes and technology change (e.g. motorcycles, mobile data).
parts.working: Knowledge (3): definitions and formula; Analysis (3): sign → type, size → strength, examples; Evaluation (2): classification depends on income level and time; new substitutes change XED; judgement.

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand
practice.stem: Invented data. Cement and steel reinforcing bars are both used in building. When the price of steel bars rose by 25%, a cement company's annual sales fell from 400,000 tonnes to 360,000 tonnes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cross elasticity of demand for cement with respect to the price of steel bars.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Real incomes are forecast to fall by 1% next year. Using an income elasticity of demand for cement of +1.8, calculate the expected change in cement sales in tonnes, starting from 360,000 tonnes.
parts.answer: −1.8%, a fall of 6,480 tonnes (to 353,520 tonnes)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether the cement company should be more concerned about changes in the price of steel bars or changes in incomes.
parts.answer: Steel: the 25% price rise cut sales by 10%; income changes are usually small (1–3%) but YED 1.8 magnifies them and a deep recession would hurt more. Concern depends on the likely size of each change, how long it lasts, and whether the firm can influence either.
parts.working: Up to 4 analysis using both elasticities and plausible size of changes; up to 2 evaluation and judgement.

practice.stem: A cinema in Islamabad cuts its ticket price from Rs 1,000 to Rs 800. Weekly ticket sales rise from 2,500 to 3,250.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand for the tickets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in the cinema's weekly total revenue.
parts.answer: Increase of Rs 100,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how your answer to (b) is linked to your answer to (a).
parts.answer: Demand is price elastic (|PED| > 1), so a price cut raises quantity by a larger percentage and total revenue rises.
parts.working: 1 elastic demand; 1 percentage rise in quantity outweighs percentage fall in price → TR rises.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The price elasticity of demand for cigarettes is −0.3. A 10% rise in their price is most likely to cause
A a 3% fall in quantity demanded and a rise in total spending on cigarettes
B a 30% fall in quantity demanded and a fall in total spending on cigarettes
C a 3% fall in quantity demanded and a fall in total spending on cigarettes
D a 0.3% fall in quantity demanded and no change in total spending
parts.answer: A a 3% fall in quantity demanded and a rise in total spending on cigarettes
parts.working: %ΔQ = −0.3 × 10 = −3%. Demand is inelastic, so the price rise outweighs the fall in quantity and total spending rises. C gets the quantity right but the revenue rule wrong.

practice.stem: Invented data. A mobile network in Pakistan raises the price of its monthly data package from Rs 500 to Rs 600. Subscriptions fall from 80,000 to 76,000 a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand for the monthly data package.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in the company's monthly revenue from the package.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why demand for the package is price inelastic.
parts.answer: e.g. few close substitutes / switching networks is inconvenient / mobile data is a necessity.
parts.working: 1 valid reason.

practice.stem: Invented data. A wholesaler sells 2,500 tonnes of sugar a week. The price elasticity of demand for its sugar is −0.4. It raises its price by 15%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected percentage change in quantity demanded and the new weekly sales.
parts.answer: −6%; 2,350 tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one factor that makes the demand for sugar price inelastic.
parts.answer: e.g. few substitutes in cooking and tea; small share of income; habit.
parts.working: 1 factor; 1 explanation of why it makes demand unresponsive.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bus company raises its fares by 20%. Its total revenue from fares rises by 8%. What is the price elasticity of demand for its bus journeys?
A −0.4
B −0.5
C −0.6
D −2.5
parts.working: New TR = 1.2 × new Q = 1.08 × old TR, so new Q = 1.08 ÷ 1.2 = 0.9 of old Q: a 10% fall. PED = −10 ÷ 20 = −0.5. A wrongly divides the revenue change by the price change (8 ÷ 20).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the price elasticity of demand for petrol is likely to be lower in the short run than in the long run.
parts.answer: Short run: few substitutes, vehicles already owned, habits and commuting fixed → inelastic. Long run: people switch to fuel-efficient or electric vehicles, public transport, move home/work → more elastic.
parts.working: Up to 2 for short-run reasons (lack of close substitutes, necessity for work travel, existing petrol vehicles); up to 2 for long-run reasons (time to find substitutes such as CNG/electric vehicles, car-sharing, relocation) with link to responsiveness.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a government should use price elasticity of demand when deciding which goods to tax.
parts.answer: Yes for revenue (tax inelastic goods raises revenue with small fall in sales) and to judge the effect on consumption; but inelastic goods are often necessities, so tax may be regressive, and PED estimates are uncertain.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): inelastic demand → tax revenue high and stable, burden mostly on consumers; elastic demand → large fall in consumption (useful for demerit goods only if elastic). Consideration (1+): equity/regressive effect on poor; aim of tax matters (revenue vs reducing consumption); PED changes over time; judgement.

practice.stem:
Invented data for three products in one year:
Electricity: price +12%, quantity −3%
A brand of shampoo: price −10%, quantity +18%
Intercity train tickets: price +5%, quantity −5%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand for each product.
parts.answer: Electricity −0.25; shampoo −1.8; train tickets −1.0

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the product for which total revenue stayed approximately the same, and explain why.
parts.answer: Train tickets: PED is −1 (unit elastic), so the percentage fall in quantity roughly matches the percentage rise in price.
parts.working: 1 train tickets; 1 unit elasticity explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The shampoo firm cut its price but its revenue rose. Explain why, and suggest why the demand for one brand of shampoo is price elastic.
parts.answer: Demand is elastic (|PED| = 1.8 > 1), so the 18% rise in quantity outweighs the 10% fall in price (TR × 0.9 × 1.18 = 1.062). Many close substitute brands.
parts.working: 1 elastic; 1 percentage comparison or calculation; 1 close substitutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the price elasticity of demand for one mobile phone network's service is likely to be greater than the price elasticity of demand for mobile phone services as a whole.
parts.answer: One network has close substitutes (other networks), so a price rise by one network makes many customers switch; for mobile services as a whole there are few substitutes, so total demand responds less.
parts.working: 1 substitutes determine PED; 1 one brand has close substitutes; 1 consumers switch between brands; 1 the whole market has no close substitute → inelastic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a mobile phone network should cut its prices to increase its revenue.
parts.answer: If its own demand is elastic, a price cut raises revenue; but rivals may match the cut (making demand less elastic), costs may rise with use, and switching costs/contracts may slow the response.
parts.working: Up to 2 analysis (elastic → TR rises); up to 2 evaluation (rival reaction, profit v revenue, time period, judgement).

practice.stem: Invented data. A museum in Lahore has 10,000 visitors a month at an entry fee of Rs 400. It estimates the price elasticity of demand for visits to be −1.6 and plans to raise the fee to Rs 500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected number of visitors and the change in monthly revenue.
parts.answer: 6,000 visitors; revenue falls by Rs 1,000,000 (Rs 4,000,000 → Rs 3,000,000)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the museum's profit is likely to fall by almost the full fall in revenue.
parts.answer: Most of the museum's costs are fixed (building, staff, security), so having fewer visitors saves very little cost.
parts.working: 1 fixed costs; 1 low cost saved per visitor lost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the estimate of price elasticity might be wrong.
parts.answer: e.g. estimated from a different season or price range; PED varies along a demand curve; other factors (tourism, weather) may change.
parts.working: 1 reason; 1 explanation.

practice.stem: The demand for a brand of bottled water is Qd = 120 − 2P, where P is the price in Rs and Q is in thousand bottles per week.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand when the price rises from Rs 10 to Rs 12.
parts.working: M1 Q falls from 100 to 96: −4%; P rises 20%. A1 −4 ÷ 20 = −0.2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand when the price rises from Rs 50 to Rs 55.
parts.answer: PED = -5
parts.working: M1 Q falls from 20 to 10: −50%; P rises 10%. A1 −50 ÷ 10 = −5.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the price elasticity of demand changes along this demand curve even though its slope is constant.
parts.answer: PED depends on percentage changes, not absolute ones. The same absolute change in Q is a small percentage at high quantities and a large percentage at low quantities, while the opposite holds for price.
parts.working: 1 slope measures absolute change (ΔP/ΔQ) but PED uses percentage changes; 1 at low prices/high quantities, %ΔQ is small and %ΔP large → inelastic; 1 at high prices/low quantities, %ΔQ large and %ΔP small → elastic (PED moves from 0 towards −∞ up the curve).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the factors that determine the price elasticity of demand for a product and consider whether a firm selling a branded product, such as a soft drink, can make the demand for its product more price inelastic.
parts.answer: Determinants: number and closeness of substitutes, proportion of income, necessity/habit, time period, definition of the market. A firm can reduce substitutability through branding, advertising and loyalty, but success is limited by rivals' actions.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: definition and formula of PED; determinants listed. Analysis: explain how each determinant changes responsiveness (e.g. close substitutes → consumers switch when price rises → elastic). Application: brand advertising, product differentiation, loyalty schemes, exclusive distribution reduce perceived substitutes → steeper demand curve, allowing price rises that raise revenue. Evaluation: rivals also advertise; advertising is costly; consumers of soft drinks are price-sensitive and many substitutes exist; effect may be temporary; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm faces the demand curve Qd = 400 − 8P, where P is in $. Point price elasticity of demand = (ΔQ ÷ ΔP) × (P ÷ Q). At which price is the point price elasticity of demand equal to −0.25?
A $10
B $25
C $40
D $50
parts.working: PED = −8P ÷ (400 − 8P) = −0.25 gives 8P = 100 − 2P, so P = $10 (Q = 320; −80 ÷ 320 = −0.25). B is where PED = −1 (the midpoint); C gives −320 ÷ 80 = −4, the reciprocal; D is where quantity is zero.

practice.stem: Invented data. The demand for bags of a snack is Qd = 600 − 15P, where P is the price in rupees and Q is thousand bags per week. Point price elasticity of demand = (ΔQ ÷ ΔP) × (P ÷ Q).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the point price elasticity of demand at P = 10 and at P = 30. Give your answers to two decimal places where necessary.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price that maximises total revenue and the maximum revenue.
parts.answer: P = 20, total revenue = 6,000 (Q = 300)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a firm that wants to maximise profit, rather than revenue, would not choose the price in (b) if its costs rise with output.
parts.answer: At the revenue-maximising price marginal revenue is zero, but each extra unit adds positive cost; reducing output slightly (higher price) cuts cost by more than revenue, raising profit.
parts.working: 1 MR = 0 at max TR; 1 positive marginal cost → profit higher at a higher price/lower output.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether the price elasticity of demand for a product is likely to stay the same over time.
parts.answer: No: PED changes with time (consumers find substitutes in the long run), with the price level (moves along a linear demand curve), with incomes and the share of income spent, with new substitutes or brand loyalty; but for habitual necessities it may be fairly stable in the short run.
parts.working: AO1/AO2 (up to 8): definition and formula; determinants – substitutes, share of income, necessity/habit, time period, breadth of definition; linear demand curve so PED varies with price; examples (fuel, mobile data). AO3 (up to 4): which changes are fast or slow; stable for necessities over short periods; firms must re-estimate; reasoned judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data. An airline flies between Karachi and Dubai. Each week it sells 200 business-class seats at $800 and 1,200 economy seats at $300. It estimates the price elasticity of demand as −0.4 for business class and −2.0 for economy class. It raises business fares by 10% and cuts economy fares by 5%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the weekly revenue from each class before and after the price changes.
parts.working: M1 business quantity −4% → 192 seats; A1 192 × $880 = $168,960; M1 economy quantity +10% → 1,320 seats; A1 1,320 × $285 = $376,200.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in total weekly revenue, to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether the airline should make further price changes in the same directions.
parts.answer: Further rises in business fares and cuts in economy fares may raise revenue again, but PED is not constant: business demand may become elastic at higher fares, economy cuts may need more seats than available, costs per passenger rise, and rivals may react.
parts.working: Up to 4 analysis (inelastic → raise price; elastic → cut price; capacity and cost limits); up to 2 evaluation and judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which event would cause a movement along the demand curve for rice, rather than a shift of the demand curve?
A a poor harvest that raises the price of rice
B a rise in the price of wheat flour
C a rise in household incomes
D an advertising campaign promoting rice
parts.answer: A a poor harvest that raises the price of rice
parts.working: A poor harvest shifts supply left; the higher price causes a contraction along the existing demand curve. B, C and D change a condition of demand, so they shift the demand curve itself.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a change in quantity supplied and a change in supply.
parts.answer: Change in quantity supplied: movement along the supply curve caused by a change in the good's own price. Change in supply: shift of the whole curve caused by a non-price factor.
parts.working: 1 each correct distinction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two events that would shift the supply curve of mangoes in Multan to the left.
parts.answer: Any two: a heatwave or pest damaging the crop; higher fertiliser, diesel or labour costs; a new indirect tax; growers switching land to more profitable crops.
parts.working: 1 each, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which event would shift the supply curve of wheat to the right?
A a rise in the price of wheat
B a rise in consumers' incomes
C the introduction of a higher-yielding seed variety
D a rise in the price of fertiliser
parts.answer: C the introduction of a higher-yielding seed variety
parts.working: Better seed lowers the cost per tonne, so more is supplied at every price. A causes a movement along the supply curve; B affects demand; D shifts supply to the left.

practice.stem: Invented data. Daily market supply of loaves of bread in a town: at Rs 100, 440 loaves; at Rs 120, 560 loaves; at Rs 140, 680 loaves. A rise in the price of flour means that, at every price, bakeries now supply 90 fewer loaves a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the new quantity supplied at each price.
parts.working: M1 subtract 90 at each price; A1 all three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether this is a decrease in supply or a contraction of supply.
parts.answer: A decrease in supply: a non-price factor (cost of flour) has changed, so less is supplied at every price and the whole supply curve shifts to the left. A contraction is a movement along the curve caused by a fall in the good's own price.
parts.working: 1 decrease/shift left; 1 caused by a non-price determinant (contrast with movement along the curve).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the bakeries' supply curve slopes upwards.
parts.answer: A higher price makes producing extra loaves more profitable (and covers the rising cost of extra output), so bakeries are willing to supply more.
parts.working: 1 higher price → more profit/incentive; 1 rising marginal cost covered.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the market for air conditioners in Karachi, distinguish between an extension of demand and an increase in demand.
parts.answer: Extension: more bought because the price of air conditioners falls (movement down the demand curve). Increase: more bought at every price because a non-price factor changes (curve shifts right).
parts.working: 1 each, with correct reference to movement v shift.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two factors that could increase the demand for air conditioners in Karachi.
parts.answer: e.g. a hotter summer; rising incomes; a fall in the price of electricity (complement); cheaper credit/instalment plans; population growth.
parts.working: 1 factor + 1 explanation, twice.

practice.stem:
Weekly demand for milk (litres) by three households in a street:
Price Rs 200: household X 7, Y 5, Z 4
Price Rs 220: X 6, Y 5, Z 3
Price Rs 240: X 5, Y 4, Z 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the market demand at each price.
parts.answer: Rs 200: 16 litres; Rs 220: 14 litres; Rs 240: 11 litres
parts.working: Horizontal summation. 2 marks all three correct; 1 mark two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A fourth household moves into the street. It buys 3 litres a week at each of the three prices. Calculate the new market demand at Rs 220 and state what happens to the market demand curve.
parts.answer: 17 litres; the market demand curve shifts to the right.
parts.working: 1 14 + 3 = 17; 1 rightward shift (more demanded at every price).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the market demand curve slopes downwards.
parts.answer: e.g. as price falls, the good becomes cheaper relative to substitutes (substitution effect) and consumers' real income rises (income effect), so more is demanded; new buyers enter the market at lower prices.
parts.working: 1 reason identified; 1 explained.

practice.stem: The supply of plastic chairs from factories near Gujranwala is Qs = −40 + 8P, where P is the price in hundreds of rupees (so P = 20 means Rs 2,000) and Q is in thousand chairs per month. A rise in electricity tariffs raises the cost of producing each chair by Rs 500 (5 in these units), shifting the supply curve upwards by this amount.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the quantity supplied at a price of Rs 2,000 per chair (P = 20) before and after the increase in costs.
parts.answer: Before: 120 thousand chairs per month; after: 80 thousand chairs per month
parts.working: 1 Qs = −40 + 8 × 20 = 120; 1 new supply Qs = −40 + 8(P − 5), so at P = 20, Qs = −40 + 120 = 80 thousand chairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two factors other than costs of production that could shift the supply curve for a manufactured good.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. improved technology (more output from same inputs → shift right); indirect taxes or subsidies; number of firms in the market; weather/natural events; prices of other goods the firms could produce.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for each factor: 1 identified, 1 explained with direction of shift.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Traders expect the price of gold to rise sharply next month. What is most likely to happen in the gold market today?
A demand shifts right and supply shifts left, so the price rises
B demand shifts left and supply shifts right, so the price falls
C there is a movement along the demand curve but no shift of either curve
D supply shifts right because sellers want to sell before the price rises
parts.answer: A demand shifts right and supply shifts left, so the price rises
parts.working: Buyers bring purchases forward (demand rises today) and sellers hold back stock to sell later at the higher price (supply falls today), so today's price rises. D reverses the sellers' incentive.

practice.stem: Invented data. Monthly demand for a good in a town is Qd = 300 − 5P + 0.02Y, where P is the price in rupees and Y is average monthly household income in rupees.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the quantity demanded at a price of Rs 100 when Y = 50,000 and when Y = 60,000.
parts.answer: 800 and 1,000 units

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the good is normal or inferior and explain how you know.
parts.answer: Normal: the coefficient on Y is positive, so demand rises as income rises.
parts.working: 1 normal; 1 reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the price at which consumers would demand 800 units after the rise in income, and explain what this shows about the shift of the demand curve.
parts.answer: P = Rs 140; the demand curve has shifted right by 200 units at each price, or equivalently upwards by Rs 40 at each quantity.
parts.working: M1 1,500 − 5P = 800; A1 P = 140; B1 shift explained.

practice.stem:
Invented data. Annual supply of rice from a district of Sindh (thousand tonnes):
Price Rs 250 per kg: before drought 40, after drought 28
Price Rs 280 per kg: before 46, after 34
Price Rs 310 per kg: before 52, after 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the change shown by the data.
parts.answer: A decrease in supply (the supply curve has shifted to the left).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in quantity supplied at a price of Rs 280. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two factors, other than the weather, that could cause the same change.
parts.answer: e.g. higher costs of fuel, fertiliser or labour; a rise in the price of an alternative crop (competitive supply, e.g. cotton); removal of a subsidy; pests or disease; higher taxes on producers.
parts.working: 1 factor + 1 explanation, twice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by effective demand.
parts.answer: The desire for a good backed by the ability (and willingness) to pay for it at a given price.
parts.working: 1 want; 1 ability to pay.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the market demand for school uniforms in a town may be less than the number of children who need a uniform.
parts.answer: Some families cannot afford the price, so their need is not effective demand and is not counted in the market demand curve.
parts.working: 1 need ≠ demand; 1 ability to pay.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two non-price factors that could change the market demand for school uniforms in the town.
parts.answer: e.g. number of children of school age (population); household incomes; a school changing its uniform rules; price of second-hand uniforms (substitute); a government voucher.
parts.working: 1 factor + 1 explanation, twice.

practice.stem: Invented data. Over one year the average price of cooking oil in Pakistan rose by 35% while the quantity bought fell by 5%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether these data are consistent with a downward-sloping demand curve.
parts.answer: Yes: a higher price with a lower quantity bought fits a movement up along a downward-sloping demand curve, e.g. caused by a fall in supply.
parts.working: 1 price up, quantity down = movement along D; 1 caused by a leftward shift of supply.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether the rise in price was more likely to result from a change in demand or a change in supply.
parts.answer: More likely a fall in supply (higher import costs, depreciation, taxes) because quantity fell; an increase in demand would raise both price and quantity. Demand may also have risen, but supply effect dominated.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): increase in demand alone → P and Q both rise, so not consistent with Q falling; decrease in supply → P up, Q down, consistent; likely causes: higher world palm-oil prices, rupee depreciation, import duties; the small fall in Q (5%) relative to the 35% price rise suggests inelastic demand. Evaluation (up to 2): both curves may have shifted (population growth raising demand while supply fell more); data cover a year and other factors change; judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data. Weekly demand and supply for a good are Qd = 1,200 − 20P and Qs = −300 + 30P, where P is in $. A rise in the cost of a raw material changes supply to Qs = −450 + 30P.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the original equilibrium price and quantity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the new equilibrium price and quantity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the vertical distance between the old and new supply curves.
parts.answer: $5 per unit
parts.working: M1 −450 + 30P = −300 + 30P′ at the same Q gives P − P′ = 150 ÷ 30. A1 $5.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the equilibrium price rose by less than the vertical shift of the supply curve.
parts.answer: Demand is not perfectly inelastic: as price rises, quantity demanded contracts, so the new equilibrium is found further down the new supply curve; only $3 of the $5 shift is passed on in the price.
parts.working: 1 demand contracts as price rises; 1 movement along demand curve, price rises only $3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the factors that may cause the supply curve of a manufactured good to shift, and consider which of these is likely to be most important for a clothing manufacturer in Faisalabad.
parts.answer: Costs of factors (wages, cotton, energy), technology/productivity, number of firms, indirect taxes and subsidies, prices of other goods the firm could make, expectations, weather for raw materials. Judgement: energy and cotton costs are likely most important for a Faisalabad textile firm, but this depends on the time period and on the share of each cost.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): shift v movement; list of factors. Analysis (3): how each shifts supply left/right. Evaluation (2): ranks factors for this firm with a reason.

practice.stem: Invented data. Over one year in Bangladesh: the average price of a smartphone fell by 10%; the number sold rose by 25%; average real incomes rose by 6%; the cost of phone components fell sharply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the data, a student calculates the price elasticity of demand for smartphones. Calculate the value the student would obtain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether the data show that the demand for smartphones is price elastic.
parts.answer: Not necessarily: PED assumes other things equal, but incomes rose (demand shifted right) and costs fell (supply shifted right) at the same time, so the observed change is a mix of a shift and a movement; the true PED could be much lower. But if the income effect was small, demand may still be elastic.
parts.working: Up to 4 analysis: both curves shifted; observed points are on different demand curves; income effect explains part of the rise in quantity. Up to 2 evaluation: need ceteris paribus data/YED estimate; judgement.

practice.stem: Five fans, A to E, want one ticket each for a qawwali concert. The most each is willing to pay is: A Rs 900, B Rs 800, C Rs 700, D Rs 600, E Rs 500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define consumer surplus.
parts.answer: The difference between the maximum amount consumers are willing to pay for a good and the price they actually pay.
parts.working: 1 willingness to pay; 1 minus the market price (area below demand curve and above price).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The tickets are priced at Rs 650. Calculate the total consumer surplus.
parts.answer: Rs 450

parts.label: c
parts.text: The organiser cuts the price to Rs 550. Calculate the new total consumer surplus.
parts.answer: Rs 800

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is producer surplus?
A the difference between a firm's total revenue and its total cost
B the difference between the price producers receive and the lowest price at which they would be willing to supply, summed over all units sold
C the amount of a good left unsold when the price is above equilibrium
D the difference between the price consumers are willing to pay and the price they actually pay
parts.answer: B the difference between the price producers receive and the lowest price at which they would be willing to supply, summed over all units sold
parts.working: Producer surplus is the area above the supply curve and below the price. A is profit; C is excess supply; D is consumer surplus.

practice.stem: Invented data. Five farmers each have one goat to sell at a cattle market. The lowest price each will accept is: F1 Rs 60,000; F2 Rs 70,000; F3 Rs 75,000; F4 Rs 85,000; F5 Rs 95,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: At a market price of Rs 80,000, state how many goats are sold and calculate the total producer surplus.
parts.answer: 3 goats; producer surplus Rs 35,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Just before Eid the price rises to Rs 90,000. Calculate the new total producer surplus.
parts.working: M1 4 sellers: 30 + 20 + 15 + 5 thousand. A1 Rs 70,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why producer surplus more than doubles even though the price rises by only 12.5%.
parts.answer: Existing sellers each gain Rs 10,000 more, and a new seller (F4) enters the market and also earns a surplus.
parts.working: 1 extra surplus on existing units; 1 extra units supplied.

practice.stem: Invented data. Daily demand for ferry trips across a harbour is P = 50 − 0.1Q, where P is the fare in $ and Q is the number of trips.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of trips and the consumer surplus when the fare is $20.
parts.answer: 300 trips; consumer surplus $4,500

parts.label: b
parts.text: The fare falls to $15. Calculate the new consumer surplus and the increase in consumer surplus.
parts.answer: $6,125; an increase of $1,625

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the two parts of the gain in consumer surplus.
parts.answer: Existing passengers pay $5 less on each of the 300 trips they already made; new passengers who value a trip between $15 and $20 now travel and gain surplus.
parts.working: 1 gain on existing units; 1 gain on new units.

practice.stem: Invented data. The most a student would pay for each cup of tea she buys in a day at a college canteen is: 1st cup Rs 300; 2nd cup Rs 220; 3rd cup Rs 150; 4th cup Rs 90.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The canteen charges Rs 120 a cup. State how many cups she buys and calculate her consumer surplus.
parts.answer: 3 cups; consumer surplus Rs 310
parts.working: M1 buys while value ≥ price: (300 − 120) + (220 − 120) + (150 − 120). A1 3 cups, Rs 310.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The price rises to Rs 160 a cup. Calculate her new consumer surplus.
parts.answer: Rs 200 (she buys 2 cups)
parts.working: M1 only 2 cups worth at least Rs 160: (300 − 160) + (220 − 160). A1 Rs 200.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the fall in her consumer surplus and explain why it is less than Rs 40 × 3 = Rs 120.
parts.answer: Rs 110. She pays Rs 40 more on each of the two cups she still buys (Rs 80), but she stops buying the third cup and loses only its surplus of Rs 30.
parts.working: 1 Rs 110; 1 third cup dropped, losing only Rs 30 not Rs 40.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a market, demand is P = 50 − 0.5Q and supply is P = 14 + 0.3Q, where P is in $ and Q in units. What is consumer surplus at equilibrium?
A $506.25
B $303.75
C $1,012.50
D $810.00

practice.stem: In the market for rooftop solar panels in Pakistan, demand is P = 120 − Q and supply is P = 20 + Q, where P is in Rs thousand per panel and Q is in thousand panels per month. Cheaper imported panels then change supply to P = Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the consumer surplus and producer surplus before the change in supply.
parts.answer: CS = Rs 1,250 million; PS = Rs 1,250 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the new consumer surplus and the change in consumer surplus.
parts.answer: New CS = Rs 1,800 million; increase of Rs 550 million

parts.label: c
parts.text: In this example producer surplus also rises. Explain why an increase in supply does not always raise producer surplus.
parts.answer: Price falls, which cuts surplus on units already sold; extra units add surplus. If demand is price inelastic, the price fall is large and PS can fall.
parts.working: 1 lower price reduces PS on existing output; 1 extra output and lower costs add PS; 1 net effect depends on PED / size of price fall (inelastic demand → PS may fall).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Demand for a good is P = 60 − 2Q, where P is in $ and Q is in units. The price falls from $30 to $20. By how much does consumer surplus increase?
A $25
B $150
C $175
D $400
parts.working: At $30, Q = 15 and CS = ½ × 15 × 30 = $225. At $20, Q = 20 and CS = ½ × 20 × 40 = $400. Increase = $175 ($150 on the 15 units already bought + $25 on the 5 new units). B counts only existing buyers; A only the new units; D is the new total.

practice.stem: Invented data. In a market, demand is P = 150 − 2Q and supply is P = 30 + Q, where P is in $ and Q is in thousand units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the original equilibrium, consumer surplus and producer surplus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Demand increases to P = 180 − 2Q. Calculate the new consumer surplus and producer surplus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why consumer surplus rises even though the price rises.
parts.answer: The increase in demand means consumers are willing to pay more for every unit (the demand curve is higher), so the gap between willingness to pay and price widens, and more units are bought.
parts.working: 1 higher willingness to pay; 1 more units bought.

practice.stem: Invented data. A small island imports all its rice. Supply to the island is perfectly elastic at the world price. Demand is Qd = 600 − 10P, where P is in $ per sack and Q is sacks per week.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the quantity imported and the consumer surplus at a world price of $20.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The world price rises to $26. Calculate the fall in consumer surplus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why producer surplus is zero in this market.
parts.answer: Supply is perfectly elastic: every unit is supplied at exactly the price received, so there is no gap between price and the minimum price sellers will accept.
parts.working: 1 perfectly elastic supply; 1 price = supply price for every unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why, for the same fall in price, the gain in consumer surplus is larger when demand is price elastic than when it is price inelastic.
parts.answer: Every consumer gains the price cut on units already bought (same in both cases if the starting quantity is equal). With elastic demand many more extra units are bought, each giving extra surplus, so the extra triangle of surplus is bigger.
parts.working: 1 gain on existing units; 1 extra units bought; 1 elastic → larger extension of demand; 1 larger additional area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether consumer surplus is a good measure of the benefit consumers get from a market.
parts.answer: It measures willingness to pay above price, so it captures benefit in money terms; but willingness to pay depends on income (rich consumers count more), consumers may lack information, and it ignores external effects.
parts.working: Up to 2 for strengths; up to 2 for limitations and judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether an increase in demand for a product always benefits both consumers and producers. Use the concepts of consumer surplus and producer surplus in your answer.
parts.answer: Producers gain (higher price and output → PS rises). Consumers: total CS may rise or fall — existing buyers pay more, but more buyers enter; outcome depends on PES and the cause of the demand increase. Not always both.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides with a diagram where relevant and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. Analysis: diagram with D shifting right; PS clearly rises (higher P and Q); CS: original buyers lose from higher price, new demand curve gives new CS triangle — with a parallel shift and elastic supply CS rises; with perfectly inelastic supply price rises and CS of original buyers falls. Consider cause: tastes (welfare of new buyers counts), population growth. Evaluation: depends on PES (time period, spare capacity), size of shift, whether a maximum price or monopoly exists; distribution between consumer groups; short run vs long run as supply responds. Judgement: producers almost always gain; consumers only sometimes.

practice.stem: Invented data. In a used-phone market in Nairobi there are six buyers and six sellers, each wanting to trade one phone. Maximum prices buyers will pay: B1 $120, B2 $110, B3 $95, B4 $80, B5 $70, B6 $55. Minimum prices sellers will accept: S1 $40, S2 $60, S3 $75, S4 $85, S5 $100, S6 $115.

parts.label: a
parts.text: At a price of $82, state how many phones are bought and sold.
parts.working: 1: buyers B1–B3 and sellers S1–S3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate consumer surplus and producer surplus at a price of $82.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that total surplus would be the same at any price at which the market clears, and calculate it.
parts.answer: Total surplus = (120 + 110 + 95) − (40 + 60 + 75) = $150; a different clearing price only transfers surplus between buyers and sellers.
parts.working: M1 total = sum of values − sum of costs of traded units; A1 150; B1 price change is a transfer.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why B4 and S4 do not trade with each other.
parts.answer: B4 values a phone at $80 but S4 will not sell for less than $85, so there is no price that benefits both: trading would reduce total surplus.
parts.working: 1 value < minimum price; 1 no mutually beneficial price.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a fall in the cost of producing a good benefits consumers more than producers.
parts.answer: A cost fall shifts supply right: price falls, quantity rises. Consumers gain CS (lower price, more units). Producers lose from the lower price but gain from lower costs and extra sales. The split depends on the relative elasticities: inelastic demand/elastic supply → most of the gain goes to consumers; elastic demand/inelastic supply → producers keep more. Market structure and time period also matter.
parts.working: AO1/AO2 (up to 8): diagram described; CS and PS areas before/after; role of PED and PES in the size of the price fall; examples. AO3 (up to 4): conditions under which each group gains more; short v long run (entry); competition; reasoned conclusion.

practice.stem: Invented data. In a market, demand is P = 200 − 2Q and supply is P = 20 + 4Q, where P is in $ and Q is in units. New technology lowers costs, and supply becomes P = 2 + 4Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium price, quantity, consumer surplus and producer surplus before and after the fall in costs.
parts.working: M1 200 − 2Q = 20 + 4Q → Q = 30; A1 CS and PS before; M1 200 − 2Q = 2 + 4Q → Q = 33; A1 CS and PS after.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in consumer surplus and in producer surplus.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The cost per unit fell by $18 but the price fell by only $6. Explain why, and link this to your answer to (b).
parts.answer: Demand (slope 2) is flatter than supply (slope 4) here, so demand is relatively more responsive; most of the cost saving is kept by producers rather than passed on as lower prices, so producer surplus rises by more.
parts.working: 1 relative slopes/elasticities; 1 only one-third of the cost fall passed on; 1 link to larger PS gain.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A supply curve is a straight line that passes through the origin. What is its price elasticity of supply?
A 0 at every price
B equal to 1 at every price
C greater than 1 at every price
D different at every point on the curve
parts.answer: B equal to 1 at every price
parts.working: Along a straight line from the origin, Q is proportional to P, so any percentage change in price gives the same percentage change in quantity: PES = 1. D is the common trap: the slope can differ between such lines but PES is still 1.

practice.stem: Invented data. Processors in Multan supply 8,000 kg of mango pulp a month at Rs 120 per kg. The price elasticity of supply of mango pulp over one month is 0.5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price per kg needed to raise the quantity supplied to 9,000 kg a month.
parts.answer: Rs 150 per kg (a 25% rise)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether supply is price elastic or price inelastic and explain what this means.
parts.answer: Inelastic: quantity supplied rises by a smaller percentage than the price.
parts.working: 1 inelastic; 1 meaning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a price elasticity of supply of zero.
parts.answer: Quantity supplied does not change at all when price changes (perfectly inelastic; vertical supply curve).
parts.working: 1 no change in Qs; 1 vertical curve.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the supply of hand-knotted carpets is price inelastic.
parts.answer: Each carpet takes months to make, so output cannot be increased quickly; skilled weavers are scarce and take years to train; little spare capacity; carpets cannot easily be stockpiled in advance in many designs.
parts.working: 1 reason + 1 explanation, twice.

practice.stem: Invented data. Egg farms near Rawalpindi supply 50,000 dozen eggs a week. The price elasticity of supply of eggs over six months is estimated at 1.4. The price of eggs rises by 10%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected percentage change in quantity supplied and the new quantity supplied.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the supply of eggs is price elastic over a period of several months.
parts.answer: Farmers can add laying hens fairly quickly and housing/feed are readily available, so output can be expanded.
parts.working: 1 reason; 1 explanation linked to time.

practice.stem: The wholesale price of chicken in Lahore rises from Rs 600 to Rs 690 per kg. Over the next fortnight the quantity supplied rises from 20,000 kg to 21,500 kg per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of supply of chicken.
parts.answer: PES = 0.5

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the supply of chicken is price inelastic in the short run.
parts.answer: Any two explained: time needed to raise birds (several weeks); limited shed capacity; chicken is perishable, so stocks cannot be held; feed and chicks must be ordered in advance.
parts.working: Up to 2 each: reason identified + explained link to slow response of quantity supplied.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The price of a good rises by 25%. The quantity supplied rises from 400 units to 460 units. What is the price elasticity of supply?
A 0.15
B 0.6
C 1.67
D 2.4
parts.working: %ΔQs = 60 ÷ 400 = 15%; PES = 15 ÷ 25 = 0.6 (inelastic). C inverts the formula (25 ÷ 15).

practice.stem: Invented data. Two straight-line supply curves: S1: Qs = 20 + 4P and S2: Qs = −30 + 3P, where P is in $ and Q in units. Point price elasticity of supply = (ΔQ ÷ ΔP) × (P ÷ Q).

parts.label: a
parts.text: For supply curve S1, calculate the price elasticity of supply at P = 10. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For supply curve S2, calculate the price elasticity of supply at P = 20.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the point where a straight-line supply curve meets the axes shows whether supply is elastic or inelastic.
parts.answer: A straight supply curve that cuts the quantity axis (positive Q intercept, like S1) is inelastic at every price; one that cuts the price axis (like S2) is elastic at every price; one through the origin has PES = 1.
parts.working: 1 quantity-axis intercept → inelastic; 1 price-axis intercept → elastic; 1 origin → unit elastic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the price elasticity of supply of rented flats in Islamabad differs between the momentary period, the short run and the long run.
parts.answer: Momentary: fixed number of flats, PES ≈ 0. Short run: owners can rent out spare rooms or convert houses, so PES rises a little. Long run: new blocks can be built, so supply becomes much more elastic.
parts.working: 1 each period correctly described; 1 reason (time to build / factor mobility).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a rise in demand for rented flats will mainly raise rents or mainly increase the number of flats available.
parts.answer: In the short run supply is inelastic, so mainly rents rise; in the long run builders respond and the number of flats rises, limiting the rent rise; depends on land availability, planning rules and cost of finance.
parts.working: Up to 2 analysis; up to 2 evaluation and judgement.

practice.stem:
Invented estimates of price elasticity of supply:
Rice: short run 0.3, long run 1.2
Cement: short run 0.8, long run 2.5
Rented flats: short run 0.1, long run 0.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: The price of each good rises by 20%. Calculate the percentage change in the quantity of cement supplied in the short run and in the long run.
parts.answer: Short run +16%; long run +50%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times larger the long-run response of rented flats is than the short-run response.
parts.answer: 9 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why each product's supply is more elastic in the long run.
parts.answer: Given more time, firms can expand capacity (new kilns, new building, more land planted), hire and train workers, and new firms can enter the market.
parts.working: 1 each for up to three relevant points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: During a summer festival the demand for hotel rooms in Hunza rises sharply. Explain why the price elasticity of supply of hotel rooms means that room prices rise sharply.
parts.answer: The number of rooms is fixed in the short run (PES close to zero), so the rise in demand cannot be met by more rooms; the shortage is removed only by a large rise in price.
parts.working: 1 PES low; 1 reason (fixed rooms, can't build quickly); 1 demand shifts right along steep supply curve; 1 large price rise, small quantity rise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether hotels in Hunza could make their supply more price elastic.
parts.answer: They could add temporary capacity (tents, renting homes), keep spare rooms, use flexible staff; but land, planning limits and seasonal demand make permanent extra rooms unprofitable.
parts.working: Up to 2 ways; up to 2 evaluation/judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define price elasticity of supply.
parts.answer: The responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in the price of the good: %ΔQs ÷ %ΔP.
parts.working: 1 responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price; 1 formula.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether the price elasticity of supply of manufactured goods is always greater than that of agricultural goods.
parts.answer: Usually yes in the short run (factories can add shifts, use stocks; crops have long growing periods and are perishable), but not always: factories at full capacity, complex goods like aircraft or chips have very inelastic supply, while some farm products (poultry, vegetables in greenhouses, stored grain) can respond quickly.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): factors – time to produce, spare capacity, stocks, factor mobility; manufacturing usually has stocks and spare capacity → elastic; agriculture has growing seasons, perishability, land constraints → inelastic. Evaluation (up to 2): counter-examples (full capacity, specialised inputs, semiconductors; stored wheat, fast-growing crops); depends on time period; judgement 'not always'.

practice.stem: Invented data. The supply of a good is Qs = 50 + 2.5P, where P is in $ and Q is in units per week.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the quantity supplied at P = 40 and at P = 60.
parts.working: 1 both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of supply for the rise from P = 40 to P = 60 using the original values as the base. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of supply for the same change using the midpoint (average) values as the base. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the price elasticity of supply is less than 1 at every price on this supply curve.
parts.answer: The curve cuts the quantity axis at Q = 50 (positive intercept), so at any price Q is more than 2.5 × P and PES = 2.5P ÷ (50 + 2.5P) < 1.
parts.working: 1 positive quantity intercept; 1 algebraic or diagrammatic reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether price elasticity of supply is more important than price elasticity of demand in explaining large changes in the prices of food.
parts.answer: Food supply is inelastic in the short run (growing seasons, weather), so shifts in supply (floods, drought) or demand cause large price swings; but inelastic demand (necessity) also magnifies supply shocks. Both matter: the size of a price change depends on both elasticities and on the size of the shift. Judgement, e.g. PES is the more important for weather shocks, PED for demand-side shocks.
parts.working: AO1/AO2 (up to 8): definitions; reasons food PES and PED are both low; supply shift with inelastic demand → big price change; demand shift with inelastic supply → big price change; examples. AO3 (up to 4): depends on source of the shock, time period, storage and trade; reasoned conclusion.

practice.stem: Invented data for a country. The price farmers receive for wheat rose by 40% and then stayed at the new level. Wheat output rose by 2% in the first year and by a total of 18% after three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of supply of wheat over one year and over three years, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: One year: 0.05; three years: 0.45

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether allowing food prices to rise is a good way to increase the supply of food.
parts.answer: Higher prices give farmers an incentive to expand (PES rises to 0.45 over three years), but the response is slow and small, poor consumers suffer high prices in the meantime, and farmers may lack credit, land or water; other measures (research, irrigation) may work better.
parts.working: Up to 4 analysis using the data (incentive function, time lags, low PES); up to 2 evaluation and judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what determines the price elasticity of supply of a product, and consider whether a firm with spare capacity will always have elastic supply.
parts.answer: Determinants: time period, spare capacity, stocks/ability to store, mobility of factors, length of production process, ease of entry. Spare capacity usually makes supply elastic, but not if a key input (skilled labour, a raw material) is scarce, if costs rise sharply as output rises, or if the firm expects the price rise to be temporary.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): definition and determinants. Analysis (3): how each raises or lowers PES. Evaluation (2): limits to the spare-capacity argument and judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the three functions of the price mechanism.
parts.answer: Signalling, incentive (transmission of preferences), rationing.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how price performs the rationing function in the market for tickets to a cricket final.
parts.answer: Seats are limited; when demand exceeds supply the price rises, so only those willing and able to pay the higher price buy tickets; demand contracts until it equals the fixed number of seats.
parts.working: 1 scarcity/excess demand; 1 price rises; 1 demand contracts to match supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the signalling function of price works when demand for rooftop solar panels in Pakistan rises.
parts.answer: Higher demand creates a shortage, so the price of panels rises; the higher price signals to sellers and importers that consumers want more panels and to consumers that panels are scarce.
parts.working: 1 demand rises; 1 price rises; 1 signal to producers; 1 signal to consumers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which producers might respond to the signal.
parts.answer: e.g. import more panels; open new assembly or installation businesses; switch resources from other products.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the incentive function of price.
parts.answer: A higher price raises the expected profit from producing a good, which encourages firms to supply more and new firms to enter.
parts.working: 1 higher price → more profit; 1 more supplied.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The price of dried apricots from Gilgit-Baltistan rises because of strong demand from abroad. Explain how the incentive function might change what local farmers produce.
parts.answer: Apricots become more profitable relative to other crops, so farmers plant more trees and dry more fruit, moving land and labour away from less profitable crops.
parts.working: 1 relative profitability; 1 more supply of apricots; 1 resources move from other uses.

practice.stem: Invented data. After floods destroy part of the crop in Punjab, the retail price of tomatoes in Lahore rises from Rs 100 to Rs 300 per kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage rise in the price of tomatoes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the higher price rations the smaller supply of tomatoes.
parts.answer: Households who are not willing or able to pay Rs 300 buy fewer tomatoes or switch to substitutes (e.g. tomato paste, yoghurt in cooking); demand contracts until it equals the reduced supply.
parts.working: 1 consumers buy less/switch; 1 contraction of demand; 1 matches the reduced supply.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the higher price acts as a signal to farmers and traders in Balochistan and Sindh where crops were not damaged.
parts.answer: The high Punjab price signals scarcity and the chance of profit, so traders transport tomatoes from undamaged areas and farmers there plant more next season.
parts.working: 1 signal of scarcity; 1 traders move supply; 1 farmers expand output.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by the price mechanism?
parts.answer: The system in which the interaction of demand and supply in markets determines prices, and those prices allocate resources.
parts.working: 1 demand and supply set prices; 1 prices allocate resources.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Identify the function of price shown in each of the following.
(i) As the price of saffron rises, some households stop buying it.
(ii) Higher lithium prices lead mining firms to open new mines.
(iii) Rice prices in Gilgit rise above those in Lahore, telling traders that rice is scarce in Gilgit.
parts.answer: (i) rationing; (ii) incentive; (iii) signalling.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the signalling, incentive and rationing functions of the price mechanism and consider how well these functions work in the market for rented housing in a fast-growing city such as Karachi.
parts.answer: Signalling: rising rents show scarcity. Incentive: higher rents encourage building and letting. Rationing: rents allocate flats to those willing and able to pay. In housing the functions work slowly because supply is inelastic, information is poor and the poor are priced out.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: definitions of the three functions. Analysis: increase in demand from migration → rents rise (signal) → landlords and developers have an incentive to build/convert property (extension of supply) → higher rents ration the existing stock. Evaluation: supply of housing is inelastic in the short run (land, planning permission, construction time); informal settlements and incomplete information; rationing by ability to pay leaves low-income families without decent housing, which may be inequitable; rent controls distort signals; judgement on 'how well'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many consumers switch from petrol cars to electric cars. Explain the likely effects on the prices of petrol cars and electric cars.
parts.answer: Demand for electric cars rises, so their price rises (shortage); demand for petrol cars falls, so their price falls (surplus).
parts.working: 1 demand shifts; 1 electric car price up; 1 petrol car price down.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the price mechanism moves factors of production between the two industries.
parts.answer: Higher profits in electric cars attract investment and raise the demand for workers with battery skills (higher wages); losses in petrol cars lead firms to cut output and release workers and capital, which move to the expanding industry.
parts.working: 1 profit signals; 1 derived demand for factors; 1 factor prices change; 1 factors move.

practice.stem: Invented data. A new university opens on the edge of a city. Within a year, rents for flats near the campus rise by 30%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the rise in rents performs the signalling and incentive functions.
parts.answer: Signal: higher rents show that flats near the campus are scarce relative to demand. Incentive: landlords earn more, so owners convert houses into flats and builders plan new flats near the campus.
parts.working: 2 signalling; 2 incentive.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider why, in the short run, the rationing function is likely to be the most important.
parts.answer: New flats take years to build, so supply is inelastic: the rent rise mainly allocates the fixed number of flats to those willing and able to pay; some students share rooms or live further away. In the long run supply responds.
parts.working: Up to 2 analysis (inelastic supply, rationing by price); up to 2 evaluation (time, planning rules, conclusion).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the price mechanism allocates goods according to ability to pay rather than need.
parts.answer: Demand curves show willingness and ability to pay; resources go to those who bid highest; people with high need but low income have little effective demand, so they are priced out.
parts.working: 1 effective demand; 1 highest bidders obtain goods; 1 low-income needs not reflected; 1 example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether this matters for bottled water after an earthquake.
parts.answer: It may: water is essential, prices may jump far above what poor victims can pay, so rationing by price is unfair; but high prices also encourage suppliers to bring water in quickly. Governments or aid agencies may prefer free distribution or rationing by quota.
parts.working: Up to 2 analysis; up to 2 evaluation and judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data. A shortage of computer chips cuts the number of new cars produced by assembly plants in Pakistan by 35%. Car makers keep their list prices unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the rationing function of price would normally deal with the shortage of new cars.
parts.answer: Excess demand would push car prices up until enough buyers drop out that demand equals the reduced supply.
parts.working: 1 excess demand; 1 price rises; 1 demand contracts to match supply.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider why car makers might keep list prices unchanged, and what happens in the market as a result.
parts.answer: Firms may fear bad publicity or want long-term goodwill; then the price does not ration, so waiting lists form and a resale market appears in which buyers pay a premium ('own money') to dealers or speculators; the premium shows the true market price.
parts.working: Up to 2 reasons for keeping prices fixed; up to 2 consequences (non-price rationing, premium, resources to middlemen).

practice.stem: Invented data. The average starting salary of software developers in Lahore rose from Rs 120,000 to Rs 150,000 a month in two years, while starting salaries in most other graduate jobs stayed the same.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the starting salary of software developers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the price mechanism in the labour market is likely to change the number of students choosing to study computing.
parts.answer: The higher salary signals a shortage of developers and gives an incentive to train; more students choose computing courses; in time supply of developers rises and the salary premium falls.
parts.working: 1 signal; 1 incentive; 1 students switch courses; 1 long-run increase in supply moderates wage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether the price mechanism allocates resources efficiently in the market for medical treatment.
parts.answer: Prices signal demand and encourage supply of doctors, clinics and medicines, rationing scarce services; but information failure (patients rely on doctors), positive externalities (vaccination), inability to pay, emergencies with very inelastic demand, and monopoly power mean the price mechanism alone is likely to under-provide and allocate unfairly. Judgement.
parts.working: AO1/AO2 (up to 8): three functions applied to medical care; reasons it may work (private clinics respond to demand); reasons it may fail (information, externalities, equity, inelastic demand). AO3 (up to 4): depends on type of treatment (cosmetic v emergency), regulation, insurance; reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the price mechanism answers the basic economic questions of what, how and for whom to produce, and consider whether it answers them fairly.
parts.answer: What: goods with high demand earn profit and are produced. How: firms choose least-cost methods, guided by factor prices. For whom: those with income and willingness to pay. Fairness: efficient in many markets, but outcomes reflect the distribution of income and wealth, so essentials may go to the rich; merit goods under-provided.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): the three questions; prices and profits. Analysis (3): signalling/incentive/rationing applied to each. Evaluation (2): efficiency v equity; judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data. In Year 1 the world price of a type of coffee was $4.00 per kg after a frost cut output. Farmers in Vietnam and Uganda planted many new trees, which take about three years to produce. World output in Year 4 was 30% higher than in Year 1 and the price was $2.50 per kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in the price of coffee between Year 1 and Year 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the price mechanism caused both the rise in output and the later fall in price.
parts.answer: The high Year 1 price signalled scarcity and gave farmers an incentive to plant more trees; because trees take about three years to bear fruit, the extra supply arrived together, shifting supply right and pushing the price down.
parts.working: 1 signal; 1 incentive; 1 time lag in supply; 1 supply shift lowers price.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether the data show that the price mechanism worked well in the coffee market.
parts.answer: It did respond: output rose 30%, ending the shortage.
