But it overshot because farmers reacted to past prices; the price fall means many farmers now earn low incomes; price swings create uncertainty. Judgement depends on time period and whether better information (futures markets) could smooth the cycle.
parts.working: Up to 4 analysis using the data; up to 2 evaluation and judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether the incentive function of prices is more important than the rationing function in dealing with the problem of scarcity.
parts.answer: Rationing allocates existing scarce goods immediately; incentive increases supply over time and so reduces scarcity itself. Importance depends on time period and PES: with inelastic supply (land, art) only rationing works; with elastic supply incentive dominates. Both rely on signalling. Judgement.
parts.working: AO1/AO2 (up to 8): explain both functions with examples; link to PES and time; show how incentive reduces future scarcity. AO3 (up to 4): conditions favouring each; equity issues of rationing; conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A consumer price index (2024 = 100) was 112.0 in 2025 and 120.4 in 2026. What was the rate of inflation in 2026?
A 7.0%
B 7.5%
C 8.4%
D 20.4%
parts.working: (120.4 − 112.0) ÷ 112.0 × 100 = 7.5%. C (8.4%) is the change in index points, not a percentage of the 2025 level; D measures the change since the base year.

practice.stem:
Invented data for a consumer price index:
Food: weight 40, price change +10%
Housing and utilities: weight 30, price change +5%
Transport: weight 20, price change +15%
Other items: weight 10, price change −2%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of the price index at the end of the year (start of year = 100).
parts.working: M1 multiply each price change by its weight: 40 × 10, 30 × 5, 20 × 15, 10 × (−2). M1 sum = 830, ÷ 100 weights = 8.3. A1 index = 108.3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why weights are used when calculating a consumer price index.
parts.answer: Households spend different shares of income on different items, so a price change in a large item (food) affects the cost of living more than one in a small item.
parts.working: 1 weights reflect share of household spending; 1 so the index measures change in cost of a typical basket accurately.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define deflation.
parts.answer: A sustained fall in the general price level, so the rate of inflation is negative.
parts.working: 1 sustained/persistent fall; 1 in the general (average) price level.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two possible consequences of deflation for an economy.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. consumers delay purchases expecting lower prices → lower AD and output; real value of debts rises → borrowers cut spending, more defaults; firms' revenues fall → wage cuts or job losses; exports become more price competitive.
parts.working: Up to 2 each: consequence identified + explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a country, inflation turns out to be much higher than anyone expected. Which group is most likely to gain?
A households that borrowed at a fixed rate of interest
B savers who hold money in fixed-interest deposits
C pensioners whose pensions are fixed in money terms
D banks that lent money at a fixed rate of interest
parts.answer: A households that borrowed at a fixed rate of interest
parts.working: Unanticipated inflation reduces the real value of debts fixed in money terms, so fixed-rate borrowers repay less in real terms. D is the main distractor: lenders at a fixed rate lose because the real value of the repayments falls. B and C lose purchasing power.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a consumer price index (CPI).
parts.answer: A weighted average of the prices of a representative basket of goods and services bought by typical households, measured against a base year that has the value 100.
parts.working: 1 weighted average of prices of a basket of consumer goods and services; 1 compared with a base year = 100.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a consumer price index may overstate the true rise in the cost of living.
parts.answer: Substitution: households switch away from items whose prices rise fastest, but the fixed basket assumes they do not. Quality: some price rises reflect better quality (e.g. phones with better cameras), which the index treats as pure inflation. Also new or cheaper outlets and new products enter the basket late.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks each for two developed reasons: substitution bias (fixed weights ignore switching to cheaper goods); quality improvements counted as price rises; new products/discount shops introduced late. 1 for identifying, 1 for explaining.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a country the annual rate of inflation falls from 9% to 4%. Which statement must be correct?
A The general price level has fallen.
B The general price level is still rising, but more slowly.
C The purchasing power of money has risen.
D The economy is experiencing deflation.
parts.answer: B The general price level is still rising, but more slowly.
parts.working: Inflation of 4% is still a rise in the average price level, just a slower one (disinflation). A and D confuse falling inflation with falling prices; C is wrong because money still loses value, only more slowly.

practice.stem: Invented data. A factory worker in Faisalabad earned Rs 50,000 a month in 2025 and Rs 56,000 a month in 2026. The consumer price index rose from 100 in 2025 to 118 in 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the worker's money wage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the worker's real wage in 2026 at 2025 prices, to the nearest rupee, and the percentage change in the real wage.
parts.answer: Rs 47,458; a fall of 5.1%

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what has happened to the worker's standard of living.
parts.answer: It has fallen: prices rose by more than the money wage, so the wage buys about 5% fewer goods and services.
parts.working: 1 real wage/purchasing power fell; 1 because inflation (18%) exceeded the money wage rise (12%).

parts.label: a
parts.text: With the help of an AD/AS diagram, explain the difference between demand-pull and cost-push inflation.
parts.answer: Demand-pull: AD shifts right faster than the economy's capacity grows → price level rises with higher real output. Cost-push: SRAS shifts left due to higher costs → price level rises while real output falls.
parts.working: 1 demand-pull: AD increases (e.g. consumer or government spending) as output nears full capacity; 1 diagram AD1→AD2, higher P and Y; 1 cost-push: higher costs (wages, imported raw materials) shift AS left; 1 diagram AS1→AS2, higher P and lower Y.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider which type of inflation is more likely in an oil-importing economy when the world price of crude oil rises by 40%.
parts.answer: Mainly cost-push: higher fuel and transport costs shift AS left. But demand-pull elements are possible if wages rise in response or the government expands spending; effect depends on oil's share of costs and the exchange rate.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): oil is an input for transport, electricity and manufacturing → costs rise → SRAS left → cost-push; import bill rises, which may reduce AD (more spending on imports), dampening demand-pull. Consideration (1+): second-round wage-price spiral; subsidies to fuel; currency movements; judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data. A retired teacher in Multan receives a fixed pension of Rs 40,000 a month from the start of 2024. Annual inflation (CPI) was 12 % in 2024, 7 % in 2025 and 5 % in 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the real value of the pension at the end of 2026, measured in prices at the start of 2024. Give your answer to the nearest rupee.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in the real value of the pension over the three years. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether linking (indexing) the pension to the consumer price index would fully protect the pensioner.
parts.answer: Indexation would keep the pension's purchasing power over the CPI basket, but not fully: the CPI basket may not match pensioners' spending (more on food and medicine), there are delays before adjustments, and it does not protect savings.
parts.working: 1 indexation keeps the money pension rising with the CPI so the real value is maintained; 1 explanation; up to 2 for consideration: pensioners' basket differs from the average (medicines, food weight higher), adjustment lags, cost to government budget, judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country Z, a technology-exporting economy, in 2026: consumer price index change −1.5 %; real GDP growth +3.8 %; unemployment rate fell from 5.2 % to 4.6 %; labour productivity growth +5.0 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the data, identify one piece of evidence that the fall in the price level in Country Z was not caused by a fall in aggregate demand.
parts.answer: Real GDP grew by 3.8 % and unemployment fell (5.2 % to 4.6 %), which would not happen if AD had fallen.
parts.working: 1 rising real output and/or falling unemployment; 1 explanation that falling AD would reduce output and raise unemployment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: With the help of an AD/AS diagram, explain how productivity growth can cause the price level to fall while real output rises.
parts.answer: Productivity gains lower unit costs and raise productive capacity, shifting SRAS (and LRAS) to the right. With AD unchanged or growing slowly, the new equilibrium has a lower price level and higher real output.
parts.working: 1 correctly labelled axes (price level, real output); 1 rightward shift of AS; 1 new equilibrium at lower price level and higher output; 1 explanation via lower costs of production per unit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the deflation in Country Z is a cause for concern.
parts.answer: Mostly benign ('good') deflation: output and employment are rising and real incomes increase. But there may be risks if households expect further price falls and delay spending, or if debtors face higher real debt burdens; the central bank may find it harder to use interest rates.
parts.working: Up to 2 for reasons it is not a concern (supply-side cause, rising living standards, competitiveness); up to 2 for possible concerns (delayed consumption, real debt, zero lower bound) with a judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a high rate of inflation is always more harmful to an economy than deflation.
parts.answer: Not always. High inflation erodes purchasing power, harms savers and fixed-income groups, reduces competitiveness and creates uncertainty; but persistent deflation can delay spending, raise real debt burdens and cause unemployment. Harm depends on the size, cause and whether it is anticipated.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides with a diagram where relevant and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. Inflation costs: menu and shoe-leather costs, redistribution from savers/lenders to borrowers, fiscal drag, loss of international competitiveness, uncertainty discouraging investment, hyperinflation risk. Deflation costs: postponed consumption, rising real value of debt, falling profits → unemployment, real interest rates rise when nominal rates can't fall below zero, deflationary spiral. Evaluation: 'good' deflation from productivity gains (AS shift right) vs 'bad' deflation from falling AD; mild, anticipated inflation is less harmful than unanticipated high inflation; effects differ for different groups; the context (debt levels, indexation). Judgement must address 'always'.

practice.stem:
Invented data for Country K:
Year: 2024, 2025, 2026
Inflation rate (%): 25, 12, 6
Central bank policy interest rate (%): 22, 18, 11

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price level at the end of 2026, taking the end of 2023 as 100. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using real interest rate ≈ nominal interest rate − inflation rate, calculate the real interest rate in 2024 and in 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the fall in inflation from 2024 to 2026 shows that the economy is performing well.
parts.answer: It helps (more stable prices, real interest rates now positive, which protects savers and confidence), but prices are still rising, high real interest rates may cut investment, output and employment, so other indicators are needed.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): lower inflation reduces uncertainty, improves competitiveness, protects real incomes; prices still rose ~48% over the three years, so living costs remain much higher; positive real rate of 5% discourages borrowing → lower AD, growth and jobs. Consideration (1+): need data on growth, unemployment, current account; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an economy, using the quantity theory of money (MV = PT), the money supply rises by 8 % in a year, the velocity of circulation is unchanged and the volume of transactions rises by 3 %. By approximately how much does the price level rise?
A 3.0 %
B 4.9 %
C 8.0 %
D 11.2 %
parts.working: P = MV ÷ T, so the new P ÷ old P = 1.08 ÷ 1.03 = 1.0485: a rise of about 4.9 % (≈ 8 % − 3 %). C ignores the growth of transactions; D adds the two changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between anticipated and unanticipated inflation, and consider which is more damaging to firms.
parts.answer: Anticipated inflation is expected and built into wage deals, prices and interest rates; unanticipated inflation is a surprise. Unanticipated inflation is usually more damaging to firms because it distorts price signals, creates uncertainty that discourages investment and can raise costs unexpectedly; but even anticipated inflation brings menu costs and loss of competitiveness if it is higher than abroad.
parts.working: Mark split (8): knowledge 3, analysis 3, evaluation 2. K: definitions of both; costs such as menu costs, shoe-leather costs, wage bargaining. A: unanticipated inflation confuses relative price signals, makes contracts and pricing risky, raises uncertainty → lower investment; firms on fixed selling contracts lose if input prices rise unexpectedly; anticipated inflation still raises menu costs and, if above trading partners, makes exports less competitive. E: depends on the rate (high anticipated inflation is still harmful), whether firms can index contracts, the exchange rate, and whether firms are borrowers (gain from surprise inflation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that inflation is always caused by excessive growth in the money supply.
parts.answer: The quantity theory (MV = PT) suggests that if V and T are stable, faster money growth raises P, so monetarists argue that sustained inflation is a monetary phenomenon. However, V is not always stable, T can grow, and inflation can start from cost-push shocks (oil, depreciation) or demand-pull from fiscal expansion; money growth may follow rather than cause inflation. A justified conclusion is that persistent high inflation usually needs monetary growth, but individual episodes have other causes.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): AO1/AO2 knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 — accurate, developed chains of reasoning with an accurate, correctly labelled diagram where relevant; AO3 evaluation up to 6 — weighs both sides, considers context and assumptions, and reaches a justified conclusion that answers the question. One-sided answers are capped at mid Level 2. Content: equation of exchange; monetarist assumptions (V and T fixed in the short run, T set by real factors); Fisher/quantity theory chain M↑ → P↑; examples of hyperinflation with rapid money creation. Counter-arguments: velocity changes (e.g. with digital payments or a fall in confidence); cost-push inflation from oil prices, wages or depreciation shown on AD/AS; demand-pull from consumer or government spending; money supply may be endogenous (banks lend as demand rises); spare capacity means extra money raises output not prices. Evaluation: distinction between triggers and sustained inflation; time period; Keynesian vs monetarist views; judgement on 'always'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an economy, consumption is $600bn, investment $150bn, government spending $200bn, exports $250bn and imports $300bn. What is aggregate demand?
A $600bn
B $900bn
C $1,200bn
D $1,500bn
parts.answer: B $900bn
parts.working: AD = C + I + G + (X − M) = 600 + 150 + 200 + (250 − 300) = $900bn. D adds imports instead of subtracting them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the aggregate demand curve slopes downwards from left to right.
parts.answer: A lower price level raises real wealth (real balance effect), lowers interest rates (more borrowing and spending) and makes exports cheaper relative to imports, so real expenditure rises.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three explained effects: wealth/real balance effect; interest rate effect; international trade (competitiveness) effect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two causes of a rightward shift of the long-run aggregate supply curve.
parts.answer: Any two: more or better-quality labour (migration, education, training); more capital (investment); new technology; discovery of natural resources; supply-side reforms raising productivity.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: With the help of an AD/AS diagram, explain the effect of a fall in consumer confidence on the price level and real output.
parts.answer: Households spend less and save more → consumption falls → AD shifts left → lower price level and lower real output.
parts.working: 1 consumption falls; 1 AD shifts left (diagram with labelled axes); 1 price level falls (or rises more slowly); 1 real output falls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two components of aggregate demand other than consumption.
parts.answer: Any two: investment; government spending; net exports (exports minus imports).
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change causes a movement along an economy's aggregate demand curve rather than a shift of the curve?
A a fall in the general price level
B a rise in government spending on hospitals
C a fall in consumer confidence
D a rise in incomes in the country's main export markets
parts.answer: A a fall in the general price level
parts.working: The AD curve shows real output demanded at each price level, so a change in the price level moves the economy along it. B, C and D change spending at every price level, so they shift AD.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) and long-run aggregate supply (LRAS).
parts.answer: SRAS shows output firms supply at each price level when input prices (e.g. money wages) are fixed; LRAS shows the economy's productive capacity when all factor prices have adjusted, set by the quantity and quality of resources.
parts.working: 1 SRAS: input/factor prices fixed in the short run; 1 LRAS: productive potential/all inputs adjust.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two changes that would shift the short-run aggregate supply curve to the right.
parts.answer: Any two: a fall in the price of imported raw materials or energy; lower money wages; a cut in indirect taxes on firms or a subsidy to producers; an appreciation that lowers import costs.
parts.working: 1 each for two valid changes.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country J. At a price level of 100 real output demanded was $500bn in January. In July real output demanded at the same price level of 100 was $540bn.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify whether the change between the two dates is a movement along the AD curve or a shift of the AD curve.
parts.answer: A shift (to the right).
parts.working: 1 shift: real output demanded is higher at the same price level of 100.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in real output demanded at a price level of 100.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two possible causes of this change.
parts.answer: Any two: lower interest rates; higher government spending; tax cuts; higher consumer or business confidence; higher foreign incomes raising exports.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would shift the short-run aggregate supply curve to the left?
A a rise in consumer confidence
B a fall in the world price of oil
C a rise in money wage rates with no change in productivity
D a cut in the rate of income tax
parts.answer: C a rise in money wage rates with no change in productivity
parts.working: Higher wages without higher productivity raise unit labour costs, so firms supply less at each price level: SRAS shifts left. A and D shift AD, not SRAS; B lowers costs and shifts SRAS to the right.

practice.stem:
Invented data for Country Q, $bn at constant prices:
2025: C 420, I 95, G 130, X 160, M 175
2026: C 438, I 88, G 150, X 172, M 186

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate aggregate demand in 2025 and 2026 and the percentage change. Give the percentage to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the component whose change made the largest contribution to the change in AD.
parts.answer: Government spending (+$20bn).

parts.label: c
parts.text: With the help of an AD/AS diagram, explain the likely effect of this change in AD on the price level and real output.
parts.answer: AD shifts right: real output rises and the price level rises; the split depends on spare capacity (flat section → mainly output, near full capacity → mainly prices).
parts.working: 1 AD shifts right (diagram labelled price level and real output/real GDP); 1 real output rises; 1 price level rises; 1 relative size depends on how close the economy is to full capacity / shape of AS.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An economy is on its vertical long-run aggregate supply curve. According to the classical (monetarist) view, what is the long-run effect of an increase in aggregate demand?
A a higher price level and the same real output
B a higher price level and higher real output
C the same price level and higher real output
D a lower price level and higher real output
parts.answer: A a higher price level and the same real output
parts.working: With LRAS vertical at full-employment output, extra AD can only raise the price level in the long run. B describes the short run (upward-sloping SRAS) or a Keynesian intermediate range.

practice.stem: Invented data. Workers' remittances to Country P rose from $27bn in 2025 to $31bn in 2026. GDP in 2026 was $370bn.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate workers' remittances as a percentage of GDP in 2026. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the rise in remittances affects aggregate demand.
parts.answer: Remittances raise households' disposable incomes, so consumption (C) rises and AD shifts to the right.
parts.working: 1 higher household income; 1 higher consumption → AD shifts right.

parts.label: c
parts.text: With the help of an AD/AS diagram, consider the effect of the rise in remittances on the price level and real output if the economy is close to full capacity.
parts.answer: AD shifts right along a steep part of AS, so the price level rises a lot and real output only a little. Effect smaller if much of the extra spending goes on imports or is saved; larger output effect if there is spare capacity.
parts.working: 1 diagram with AD shift; 1 steep AS near capacity → mainly higher price level; 1 small output rise; 1 consideration (leakage into imports/saving, spare capacity in some sectors, possible supply response).

practice.stem: Invented extract. Severe floods in a farming region destroyed 30 % of the cotton and rice crop, washed away roads and bridges and damaged irrigation canals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the likely effect of the floods on short-run and long-run aggregate supply.
parts.answer: SRAS shifts left at once because crop losses and damaged transport raise costs and cut output; LRAS also shifts left because capital (roads, irrigation) and productive land are destroyed, reducing productive capacity until rebuilt.
parts.working: 1 SRAS left; 1 reason (higher costs/less output); 1 LRAS left; 1 reason (loss of capital and land).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether government spending on reconstruction can offset the effects of the floods.
parts.answer: Reconstruction raises AD at once and, once completed, restores LRAS. But it takes time, may raise inflation if supply is still constrained, needs finance (borrowing or aid) and may import materials; a lasting offset depends on building better infrastructure.
parts.working: Up to 2 for how it helps (AD rises, LRAS restored, jobs); up to 2 for limits (time lags, inflationary pressure, funding, import leakage) with a judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a large rise in world oil prices shifts the short-run aggregate supply curve of an oil-importing economy.
parts.answer: Oil is a key input in transport, power and manufacturing, so firms' costs of production rise and they supply less at each price level: SRAS shifts left.
parts.working: 1 higher costs of production; 1 SRAS shifts left (upwards).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether a large rise in world oil prices is likely to reduce real output more than it raises the price level in an oil-importing economy.
parts.answer: Both effects occur (stagflation). Which is larger depends on the slope of AD and AS, whether AD also falls as the import bill rises, policy responses and how long the shock lasts.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): SRAS left → higher price level and lower real output; AD may also fall because spending leaks to imports and real incomes fall → output falls further while dampening the price rise; if AD is steep/inelastic, effect is mainly on price; second-round wage rises push prices further. Evaluation (up to 2): depends on oil intensity, fuel subsidies, monetary policy response (rate rises cut output more), exchange rate, whether the shock is temporary; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how an increase in investment affects both aggregate demand and aggregate supply, and consider whether its effect on the price level is likely to be inflationary.
parts.answer: Investment is a component of AD (short run: AD right) and adds to productive capacity (long run: LRAS right). Price level rises in the short run but may be stable or fall in the long run if capacity rises enough.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: investment as spending on capital goods; AD = C + I + G + (X − M); LRAS/capacity. Analysis: higher I → AD shifts right → higher price level and output (with multiplier); new capital raises productivity → LRAS shifts right → lower price level, higher output. Evaluation: timing (AD effect immediate, AS effect delayed); type of investment (replacement vs new capacity); spare capacity; size of the shifts; judgement on whether net effect is inflationary.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using a Keynesian aggregate supply curve, how the effect of an increase in aggregate demand depends on the amount of spare capacity in the economy, and consider whether the Keynesian view is more realistic than the classical view.
parts.answer: Keynesian AS is horizontal at low output (large spare capacity: AD rise increases output, not prices), upward-sloping as bottlenecks appear (both rise), and vertical at full employment (only prices rise). Whether this is more realistic than the classical vertical LRAS depends on the time period and how flexible wages and prices are.
parts.working: Mark split (8): knowledge 3, analysis 3, evaluation 2. K: shape of Keynesian AS (three ranges); classical SRAS/LRAS. A: in deep recession unemployed resources mean extra AD raises real output; nearer full employment, bottlenecks raise costs; at full capacity only inflation. E: wages are sticky downward so Keynesian view fits the short run/recessions; classical view fits the long run when expectations adjust; evidence from recessions vs booms; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether supply-side shocks are more damaging to an economy than demand-side shocks.
parts.answer: Negative supply shocks (oil, drought, war) shift SRAS left, raising prices and cutting output at the same time (stagflation), which is hard for policy to fix. Negative demand shocks lower output and prices, which can be offset by fiscal and monetary stimulus. However, deep demand shocks can last longer and cause hysteresis, and some supply shocks are temporary. Judgement depends on size, duration and whether LRAS is affected.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides, diagram where relevant, and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is only asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. Content: AD/AS diagrams for both; supply shock → higher price level + lower output, policy dilemma (stimulus worsens inflation, tightening worsens recession); demand shock → lower output, lower inflation, policy can respond with lower interest rates/higher spending. Evaluation: permanent supply shocks shift LRAS; prolonged demand shortfalls can damage LRAS via hysteresis; policy room (debt, zero rates); open economy effects.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's nominal GDP rises from $800bn to $880bn in a year. Over the same year the GDP deflator rises from 100 to 106. What is the rate of real economic growth, correct to one decimal place?
A 3.8%
B 4.0%
C 10.0%
D 16.6%
parts.working: Real GDP = 880 ÷ 1.06 = $830.2bn (at last year's prices); (830.2 − 800) ÷ 800 × 100 = 3.8%. B uses the shortcut 10% − 6%, which is only an approximation and is not correct to one decimal place; C is nominal growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between actual economic growth and potential economic growth.
parts.answer: Actual growth: an increase in real GDP (output actually produced). Potential growth: an increase in the economy's productive capacity (LRAS/PPC shifts out).
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how more spending on education can lead to potential economic growth.
parts.answer: Education raises skills and the productivity of labour, increasing the quality of the factor labour; the productive capacity of the economy rises, shifting LRAS (or the PPC) outward.
parts.working: 1 better skills/human capital; 1 higher labour productivity; 1 LRAS or PPC shifts right/outward (over time).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's real GDP grows at a steady 3.5 % a year. Approximately how many years will it take for real GDP to double?
A 10 years
B 20 years
C 35 years
D 70 years
parts.answer: B 20 years
parts.working: Using the rule of 70, 70 ÷ 3.5 = 20 years (exactly ln 2 ÷ ln 1.035 ≈ 20.1). C simply uses 10 × the growth rate; D is the rule-of-70 number itself, ignoring the growth rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between nominal and real economic growth.
parts.answer: Nominal growth is the rise in GDP at current prices, including price rises; real growth removes the effect of inflation and measures the change in the volume of output.
parts.working: 1 nominal at current prices; 1 real adjusted for inflation/volume.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a year, nominal GDP rises by 14 % and the GDP deflator rises by 9 %. Calculate the rate of real economic growth. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.working: M1 1.14 ÷ 1.09 = 1.0459. A1 4.6 % (not 5 %, which is only an approximation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of the recovery phase of the economic cycle.
parts.answer: Any two: real GDP starts to rise again; unemployment begins to fall; business and consumer confidence improve; investment picks up; spare capacity starts to be used.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a large fall in the number of working-age people in a country could reduce its potential growth.
parts.answer: Fewer workers means a smaller labour force, a factor of production, so the productive capacity of the economy grows more slowly (LRAS/PPC shifts outward less or inward), unless productivity rises enough to compensate.
parts.working: 1 smaller labour supply; 1 less productive capacity/LRAS; 1 development (skills lost, unless offset by productivity or capital).

practice.stem:
Invented data for Country R:
Year: 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026
Real GDP ($bn): 300, 309, 315, 330
Population (million): 200, 204, 208, 212

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of economic growth in 2026. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in real GDP per head between 2023 and 2026. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a rise in real GDP per head may overstate the improvement in living standards.
parts.answer: Average figure hides inequality; ignores pollution, longer working hours and loss of leisure; output may be military or exports rather than consumer goods; informal economy changes; quality of life measures like health are excluded.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three explained points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one cause of actual economic growth that comes from the demand side of the economy.
parts.answer: e.g. a rise in consumer spending or exports increases AD; if there is spare capacity, firms raise output so real GDP grows.
parts.working: 1 demand-side cause; 1 explained link to higher real output when spare capacity exists.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether an increase in government spending on roads and electricity grids will lead to sustained economic growth.
parts.answer: Short run: AD rises (actual growth); long run: lower transport and energy costs raise productivity, shifting LRAS → potential growth. Sustained only if projects are well chosen, completed and maintained, and financed without crowding out or debt problems.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): AD effect with multiplier; supply-side effect on productivity and capacity; attracts investment. Consideration (1+): time lags, poor project choice/corruption, borrowing costs, maintenance; judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country E, real GDP ($bn): 2024 actual 590, potential 600; 2025 actual 625, potential 618; 2026 actual 640, potential 637.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output gap in each year as a percentage of potential GDP. Give your answers to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what a positive output gap suggests about inflation.
parts.answer: Actual output is above sustainable capacity, so resources are over-used, costs and wages rise and demand-pull inflation is likely.
parts.working: 1 output above potential/over-full use of resources; 1 upward pressure on prices.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the economy was performing well in 2026.
parts.answer: Actual growth was (640 − 625)/625 = 2.4 % while potential grew by about 3.1 %, so the gap closed: output close to capacity with low inflation pressure. But growth slowed, and the data say nothing about unemployment, inflation or distribution.
parts.working: 1 uses data (gap narrowing / close to potential); 1 slower growth than potential; 1 judgement noting missing data.

practice.stem: Invented data. Quarterly real GDP growth (%) for Country H: Q1 +0.6, Q2 +0.2, Q3 −0.3, Q4 −0.5, Q5 +0.1, Q6 +0.8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the common definition of a recession, identify when Country H was in recession.
parts.answer: Quarters 3 and 4 (two consecutive quarters of negative real growth).
parts.working: 1 Q3–Q4 with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Taking real GDP in the quarter before Quarter 1 as 100, calculate real GDP at the end of Quarter 6. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two likely effects on firms of the economy entering the recession phase of the economic cycle.
parts.answer: Falling sales and profits as demand drops, leading to cuts in output and jobs; firms postpone investment because of spare capacity and pessimism; some go out of business or face cash-flow problems.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed effects (effect + reason).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, with the help of an LRAS or production possibility curve diagram, how technological progress causes economic growth, and consider whether it always increases employment.
parts.answer: New technology raises productivity, shifting LRAS (or the PPC) outwards so potential output rises; if AD grows too, actual output rises. Employment may rise as new industries and higher incomes create jobs, but labour-saving technology can cause structural unemployment where skills do not match.
parts.working: Mark split (8): knowledge 3, analysis 3, evaluation 2. K: definition of economic growth; diagram with LRAS/PPC outward shift. A: higher output per worker, lower costs, new products; income effect creating demand and jobs. E: labour-saving vs labour-using technology; retraining and mobility; short run vs long run; whether AD keeps pace.

practice.stem: Invented data. Country L has real GDP per head of $1,500 growing at 6 % a year. Country M has real GDP per head of $12,000 growing at 1.5 % a year. Assume these growth rates continue for 10 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate real GDP per head in each country after 10 years. Give your answers to the nearest dollar.
parts.answer: Country L $2,686; Country M $13,926

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the absolute gap in real GDP per head after 10 years, and the ratio of M's to L's real GDP per head. Give the ratio to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Gap $11,240 (up from $10,500); ratio 5.2 (down from 8.0)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether Country L is catching up with Country M.
parts.answer: In relative terms yes (ratio falls from 8.0 to 5.2) but in absolute dollars the gap widens. Catching up depends on L keeping its higher growth rate; figures ignore distribution, prices (PPP) and quality of life.
parts.working: 1 relative catch-up; 1 absolute gap widens; 1 judgement/limitation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether the benefits of economic growth always outweigh its costs for a developing economy such as Pakistan.
parts.answer: Growth brings higher incomes, jobs, tax revenue for health and education and less poverty; costs include pollution, depletion of resources, inequality, inflation and current-account pressures. Benefits usually outweigh costs for a low-income country, but not always: it depends on the type, sustainability and distribution of growth.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides with a diagram where relevant and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. Benefits: higher real incomes and living standards, lower unemployment, more tax revenue without higher tax rates, reduced poverty. Costs: environmental damage (smog, water stress), resource depletion, rising inequality, inflation if AD outruns capacity, import surge and current-account deficits (boom–bust cycles), urban congestion. Evaluation: growth led by consumption/imports vs by investment/exports; whether gains reach the poor; opportunity cost of investment (less consumption now); sustainability; policy can reduce costs. Judgement must address 'always'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether investment in human capital is more important than investment in physical capital for long-term economic growth in a country such as Pakistan.
parts.answer: Both shift LRAS right. Human capital (education, health, skills) raises labour productivity, helps adopt technology and has long-lasting effects; physical capital (machines, power, roads) is needed for workers to be productive and can raise output faster. In Pakistan low literacy and skills gaps suggest high returns to human capital, but energy and infrastructure shortages also bind. Judgement: they are complements; priority depends on the main bottleneck.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides, diagram where relevant, and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is only asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. Content: LRAS/PPC shift; productivity chains for each; diminishing returns to physical capital alone; long time lags for education; brain drain risk; quality of schooling; financing constraints. Evaluation: complementarity, time period, evidence about bottlenecks, role of private sector and FDI.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether economic growth led by export manufacturing, as in Bangladesh's garment industry, is likely to be sustainable.
parts.answer: Export manufacturing raises AD, employment, foreign exchange and skills, and can attract investment. Sustainability is threatened by dependence on one product and few markets, low wages as the main advantage (lost as wages rise or to automation), environmental damage, and loss of trade preferences. Sustained growth needs diversification, upgrading and investment in education and infrastructure.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): AO1/AO2 knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 — accurate, developed chains of reasoning with an accurate, correctly labelled diagram where relevant; AO3 evaluation up to 6 — weighs both sides, considers context and assumptions, and reaches a justified conclusion that answers the question. One-sided answers are capped at mid Level 2. Content: actual and potential growth; export-led growth through X in AD and the multiplier; economies of scale; learning by doing; FDI. Risks: narrow export base, world demand shocks, rising wages/competition from other low-wage countries, automation, environmental and social costs (pollution, working conditions), reliance on imported inputs. Evaluation: meaning of 'sustainable' (lasting vs environmental); policy responses; evidence from East Asian economies; justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Invented data for three countries in 2026: Country A investment 15 % of GDP, real growth 3 %; Country B investment 30 % of GDP, real growth 6 %; Country C investment 25 % of GDP, real growth 2 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the investment share of GDP to the growth rate for each country. Give your answers to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Country A 5.0; Country B 5.0; Country C 12.5

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, consider whether higher investment always leads to faster economic growth.
parts.answer: Not always: A and B suggest more investment brings faster growth, but C invests 25 % of GDP yet grows only 2 %. The quality and type of investment (e.g. housing or unproductive projects), the education of the workforce and the level of AD also matter; only three countries and one year are shown.
parts.working: 1 uses A/B as support; 1 uses C as counter-evidence; 1 reason why investment may not raise growth (quality, diminishing returns, lack of human capital, AD weak); 1 judgement noting limits of the data.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country has a labour force of 64 million, of whom 59.2 million are employed. What is the unemployment rate?
A 4.8%
B 7.5%
C 8.1%
D 92.5%
parts.working: Unemployed = 64 − 59.2 = 4.8 million. Rate = 4.8 ÷ 64 × 100 = 7.5%. C divides by the number employed instead of the labour force; D is the employment rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify the type of unemployment in each case:
(1) Weavers in Faisalabad lose their jobs when mills install automatic looms.
(2) A new graduate spends three months searching for a suitable job.
(3) Construction workers are laid off when spending falls during a recession.
parts.answer: (1) structural (technological); (2) frictional; (3) cyclical (demand-deficient)
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one consequence of high unemployment for the government's budget.
parts.answer: Tax revenue falls (less income tax and spending taxes) and spending on benefits/support rises, so the budget deficit increases.
parts.working: 1 lower tax revenue or higher welfare spending; 1 budget deficit increases / borrowing rises.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Using the International Labour Organization (ILO) definition, which person is counted as unemployed?
A a person without a job who has looked for work in the past four weeks and can start within two weeks
B a full-time university student who is not looking for work
C a part-time shop assistant who would like to work more hours
D a 62-year-old who has retired early and does not want a job
parts.answer: A a person without a job who has looked for work in the past four weeks and can start within two weeks
parts.working: The ILO measure counts people without work who are actively seeking and available to start. C is the main distractor: the person is underemployed but counts as employed. B and D are economically inactive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between frictional unemployment and structural unemployment.
parts.answer: Frictional: short-term unemployment while people move between jobs or search for work. Structural: longer-term unemployment caused by a mismatch between workers' skills or location and the jobs available, often after an industry declines.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why hotel workers in the mountain resorts of northern Pakistan may experience seasonal unemployment.
parts.answer: Demand for hotel services depends on the tourist season; in winter, when roads close and visitor numbers fall, hotels need fewer workers so staff are laid off.
parts.working: 1 demand varies with the season; 1 developed link to fewer jobs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two costs of unemployment for the people who are unemployed.
parts.answer: Loss of income lowers living standards and may cause debt or poverty; long spells cause loss of skills and confidence, making it harder to get a job (and possible health/stress problems).
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed costs: lower income/consumption; deskilling and lower future earnings; health and social effects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one cost of unemployment for the economy as a whole.
parts.answer: Lost output: the economy produces inside its PPC, so goods and services that could have been produced are lost for good (or lower tax revenue/higher benefit spending).
parts.working: 1 identification; 1 explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by underemployment.
parts.answer: People in work who want to work more hours or whose jobs do not use their skills.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the official unemployment rate in a country such as Pakistan may understate how many people lack adequate work.
parts.answer: Many people work in the informal sector for a few hours or very low pay but count as employed (underemployment); discouraged workers stop searching and are classed as inactive, not unemployed; family helpers on farms are counted as employed.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed reasons.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country S: working-age population 120 million; labour force 78 million; unemployed according to the labour force survey 5.46 million; people claiming unemployment benefits 3.12 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the unemployment rate shown by each measure.
parts.answer: Labour force survey: 7%; claimant count: 4%
parts.working: 1 5.46 ÷ 78 × 100 = 7%; 1 3.12 ÷ 78 × 100 = 4%. (Use the labour force, not the working-age population.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the claimant count measure is lower than the labour force survey measure.
parts.answer: Some unemployed people are not eligible for benefits (e.g. partner's income, recently left education, informal workers); some choose not to claim (stigma, small benefit, don't know how); the survey uses the international definition (looking for work and available).
parts.working: Up to 2 each: reason identified + explained.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country F: labour force 72 million in 2025 and 75 million in 2026; unemployment rate 6.5 % in 2025 and 6.2 % in 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of people unemployed and the number employed in each year, in millions.
parts.answer: 2025: unemployed 4.68m, employed 67.32m; 2026: unemployed 4.65m, employed 70.35m

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how employment can rise by much more than unemployment falls.
parts.answer: The labour force grew by 3 million (new entrants, migrants); most of the new jobs went to these extra people rather than to those already unemployed, so employment rose by 3.03m while unemployment fell by only 0.03m.
parts.working: 1 labour force growth; 1 use of figures.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country G in 2026: overall unemployment rate 6 %; unemployment rate among 15–24 year-olds 18 %; about 40 % of unemployed graduates studied courses with few related job openings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the youth unemployment rate with the overall unemployment rate in 2026.
parts.answer: Youth unemployment (18 %) was three times the overall rate (6 %).
parts.working: 1 for a comparison using the figures (×3 or 12 points higher).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why unemployment among young people is usually higher than among older workers.
parts.answer: Young people lack experience and skills employers want; they are often first to be laid off ('last in, first out'); they spend more time searching between first jobs (frictional); courses may not match labour market needs.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed reasons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether paying firms a subsidy for each young worker they hire is likely to reduce youth unemployment.
parts.answer: It lowers the cost of employing young people, so firms may hire more and the workers gain experience. But firms may replace older workers or hire people they would have hired anyway (deadweight); jobs may end when the subsidy ends; it is costly; it does not fix skills mismatch.
parts.working: Up to 2 for how it works; up to 2 for limitations with a judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between voluntary and involuntary unemployment, and consider whether an increase in unemployment benefits will increase unemployment.
parts.answer: Voluntary unemployment: people choose not to accept jobs at the going wage (e.g. searching for better offers or because benefits are close to wages). Involuntary: people willing to work at the going wage cannot find jobs because of too little demand. Higher benefits may raise voluntary/frictional unemployment by lengthening job search, but the effect is small if jobs are scarce, if benefits are low relative to wages or conditional on job search; benefits also support AD in recessions.
parts.working: Mark split (8): knowledge 3, analysis 3, evaluation 2. K: definitions. A: replacement ratio, longer job search, unemployment trap; benefits sustain consumption → AD. E: size of benefits relative to wages, conditions attached, state of the economy (cyclical unemployment is involuntary), better job matching may raise productivity; judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country N: unemployment rate (%) and inflation rate (%): 2020: 4.0, 6.5; 2021: 5.0, 4.5; 2022: 6.5, 3.0; 2023: 5.0, 9.0; 2024: 5.5, 11.5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the only pair of consecutive years in the data that is not consistent with a movement along a single short-run Phillips curve, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 2023 to 2024: unemployment rose (5.0 % to 5.5 %) and inflation also rose (9.0 % to 11.5 %); a short-run trade-off would need them to move in opposite directions.
parts.working: 1 correct pair (2023–2024); 1 explanation that both variables rose together (every other pair moves in opposite directions).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how changes in inflation expectations could explain the data for 2023 and 2024.
parts.answer: After inflation rose in 2023, workers and firms expected higher inflation and built it into wage claims and prices, shifting the short-run Phillips curve upward. So inflation was much higher at a given unemployment rate: at 5.0 % unemployment inflation was 9.0 % in 2023 against 4.5 % in 2021, and in 2024 inflation rose further even though unemployment rose.
parts.working: 1 expectations of inflation rise; 1 higher wage claims/price setting; 1 SRPC shifts up; 1 use of data (5.0 % unemployment with 4.5 % inflation in 2021 but 9.0 % in 2023, or both rising in 2024).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a recession causes cyclical unemployment.
parts.answer: Falling AD means firms sell less, so they need fewer workers (labour is a derived demand) and cut jobs.
parts.working: 1 fall in AD/output; 1 lower derived demand for labour → job losses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether structural unemployment is more harmful than cyclical unemployment to an economy.
parts.answer: Structural unemployment is often longer lasting and concentrated in regions/industries; skills become obsolete and it does not disappear when the economy recovers. Cyclical unemployment can be widespread and severe but usually falls as AD recovers. Judgement depends on scale, duration and policy response.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): structural – mismatch of skills/location, long duration, hysteresis, regional decline, needs costly retraining; cyclical – affects many sectors, lost output across the economy, falling AD can deepen recession, but responds to fiscal/monetary policy. Evaluation (up to 2): a deep recession can turn cyclical into long-term unemployment; structural change also brings efficiency gains; depends on labour mobility and retraining; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether technological change, such as artificial intelligence and automation, is likely to cause long-term unemployment.
parts.answer: Automation can replace routine jobs, causing structural unemployment for workers whose skills become obsolete. But technology raises productivity and incomes, lowers prices, creates new products and jobs, and historically employment has recovered. Long-term unemployment depends on how fast workers can retrain and move, the speed of change and policy.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides, diagram where relevant, and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is only asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. Content: structural unemployment and occupational/geographical immobility; productivity → lower costs → higher real incomes → demand for other goods; new industries; complementarity of technology with skilled labour. Evaluation: time period, type of job (routine vs creative/care), education system, labour market flexibility, inequality effects, evidence from earlier technological waves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether government policy can reduce the natural rate of unemployment.
parts.answer: The natural rate is the unemployment that remains when the labour market is in equilibrium (frictional + structural), consistent with stable inflation. Demand-side policy cannot reduce it in the long run (expectations-augmented Phillips curve: only higher inflation). Supply-side policies — training, better job matching, housing mobility, reforming benefits, reducing labour market rigidities — can lower it, but take time, cost money and may raise inequality.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): AO1/AO2 knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 — accurate, developed chains of reasoning with an accurate, correctly labelled diagram where relevant; AO3 evaluation up to 6 — weighs both sides, considers context and assumptions, and reaches a justified conclusion that answers the question. One-sided answers are capped at mid Level 2. Content: definition and link to the long-run Phillips curve/NAIRU; why AD stimulus only reduces unemployment temporarily as expectations adjust; supply-side measures and how each reduces frictional or structural unemployment. Evaluation: time lags, government failure, effectiveness evidence, hysteresis (long recessions raise the natural rate, so demand policy may matter), costs vs benefits, different labour markets; justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country W. Year 1: working-age population 40 million, labour force 26 million, unemployed 2.08 million. Year 2: working-age population 40.5 million, labour force 25.6 million, unemployed 1.92 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the unemployment rate and the labour force participation rate (labour force as a percentage of the working-age population) in each year. Give your answers to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Year 1: unemployment 8.0 %, participation 65.0 %; Year 2: unemployment 7.5 %, participation 63.2 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in the number of people employed between the two years.
parts.answer: A fall of 0.24 million (23.92m to 23.68m)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the fall in the unemployment rate shows that the labour market improved.
parts.answer: No clear improvement: the rate fell only because people left the labour force (participation fell despite a larger working-age population), probably discouraged workers; employment actually fell. The data do not show hours, wages or underemployment.
parts.working: 1 participation fell/workers leaving labour force; 1 employment fell; 1 judgement.

practice.stem:
Invented data for an open economy, $bn per year:
Investment 120, Government spending 200, Exports 180
Saving 100, Taxation 210, Imports 220

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total injections and the total withdrawals.
parts.answer: Injections $500bn; withdrawals $530bn

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what will happen to the level of national income.
parts.answer: Withdrawals exceed injections by $30bn, so less is spent on domestic output than is earned; national income will fall until withdrawals equal injections.
parts.working: 1 W > I so spending in the flow falls; 1 national income falls to a new equilibrium where injections = withdrawals.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the two main flows between households and firms in the circular flow.
parts.answer: Households supply factor services and receive factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit); households spend on goods and services, which is revenue for firms.
parts.working: 1 factor incomes from firms to households; 1 consumer spending from households to firms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the three injections into the circular flow of income in an open economy with a government.
parts.answer: Investment, government spending and exports.
parts.working: 2 for all three; 1 for two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why spending on a country's exports is treated as an injection.
parts.answer: Exports are spending by foreigners on domestic output, which comes from outside the domestic household–firm flow; it adds to firms' revenue and so to incomes paid to domestic households.
parts.working: 1 spending from abroad/outside the flow; 1 on domestically produced output; 1 raises firms' revenue and household income.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between real flows and money flows in the circular flow of income between households and firms.
parts.answer: Real flows are the movements of factor services (labour, land) from households to firms and goods and services from firms to households; money flows are the payments in the opposite direction: incomes to households and spending to firms.
parts.working: 1 real flows; 1 money flows in opposite direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a real flow and one example of a money flow.
parts.answer: Real: a factory worker's labour supplied to a textile mill (or furniture sold to a household). Money: the worker's wage (or household spending on the furniture).
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Households in a country spend more on imported smartphones and less on domestically made goods. Explain the effect on the circular flow of income.
parts.answer: Spending on imports is a withdrawal: money leaves the domestic flow and becomes income for foreign producers. Domestic firms' revenue falls, so they pay less in wages and profits and national income falls.
parts.working: 1 imports are a withdrawal; 1 domestic firms' revenue falls; 1 lower incomes/output (multiplier).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where taxation is withdrawn from the circular flow and how it can re-enter it.
parts.answer: Taxes are paid by households and firms to the government (withdrawal); they re-enter when the government spends on goods and services such as schools and roads (an injection).
parts.working: 1 withdrawal to government; 1 re-enters as G.

parts.label: a
parts.answer: (1) injection (investment); (2) withdrawal (saving); (3) injection (export of a service); (4) withdrawal (taxation); (5) neither — consumption of domestic output.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the circular flow of income, which is an injection?
A income tax paid by households
B spending on imported goods
C spending by foreigners on a country's exports
D money saved by households in banks
parts.answer: C spending by foreigners on a country's exports
parts.working: Injections are investment, government spending and exports – spending that enters the flow from outside the household–firm loop. A, B and D are withdrawals (taxation, imports and saving).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an economy, the marginal propensity to save is 0.1, the marginal rate of tax is 0.2 and the marginal propensity to import is 0.15. Investment rises by $9bn. What is the eventual increase in national income?
A $9bn
B $20bn
C $40.5bn
D $90bn
parts.answer: B $20bn

practice.stem: Invented data for an open economy, $bn per year. Year 1: investment 90, government spending 160, exports 110, saving 85, taxation 150, imports 120. Year 2: investment 85, government spending 165, exports 100, saving 95, taxation 155, imports 125.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate total injections and total withdrawals in each year.
parts.answer: Year 1: injections $360bn, withdrawals $355bn. Year 2: injections $350bn, withdrawals $375bn.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the year in which national income was likely to be rising, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Year 1: injections exceeded withdrawals by $5bn, so spending into the flow was greater than leakages and income rose.
parts.working: 1 Year 1; 1 explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why national income stops changing once it reaches equilibrium.
parts.answer: As income changes, withdrawals (saving, tax, imports) change with it until they equal injections; then there is no net addition to or leakage from spending.
parts.working: 1 withdrawals depend on income; 1 equality J = W.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the circular flow of income in a closed economy with no government, and consider whether an increase in saving by households is harmful to the economy.
parts.answer: Households supply factors to firms and receive incomes; they spend on firms' output; saving is a withdrawal and investment an injection. More saving lowers consumption, so income falls (paradox of thrift) unless banks lend the savings for investment; in the long run more saving can finance investment and growth.
parts.working: Mark split (8): knowledge 3, analysis 3, evaluation 2. K: two-sector flow; income = spending = output; saving as withdrawal, investment as injection. A: higher saving → lower spending → lower firms' revenue → lower output and incomes, multiplier effect; paradox of thrift. E: depends whether saving is channelled into investment, interest rates, spare capacity, the long run growth benefits; judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data. In Country D, government spending rose by $6bn and, after all the rounds of spending, national income rose by $15bn. Assume nothing else changed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of the multiplier.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the marginal propensity to withdraw.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two changes that would make the multiplier larger.
parts.answer: A lower marginal propensity to import (more spending stays in the domestic flow); a lower marginal rate of tax; a lower marginal propensity to save. Each means less of each round of extra income leaks out, so more is re-spent.
parts.working: 2 marks each: identify a lower leakage + explain more re-spending in each round.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the circular flow of income in an open economy with a government sector, and consider whether an increase in spending on imports will always reduce national income.
parts.answer: Households and firms exchange factor services and spending; saving, taxes and imports leak out; investment, government spending and exports are injected. More imports are a withdrawal and reduce national income unless offset by higher injections (e.g. imported capital raising investment and exports, or rising exports).
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: households, firms, government, foreign sector; injections (I, G, X) and withdrawals (S, T, M); equilibrium where I + G + X = S + T + M. Analysis: higher M → greater withdrawal → spending on domestic output falls → national income falls (multiplier). Evaluation: imports of capital goods and raw materials may raise investment and export capacity; foreigners may spend their earnings on the country's exports; if imports replace saving rather than domestic consumption, effect differs; judgement on 'always'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why, in equilibrium, total injections must equal total withdrawals but saving need not equal investment.
parts.answer: Equilibrium requires I + G + X = S + T + M; the totals balance, but individual pairs need not: e.g. a budget deficit (G > T) or trade surplus (X > M) can be offset by saving exceeding investment.
parts.working: 1 J = W condition; 1 components can differ; 1 example of offsetting imbalance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A government runs a budget deficit. Consider whether this means that national income must be rising.
parts.answer: Not necessarily: G > T is one injection exceeding one withdrawal, but if S > I or M > X by more, total withdrawals can exceed injections and income falls. Income rises only if total J > W.
parts.working: 1 deficit adds net injection; 1 other balances may offset; 1 example; 1 judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country K: marginal propensity to save 0.15; marginal rate of tax 0.25; marginal propensity to import 0.20. The government spends an extra $3bn on a railway project.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of the multiplier.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the eventual increase in national income and the increases in tax revenue, imports and saving that result.
parts.answer: National income +$5bn; tax revenue +$1.25bn; imports +$1.0bn; saving +$0.75bn

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answers, explain why the effect of the project on the budget deficit is less than $3bn.
parts.answer: Higher income raises tax revenue by $1.25bn, so the deficit rises by only $1.75bn; withdrawals rise by 1.25 + 1.0 + 0.75 = $3bn, equal to the injection.
parts.working: 1 extra tax revenue offsets part; 1 net effect 1.75bn / withdrawals equal injection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that an increase in investment will always lead to a large increase in national income.
parts.answer: An increase in investment is an injection, raising income by a multiple via the multiplier, and also adds to productive capacity. But the multiplier is small where leakages (saving, tax, imports) are high; if the economy is near full capacity, the rise is mostly in prices; investment financed by government borrowing may crowd out other spending; time lags and confidence matter. So the effect is not always large.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): AO1/AO2 knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 — accurate, developed chains of reasoning with an accurate, correctly labelled diagram where relevant; AO3 evaluation up to 6 — weighs both sides, considers context and assumptions, and reaches a justified conclusion that answers the question. One-sided answers are capped at mid Level 2. Content: injection; multiplier process and formula 1/(mps + mpt + mpm); worked example; accelerator link; supply-side effect (LRAS). Evaluation: size of leakages in an open economy (high mpm), spare capacity and the AS curve, crowding out, financing and interest rates, quality of investment, imported capital goods, time lags; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether government spending is a more reliable injection into the circular flow of income than private investment.
parts.answer: Government spending is decided by policy, so it can be planned and kept up in a recession, whereas investment depends on business confidence, interest rates and expected profits and is volatile. But government spending is limited by budget deficits, debt, political cycles and time lags, and can crowd out private investment; investment also adds to productive capacity. Judgement depends on the economy's fiscal position and the purpose of spending.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides, diagram where relevant, and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is only asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. Content: definitions of injections; multiplier for both; determinants of investment (confidence, interest rates, accelerator) vs government spending (policy choice, revenue). Evaluation: fiscal constraints (IMF programmes, debt), efficiency of public projects, crowding out, quality of investment, time lags; justified conclusion.

practice.stem:
Invented data for Country T, $bn:
GDP at market prices: 350
Primary income (profits, interest, dividends) received from abroad: 12
Primary income paid to foreign owners: 20
Capital consumption (depreciation): 30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate gross national income (GNI).
parts.working: M1 GNI = GDP + primary income from abroad − primary income paid abroad = 350 + 12 − 20. A1 $342bn.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate net national income (NNI).
parts.working: M1 NNI = GNI − capital consumption (depreciation) = 342 − 30. A1 $312bn.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why GNI may be lower than GDP for a country where many firms are foreign-owned.
parts.answer: Profits and interest earned by foreign owners from production in the country are counted in GDP but paid abroad, so they are subtracted to give GNI.
parts.working: 1 foreign-owned firms send profits/dividends abroad; 1 these are primary income outflows deducted from GDP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define gross domestic product (GDP).
parts.answer: The total value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period, usually a year.
parts.working: 1 value of final output; 1 within the country in a period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between GDP and gross national income (GNI).
parts.answer: GNI is GDP plus primary income (profits, interest, dividends, wages) received from abroad minus primary income paid to foreign residents; GDP measures output produced in the country, GNI income earned by its residents.
parts.working: 1 net primary income from abroad; 1 domestic output vs residents' income.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country B, $bn: consumer spending 220; fixed investment 60; increase in inventories (stocks) 5; government spending on goods and services 75; exports 90; imports 105.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate GDP at market prices.
parts.working: M1 C + I + change in inventories + G + X − M; A1 220 + 60 + 5 + 75 + 90 − 105 = 345.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why spending on imports is subtracted when measuring GDP by the expenditure method.
parts.answer: Consumption, investment and government spending include spending on goods made abroad; imports are subtracted so that only output produced inside the country is counted.
parts.working: 1 C, I, G include imported goods; 1 GDP measures domestic output only.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country Y, $bn: wages and salaries 180; company profits 90; rent 30; interest 20; state pensions and unemployment benefits 25.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the income method, calculate the value of national income.
parts.working: M1 add factor incomes only: 180 + 90 + 30 + 20; A1 320. State pensions and unemployment benefits are excluded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why state pensions and unemployment benefits are not included in the income method.
parts.answer: They are transfer payments: income received without any good or service being produced in return, so including them would overstate the value of output.
parts.working: 1 transfer payments; 1 no corresponding output.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why official GDP figures may underestimate the total output of an economy such as Pakistan.
parts.answer: A large informal (hidden) economy: street vendors and small workshops do not report their output; unpaid household production (cooking, childcare, growing food for the family) is not sold so is not counted.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed reasons: informal/shadow economy; non-marketed/subsistence output; tax evasion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one problem of comparing GDP between countries by converting it into US dollars at market exchange rates.
parts.answer: Market exchange rates do not reflect differences in price levels (cost of living), so poorer countries' real output is understated (or exchange rates fluctuate).

practice.stem: Invented data for Country U: GDP at market prices $500bn; indirect taxes on spending $60bn; subsidies on products $15bn.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate GDP at basic prices.
parts.working: M1 GDP at basic prices = GDP at market prices − indirect taxes + subsidies = 500 − 60 + 15. A1 $455bn.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the output, income and expenditure methods of measuring GDP should give the same total.
parts.answer: The value of output produced is either spent (expenditure) and the revenue from it is paid out as factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) to those who produced it, so all three measure the same flow.
parts.working: 1 output is sold/spent (output = expenditure, counting changes in inventories); 1 the money received is paid as incomes to factors; 1 so the three measure the same circular flow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why the three totals differ in practice.
parts.answer: Statistical discrepancy: errors and omissions, hidden/informal economy, different data sources and timing.
parts.working: 1 any valid reason.

practice.stem: Invented data for one shirt's chain of production (all values in rupees): a cotton farmer sells cotton to a spinner for 200; the spinner sells yarn to a weaver for 450; the weaver sells cloth to a tailor for 800; the tailor sells the finished shirt to a customer for 1,500. Assume the farmer buys no inputs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value added at each stage and the total contribution of this chain of production to GDP.
parts.answer: Farmer Rs 200; spinner Rs 250; weaver Rs 350; tailor Rs 700; total Rs 1,500
parts.working: M1 value added = sales − bought-in inputs: 200, 450 − 200 = 250, 800 − 450 = 350, 1,500 − 800 = 700. A1 all four. A1 total 1,500 = value of the final product.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why adding up the sales of every firm would overstate GDP.
parts.answer: It would count the value of intermediate goods (cotton, yarn, cloth) several times — double counting; only the final output or value added should be counted.
parts.working: 1 double counting; 1 intermediate goods counted repeatedly.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country X: nominal GDP $420bn in 2024 and $470bn in 2025; GDP deflator (2020 = 100) 140 in 2024 and 154 in 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate real GDP in 2024 and 2025 at 2020 prices. Give your answers to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of real economic growth and the rate of nominal GDP growth in 2025. Give your answers to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Real growth 1.7 %; nominal growth 11.9 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate of inflation shown by the GDP deflator in 2025, and explain why it differs from the change in nominal GDP.
parts.answer: 10 %; nominal GDP growth includes both higher prices (10 %) and higher real output (1.7 %).

practice.stem: Invented data for 2026. Country P: GDP $340bn, population 240 million, mainly farming and services. Country Q: GDP $95bn, population 22 million; 60 % of its GDP comes from oil fields owned by foreign companies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate GDP per head in each country, in US dollars, to the nearest dollar.
parts.answer: Country P $1,417; Country Q $4,318

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater GDP per head is in Country Q than in Country P. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: 3.0 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether people in Country Q must enjoy a higher standard of living than people in Country P.
parts.answer: Not necessarily: Q has three times the GDP per head, but income may be very unequally shared, hours of work may be longer, prices may be higher (need PPP), and Q's oil output may be foreign-owned (profits flow abroad, so GNI lower). Health, education and environment also matter.
parts.working: 1 GDP per head suggests yes; up to 3 for reasons why not (distribution, foreign ownership/GNI, price levels, non-income factors), including use of the information on oil; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the three methods of measuring national income, and consider why the statistics produced may be inaccurate.
parts.answer: Output method sums value added by each industry; income method sums factor incomes (wages, profits, rent, interest); expenditure method sums C + I + G + X − M. They should be equal because spending by one is income for another and pays for output. Inaccuracies: the informal economy, tax evasion, non-marketed output, double counting risks, revisions, sampling errors and statistical discrepancies.
parts.working: Mark split (8): knowledge 3, analysis 3, evaluation 2. K: the three methods with components. A: why they are equal (circular flow); adjustments (transfer payments excluded, value added, imports subtracted).
