E: sources of inaccuracy and which method is most affected; size of the informal sector in developing countries; data revised over time.

practice.stem:
Invented data for Country V:
2020: nominal GDP Rs 50 trillion, GDP deflator 100, population 220 million
2026: nominal GDP Rs 105 trillion, GDP deflator 190, population 245 million

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate real GDP in 2026 at 2020 prices, in Rs trillion, to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Rs 55.3 trillion
parts.working: M1 real GDP = nominal ÷ (deflator ÷ 100) = 105 ÷ 1.9. A1 Rs 55.3 trillion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in real GDP per head between 2020 and 2026, to one decimal place.
parts.working: M1 2020: 50 trillion ÷ 220 million = Rs 227,273; M1 2026: 55.26 trillion ÷ 245 million = Rs 225,564. A1 -0.8% (a small fall, although real GDP rose by 10.5%).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why economists use real GDP per head rather than nominal GDP when comparing living standards over time.
parts.answer: Nominal GDP rises with inflation even if output does not; real GDP removes price changes. Dividing by population shows the average output per person, as a growing population shares the output.
parts.working: 1 real removes the effect of inflation; 1 per head allows for population growth.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country R, $bn: GDP at market prices 380; primary income received from abroad 4; primary income paid abroad 9; workers' remittances received from citizens working abroad 30; capital consumption (depreciation) 42.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate gross national income (GNI).
parts.working: M1 GNI = GDP + primary income received − primary income paid; A1 380 + 4 − 9 = 375. Workers' remittances are not included.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate net national income (NNI).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the workers' remittances are not included in GNI even though they add to households' incomes.
parts.answer: Remittances from emigrants who live abroad are current transfers (secondary income), not payments for factor services supplied by the country's residents; GNI only adds primary income (wages, profits, interest, dividends) earned from abroad. They raise disposable income but not national income.
parts.working: 1 remittances are secondary income/transfers; 1 GNI includes only primary/factor income; 1 they still raise household spending power (disposable income).

practice.stem: Invented data for 2026. GDP per head in Pakistan was about PKR 520,000. Market exchange rate US$1 = PKR 280. Purchasing power parity exchange rate US$1 = PKR 75.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate GDP per head in US dollars using (i) the market exchange rate and (ii) the purchasing power parity (PPP) exchange rate. Give your answers to the nearest dollar.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the two figures are so different.
parts.answer: Many goods and services, especially non-traded ones such as food, housing and haircuts, are much cheaper in Pakistan than in the US. The PPP rate converts at the rate that buys the same basket in both countries, so each rupee buys more than the market rate suggests.
parts.working: 1 lower price level in the country; 1 non-traded goods; 1 PPP equalises purchasing power of a common basket.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether GDP per head at PPP is the best measure for comparing living standards between countries.
parts.answer: Better than market rates for comparing what incomes can buy, but it is still an average that ignores distribution, informal and non-market output, leisure, environment, health and education; baskets differ between countries and PPP estimates are uncertain. Composite measures such as the HDI or MPI add other dimensions. Conclusion: a useful starting point but not sufficient on its own.
parts.working: Up to 3 for advantages of PPP figures; up to 3 for limitations (inequality, non-market output, quality of life, estimation problems, alternative measures HDI/MEW/MPI); 1–2 for a justified judgement. Max 7.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether gross national income (GNI) per head is a reliable indicator of differences in living standards between countries.
parts.answer: GNI per head measures average income available to residents, so it is a common, easily compared indicator linked to spending power, health and education. But it ignores distribution, non-market and informal output, quality of goods, leisure, working conditions, environmental damage and life expectancy; conversion at market exchange rates distorts comparisons unless PPP is used. Composite indicators (HDI, MEW, MPI) address some weaknesses. Conclusion: a necessary but incomplete indicator.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): AO1/AO2 knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 — accurate, developed chains of reasoning with an accurate, correctly labelled diagram where relevant; AO3 evaluation up to 6 — weighs both sides, considers context and assumptions, and reaches a justified conclusion that answers the question. One-sided answers are capped at mid Level 2. Content: definition of GNI and why per head; why it is used (data availability, correlation with HDI components); limitations listed above; PPP vs market exchange rates; alternatives HDI (income, health, education), MEW, MPI and their own weaknesses. Evaluation: purpose of comparison, levels of development, data quality, judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether real GDP statistics are useful for comparing living standards in a country over time.
parts.answer: Real GDP per head shows changes in average output and income after removing inflation, so it is a useful headline indicator. But it ignores how income is distributed, changes in quality and new products, the informal economy, leisure, environmental costs and what output is produced (e.g. defence vs health); population growth must be allowed for. Other indicators should be used too.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides, diagram where relevant, and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is only asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. Content: nominal vs real; need for per head figures; usefulness (consistent, regular, comparable across years). Limitations above, plus changes in the size of the informal sector over time, accuracy of the price index. Evaluation: still the best single available measure; usefulness depends on the period and the country; combine with HDI, poverty and inequality data; judgement.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which policy is an expenditure-switching policy to reduce a current account deficit?
A a devaluation of the country's currency
B an increase in income tax rates
C a cut in government spending on public services
D a rise in interest rates to reduce consumer spending
parts.answer: A a devaluation of the country's currency
parts.working: A devaluation makes imports dearer and exports cheaper, switching spending by both residents and foreigners towards domestically produced goods. B, C and D are expenditure-reducing: they cut total spending, including spending on imports.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances
practice.stem: A North African country has a current account deficit equal to 5 % of its GDP, mainly because of high imports of consumer goods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two expenditure-reducing policies a government could use to reduce a current account deficit.
parts.answer: Any two of: higher income tax or sales tax; lower government spending; higher interest rates; a reduction in the money supply/credit.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two (contractionary fiscal or monetary measures).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a fall in national income is likely to reduce spending on imports.
parts.answer: With lower incomes households and firms spend less in total, and part of every unit of spending goes on imports (the marginal propensity to import), so imports fall.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower income → lower total spending/consumption; 1 mark: some of that spending is on imported goods (imports depend on income, normal goods), so import spending falls.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a fall in a country's exchange rate is called an expenditure-switching policy.
parts.answer: It makes exports cheaper in foreign currency and imports dearer in domestic currency, so both domestic and foreign buyers switch spending from foreign goods to the country's goods, improving the current account.
parts.working: 1 exports cheaper abroad; 1 imports dearer at home; 1 spending switches towards domestic output.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one supply-side policy that could reduce a current account deficit in the long run.
parts.answer: Any one: spending on education and training; investment grants for export industries; improving infrastructure such as ports and power; deregulation to raise productivity.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how an increase in income tax could reduce a current account deficit.
parts.answer: Higher income tax lowers households' disposable income, so they spend less on all goods, including imports; the fall in import spending reduces the deficit. It is an expenditure-reducing policy.
parts.working: 1 lower disposable income; 1 less spending on imports; 1 deficit falls/expenditure-reducing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one disadvantage of using this policy.
parts.answer: Any one: it also reduces spending on domestic goods, so output and employment fall; reduces incentives to work; unpopular.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a subsidy to exporters could reduce a current account deficit.
parts.answer: It lowers exporters' costs so they can cut prices in foreign markets; export volumes and earnings rise if demand is price elastic.
parts.working: 1 lower costs/prices of exports; 1 more export earnings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why export subsidies may not be a successful long-term policy.
parts.answer: Trading partners may impose countervailing duties or retaliate, and subsidies may break international trade rules (WTO); they cost the government money and may protect inefficient firms.
parts.working: 1 identification; 1 explanation.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances
practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): A South Asian country's imports of mobile phones rose to US$2.1 billion last year. Its current account deficit is 3.8 % of GDP. The government proposes a 25 % tariff on imported phones. Most local phone factories assemble phones from imported parts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between expenditure-switching and expenditure-reducing policies.
parts.answer: Expenditure-switching policies change the relative price or availability of imports and domestic goods so spending moves towards domestic output (e.g. tariffs, devaluation); expenditure-reducing policies lower total spending in the economy, which reduces spending on imports (e.g. higher taxes or interest rates).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correctly explained type (with or without an example).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether the proposed tariff on mobile phones is likely to reduce the current account deficit.
parts.answer: It may reduce imports of phones if demand is price elastic and domestic substitutes exist, but if demand is inelastic and there are no local producers, spending on imports may fall only a little; retaliation and higher costs for businesses may also reduce exports.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for analysis: tariff raises the domestic price of imported phones → quantity of imports falls; switch to domestic assemblers; tariff revenue. Up to 1 mark for evaluation: effect depends on PED for phones (likely inelastic for a necessity), availability of domestic substitutes (domestic phones may use imported parts), retaliation against exports, smuggling, and it treats a symptom not the cause (low competitiveness).

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a rise in interest rates could reduce a current account deficit, and consider the possible costs of this policy for the domestic economy.
parts.answer: Higher interest rates reduce consumption and investment, so national income and spending on imports fall (expenditure-reducing); costs include lower growth and higher unemployment, and an appreciation that may hurt exporters.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: current account deficit; expenditure-reducing policy; meaning of interest rate rise. Analysis: higher cost of borrowing and reward for saving → lower C and I → lower national income → lower spending on imports; lower inflation may improve competitiveness over time. Evaluation: costs — slower growth, higher unemployment, lower investment reduces future capacity; inflows of hot money may cause appreciation, making exports less competitive and partly offsetting the effect; heavy cost for indebted households and firms; judgement on whether the cost is worth paying.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country with a current account deficit devalues its currency. The price elasticity of demand for its exports is 0.3 and the price elasticity of demand for its imports is 0.4. What is the most likely effect on the current account?
A It worsens, because the sum of the elasticities is less than 1.
B It improves, because both demands are price inelastic.
C It improves, because the demand for imports is more elastic than the demand for exports.
D It is unchanged, because the devaluation affects export and import prices equally.
parts.answer: A It worsens, because the sum of the elasticities is less than 1.
parts.working: Marshall–Lerner condition: a devaluation improves the balance only if PEDx + PEDm > 1. Here 0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7 < 1, so export volumes rise and import volumes fall too little to offset the lower foreign-currency export prices and the higher domestic-currency import prices. B wrongly treats inelastic demand as favourable.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances
practice.stem: Invented extract. An East Asian manufacturing economy has had a current account surplus of 7–9 % of GDP for six years. Its main trading partners complain that its low household spending and undervalued currency harm their industries.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two policies the government of a country with a large current account surplus could use to reduce the surplus.
parts.answer: Expansionary fiscal policy (more government spending or lower taxes) raises incomes and so spending on imports; allowing or encouraging the currency to appreciate makes exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper (or lower interest rates to raise domestic demand).
parts.working: 2 marks each: policy + mechanism (income effect on imports, or relative price effect).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether the government should try to reduce the surplus.
parts.answer: A surplus brings foreign exchange, jobs in export industries and foreign assets, so it may be fine; but a large, persistent surplus can mean domestic consumption is held down, causes inflation pressure, and draws protectionist retaliation from trading partners with deficits. Answer depends on the cause and size.
parts.working: Up to 2 for reasons to keep it; up to 2 for reasons to reduce it, with a judgement.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances
practice.stem: Invented data for Country S: GDP $300bn; current account deficit 4.5 % of GDP; marginal propensity to import 0.3. The government cuts its spending by $6bn. The value of the multiplier is 1.5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current account deficit in $bn before the spending cut.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fall in national income and the fall in imports that the spending cut causes.
parts.answer: National income falls by $9bn; imports fall by $2.7bn

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assuming exports are unchanged, calculate the new current account deficit as a percentage of the new GDP. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Consider whether cutting government spending is a good way to reduce this deficit.
parts.answer: It works (deficit falls from 4.5 % to 3.7 % of GDP) but at a high cost: $9bn of lost output and higher unemployment to save $2.7bn of imports. It does not tackle competitiveness; other policies (supply-side, exchange rate) may be better in the long run.
parts.working: 1 effective in reducing imports; 1 large output/jobs cost relative to import saving; 1 judgement/alternative.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances
practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): Before a 10 % devaluation, a country's exports were worth US$30 billion and its imports US$45 billion a year, both priced in US dollars. In the first year after the devaluation, the US dollar price of its exports fell by 10 % and export volumes rose by 4 %. The US dollar price of its imports was unchanged and import volumes fell by 3 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the export earnings and import spending, in US$ billion, one year after the devaluation, and state whether the trade deficit has become larger or smaller. Give your answers to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Exports US$28.08 bn; imports US$43.65 bn; the deficit rises from US$15.00 bn to US$15.57 bn, so it becomes larger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the trade deficit might become smaller over a longer period after the devaluation.
parts.answer: In the short run demand for exports and imports is price inelastic because contracts are fixed and buyers take time to find substitutes; over time demand becomes more elastic, export volumes rise more and import volumes fall more, so earnings rise and the deficit falls (a J-curve pattern).
parts.working: 1 mark: short-run demand is inelastic (contracts, habits, lack of substitutes); 1 mark: over time PED for exports and imports rises as buyers adjust; 1 mark: when the combined responsiveness is large enough, export earnings rise relative to import spending and the deficit narrows (J-curve).

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether expenditure-switching policies are more effective than expenditure-reducing policies in correcting a current account deficit.
parts.answer: Expenditure-switching avoids a deliberate fall in national income and targets competitiveness, but depends on price elasticities, retaliation and inflation; expenditure-reducing policies work more reliably on imports but at the cost of lower growth and higher unemployment. The more effective choice depends on the cause of the deficit.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: switching (devaluation, tariffs, quotas, export subsidies) changes relative prices so domestic and foreign buyers move to domestic goods; reducing (contractionary fiscal and monetary policy) lowers income and therefore imports; diagrams of AD shifts where useful. Evaluation: switching may fail if demand for imports and exports is price inelastic, if devaluation raises import costs and inflation, or if tariffs bring retaliation/break trade agreements; reducing works whatever the elasticities but creates unemployment and may harm investment; if the deficit is due to excess demand, reducing is appropriate; if due to low competitiveness, switching plus supply-side policy is better; justified conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances
practice.stem: Invented data. Country V devalued its currency by 15 % at the end of Quarter 0. Its trade balance in goods and services ($bn) was: Q0 −4.0; Q1 −4.8; Q2 −5.1; Q3 −4.2; Q4 −3.0; Q5 −1.9.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in the trade balance between Quarter 0 and Quarter 2, and between Quarter 0 and Quarter 5.
parts.answer: Q0 to Q2: worsened by $1.1bn; Q0 to Q5: improved by $2.1bn

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the J-curve effect accounts for the pattern in the data.
parts.answer: Straight after a devaluation, trade volumes respond slowly because contracts are fixed and demand is price inelastic in the short run, so higher import prices raise import spending and the deficit widens (Q1–Q2). Over time buyers switch to the cheaper exports and away from dearer imports; once the Marshall–Lerner condition holds the balance improves (Q3–Q5).
parts.working: 1 short-run inelastic demand/contracts; 1 deterioration explained; 1 elasticities rise over time; 1 Marshall–Lerner condition met → improvement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the data, evaluate whether the devaluation has been successful in correcting the trade deficit.
parts.answer: Partly: after five quarters the deficit is less than half its original size, suggesting expenditure-switching is working. But the deficit has not been eliminated; other factors (world demand, oil prices, a domestic slowdown) may explain the change; devaluation raises import prices and inflation, which may erode competitiveness; costs to consumers and debt in foreign currency. Longer data and data on inflation and GDP are needed.
parts.working: Up to 4 for analysis using the data (improvement after an initial worsening, size of change, J-curve); up to 4 for evaluation (other causes, inflation erodes the effect, deficit remains, side effects, short time period) with a justified judgement.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether supply-side policies are the best way for a country such as Sri Lanka to correct a persistent current account deficit.
parts.answer: Supply-side policies (education, infrastructure, export diversification, productivity) raise competitiveness and export capacity and reduce dependence on imports, tackling the root cause without cutting output. But they take years, are costly when public finances are weak, and results are uncertain. In a crisis, expenditure-reducing (tighter fiscal/monetary policy) and expenditure-switching (depreciation) policies act faster. A combination is likely best.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides, diagram where relevant, and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is only asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. Content: causes of persistent deficits (low competitiveness, narrow export base, high import dependence for fuel/food); how supply-side policy shifts LRAS and lowers costs; alternatives and how they work. Evaluation: time lags, cost and financing, IMF conditions, inflation side-effects of depreciation, recession side-effects of austerity; judgement on 'best'.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that a country with a persistent current account deficit should allow its currency to depreciate rather than use contractionary fiscal and monetary policy.
parts.answer: Depreciation switches expenditure towards domestic output without reducing total demand, preserving jobs, and can work if the Marshall–Lerner condition holds (after the J-curve). But it raises import prices and inflation, increases the cost of foreign-currency debt and may be eroded by wage rises. Contractionary policy cuts imports through lower incomes but at a cost in output and jobs; it also curbs inflation. The best choice depends on elasticities, the cause of the deficit, inflation, debt and the economy's cycle; supply-side policy is needed for a lasting cure.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): AO1/AO2 knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 — accurate, developed chains of reasoning with an accurate, correctly labelled diagram where relevant; AO3 evaluation up to 6 — weighs both sides, considers context and assumptions, and reaches a justified conclusion that answers the question. One-sided answers are capped at mid Level 2. Content: expenditure-switching vs expenditure-reducing; Marshall–Lerner and J-curve; AD/AS effects of each; interest rates and capital flows. Evaluation: elasticities in the short and long run, import dependence (fuel, inputs), inflation pass-through, foreign debt, fixed vs floating regime, unemployment costs, whether the deficit reflects high investment; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would most likely cause a country's floating exchange rate to appreciate?
A a rise in its interest rates relative to those in other countries
B a rise in its inflation rate relative to that in other countries
C an increase in its residents' demand for imported goods
D an outflow of investment funds to other countries
parts.answer: A a rise in its interest rates relative to those in other countries
parts.working: Higher relative interest rates attract financial inflows, raising demand for the currency, so it appreciates. B, C and D each raise the supply of the currency or reduce demand for it, causing depreciation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a floating exchange rate and a fixed exchange rate.
parts.answer: A floating rate is determined by the demand for and supply of the currency in the foreign exchange market with no government target; a fixed rate is set by the government or central bank at a chosen value and maintained by intervention (buying/selling currency, interest rates).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a large increase in the number of foreign tourists visiting Thailand would affect the value of the Thai baht in a floating exchange rate system.
parts.answer: Tourists must buy baht to pay for hotels and services, so demand for the baht rises; the demand curve shifts to the right while supply is unchanged; the equilibrium exchange rate rises, so the baht appreciates (and the quantity traded increases).
parts.working: 1 mark: tourists need baht → demand for baht increases; 1 mark: demand curve shifts right (axes: price of baht in foreign currency, quantity of baht); 1 mark: excess demand at the old rate; 1 mark: new higher equilibrium rate — appreciation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A UK textbook costs £25. The exchange rate changes from £1 = PKR 350 to £1 = PKR 375. What happens to the price of the textbook for a Pakistani student, assuming its sterling price is unchanged?
A It rises by PKR 625.
B It falls by PKR 625.
C It rises by PKR 25.
D It is unchanged.
parts.answer: A It rises by PKR 625.
parts.working: 25 × 350 = PKR 8,750 before; 25 × 375 = PKR 9,375 after, a rise of PKR 625 because the rupee has depreciated. B gets the direction wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Pakistan has a floating exchange rate. Which change would most likely cause the rupee to depreciate against the US dollar?
A a rise in Pakistan's spending on imported oil
B a rise in remittances sent home by Pakistanis working abroad
C a rise in foreign direct investment into Pakistan
D a rise in Pakistan's interest rates relative to the US
parts.answer: A a rise in Pakistan's spending on imported oil
parts.working: Paying for more imported oil means more rupees are supplied to buy dollars, so the rupee falls. B, C and D all increase demand for rupees, causing an appreciation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a depreciation of a floating exchange rate.
parts.answer: A fall in the value of a currency against other currencies, caused by market forces (changes in demand and supply), not by government decision.
parts.working: 1 fall in value against other currencies; 1 market forces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two factors that could increase the demand for a country's currency.
parts.answer: Any two: higher exports; more inward tourism; more inward foreign direct investment; higher interest rates attracting hot money; speculation that the currency will rise.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The exchange rate changes from US$1 = PKR 280 to US$1 = PKR 300. A Pakistani exporter keeps the rupee price of a shirt at PKR 4200. What has happened?
A The rupee has depreciated and the US dollar price of the shirt has fallen from $15.00 to $14.00.
B The rupee has appreciated and the US dollar price of the shirt has fallen from $15.00 to $14.00.
C The rupee has depreciated and the US dollar price of the shirt has risen from $14.00 to $15.00.
D The rupee has appreciated and the US dollar price of the shirt has risen from $14.00 to $15.00.
parts.answer: A The rupee has depreciated and the US dollar price of the shirt has fallen from $15.00 to $14.00.
parts.working: More rupees are needed to buy one dollar, so the rupee has depreciated. Dollar price = 4200 ÷ 280 = $15.00 before and 4200 ÷ 300 = $14.00 after. B gives the right prices but the wrong direction for the rupee.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a managed float exchange rate system works, and consider whether it is better than a fixed exchange rate for a small open economy.
parts.answer: In a managed float, market forces set the rate but the central bank intervenes (buying or selling currency, changing interest rates) to limit large or unwanted movements. It combines some flexibility with some stability, but needs reserves and may lack credibility; a fixed rate gives more certainty but removes an adjustment tool.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: definitions of managed float and fixed exchange rate; tools of intervention (foreign currency reserves, interest rates). Analysis: if the currency falls too fast, the central bank sells foreign currency and buys domestic currency, raising demand (diagram); it can let the rate adjust gradually to shocks, helping the current account; under a fixed rate the government must defend the peg whatever happens. Evaluation: for a small open economy heavily dependent on trade, stability of a fixed rate helps traders and controls imported inflation, but defending it can exhaust reserves and requires interest rates to follow the anchor country; a managed float keeps monetary independence but may cause uncertainty and speculative pressure; judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data. Exchange rates: US$1 = PKR 280; US$1 = AED 3.67 (the UAE dirham is pegged to the US dollar).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the exchange rate between the UAE dirham and the Pakistani rupee (PKR per AED). Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.answer: AED 1 = PKR 76.29

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price in rupees of a phone that costs AED 2,500 in Dubai, to the nearest rupee.
parts.working: 2,500 × 280 ÷ 3.67 = 190,736 (using the unrounded rate; 2,500 × 76.29 = 190,725 also accepted).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider how a depreciation of the rupee against the US dollar would affect Pakistani importers of goods from the UAE.
parts.answer: The dirham is pegged to the dollar, so the rupee also falls against the dirham; imports cost more rupees, so importers face higher costs, may raise prices and sell less. The effect depends on whether they can pass costs on, on the PED of the goods, and on whether contracts were agreed in advance or hedged.
parts.working: 1 dirham pegged so rupee falls against dirham; 1 higher rupee cost of imports; up to 2 consideration (pass-on to consumers, PED, hedging/contracts, switch to local suppliers) with judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: With the help of a demand and supply diagram for a currency, explain how speculation that the currency will fall in value can cause it to fall.
parts.answer: Speculators expecting a fall sell the currency (supply shifts right) and foreign buyers delay buying it (demand shifts left), so the equilibrium exchange rate falls — the expectation is self-fulfilling.
parts.working: 1 axes (price of currency in foreign currency, quantity of currency); 1 supply shifts right; 1 demand shifts left; 1 lower equilibrium rate explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether the central bank should intervene to stop the fall.
parts.answer: Buying the currency with foreign reserves or raising interest rates can stabilise it and limit imported inflation; but reserves are limited, higher rates slow growth, and resisting a fall justified by fundamentals may fail. A fall may also help exporters.
parts.working: Up to 2 for reasons to intervene; up to 2 for reasons not to, with a judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data. Country W's trade weights and the change in the value of its currency over a year: against the US dollar (weight 0.40) −5 %; against the Chinese yuan (weight 0.35) +2 %; against the euro (weight 0.25) −1 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the trade-weighted exchange rate index of Country W's currency and its new value (starting value 100). Give the index to two decimal places.
parts.answer: −1.55 %; new index 98.45

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a trade-weighted index is more useful than a single bilateral exchange rate for judging a country's international competitiveness.
parts.answer: A country trades with many partners; the TWI weights each currency by its share of trade, so it reflects the overall change in the price of the country's goods abroad. One bilateral rate can move differently from others (here the currency rose against the yuan but fell against the dollar and euro).
parts.working: 1 many trading partners; 1 weights by trade shares; 1 use of the data to show bilateral rates can mislead.

practice.stem:
Table 7: Exchange rate of the Country Q dollar (data invented for practice)
January: US$1 = 160 Q-dollars
December: US$1 = 184 Q-dollars

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the value of the Country Q dollar measured in US dollars between January and December. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: −13.0 % (a depreciation of about 13.0 %)
parts.working: M1: value of one Q-dollar in US$ = 1 ÷ 160 = 0.006250 in January and 1 ÷ 184 = 0.005435 in December. A1: (0.005435 − 0.006250) ÷ 0.006250 × 100 = −13.0 %. (The 15 % rise in Q-dollars per US$ is not the same as a 15 % fall in the Q-dollar.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider how the change in the exchange rate is likely to affect inflation in Country Q.
parts.answer: Inflation is likely to rise: imported goods, fuel and raw materials cost more in Q-dollars (cost-push), and cheaper exports raise net exports and AD (demand-pull). The size depends on the import content of consumption, how much firms pass on and whether the depreciation is expected to last.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for analysis: higher domestic price of imported consumer goods → CPI rises directly; dearer imported inputs → higher costs → AS shifts left (cost-push); exports become cheaper abroad → higher net exports → AD rises (demand-pull); possible wage-price spiral. Up to 1 mark for evaluation: effect depends on the share of imports in spending, PED for imports, profit margins absorbing costs, contracts priced earlier, and the central bank's response.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a depreciation of a country's currency is always beneficial for its economy.
parts.answer: No: a depreciation can raise exports, output and employment and help a current account deficit, but it also raises import prices and inflation, increases the burden of foreign-currency debt and reduces living standards; its benefits depend on elasticities, spare capacity and the cause of the fall.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: depreciation makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home → net exports and AD rise → growth and jobs (AD/AS); current account may improve if demand is price elastic enough; competitiveness improves. Costs: imported inflation, higher costs for firms using imported inputs, lower real incomes, larger burden of debt in foreign currency, possible capital flight. Evaluation: depends on price elasticities (short-run J-curve), spare capacity, import content of exports, size of foreign debt, whether trading partners are growing, and whether the depreciation is gradual or a sudden crisis; 'always' is too strong; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a government maintains a fixed exchange rate, and consider whether a fixed exchange rate is desirable for an oil-exporting economy.
parts.answer: The central bank buys its own currency with foreign reserves when there is excess supply and sells it when there is excess demand; it can also change interest rates or use exchange controls. For an oil exporter, a peg (often to the US dollar, the currency oil is priced in) gives certainty and stable import prices, and large oil reserves make it credible; but the economy cannot use the exchange rate to absorb oil price shocks, and monetary policy must follow the anchor country.
parts.working: Mark split (8): knowledge 3, analysis 3, evaluation 2. K: fixed rate defined; intervention through reserves, interest rates, controls. A: diagram of intervention; how reserves are used up when defending against falls. E: oil revenues in dollars; stability vs loss of flexibility; falling oil prices drain reserves; loss of independent monetary policy; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a country's floating exchange rate is mainly determined by its trade in goods and services.
parts.answer: Trade flows affect demand for (exports) and supply of (imports) the currency. But financial flows are often much larger: hot money responding to interest rates, FDI, portfolio investment, remittances, speculation and central bank intervention. In the short run financial flows and expectations dominate; in the long run competitiveness and trade matter more.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides, diagram where relevant, and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is only asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. Content: demand and supply of currency diagram; trade effects; interest rate differentials and hot money; FDI; remittances (important for Pakistan, Bangladesh); speculation; government intervention and managed floats. Evaluation: relative size of flows, time period, type of economy, confidence; justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Invented data for one year. The exchange rate moved from US$1 = PKR 250 to US$1 = PKR 275. Over the same year Pakistan's price level rose by 20 % and the US price level rose by 3 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the nominal value of the rupee against the US dollar. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: A depreciation of 9.1 %
parts.working: The rupee's value in dollars falls from 1/250 to 1/275: 250 ÷ 275 = 0.909, a fall of 9.1 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the real exchange rate of the rupee against the US dollar, using: real exchange rate = nominal exchange rate (US$ per rupee) × Pakistan price level ÷ US price level. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: A real appreciation of 5.9 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Pakistani exporters may have become less competitive even though the rupee depreciated.
parts.answer: Pakistani prices rose by 20 % but US prices by only 3 %; the 9.1 % nominal depreciation did not offset the inflation gap, so in real terms Pakistani goods became dearer relative to US goods.
parts.working: 1 inflation differential; 1 depreciation smaller than the differential; 1 real appreciation → loss of price competitiveness.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms of trade.
parts.answer: The ratio of a country's index of export prices to its index of import prices, multiplied by 100.
parts.working: 1 mark: export price index ÷ import price index × 100 (or the quantity of imports that a unit of exports can buy).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the terms of trade index for the year when the export price index is 108 and the import price index is 90.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what this index value shows about the country's position compared with the base year.
parts.answer: The terms of trade have improved by 20 %: each unit of exports now buys 20 % more imports than in the base year.
parts.working: 1 mark: an improvement (index above 100); 1 mark: a given quantity of exports pays for more imports.

practice.stem:
Table 8: Price indices for Country C, a cocoa exporter (2023 = 100; data invented for practice)
2023: export prices 100, import prices 100
2024: export prices 120, import prices 105
2025: export prices 96, import prices 112
Extract: After a record harvest in other producing countries, world cocoa prices fell sharply in 2025. Country C imports most of its fuel and machinery.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the terms of trade index for 2024 and 2025. Give your answers to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the extract, explain one likely cause of the change in the terms of trade between 2024 and 2025.
parts.answer: The world price of cocoa, the main export, fell (export prices index from 120 to 96) while import prices of fuel and machinery kept rising, so the terms of trade deteriorated.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies the fall in export prices (cocoa) and/or rise in import prices; 1 mark: links this to the fall in the index from 114.3 to 85.7.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would improve a country's terms of trade?
A Export prices rise by 4 % and import prices rise by 1 %.
B Export prices rise by 3 % and import prices rise by 6 %.
C Export prices fall by 2 % and import prices are unchanged.
D Export prices and import prices both rise by 5 %.
parts.answer: A Export prices rise by 4 % and import prices rise by 1 %.
parts.working: Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100; it improves when export prices rise relative to import prices: 104 ÷ 101 × 100 = 103.0. B gives 97.2 (worse); D leaves it at 100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a country's terms of trade might improve.
parts.answer: A rise in world demand for its main exports (e.g. a commodity boom) raises export prices; an appreciation of its currency raises export prices in foreign currency and lowers import prices in domestic currency; a fall in the world price of a key import such as oil; higher-quality exports commanding higher prices.
parts.working: 2 marks each: cause + effect on export or import prices.

practice.stem: Invented data. Over one year (start of year = 100): Country A export prices 110, import prices 105; Country B export prices 95, import prices 85; Country C export prices 120, import prices 118.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the terms of trade index at the end of the year for each country. Give your answers to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Country A 104.8; Country B 111.8; Country C 101.7

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how Country B's terms of trade improved the most even though its export prices fell.
parts.answer: Its import prices fell by more (15 %) than its export prices (5 %), so export prices rose relative to import prices.
parts.working: 1 import prices fell further; 1 relative prices determine the terms of trade.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Over a year, a country's index of export prices rises from 100 to 110 and its index of import prices rises from 100 to 125. What is its terms of trade index at the end of the year?
A 88.0
B 113.6
C 115.0
D 85.0
parts.working: Terms of trade = (index of export prices ÷ index of import prices) × 100 = 110 ÷ 125 × 100 = 88.0: a deterioration. B inverts the ratio (125 ÷ 110 × 100).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a large rise in world oil prices would affect the terms of trade of an oil-importing country such as Pakistan.
parts.answer: Oil is a large part of its imports, so the import price index rises relative to the export price index and the terms of trade deteriorate (fall).
parts.working: 1 mark: import prices rise; 1 mark: index falls/deteriorates (each unit of exports buys fewer imports).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether this change in the terms of trade will reduce living standards in the country.
parts.answer: Likely yes in the short run: more exports are needed to pay for the same imports, real incomes fall, fuel and transport costs raise inflation and the current account deficit widens; the effect may be smaller if demand shifts to other energy sources, if the price rise is temporary, or if export prices also rise.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for analysis: deterioration means more resources must be exported to buy the same oil; higher import bill → current account worsens/currency may depreciate; higher fuel prices → cost-push inflation → real incomes fall; firms' costs rise → output and jobs may fall. Up to 1 mark for evaluation: depends on PED for oil (inelastic → larger import bill), duration of the shock, government subsidies, rising remittances from oil-exporting Gulf countries, and whether export prices rise too.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country L (2020 = 100). In 2026 its export price index was 115 and its terms of trade index was 92.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the import price index for 2026.
parts.working: M1 import price index = export price index ÷ terms of trade × 100; A1 115 ÷ 92 × 100 = 125.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the percentage changes in export prices and in import prices between 2020 and 2026, and explain what the terms of trade index of 92 shows.
parts.answer: Export prices rose by 15 % and import prices by 25 %; the terms of trade worsened by 8 %, so a given volume of exports buys about 8 % fewer imports than in 2020.
parts.working: 1 both percentage changes (15 % and 25 %); 1 deterioration: each unit of exports buys fewer imports (8 % fewer).

practice.stem: Invented data. A cotton-exporting country sells cotton for $1,800 a tonne in 2025 and $2,070 a tonne in 2026. It imports tractors that cost $45,000 each in 2025 and $46,800 each in 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the terms of trade index for 2026 (2025 = 100). Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many tractors 10,000 tonnes of cotton exports could buy in 2025 and in 2026 (to the nearest whole tractor).
parts.answer: 2025: 400 tractors; 2026: 442 tractors

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what your answers show about the meaning of an improvement in the terms of trade.
parts.answer: Each unit of exports now buys more imports (about 10.6 % more), so the country can obtain more imported goods for the same volume of exports.
parts.working: 1 more imports per unit of exports; 1 link to the 10.6 % / 400 → 442.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how an appreciation of a country's currency affects its terms of trade.
parts.answer: If exporters keep domestic-currency prices unchanged, export prices in foreign currency rise; import prices in domestic currency fall. Export prices rise relative to import prices (measured in a common currency), so the terms of trade improve.
parts.working: 1 export prices rise abroad; 1 import prices fall at home; 1 terms of trade improve.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether this improvement in the terms of trade is good for the country.
parts.answer: Imports become cheaper, which lowers inflation and raises real incomes; but exports become less price competitive, so export volumes may fall, the current account may worsen and jobs in export industries may be lost. Depends on the PED for exports and imports.
parts.working: Up to 2 benefits; up to 2 costs; judgement referring to elasticities.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): A garment-exporting country lowered its export prices to win orders. Between 2024 and 2025 its export price index fell from 100 to 95, its import price index rose from 100 to 104, and the volume of its exports rose by 15 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the terms of trade index for 2025. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the value of the country's export earnings between 2024 and 2025. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1: value index = price index × volume index ÷ 100 = 95 × 115 ÷ 100 = 109.25. A1: export earnings rose by 9.25 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether the deterioration in the terms of trade is harmful to this country.
parts.answer: Not necessarily: export prices fell, but because demand for its exports is price elastic, export volumes rose by more and export earnings rose; the fall in the terms of trade may reflect greater competitiveness. It would be harmful if caused by rising import prices or falling world demand.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for analysis: a deterioration means each unit of exports buys fewer imports; but the cause matters — here export prices fell as firms became more competitive and volumes rose 15 %, so earnings rose (calculation), helping output, jobs and the current account; if import prices rise (e.g. oil), real income falls. Up to 2 marks for evaluation: depends on the cause of the change, PED for exports and imports, the import bill (import prices rose 4 %), whether the gain is sustained; justified judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a country that depends on exporting primary products will always benefit from a rise in world commodity prices.
parts.answer: A rise in commodity prices improves its terms of trade and usually raises export earnings, incomes and government revenue, but benefits may be temporary, unevenly shared and may cause appreciation that harms other exporters; it does not always benefit.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: higher export prices → terms of trade improve → more imports per unit of exports; export revenue rises if demand is price inelastic; current account improves; higher incomes, employment and tax revenue (royalties) → growth; supply of exports may expand. Evaluation: the gain depends on whether the price rise reflects higher world demand or a supply shortage at home (poor harvest — lower volumes); commodity prices are volatile, so dependence increases instability; currency appreciation can harm manufacturing and tourism; revenue may go to a few firms or MNCs; rising import prices may offset; it may discourage diversification; justified conclusion on 'always'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the terms of trade are measured, and consider whether a deterioration in the terms of trade caused by higher productivity in a country's export industries is harmful.
parts.answer: Terms of trade = (index of average export prices ÷ index of average import prices) × 100. Higher productivity lowers unit costs, so firms cut export prices and the index falls. But lower prices make exports more competitive; if demand is price elastic, export volumes and revenue rise, creating jobs and growth, so the deterioration is not harmful. If demand is inelastic, revenue falls.
parts.working: Mark split (8): knowledge 3, analysis 3, evaluation 2. K: formula; meaning of deterioration. A: productivity → lower costs → lower export prices; effect on export volumes and revenue depending on PED; effect on current account and employment. E: cause of the change matters more than the direction; PED; whether competitors also gain productivity; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether changes in a country's terms of trade are more important than changes in its exchange rate in determining its current account balance.
parts.answer: Terms of trade affect how much export revenue buys in imports; a commodity price rise can transform a commodity exporter's current account. Exchange rates affect price competitiveness of all traded goods and also feed into the terms of trade. Other factors — income growth at home and abroad, inflation, productivity, primary and secondary income flows — also matter. Which is more important depends on the structure of trade and elasticities.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides, diagram where relevant, and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is only asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. Content: definitions; links between the two (appreciation improves ToT); effect on export and import values with PED; Marshall–Lerner. Evaluation: commodity exporters vs manufactured exporters; short run vs long run; non-price factors; remittances and income flows; judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data. Terms of trade index of a copper-exporting country (2000 = 100): 2005 140; 2010 175; 2015 110; 2020 120; 2025 150. Copper makes up about 55 % of the country's exports.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the terms of trade index between 2005 and 2010, between 2010 and 2015 and between 2015 and 2025. Give your answers to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the terms of trade of a country that relies on one primary export are often volatile.
parts.answer: World demand and supply for commodities are price inelastic in the short run, so shifts (e.g. a boom in construction abroad, new mines) cause large price swings; with one main export, these swings dominate the export price index.
parts.working: 1 inelastic demand/supply; 1 shocks to world demand or supply; 1 export price index dominated by one good.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether the government should try to reduce the country's dependence on copper exports.
parts.answer: Volatile terms of trade cause unstable export earnings, government revenue and exchange rates; long-run decline in primary prices relative to manufactures (Prebisch–Singer) is a risk. Diversification reduces this but is costly, slow and may mean giving up comparative advantage; copper demand may rise with electric vehicles and renewable energy. Alternatives: a sovereign wealth fund to smooth revenues, processing copper locally.
parts.working: Up to 4 for analysis of the costs of dependence using the data; up to 4 for evaluation (comparative advantage, future demand, alternatives such as stabilisation funds or downstream processing, time and cost) with a judgement.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between absolute advantage and comparative advantage, and consider whether free trade benefits all countries.
parts.answer: Absolute advantage is producing more of a good with the same resources; comparative advantage is producing at a lower opportunity cost. Trade based on comparative advantage can raise total output and welfare, but not every country or group gains equally.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: definitions of absolute and comparative advantage, opportunity cost, free trade. Analysis: a numerical or worked example showing that specialisation by comparative advantage raises total world output even when one country has absolute advantage in both goods; gains shared through the terms of trade; consumers gain from lower prices and more choice. Evaluation: gains depend on the terms of trade, transport costs and factor mobility; some industries and workers lose jobs; countries specialising in primary products face volatile prices; infant industries may never develop; benefits are not automatic for all; judgement.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define absolute advantage.
parts.answer: A country has an absolute advantage when it can produce more of a good than another country with the same resources.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons, other than comparative advantage, why countries trade with each other.
parts.answer: To obtain goods they cannot produce or lack resources for (e.g. oil, tropical fruit, rare minerals); to gain economies of scale from selling to larger markets; to give consumers more variety and choice; to access technology.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed reasons.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two assumptions of the theory of comparative advantage.
parts.answer: Any two: no transport costs; no trade barriers; constant opportunity costs (constant returns); factors of production are perfectly mobile within a country but immobile between countries; perfect knowledge.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a country may import a good that it could produce using fewer resources than the exporting country.
parts.answer: Even with an absolute advantage, its opportunity cost of producing that good may be higher than its trading partner's; it gains by using resources where its comparative advantage is greatest and importing the good.
parts.working: 1 opportunity cost higher; 1 resources used better elsewhere.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage
practice.stem: Invented data. Output per worker per week: Kenya — 30 kg of tea or 10 bicycles; Vietnam — 20 kg of tea or 25 bicycles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of producing one bicycle in each country, in kg of tea.
parts.answer: Kenya 3 kg of tea; Vietnam 0.8 kg of tea
parts.working: Kenya 30 ÷ 10 = 3; Vietnam 20 ÷ 25 = 0.8. 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify which country has an absolute advantage in each good.
parts.answer: Kenya in tea (30 kg vs 20 kg per worker); Vietnam in bicycles (25 vs 10).
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which good each country should specialise in.
parts.answer: Kenya: tea; Vietnam: bicycles.
parts.working: 1 both correct.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage

parts.label: a
parts.text:
One worker in Country X can produce either 10 tonnes of rice or 5 units of cloth. One worker in Country Y can produce either 6 tonnes of rice or 4 units of cloth. Which statement is correct?
A Country X has an absolute advantage in both goods, but Country Y has a comparative advantage in cloth.
B Country X has a comparative advantage in both goods.
C Country Y has a comparative advantage in rice.
D Neither country can gain from trade because Country X is more efficient at producing both goods.
parts.answer: A Country X has an absolute advantage in both goods, but Country Y has a comparative advantage in cloth.
parts.working: X produces more of both goods per worker (absolute advantage in both). Opportunity cost of 1 unit of cloth: X = 10 ÷ 5 = 2 tonnes of rice; Y = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 tonnes of rice. Y gives up less rice, so it has the comparative advantage in cloth (and X in rice). D ignores that gains come from differences in opportunity cost.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage
practice.stem:
Table 9: Output per worker per week (data invented for practice)
Country A: 8 tonnes of wheat or 24 units of textiles
Country B: 6 tonnes of wheat or 12 units of textiles

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of wheat in each country.
parts.answer: Country A: 3 units of textiles; Country B: 2 units of textiles.
parts.working: 24 ÷ 8 = 3 textiles (1); 12 ÷ 6 = 2 textiles (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify which good each country should specialise in. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Country B should specialise in wheat (lower opportunity cost: 2 textiles vs 3); Country A should specialise in textiles (opportunity cost 1/3 tonne of wheat vs 1/2 in B).
parts.working: 1 mark: B wheat, A textiles; 1 mark: justified by lower opportunity cost (comparative advantage).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State a rate of exchange of textiles for wheat at which both countries could gain from trade.
parts.answer: Any rate strictly between 2 and 3 units of textiles per tonne of wheat, e.g. 2.5 units of textiles for 1 tonne of wheat.
parts.working: 1 mark: a rate between the two opportunity cost ratios (2 < rate < 3).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain one reason why the gains from specialisation might be smaller in practice than the theory suggests.
parts.answer: For example, transport costs may use up the gain; or factors are not perfectly mobile between industries, so workers cannot easily move from wheat to textiles; or opportunity costs rise as production expands (increasing costs).
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies a valid limitation (transport costs, factor immobility, increasing costs, trade barriers, exchange rates); 1 mark: explains how it reduces the gain.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In Country A the opportunity cost of 1 unit of cloth is 2 units of food. In Country B the opportunity cost of 1 unit of cloth is 4 units of food. At which rate of exchange could both countries gain from trade?
A 1 unit of cloth for 1.5 units of food
B 1 unit of cloth for 3 units of food
C 1 unit of cloth for 4.5 units of food
D 1 unit of cloth for 5 units of food
parts.answer: B 1 unit of cloth for 3 units of food
parts.working: A specialises in cloth (lower opportunity cost) and gains if it gets more than 2 food per cloth; B gains if it pays less than 4 food per cloth. Only 3 lies between 2 and 4. A (1.5) is worse for A than producing food itself.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage
practice.stem: Invented data. Labour hours needed to produce one unit: Pakistan — 1 tonne of mangoes 4 hours, 1 laptop 50 hours; Germany — 1 tonne of mangoes 6 hours, 1 laptop 20 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of producing one laptop in each country, in tonnes of mangoes.
parts.answer: Pakistan 12.5 tonnes; Germany 3.33 tonnes
parts.working: Pakistan 50 ÷ 4 = 12.5; Germany 20 ÷ 6 = 3.33. 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify which country has the comparative advantage in each good and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Germany in laptops (opportunity cost 3.33 t of mangoes vs 12.5 t); Pakistan in mangoes (opportunity cost 0.08 laptop per tonne vs 0.30 in Germany).
parts.working: 1 Germany laptops; 1 Pakistan mangoes; 1 comparison of opportunity costs (lower opportunity cost).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which country has an absolute advantage in mangoes.
parts.answer: Pakistan (4 hours per tonne compared with 6 hours).

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, with the help of production possibility curves, how specialisation according to comparative advantage can increase world output.
parts.answer: Each country's PPC has a different slope (different opportunity costs). By specialising in the good with the lower opportunity cost and trading, each country can consume at a point outside its own PPC, so total world output rises.
parts.working: 1 PPCs with different slopes/opportunity costs; 1 specialisation; 1 trade; 1 consumption beyond the PPC.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider why high transport costs may reduce or remove these gains from trade.
parts.answer: Transport costs add to the price of traded goods; if they exceed the difference in opportunity costs, it is cheaper to produce at home. Gains are smaller for bulky, low-value goods; but improved logistics, containers and digital trade in services reduce these costs.
parts.working: 1 raises cost of imports; 1 can outweigh cost differences; up to 2 consideration (type of good, distance, services trade, falling transport costs) with judgement.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between specialisation and free trade.
parts.answer: Specialisation means concentrating production on a limited range of goods; free trade is the exchange of goods and services between countries without barriers such as tariffs and quotas.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a high degree of specialisation in one export increases the economic risks a country faces.
parts.answer: Yes: dependence on one export means falls in world demand or price (or a crop failure) cut export earnings, jobs and government revenue, and can destabilise the exchange rate. But specialisation raises efficiency and income, and risks can be reduced by stabilisation funds, insurance and diversification over time.
parts.working: Up to 2 risks explained; up to 2 counter-arguments/mitigation with a judgement.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether specialising according to comparative advantage is the best trade strategy for a low-income country.
parts.answer: Specialisation by comparative advantage raises efficiency and income in the short run, but a low-income country's current comparative advantage is often in primary products with volatile prices and falling terms of trade; diversification and developing new advantages may be better long-run strategies.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: comparative advantage theory; gains from specialisation and trade (higher output, economies of scale, foreign currency earnings, access to imported capital goods); compare with alternatives such as diversification, protection of infant industries, regional trade agreements. Evaluation: risks of over-specialisation (price volatility, weather, exhaustion of resources, deteriorating terms of trade); comparative advantage can change over time through investment in skills and technology (dynamic comparative advantage); protection may lead to inefficiency and retaliation; examples (e.g. garment exports, cocoa, copper); justified conclusion on 'best'.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage
practice.stem: Invented data. Country A and Country B each have 100 workers. Output per worker per week: Country A 8 tonnes of wheat or 2 units of cloth; Country B 3 tonnes of wheat or 3 units of cloth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total world output of wheat and cloth when each country divides its workers equally between the two goods.
parts.answer: 550 tonnes of wheat and 250 units of cloth
parts.working: A: 50 × 8 = 400 wheat, 50 × 2 = 100 cloth; B: 50 × 3 = 150 wheat, 50 × 3 = 150 cloth. Totals 550 and 250.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the good in which each country has a comparative advantage, and calculate world output if each country specialises completely.
parts.answer: A: wheat (cloth costs 4 wheat in A but 1 in B); B: cloth. Output 800 wheat and 300 cloth.
parts.working: 1 comparative advantage with opportunity costs; 1 A 100 × 8 = 800 wheat; 1 B 100 × 3 = 300 cloth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the gain in world output from specialisation.
parts.answer: 250 more tonnes of wheat and 50 more units of cloth

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why Country A gains from specialisation even though it has an absolute advantage in wheat and B has an absolute advantage only in cloth.
parts.answer: Gains come from differences in opportunity costs: each country produces the good it gives up least to make, so total output rises and, by trading at a rate between 1 and 4 wheat per cloth, both can consume more.
parts.working: 1 differences in opportunity cost; 1 trade at a rate between the two opportunity costs benefits both.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a country's comparative advantage can change over time, and consider whether a country such as Pakistan should try to develop a comparative advantage in information technology (IT) services.
parts.answer: Comparative advantage depends on relative factor endowments, skills, technology and costs, which change through investment in education, capital accumulation, rising wages and new technology. Pakistan has a large young population and growing IT exports; developing this can add higher value-added exports and reduce dependence on textiles. But it needs investment in skills, reliable internet and power, and faces strong competition (India, Philippines).
parts.working: Mark split (8): knowledge 3, analysis 3, evaluation 2. K: comparative advantage; dynamic comparative advantage. A: how education, investment, technology and wage changes alter opportunity costs; example of East Asian economies. E: costs and time; competition; brain drain; opportunity cost of resources; role of government vs market; judgement.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether the theory of comparative advantage explains the pattern of international trade in the world today.
parts.answer: It explains much trade between different countries: low-wage economies export labour-intensive goods, resource-rich countries export commodities. But much trade is between similar high-income countries in similar products (intra-industry trade), driven by economies of scale, brands and consumer variety; global supply chains, FDI by multinationals, protection and trade agreements also shape trade. So it explains part, not all, of trade.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides, diagram where relevant, and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is only asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. Content: theory and assumptions (constant costs, no transport costs, perfect mobility within countries, free trade). Evidence for and against. Evaluation: unrealistic assumptions; dynamic changes; political factors (tariffs, sanctions, trade blocs); judgement.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that the theory of comparative advantage shows that all countries gain from globalisation.
parts.answer: Comparative advantage shows that specialisation and trade increase total world output and that every country can consume beyond its PPC. Globalisation spreads technology, FDI and larger markets. But gains are not shared equally: terms of trade may move against primary exporters, some industries and workers lose jobs (structural unemployment), inequality can rise within countries, infant industries may be prevented from developing, and global shocks spread. Gains for a country overall may still leave many losers.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): AO1/AO2 knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 — accurate, developed chains of reasoning with an accurate, correctly labelled diagram where relevant; AO3 evaluation up to 6 — weighs both sides, considers context and assumptions, and reaches a justified conclusion that answers the question. One-sided answers are capped at mid Level 2. Content: the theory with a numerical or PPC illustration; features of globalisation (trade, capital flows, MNCs, technology). Evaluation: unrealistic assumptions; distribution of gains between and within countries; dynamic effects; dependence and volatility; environmental costs; role of policy and compensation; justified conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which transaction is recorded as a credit in the secondary income section of Pakistan's current account?
A money sent home by Pakistani workers employed in Saudi Arabia
B profits sent abroad by a foreign-owned car factory in Pakistan
C a foreign company building a new factory in Pakistan
D rice exported from Pakistan to China
parts.answer: A money sent home by Pakistani workers employed in Saudi Arabia
parts.working: Workers' remittances are current transfers and are recorded in secondary income. B is primary income (a debit), C is foreign direct investment (financial account), D is trade in goods.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the four components of the current account of the balance of payments.
parts.answer: Trade in goods, trade in services, primary income, secondary income.
parts.working: 2 marks for all four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a country might have a large surplus on its current account.
parts.answer: For example: strong international competitiveness (high productivity, quality, low costs) so exports far exceed imports; high domestic saving and low consumption, so spending on imports is low; an undervalued exchange rate; large exports of a high-priced commodity such as oil.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for identification and 1 mark for explaining how it raises exports relative to imports (or income inflows relative to outflows).

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.answer: (1) trade in goods, credit; (2) trade in services, debit; (3) primary income, debit; (4) secondary income, credit.
parts.working: 1 each (section and direction both correct).

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments
practice.stem: Invented data for Country M, 2026 ($bn): exports of goods 32.1, imports of goods 54.8; exports of services 7.9, imports of services 10.4; primary income credits 1.2, debits 9.0; secondary income credits 31.5, debits 1.6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the balance on trade in goods, trade in services, primary income and secondary income.
parts.answer: Goods −22.7; services −2.5; primary income −7.8; secondary income +29.9 ($bn)
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current account balance.
parts.answer: −$3.1bn (a deficit)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the component that does most to reduce the size of the current account deficit.
parts.answer: Secondary income (mainly workers' remittances), +$29.9bn.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between visible trade and invisible trade.
parts.answer: Visible trade is trade in physical goods (trade in goods); invisible trade is trade in services such as tourism, banking, shipping and IT, plus income flows.
parts.working: 1 visible = goods; 1 invisible = services.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a visible export and one example of an invisible export for Pakistan.
parts.answer: Visible: cotton textiles, rice, surgical instruments. Invisible: software and IT services sold abroad, a foreign tourist's spending in Pakistan, freight services.
parts.working: 1 each.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments
practice.stem:
Table 10: Current account of Country N, 2025 (US$ billion; data invented for practice)
Trade in goods: −27.5
Trade in services: −2.9
Primary income: −8.1
Secondary income: +31.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current account balance for 2025.
parts.answer: A deficit of US$7.3 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a current account deficit of this kind is a problem for the country.
parts.answer: It may be: it must be financed by borrowing or by selling assets, and the large deficit on goods shows weak competitiveness. But the deficit is small relative to the trade gap because of large remittances, and if imports are capital goods it may support future growth.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for analysis: the deficit must be financed through the financial account (borrowing, running down reserves, FDI); persistent deficits may lead to depreciation and higher debt; large goods deficit suggests low competitiveness and reliance on remittances; primary income deficit reflects interest and profit payments abroad. Up to 1 mark for evaluation: depends on the size relative to GDP, how it is financed (FDI vs short-term loans), what is imported (capital goods vs consumer goods), and whether remittances are stable.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which transaction is recorded as a debit in the primary income section of Pakistan's current account?
A dividends paid by a Pakistani subsidiary to its parent company in China
B airline tickets sold by a Pakistani airline to foreign tourists
C wheat imported from Australia
D a grant of food aid given to Pakistan by a foreign government
parts.answer: A dividends paid by a Pakistani subsidiary to its parent company in China
parts.working: Dividends paid to foreign owners are investment income flowing out: a primary income debit. B is a services credit, C a goods debit, D a secondary income credit (current transfer).

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two possible causes of a current account deficit.
parts.answer: High domestic incomes/rapid growth raising demand for imports; low price competitiveness from high inflation or an overvalued exchange rate; poor quality or narrow range of exports; large interest and profit payments to foreign investors.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed causes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a current account deficit caused by importing machinery and capital goods is a problem.
parts.answer: Less of a problem than one caused by consumer imports: the machinery raises productive capacity and future exports, which can repay the deficit. But it must be financed (borrowing, reserves), may pressure the currency, and the investment may not raise exports if poorly chosen.
parts.working: Up to 2 why it is not a problem; up to 2 why it may be, with judgement.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments
practice.stem: Invented data for Country D: current account deficit $18bn in 2025 and $12bn in 2026; nominal GDP $450bn in 2025 and $480bn in 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current account deficit as a percentage of GDP in each year. Give your answers to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why economists usually measure a current account balance as a percentage of GDP.
parts.answer: It shows the deficit relative to the size of the economy and its ability to finance it, and allows comparison over time and between countries of different size.
