parts.label: a
parts.text: A city government sets a maximum monthly rent for flats that is below the market equilibrium rent. Explain why this causes a shortage of rented flats.
parts.answer: At the lower rent, quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls, so demand exceeds supply.
parts.working: 1 mark: maximum rent is below equilibrium so it is binding. 1 mark: more households want to rent at the lower price (extension of demand). 1 mark: landlords supply fewer flats as returns fall (contraction of supply), e.g. convert them to offices or sell them – excess demand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an illegal (shadow) market may develop for rented flats.
parts.answer: Because some tenants are willing to pay more than the legal maximum, landlords can charge extra payments secretly.
parts.working: 1 mark: at the quantity supplied, tenants' willingness to pay is above the legal maximum. 1 mark: so landlords ask for illegal side payments (e.g. large 'key money' deposits), and flats go to those who can pay rather than those in most need.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one effect of the maximum rent on the quality of rented flats.
parts.answer: Quality falls because landlords have less incentive and income to maintain them.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A government sets a maximum price for bread above the current equilibrium price. What is the immediate effect?
A a shortage of bread
B a surplus of bread
C no change in the price or quantity of bread
D a rise in the price of bread to the maximum price
parts.answer: C no change in the price or quantity of bread
parts.working: A maximum price only affects the market if it is below equilibrium. Set above equilibrium it is not binding, so price and quantity stay the same. D is wrong because the maximum is a ceiling, not a target.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A government sets a minimum price for milk above the equilibrium price. It does not buy any milk itself. What is most likely to happen?
A Producers sell all the milk they produce at the higher price.
B The quantity of milk bought and sold falls to the quantity demanded at the minimum price, leaving unsold milk.
C Consumer surplus in the milk market increases.
D A shortage of milk develops.
parts.answer: B The quantity of milk bought and sold falls to the quantity demanded at the minimum price, leaving unsold milk.
parts.working: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded; without government purchases only the quantity demanded is sold, so there is a surplus. A ignores that consumers buy less at the higher price; C is wrong because consumers pay more and buy less; D describes a maximum price below equilibrium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why a government might set a minimum (support) price for sugarcane paid to growers by sugar mills.
parts.answer: To raise and stabilise farmers' incomes: sugarcane growers are numerous and small while a few mills buy the crop, so mills could push the price down; a minimum price protects growers and encourages them to keep growing the crop.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason (protect farm incomes/buyer power of mills/food security); 1 mark: explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the minimum price might lead to an inefficient use of scarce resources.
parts.answer: If the price is above equilibrium, farmers grow more sugarcane than buyers want; land and very large amounts of irrigation water are pulled into sugarcane instead of crops that consumers value more, and surplus cane or sugar may be wasted or exported at a loss.
parts.working: 1 mark: overproduction/excess supply; 1 mark: resources (land, water) diverted from higher-valued uses.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a market, demand is Qd = 200 − 4P and supply is Qs = 20 + 2P, where P is the price in dollars. The government sets a maximum price of $20. What is the size of the resulting shortage?
A 20 units
B 40 units
C 60 units
D 80 units
parts.answer: C 60 units
parts.working: Equilibrium: 200 − 4P = 20 + 2P gives P = $30, Q = 80. At $20, Qd = 120 and Qs = 60, so the shortage is 60. D is the equilibrium quantity, not the shortage.

practice.stem:
The table shows the demand and supply schedules for rice in a country (invented data).
Price (Rs per kg): quantity demanded (thousand tonnes), quantity supplied (thousand tonnes)
150: 900, 500
175: 800, 600
200: 700, 700
225: 600, 800
250: 500, 900

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.answer: Rs 200 per kg; 700 thousand tonnes
parts.working: B1 both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government sets a minimum price of Rs 250 per kg and buys any surplus. Calculate the surplus and the cost to the government of buying it.
parts.answer: Surplus 400 thousand tonnes; cost Rs 100 billion
parts.working: Surplus = 900 − 500 = 400 thousand tonnes (M1 A1); cost = 400,000 tonnes × 1000 kg × Rs 250 = Rs 100,000,000,000 = Rs 100 billion (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the change in farmers' total revenue from rice as a result of the scheme.
parts.answer: Rises by Rs 85 billion (from Rs 140 billion to Rs 225 billion)
parts.working: Before: 700,000 × 1000 × 200 = Rs 140 billion; after: 900,000 × 1000 × 250 = Rs 225 billion (M1); increase Rs 85 billion (A1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage of this scheme for consumers.
parts.answer: Consumers pay a higher price (Rs 250 instead of Rs 200) and buy less, losing consumer surplus; they also pay taxes to finance the surplus.
parts.working: 1 mark point, 1 mark development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: With the help of a diagram, explain why a maximum price set below the equilibrium price may cause a shortage, and consider whether such a policy will help low-income households.
parts.answer: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the controlled price; poor households may or may not benefit depending on rationing and supply response.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): definition of a maximum price; correctly labelled demand and supply diagram with maximum price line below equilibrium; shortage shown as Qd − Qs. Analysis (3): lower price extends demand and contracts supply; quantity actually traded falls; producers may cut quality; shortage leads to queues and shadow markets. Evaluation (2): households who obtain the good gain from the lower price; but those who cannot get it lose; benefit depends on PES and PED, rationing system (e.g. ration cards), enforcement; justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Invented data: in a country, the retail price of sugar rose to Rs 165 per kg after a poor sugar-cane harvest. The government then imposed a maximum retail price of Rs 140 per kg. A month later, newspapers reported that many shops had no sugar on their shelves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the maximum price is below the previous market price. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two likely effects of the maximum price on the sugar market.
parts.answer: Shortage as Qd rises and Qs falls; illegal market or hoarding; supply diverted to other uses or smuggled abroad.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained effects: shortage (excess demand) with empty shelves; illegal resale at higher prices; hoarding by traders expecting the control to end; mills cut supply or export; queues and time costs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether a maximum price is more effective than a cash transfer to poor households for making sugar affordable.
parts.answer: A cash transfer targets the poor and avoids shortages; a maximum price is cheaper for the budget but benefits all buyers and causes shortages.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): maximum price helps everyone who buys, including rich households and confectionery firms; causes shortage; no budget cost. Cash transfer targets poor, keeps market price, no shortage, but costs the government and may be spent on other goods. Evaluation (1): judgement, e.g. a cash transfer is likely more effective if there is a reliable register of poor households.

practice.stem:
Daily demand and supply schedules for petrol in a country (invented data):
Price (Rs per litre): 240, 260, 280, 300, 320
Quantity demanded (million litres): 60, 56, 52, 48, 44
Quantity supplied (million litres): 40, 46, 52, 58, 64

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the equilibrium price and quantity of petrol.
parts.answer: Rs 280 per litre; 52 million litres a day.
parts.working: 1 mark for both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government sets a maximum price of Rs 260 per litre. Calculate the resulting shortage.
parts.answer: 10 million litres a day
parts.working: M1: Qd = 56, Qs = 46; A1: 56 − 46 = 10 million litres.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the change in the total daily revenue of petrol sellers. Give your answer in Rs million.
parts.answer: A fall of Rs 2 600 million a day
parts.working: M1: before 280 × 52 = 14 560; after 260 × 46 = 11 960; A1: change = −2 600 (Rs million).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the available petrol might be allocated when the price is not allowed to rise.
parts.answer: Any two: queues/first come, first served; rationing by coupons or limits per vehicle; favouritism by sellers; illegal (black) market sales at higher prices.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the effect of a minimum price set above equilibrium in a market where demand is price inelastic, and consider whether producers always gain from such a minimum price.
parts.answer: Explain: price rises to the minimum; quantity demanded falls only a little because demand is inelastic; quantity supplied rises, creating a surplus; with inelastic demand, consumer spending (producer revenue from sales) rises. Consider: producers who sell gain, but those who cannot sell the surplus lose unless the government buys it; higher output raises total costs; in the long run, extra entry can drive surplus up; if the government stops buying or the minimum is not enforced, prices may collapse; consumers may switch to substitutes over time (demand becomes more elastic). Judgement: producers as a group usually gain when demand is inelastic and the surplus is bought, but not always.
parts.working: Marks: 3 knowledge and understanding, 3 analysis, 2 evaluation. Knowledge: definition of minimum price, PED. Analysis: diagram described with Pmin above Pe, Qd and Qs, surplus; revenue effect with inelastic demand. Evaluation: conditions under which producers lose (unsold surplus, costs, long run).

practice.stem: In the market for a basic medicine, demand is P = 100 − Q and supply is P = 20 + Q, where P is the price in dollars and Q is the quantity in thousands of packs per month (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity, and the consumer surplus and producer surplus at equilibrium.
parts.answer: P = $60, Q = 40 thousand; consumer surplus $800 thousand; producer surplus $800 thousand

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government imposes a maximum price of $40. Calculate the new consumer surplus and producer surplus, assuming the units supplied go to the consumers who value them most.
parts.answer: Consumer surplus $1000 thousand; producer surplus $200 thousand
parts.working: Quantity supplied at $40: 40 = 20 + Q so Q = 20 (M1). CS = trapezium between demand and $40 from 0 to 20 = ½ × (60 + 40) × 20 = 1000 (A1). PS = ½ × 20 × 20 = 200 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the deadweight (welfare) loss and comment on whether consumers as a group gain from the maximum price.
parts.answer: Welfare loss $400 thousand; consumers who obtain the good gain (CS rises by $200 thousand) but 20 thousand units of demand are no longer met.
parts.working: Total surplus 1600 − 1200 = 400 (B1). Comment (B1): consumers as a group gain only if goods reach those who value them most; queuing or illegal markets would reduce this gain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a guaranteed minimum price for wheat is the best way for a government to support farmers' incomes.
parts.answer: A minimum price raises incomes of farmers who sell, but creates surpluses, higher food prices and fiscal costs; alternatives may be better.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 8): diagram of minimum price above equilibrium; surplus Qs − Qd; government must buy and store the surplus; farmers' revenue rises (price × quantity sold); larger farmers with more output gain most; consumers pay more, which hurts poor households for whom wheat flour is a staple; storage costs, wastage, opportunity cost of government spending; possible over-production of wheat at the expense of other crops. Comparison with alternatives: direct cash transfers to small farmers, input subsidies, buffer stocks, crop insurance, investment in irrigation and research. Evaluation (up to 4): depends on PED and PES, budget position, how well the scheme is targeted, world prices; 'best' requires a comparison and a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A government introduces a minimum retail price of Rs 360 for a pack of cigarettes. The previous market price was Rs 300. Assume the price elasticity of demand for cigarettes is −0.4 (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the quantity of cigarettes demanded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in total consumer spending on cigarettes.
parts.working: New spending ÷ old spending = 1.20 × 0.92 = 1.104 (M1), a rise of 10.4 % (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answers, explain why a minimum price on cigarettes may not greatly reduce smoking, and suggest one problem it could create.
parts.answer: Demand is price inelastic, so consumption falls only slightly while spending rises; it may encourage illegal or smuggled cigarettes.
parts.working: 1 mark: PED is inelastic (addiction, few substitutes). 1 mark: quantity falls by only 8 % while smokers spend more, which may hurt poor smoking households. 1 mark: problem, e.g. smuggling/counterfeit cigarettes, extra revenue goes to sellers not the government (unlike a tax).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a market, demand is Qd = 150 − 5P and supply is Qs = −30 + 4P, where P is the price in dollars and Q is in thousands of units. The government sets a maximum price of $14. What is the resulting shortage?
A 54 thousand units
B 24 thousand units
C 30 thousand units
D there is no shortage
parts.answer: A 54 thousand units
parts.working: Equilibrium: 150 − 5P = −30 + 4P gives P = $20, Q = 50. At $14: Qd = 150 − 70 = 80, Qs = −30 + 56 = 26, shortage = 80 − 26 = 54. B (50 − 26) and C (80 − 50) measure the gap from the old equilibrium quantity only; D would apply only if the maximum price were above $20.

practice.stem: In the market for a cereal crop, demand is P = 120 − 2Q and supply is P = 20 + 2Q, where P is the price in dollars per tonne and Q is in thousands of tonnes (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity before the scheme.
parts.answer: $70 per tonne; 25 thousand tonnes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government sets a minimum price of $80 and buys any surplus. Calculate the quantity demanded, the quantity supplied and the cost to the government.
parts.answer: Qd = 20, Qs = 30 (thousand tonnes); cost $800 thousand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the change in consumer surplus and in producer surplus.
parts.answer: Consumer surplus falls by $225 thousand (625 → 400); producer surplus rises by $275 thousand (625 → 900).
parts.working: 1 mark: CS before ½ × 25 × 50 = 625, after ½ × 20 × 40 = 400; 1 mark: PS before ½ × 25 × 50 = 625, after ½ × 30 × 60 = 900.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Using your answers, explain why the scheme reduces economic welfare even though producers gain.
parts.answer: Producers gain $275 thousand but consumers lose $225 thousand and taxpayers pay $800 thousand: a net loss of $750 thousand (unless the stored crop has value), because resources are used to produce output that consumers do not want at that price.
parts.working: 1 mark: net calculation (275 − 225 − 800 = −750); 1 mark: explanation – overproduction/allocative inefficiency.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's Gini coefficient rises from 0.30 to 0.38. What does this show?
A income has become more equally distributed
B income has become less equally distributed
C average income in the country has fallen
D the number of people living in poverty has risen
parts.answer: B income has become less equally distributed
parts.working: A higher Gini coefficient means the Lorenz curve is further from the line of equality, so distribution is less equal. It says nothing about the level of average income (C) or the absolute number in poverty (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between income and wealth, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: Income is a flow of money received over a period (e.g. monthly wages); wealth is a stock of assets owned at a point in time (e.g. a house or land).
parts.working: 1 mark each correct distinction with example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how inequality of wealth can lead to inequality of income.
parts.answer: Wealth generates income (rent, interest, dividends, profit), so those with more assets receive more income.
parts.working: 1 mark: assets yield income such as rent and dividends. 1 mark: wealth also allows better education and business start-up, raising future earnings, so the gap widens across generations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two causes of income inequality other than inequality of wealth.
parts.answer: Differences in skills/education; discrimination; regional differences; unemployment; differences in bargaining power.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid causes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what a Lorenz curve shows.
parts.answer: It plots the cumulative percentage of households (from poorest to richest) against the cumulative percentage of income (or wealth) they receive, showing how equally income is distributed.
parts.working: 1 mark: cumulative % of population against cumulative % of income; 1 mark: the further it is from the diagonal, the greater the inequality.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the line of perfect equality represents.
parts.answer: Each percentage of households receives the same percentage of income (e.g. the poorest 40 % receive 40 %).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the value of the Gini coefficient for perfect equality and for perfect inequality.
parts.answer: 0 for perfect equality; 1 for perfect inequality.
parts.working: 1 mark for both.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two causes of wealth inequality.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: inheritance – wealth passed between generations so some start with large assets; differences in income allow richer people to save more and buy assets; rising asset prices (land, shares) raise the wealth of those who already own them; access to credit/entrepreneurial success.
parts.working: For each cause: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two measures, other than taxation, that a government could use to reduce income inequality.
parts.answer: Any two: cash transfers/benefits to poor households; national minimum wage; free or subsidised education and health care; job-creation or training schemes; land reform.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how free secondary education could reduce income inequality in the long run.
parts.answer: Children from poor families gain skills and qualifications they could not otherwise afford, so they can get higher-paid jobs as adults, narrowing the gap between their incomes and those of richer families.
parts.working: 1 mark: improves human capital of poor children; 1 mark: leads to higher future earnings/greater equality of opportunity.

practice.stem:
Invented income tax bands for a country (annual income):
first Rs 600,000: 0 %
Rs 600,001 to Rs 1,200,000: 5 %
Rs 1,200,001 to Rs 2,400,000: 15 %
above Rs 2,400,000: 25 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the income tax paid by Bilal, who earns Rs 1,000,000 a year, and by Sana, who earns Rs 3,000,000 a year.
parts.answer: Bilal Rs 20,000; Sana Rs 360,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of tax paid by each person, and state Sana's marginal rate of tax.
parts.answer: Bilal 2 %; Sana 12 %; Sana's marginal rate 25 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this tax system is described as progressive.
parts.answer: The average rate of tax rises as income rises (2 % to 12 %), so higher earners pay a larger proportion of their income.
parts.working: 1 mark: average rate rises with income. 1 mark: use of the figures calculated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the causes of income inequality within a country and consider whether some degree of inequality is necessary for an economy to work well.
parts.answer: Causes include differences in skills, education, wealth, discrimination and bargaining power; some inequality provides incentives, but too much harms growth and welfare.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): meaning of income inequality; measurement by Lorenz curve or Gini coefficient; causes such as differences in education and skills, wealth/inheritance, labour market discrimination, regional differences, unemployment, tax and benefit systems. Analysis (3): explain how each cause leads to different wage or non-wage incomes, e.g. scarce skills command high wages. Evaluation (2): wage differences signal where labour is needed and reward effort, risk and training; but extreme inequality reduces social mobility, health and demand, and may cause social unrest; justified conclusion.

practice.stem:
Invented data for a country.
Year: share of income of poorest 20 % of households, share of income of richest 20 %
2015: 8 %, 45 %
2025: 7 %, 49 %
Real national income grew by 40 % between 2015 and 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the income share of the richest 20 % to that of the poorest 20 % in 2015 and in 2025. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the change in the ratio suggests about the distribution of income.
parts.answer: Income has become less equally distributed, as the richest group's share rose while the poorest group's share fell.
parts.working: 1 mark: less equal. 1 mark: use of data (ratio rose from 5.6 to 7.0).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the data prove that the poorest 20 % of households were worse off in 2025 than in 2015.
parts.answer: No: the data are shares, not amounts; if total real income grew enough, the poorest may have had higher real incomes despite a smaller share.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): shares vs absolute incomes; real GDP growth of 40 % (invented) means the poorest 20 %'s real income changed by 1.4 × 7/8 − 1 = +22.5 %; but price changes for basic goods, household size and non-income factors (services, wealth) also matter. Evaluation (1): a judgement, e.g. relatively worse off but probably not absolutely.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which tax is regressive?
A an income tax with marginal rates that rise as income rises
B a tax of a fixed amount per adult, the same for everyone
C a tax of 10 % on all income
D a wealth tax on property worth more than a high threshold
parts.answer: B a tax of a fixed amount per adult, the same for everyone
parts.working: A fixed amount is a larger proportion of a low income than of a high income, so the average rate falls as income rises – regressive. C is proportional (same percentage for all); A and D are progressive.

practice.stem: Invented data: when Kamran's annual income is Rs 2 000 000 he pays Rs 180 000 in income tax. When his income rises to Rs 2 400 000 he pays Rs 260 000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Kamran's average rate of tax at each income and his marginal rate of tax on the extra income. Give your answers to 2 decimal places where necessary.
parts.answer: Average rate 9 % before and 10.83 % after; marginal rate 20 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using your answers, explain whether the tax system is progressive.
parts.answer: Yes: the average rate rises as income rises (9 % → 10.83 %), because the marginal rate (20 %) is above the average rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: progressive; 1 mark: justification using average rising/marginal above average.

practice.stem:
Invented data: share of national income received by the poorest 20 % and the richest 20 % of households.
Country A: poorest 20 % receive 9 %; richest 20 % receive 38 %
Country B: poorest 20 % receive 4 %; richest 20 % receive 58 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the income share of the richest 20 % to that of the poorest 20 % in each country. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Country A: 4.22; Country B: 14.50.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which country is likely to have the higher Gini coefficient.
parts.answer: Country B
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why income distribution data may be unreliable in a country with a large informal sector.
parts.answer: Informal incomes are unrecorded and often under-reported in surveys; the very rich may also under-report or hold income abroad; in-kind and seasonal income is hard to measure; so measured shares may be biased in either direction.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three developed points.

practice.stem: Invented data: the share of national income received by each fifth (quintile) of households in a country, from poorest to richest, is 6 %, 10 %, 15 %, 22 % and 47 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cumulative share of income received by the poorest 60 % of households.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Treating the Lorenz curve as straight lines joining the cumulative points, calculate the area under the Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient. Give the Gini coefficient to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Area under Lorenz curve = 0.312; Gini coefficient = 0.38

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what would happen to the Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient if a new tax and transfer scheme took income from the richest 20 % and gave it to the poorest 20 %.
parts.answer: The Lorenz curve moves closer to the line of equality and the Gini coefficient falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: the cumulative shares at each point rise, so the curve moves towards the 45° line. 1 mark: the area between the curve and the line of equality falls, so the Gini coefficient falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a progressive income tax is the best way to reduce income inequality in a lower-middle-income country.
parts.answer: It can narrow post-tax income gaps, but its effect is limited where few people pay income tax and the informal sector is large; spending and other taxes may matter more.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 8): how a progressive tax works (rising average rate) and narrows post-tax incomes; revenue can fund transfers, health and education. Limits: small tax base, large informal sector, tax avoidance and evasion, disincentive effects on work and enterprise, capital flight; poorest households are below the threshold so gain nothing directly. Alternatives: cash transfers, free education and health (raise human capital), wealth or property taxes, minimum wages, land reform. Evaluation (up to 4): effectiveness depends on tax collection capacity and how revenue is spent; long-term inequality is better reduced by education; a judgement on 'best'.

practice.stem: Invented data: a government pays a monthly benefit of Rs 8 000 to families whose monthly earnings are Rs 40 000 or less. Families earning more than Rs 40 000 receive nothing. A parent earning Rs 38 000 a month is offered extra hours that would raise earnings to Rs 44 000 a month. Ignore income tax.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in the family's total monthly income (earnings plus benefit) if the parent accepts the extra hours.
parts.answer: A fall of Rs 2 000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a poverty trap, using the data.
parts.answer: Because the benefit is withdrawn completely once income exceeds Rs 40 000, earning Rs 6 000 more leaves the family Rs 2 000 worse off – an effective marginal 'tax' of more than 100 %. Low-income households have little incentive to work more or seek promotion, so they stay poor.
parts.working: 1 mark: loss of benefit as earnings rise; 1 mark: uses data – effective marginal rate above 100 %; 1 mark: disincentive to work keeps family in poverty.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the benefit could be redesigned to reduce this problem.
parts.answer: Withdraw the benefit gradually (taper), e.g. reduce it by Rs 30 for every Rs 100 earned above the threshold, so extra work always raises total income.
parts.working: 1 mark: gradual withdrawal/taper; 1 mark: explanation that work then always pays.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether economic growth is likely to reduce income inequality in a developing economy.
parts.answer: Reduce: growth creates jobs, moving workers from low-productivity farming into higher-paid industry and services; rising tax revenue funds transfers, education and health; tight labour markets raise low wages. Increase: early growth may benefit owners of capital, land and skills most (Kuznets-type pattern); growth concentrated in cities or in capital-intensive sectors (mining, finance) leaves rural poor behind; skill-biased technology raises returns to education; asset prices rise. Judgement: growth raises average incomes and can reduce poverty, but whether inequality falls depends on the kind of growth (labour-intensive vs capital-intensive), access to education and the government's redistributive policies.
parts.working: Higher-band answers need accurate, developed analysis (with a relevant diagram where useful) of both sides, applied to the context, and a reasoned judgement that answers the 'assess' question directly; one-sided or descriptive answers stay in the lower bands. Expect clear distinction between poverty and inequality, mechanisms both ways, use of Gini/Lorenz concepts, and a judgement on 'likely' that depends on the type of growth and policy.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why would a free market fail to provide a public good such as a flood defence wall?
A the good is rival in consumption
B consumers would demand too much of it
C people can benefit without paying, so firms cannot earn revenue
D the government has better information than consumers
parts.answer: C people can benefit without paying, so firms cannot earn revenue
parts.working: Because a public good is non-excludable, people can be free riders, so firms cannot charge and will not supply it. A is wrong: public goods are non-rival.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many people in rural areas do not have regular dental check-ups, even when they can afford them. Explain how information failure can lead to the under-consumption of dental check-ups.
parts.answer: People underestimate the long-term benefits (preventing serious disease), so their demand is below the level that would maximise their welfare.
parts.working: 1 mark: information failure = consumers lack full/accurate information. 1 mark: they do not realise that problems can be prevented cheaply / focus on short-term cost. 1 mark: so demand and consumption are lower than they would choose with full information – a merit good is under-consumed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two policies the government could use to increase consumption of dental check-ups.
parts.answer: Free or subsidised check-ups; information campaigns in schools; direct provision through clinics.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why is a merit good likely to be under-consumed in a free market?
A Consumers underestimate the benefit they would receive because they lack full information.
B Nobody can be prevented from consuming it once it is provided.
C Its price is set too low by producers.
D Producers of the good make supernormal profit.
parts.answer: A Consumers underestimate the benefit they would receive because they lack full information.
parts.working: Under-consumption of a merit good comes from information failure: people do not realise how much it would benefit them. B describes non-excludability, a feature of public goods; C and D do not explain under-consumption.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why shisha (water-pipe) smoking is classified as a demerit good.
parts.answer: Its harm to the user's health is greater than users realise (imperfect information, e.g. belief that water filters out toxins), so it is over-consumed in a free market.
parts.working: 1 mark: consumers underestimate private harm/information failure; 1 mark: over-consumption relative to the socially desirable level.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which a government could reduce consumption of shisha.
parts.answer: Any two: indirect tax; ban or licensing of shisha cafés; minimum age; health warnings/education campaigns; advertising ban.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Spraying a whole neighbourhood to kill dengue mosquitoes protects every household in the area. Explain why this service is unlikely to be provided by the market.
parts.answer: It is non-excludable (households that do not pay are still protected) and non-rival (one household's protection does not reduce another's), so people free ride, revealing little willingness to pay, and a private firm cannot earn enough revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark: non-excludable; 1 mark: non-rival; 1 mark: free-rider problem means no profitable market.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the government could ensure that the service is provided.
parts.answer: Provide it directly (or contract a firm) and finance it from taxation.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why smokeless tobacco products are regarded as demerit goods.
parts.answer: Consumers underestimate the harm (e.g. oral cancer), and may be addicted, so consumption is higher than is in their own interest.
parts.working: 1 mark: demerit good = over-consumed in a free market. 1 mark: information failure – users underestimate health risks. 1 mark: addiction / habit, so the good's harm to the user is not fully reflected in demand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of banning the sale of such products.
parts.answer: Advantage: consumption should fall sharply, improving health. Disadvantage: an illegal market may develop, with no quality control and no tax revenue.
parts.working: 2 marks each: advantage explained (removes legal supply, clear signal); disadvantage explained (illegal markets, enforcement costs, loss of jobs/tax revenue, consumers may switch to other harmful products).

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why public goods would not be provided in a free market, and consider whether the government should provide all public goods itself.
parts.answer: Non-excludability causes free riding, so there is a missing market; the government must ensure provision, but it may contract private firms to produce them.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): definitions of non-rival and non-excludable; examples (national defence, street lighting, lighthouses, flood defences). Analysis (3): firms cannot charge non-payers, so consumers do not reveal willingness to pay; free-rider problem; zero marginal cost of an extra user means charging would be inefficient; so the market is missing. Evaluation (2): government must finance them through taxation but need not produce them – private firms can build and maintain under contract, possibly more efficiently; deciding the right quantity is difficult without prices; justified conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using sugar-sweetened drinks as an example, explain how information failure can lead to the over-consumption of a demerit good.
parts.answer: Consumers do not know or underestimate the long-term health effects (diabetes, obesity, tooth decay); they act on short-term enjoyment and advertising; so they buy more than they would with full information – the market quantity exceeds the socially desirable quantity.
parts.working: 1 mark: consumers lack/ignore information on harm; 1 mark: perceived private benefit exceeds true benefit; 1 mark: consumption above the optimum.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a government campaign of health warnings may have only a limited effect on consumption.
parts.answer: People may ignore warnings or discount future harm (present bias); habits and addiction to sugar; marketing by drinks firms is stronger; warnings are less effective for children; the campaign costs money and needs to be repeated.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three explained reasons.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)
practice.stem: Invented data for rural districts of a province: the enrolment rate of girls in secondary school was 45 % when fees were charged. After fees were abolished and a stipend of Rs 1 000 a month was paid to girls who attend, the enrolment rate rose to 68 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in the enrolment rate in percentage points and as a percentage. Give the percentage to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: +23 percentage points; +51.1 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why secondary education for girls is regarded as a merit good.
parts.answer: Families may underestimate the private benefits (higher future earnings, better health), so in a free market too little is consumed; there are also large external benefits (healthier children, lower fertility).
parts.working: 1 mark: information failure/underestimated benefit; 1 mark: under-consumption (or external benefits).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the government's spending on the stipend is justified.
parts.answer: For: enrolment rose by half; benefits to the girls and society are large and long-lasting. Against: cost; some families would have enrolled anyway (spending on them achieves nothing); quality of schooling matters as much as enrolment; other factors (new schools, roads) may explain part of the rise. Judgement.
parts.working: 1 mark: argument for with data; 1 mark: argument against; 1 mark: development (e.g. causation, alternative use of money); 1 mark: judgement.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a free market may fail to provide the socially optimal quantity of merit goods, and consider whether merit goods should always be provided free of charge.
parts.answer: Explain: consumers underestimate the benefits (information failure), and many merit goods also have positive externalities; people on low incomes may be unable to afford them; demand is therefore below the optimal level and the market under-consumes. Consider: free provision raises consumption and equity, but costs taxpayers, can cause over-use or waste, and may lower quality if funding is limited; partial subsidies, vouchers, regulation (compulsory vaccination) or information campaigns may be cheaper. Judgement: free provision is justified when information failure is severe and the poor would be excluded, but not always.
parts.working: Marks: 3 knowledge and understanding, 3 analysis, 2 evaluation. Knowledge: definition of merit good and information failure. Analysis: diagram described with demand based on perceived benefit below true benefit, under-consumption. Evaluation: costs and alternatives to free provision, reaching a judgement on 'always'.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a ban is a better policy than an indirect tax for reducing the consumption of a demerit good.
parts.answer: A ban gives the biggest reduction in theory but causes illegal markets; a tax keeps the market legal and raises revenue but has small effect when demand is price inelastic.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 8): a ban removes legal supply, sends a clear signal, but creates illegal markets, enforcement costs, loss of tax revenue and possible harm from unregulated products; indirect tax shifts supply left, raises price and reduces quantity, generates revenue to fund health care or education, but if PED is inelastic consumption falls little and the tax is regressive. Discuss the role of information (education campaigns), the nature of the good (addictive or not, how harmful), enforcement capacity. Evaluation (up to 4): depends on the good and the country – a ban may suit very harmful goods with easy enforcement; a tax suits goods where moderate consumption is accepted; a judgement.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)
practice.stem:
Invented data on the percentage of children fully vaccinated in a country.
Year: urban districts, rural districts
2020: 88 %, 62 %
2025: 88 %, 71 %
Free mobile vaccination clinics began visiting rural villages in 2021.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in vaccination rates between urban and rural districts in 2025, and state whether it was larger or smaller than in 2020.
parts.answer: 17 percentage points in 2025, smaller than 26 percentage points in 2020

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why vaccinations may be under-consumed in rural districts if left to the market.
parts.answer: Information failure (parents underestimate benefits), cost and travel time, low incomes, myths and mistrust.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: merit good definition (1); information failure explained (1); low incomes and distance raise the effective price (1); result – consumption below the socially desirable level (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether the data show that free mobile vaccination clinics are the best policy to raise vaccination rates.
parts.answer: The data suggest the clinics helped, but other factors may have contributed and the cost is not shown.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): rural rate rose 9 points after clinics began while the urban rate stayed at 88 %, which supports the policy; but correlation is not causation – information campaigns, rising incomes or school requirements might also explain it; no data on cost per extra child vaccinated; rate still 71 %, so barriers remain (information, trust). Alternatives: conditional cash transfers, school-entry requirements, community health workers. Evaluation (up to 2): a justified judgement.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether government intervention to correct market failure always improves the allocation of resources.
parts.answer: Improves: taxes on demerit goods, subsidies or provision of merit goods and public goods can move output towards the socially optimal level; information campaigns correct information failure. Government failure: lack of information to set the right tax or subsidy; political pressures and lobbying; administrative costs; unintended consequences (illegal markets after bans, smuggling after high taxes); inefficient state providers lacking profit incentives; policy time lags. Judgement: intervention can improve allocation, but only when its benefits exceed the cost of government failure; outcomes depend on the policy chosen and the quality of institutions – 'always' is too strong.
parts.working: Higher-band answers need accurate, developed analysis (with a relevant diagram where useful) of both sides, applied to the context, and a reasoned judgement that answers the 'assess' question directly; one-sided or descriptive answers stay in the lower bands. Expect explanation of market failure types and corrective policies, a clear concept of government failure with examples, and a judgement.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)
practice.stem: Extract (invented): A health ministry proposes to ban the sale of high-caffeine energy drinks to people under 18. A survey found that 60 % of teenagers who drink them 'did not know they could cause heart problems'. Shopkeepers say they cannot check every buyer's age.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the proposed ban would deal with the information failure described in the extract.
parts.answer: Young people underestimate the harm of high-caffeine drinks; the ban removes the choice for the group least able to judge the risks, cutting their consumption towards the socially desirable level.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies information failure/underestimated harm; 1 mark: ban reduces consumption by under-18s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one unintended consequence of the ban.
parts.answer: e.g. under-18s buy from unlicensed sellers or ask older friends (an illegal market), so the ban is hard to enforce and sellers face no quality checks; or the drinks become more attractive as 'forbidden'.
parts.working: 1 mark: consequence; 1 mark: explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether a health-education campaign in schools would be a better policy than the ban.
parts.answer: Education: tackles the root cause (information failure), keeps freedom of choice, has long-lasting effects, cheap per pupil; but slow, may be ignored, does not reach those out of school. Ban: immediate, clear rule; but enforcement costs, illegal markets, restricts freedom, does nothing about adults. Judgement: possibly both together; depends on the scale of harm and enforcement capacity.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks: analysis of education campaign; up to 2 marks: comparison with the ban; up to 2 marks: reasoned judgement.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)
practice.stem: Invented data: a village of 3 000 households needs a flood embankment costing Rs 9 million. A survey shows that each household values the protection at Rs 4 000. When the village council asks for voluntary contributions of Rs 4 000, only 900 households pay.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total value of the embankment to the households and the shortfall between voluntary contributions and the cost.
parts.answer: Total value Rs 12 million; shortfall Rs 5.4 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the embankment is not built by voluntary contribution even though its total benefit exceeds its cost.
parts.answer: The embankment protects every household whether or not it pays (non-excludable) and protecting one house does not reduce protection for others (non-rival); so each household has an incentive to free ride, hoping others will pay; contributions reveal much less than the true valuation and the project is not funded, although benefits (12m) exceed cost (9m).
parts.working: 1 mark: non-excludable/non-rival; 1 mark: free-rider incentive; 1 mark: links to data – benefit 12m > cost 9m but only 3.6m raised.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way the village council could ensure the embankment is built.
parts.answer: Levy a compulsory local tax (e.g. Rs 3 000 per household) or obtain government funding.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How does an ad valorem tax on a good affect its supply curve?
A The supply curve shifts upwards by the same amount at every quantity.
B The supply curve pivots upwards, so the vertical gap between the old and new curves widens as price rises.
C The supply curve shifts downwards.
D The supply curve does not move; the demand curve shifts to the left.
parts.answer: B The supply curve pivots upwards, so the vertical gap between the old and new curves widens as price rises.
parts.working: An ad valorem tax is a percentage of price, so the tax per unit is larger at higher prices and the new supply curve is steeper. A describes a specific (fixed amount per unit) tax; C describes a subsidy; D confuses a tax on sellers with a change in demand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a specific subsidy.
parts.answer: A fixed amount of money paid by the government to producers for each unit of a good they produce or sell.
parts.working: 1 mark: payment from government to producers; 1 mark: fixed amount per unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a government might subsidise the installation of rooftop solar panels on homes.
parts.answer: Solar power creates external benefits (less air pollution and lower greenhouse-gas emissions than electricity from oil or coal plants) that households ignore; a subsidy lowers the installation price so more panels are installed, moving output towards the socially optimal level (it can also reduce fuel imports).
parts.working: 1 mark: reason (positive externality/environmental benefit, energy security, lower import bill); 1 mark: explanation of how the subsidy lowers price and raises quantity towards the social optimum.

practice.stem: A specific tax of Rs 30 per unit is placed on a good. The price paid by consumers rises from Rs 200 to Rs 220 and the quantity sold falls from 10 000 to 8 000 units a week (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of the tax per unit paid by consumers and by producers.
parts.answer: Consumers Rs 20; producers Rs 10.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total tax revenue and the part of it paid by consumers.
parts.answer: Revenue Rs 240 000; consumers pay Rs 160 000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mobile phone has a price of Rs 50 000 before sales tax. Calculate the price including an 18 % sales tax, and the amount of tax.
parts.answer: Price Rs 59 000; tax Rs 9 000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The tax rate rises to 25 %. Calculate the new price, assuming the pre-tax price is unchanged, and state what type of indirect tax this is.
parts.answer: Rs 62 500; an ad valorem tax.
parts.working: 1 mark: 50 000 × 1.25 = 62 500; 1 mark: ad valorem (percentage of price).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Before a specific tax is imposed on a good, its price is $50 and 100 units are sold. After a specific tax of $10 per unit, the price paid by consumers is $56 and 90 units are sold. What is the government's tax revenue?
A $360
B $540
C $900
D $1000
parts.working: Revenue = tax per unit × quantity sold after the tax = $10 × 90 = $900. D wrongly uses the original quantity; A is the producers' share ($4 × 90) and B the consumers' share ($6 × 90).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a specific tax and an ad valorem tax.
parts.answer: A specific tax is a fixed amount per unit; an ad valorem tax is a percentage of the price.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Specific: supply curve shifts up in parallel. Ad valorem: the vertical gap widens as price rises (curve pivots).

parts.label: b
parts.text: With the help of a diagram described in words, explain why the burden (incidence) of an indirect tax falls mainly on consumers when demand is price inelastic.
parts.answer: Supply shifts up by the tax; with steep demand the price rises by most of the tax and quantity falls little.
parts.working: Diagram: original D and S, S shifts vertically up by the tax (1). With inelastic (steep) demand, price paid by consumers rises by most of the tax (1). Price received by producers (new price minus tax) falls only a little (1). Consumers' share = rise in price × new quantity, larger than producers' share; quantity falls little (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a tax on petrol raises a large amount of revenue but reduces petrol consumption only slightly.
parts.answer: Demand for petrol is price inelastic (few substitutes in the short run, a necessity for transport); so the price rise causes a proportionately smaller fall in quantity; most of the tax is passed to consumers and quantity stays high; revenue = tax per unit × large quantity sold.
parts.working: 1 mark: inelastic demand; 1 mark: reason (few substitutes/necessity); 1 mark: small fall in quantity/most burden on consumers; 1 mark: revenue linked to large quantity.

practice.stem: Invented data: a government pays producers a subsidy of Rs 1 000 for each bag of fertiliser sold. Before the subsidy the price was Rs 4 500 a bag and farmers bought 2.4 million bags a month. With the subsidy farmers pay Rs 3 900 a bag and buy 2.9 million bags a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total monthly cost of the subsidy to the government. Give your answer in Rs billion.
parts.answer: Rs 2.9 billion
parts.working: 1 000 × 2.9 million = Rs 2 900 million = Rs 2.9 billion (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much of the Rs 1 000 subsidy per bag benefits farmers and how much benefits fertiliser producers.
parts.answer: Farmers Rs 600 per bag; producers Rs 400 per bag.
parts.working: 1 mark: 4 500 − 3 900 = 600 to farmers; 1 mark: 1 000 − 600 = 400 to producers (they now receive 4 900).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the change in price paid by farmers, calculate the price elasticity of demand for fertiliser. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why producers capture part of the subsidy.
parts.answer: The subsidy shifts supply down by Rs 1 000; because supply is not perfectly elastic (and demand is not perfectly inelastic), the market price falls by less than the subsidy, so producers receive more per bag than before (Rs 4 900 instead of 4 500).
parts.working: 1 mark: price falls by less than the subsidy; 1 mark: linked to elasticities of demand and supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: With the help of a diagram described in words, explain the effect of a specific tax on consumer surplus and producer surplus.
parts.answer: Supply shifts up by the tax; consumers pay a higher price and buy less, so consumer surplus (area under demand above price) shrinks; producers receive a lower net price (price minus tax) on fewer units, so producer surplus shrinks; part of the lost surplus becomes tax revenue (tax × new quantity) and the rest is a deadweight loss triangle between the old and new quantities.
parts.working: 1 mark: diagram description – supply shifts up by tax, new P and Q; 1 mark: CS falls; 1 mark: PS falls; 1 mark: tax revenue rectangle and deadweight loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a subsidy to producers of a merit good affects its price and the quantity consumed, and consider whether a subsidy is better than direct provision by the government.
parts.answer: Explain: subsidy lowers costs, supply shifts right (down by the subsidy), price falls, quantity consumed rises towards the socially optimal level; incidence shared between consumers and producers depending on elasticities. Consider: subsidy keeps private providers and competition, can be targeted, cheaper than running services; but price may still exclude the poorest, producers may capture the subsidy, needs monitoring. Direct provision guarantees access free of charge but may be inefficient and costly to taxpayers. Judgement depends on the good and the capacity of government.
parts.working: Marks: 3 knowledge and understanding, 3 analysis, 2 evaluation. Knowledge: subsidy and merit good definitions. Analysis: diagram described with supply shift, new price and quantity, share of subsidy. Evaluation: comparison with direct provision reaching a judgement.

practice.stem: In the market for solar water heaters, demand is Qd = 120 − 2P and supply is Qs = −30 + 3P, where P is the price in dollars and Q is in thousands per year (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity before the subsidy.
parts.answer: P = $30, Q = 60 thousand

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government pays producers a subsidy of $10 per unit. The supply equation becomes Qs = −30 + 3(P + 10). Calculate the new equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.answer: P = $24, Q = 72 thousand

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the subsidy to the government, and the share of the subsidy per unit received by consumers and by producers.
parts.answer: Cost $720 thousand; consumers $6 per unit; producers $4 per unit
parts.working: Cost = 10 × 72 = $720 thousand (B1). Consumers' price falls from $30 to $24, so they gain $6 per unit (B1). Producers receive $24 + $10 = $34, a gain of $4 per unit (B1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why consumers receive the larger share of the subsidy in this market.
parts.answer: Demand is less price elastic than supply at the original equilibrium, so more of the benefit passes to consumers.
parts.working: B1: at P = 30, Q = 60 the PED is 2 × 30/60 = 1.0 and the PES is 3 × 30/60 = 1.5; the less elastic side receives the larger share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether an indirect tax on sugary drinks is likely to reduce their consumption significantly.
parts.answer: It raises price and reduces quantity, but the effect depends on PED, the size of the tax, pass-through to consumers and the availability of untaxed substitutes.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 8): diagram showing supply shifting up by the tax; new higher price and lower quantity; incidence depends on PED/PES; if demand is price inelastic (habit, brand loyalty, low share of income for richer groups) consumption falls little; producers may absorb part of the tax or reformulate recipes with less sugar (a desired effect); consumers may switch to untaxed sugary foods; tax is regressive; revenue could fund health education. Evaluation (up to 4): significance depends on the tax rate, the price sensitivity of young and low-income consumers (more elastic), complementary policies (labelling, school bans); a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: In a market, demand is P = 90 − Q and supply is P = 10 + Q, where P is in dollars and Q is in thousands of units. The government imposes a specific tax of $20 per unit on producers (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity before and after the tax, and the price received by producers after the tax.
parts.answer: Before: P = $50, Q = 40; after: consumers pay $60, Q = 30, producers receive $40.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the tax revenue and the deadweight (welfare) loss.
parts.answer: Revenue $600 thousand; deadweight loss $100 thousand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the fall in consumer surplus plus producer surplus equals the tax revenue plus the deadweight loss.
parts.answer: CS falls from 800 to 450 (−350) and PS falls from 800 to 450 (−350): total −700 = 600 revenue + 100 deadweight loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a subsidy is the best way to increase the use of public transport in a large city.
parts.answer: Subsidy: lowers fares, raises demand along the demand curve, corrects under-consumption due to external benefits (less congestion, pollution); helps low-income users. Limits: demand for public transport may be price inelastic – reliability, safety, journey time and coverage matter more than price; subsidy can be captured by operators or cause inefficiency; cost to taxpayers and opportunity cost. Alternatives: direct investment in new routes (metro, BRT), congestion charges or parking fees on cars (raising the price of the substitute), regulation (bus lanes), information. Judgement: a subsidy helps most when fares are a barrier and the service is good; it is usually most effective combined with investment in quality and charges on car use.
parts.working: Higher-band answers need accurate, developed analysis (with a relevant diagram where useful) of both sides, applied to the context, and a reasoned judgement that answers the 'assess' question directly; one-sided or descriptive answers stay in the lower bands. Expect a subsidy diagram described (supply shifts down, lower price, higher quantity), elasticity argument, alternatives compared, and a judgement on 'the best way'.

practice.stem: Invented data: to reduce plastic waste, a government places a tax of Rs 15 on each single-use plastic bottle of drink. Before the tax the price was Rs 60 and 50 million bottles a year were sold. After the tax the price is Rs 72 and 44 million bottles are sold.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand for bottled drinks over this price change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the tax revenue and the share of the tax paid by consumers.
parts.answer: Revenue Rs 660 million; consumers pay 80 % of the tax.
parts.working: 1 mark: 15 × 44 million = 660 million; 1 mark: (72 − 60) ÷ 15 = 80 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether this tax is likely to achieve the government's aim of reducing plastic waste.
parts.answer: For: consumption fell 12 % (6 million fewer bottles); revenue can fund recycling and water fountains. Against: demand is inelastic, so the fall is small and most of the burden falls on consumers; people may switch to other single-use plastics not taxed; waste depends on disposal not just purchases; the tax is regressive. Judgement: a modest effect alone; more effective with deposit-return schemes, recycling investment and alternatives.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks: effect using data; up to 2 marks: limits; up to 2 marks: reasoned judgement.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments
practice.stem: A government's cash-transfer programme pays Rs 10,500 every quarter (three months) to each of 9 million low-income families. The country's GDP is Rs 105 trillion (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual cost of the cash-transfer programme. Give your answer in Rs billion.
parts.answer: Rs 378 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of the programme as a percentage of GDP. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a transfer payment and why it is not counted as part of GDP.
parts.answer: A payment from the government for which no good or service is provided in return; it redistributes existing income rather than paying for new output.
parts.working: 1 mark definition. 1 mark: no production takes place in return, so counting it would double-count income.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between direct provision and a subsidy as ways of increasing the consumption of a merit good.
parts.answer: Direct provision: the government itself produces/supplies the good, often free at the point of use; subsidy: the government pays private producers (or consumers) to lower the price, while private firms still supply it.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of direct provision by the government in your country and state one reason for it.
parts.answer: e.g. government schools or basic health units; reason: to ensure access for the poor / under-consumption of merit goods.
parts.working: 1 mark: example; 1 mark: reason.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of giving poor households cash transfers rather than providing them with food rations.
parts.answer: Advantage: cash lets families choose what they need most (freedom, efficiency), and is cheaper to deliver than storing and distributing food. Disadvantage: cash may be spent on non-essentials or demerit goods; its value can be eroded by inflation; food rations guarantee nutrition.
parts.working: 1 mark: advantage; 1 mark: explanation; 1 mark: disadvantage; 1 mark: explanation.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a buffer stock scheme can stabilise the price of cotton.
parts.answer: The agency sets a target price range. When a good harvest pushes the price below the floor, it buys cotton and stores it, raising demand; when a poor harvest pushes the price above the ceiling, it sells from its stock, raising supply; so price stays within the range.
parts.working: 1 mark: target range/floor and ceiling; 1 mark: buys in surplus years; 1 mark: sells in shortage years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one cost of operating a buffer stock scheme.
parts.answer: Any one: buying the surplus; storage and insurance; wastage/deterioration; administration.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments
practice.stem: Invented data: a cocoa buffer stock agency aims to keep the price at $2 500 per tonne. After a very good harvest, there is a surplus of 120 000 tonnes at that price, which the agency buys. Storage costs $40 per tonne per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of buying the surplus. Give your answer in $ million.
parts.answer: $300 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of storing this cocoa for one year.
parts.answer: $4.8 million

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the agency hopes to recover most of these costs later.
parts.answer: When a poor harvest pushes the price above the target, it sells stored cocoa, receiving revenue that offsets earlier purchase costs.
parts.working: 1 mark: sells in poor harvest years; 1 mark: revenue recovers purchase cost.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments
practice.stem: A buffer stock agency for coffee beans aims to keep the price between a floor of $1.80 per kg and a ceiling of $2.20 per kg. After a very good harvest, the free-market price would fall to $1.50 per kg, so the agency buys 300,000 tonnes of coffee beans at $1.80 per kg (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost to the agency of the purchases it makes after the good harvest. Give your answer in $ million.
parts.answer: $540 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the agency would do if a poor harvest caused the free-market price to rise to $2.50 per kg.
parts.answer: Sell coffee from its stock to increase supply and bring the price down to the ceiling of $2.20.
parts.working: 1 mark: sell from the stock. 1 mark: the extra supply shifts the supply curve right and keeps the price at or below $2.20.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why such a scheme might fail in the long run.
parts.answer: Floor set too high (persistent surpluses and rising costs); storage costs and perishability; stocks run out after several poor harvests; producers expand output; funding problems.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained reasons.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the direct provision of health care by the government can increase the consumption of a merit good, and consider the problems that direct provision may cause.
parts.answer: Free provision removes the price barrier and raises consumption towards the desired level; but it is costly, may cause excess demand and can be inefficient.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): meaning of direct provision (government produces and supplies, often free at the point of use); health care as a merit good under-consumed due to information failure and low incomes. Analysis (3): zero price means quantity demanded rises (movement along demand to where price = 0); access no longer depends on income; equity improves. Evaluation (2): high opportunity cost for the budget; excess demand leads to waiting lists; lack of profit motive may reduce efficiency and quality; information failure remains if people still do not use services; justified conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments
practice.stem:
Invented data: the surplus (+) or shortage (−) of a commodity at the buffer stock agency's target price, in thousand tonnes:
Year 1: +50; Year 2: +30; Year 3: −20; Year 4: +40
The agency buys every surplus and sells to meet every shortage. It starts with no stock.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the size of the agency's stock at the end of Year 4.
parts.answer: 100 thousand tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text: The agency buys and sells at $300 per tonne and started with funds of $25 million. Calculate its spending on net purchases by the end of Year 3 and by the end of Year 4, and state when it runs out of funds.
parts.answer: $18 million by the end of Year 3; $30 million by the end of Year 4; the funds run out during Year 4.
parts.working: M1: Year 3 net 60 000 × 300 = $18 million; M1: Year 4 net 100 000 × 300 = $30 million; A1: exceeds $25 million in Year 4.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why buffer stock schemes often run out of money when the target price is set too high.
parts.answer: If the floor is above the long-run average market price, surpluses occur in most years, so the agency keeps buying and rarely sells; stocks and storage costs grow until funds are exhausted.
parts.working: 1 mark: target above average equilibrium price; 1 mark: purchases exceed sales, funds and storage exhausted.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments
practice.stem: Invented data: a country with a population of 240 million has 6 public hospital beds per 10 000 people. Patients at public hospitals wait an average of 5 hours to see a doctor, compared with 40 minutes at private hospitals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of public hospital beds in the country.
parts.answer: 144 000 beds

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why direct provision of health care by the government may be inefficient.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: no profit motive to cut costs or improve quality; overstaffing or political appointments; lack of competition; free at point of use leads to excess demand and long waiting times; poor information on patients' preferences; budget allocations not linked to performance.
parts.working: For each reason: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the government still provides health care directly.
parts.answer: Health care is a merit good with external benefits (e.g. vaccination stops disease spreading); poor households could not afford private care, so direct provision ensures access and equity.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason; 1 mark: explanation.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between means-tested and universal transfer payments.
parts.answer: Means-tested benefits are paid only to those whose income/wealth is below a limit; universal benefits are paid to everyone in a group (e.g. all pensioners) regardless of income.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of each type.
parts.answer: Means-tested: lower cost, money targeted at those in need. Universal: simple and cheap to administer, high take-up, no stigma, no poverty trap.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why take-up of means-tested benefits is often low.
parts.answer: Eligible people may not know about them, find the forms complex, lack documents (e.g. ID cards), or feel stigma.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two reasons.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a government can use transfer payments to reduce poverty, and consider whether transfer payments reduce the incentive to work.
parts.answer: Explain: transfers (cash benefits, pensions, child allowances, unemployment benefits) raise the disposable income of poor households; financed by progressive taxes they redistribute income; targeted payments can lift households above the poverty line and protect against shocks. Consider: benefits withdrawn as income rises create high effective marginal tax rates (poverty/unemployment trap) and reduce the incentive to work; generous benefits may raise the reservation wage; but many recipients cannot work (elderly, disabled, children), benefits may be too low to change behaviour, and conditional transfers (e.g. linked to school attendance) can raise future productivity. Judgement: design matters (tapers, conditions).
parts.working: Marks: 3 knowledge and understanding, 3 analysis, 2 evaluation. Knowledge: definition of transfer payments and poverty. Analysis: chain from transfer → disposable income → consumption of essentials. Evaluation: incentive effects, design and a judgement.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether buffer stock schemes are an effective way to stabilise the prices of agricultural products.
parts.answer: They can smooth short-term fluctuations, but often fail because of wrongly set price bands, storage costs, perishability and lack of funds.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 8): agricultural prices are unstable because supply varies with weather and both demand and supply are price inelastic in the short run; diagram of a price band, buying in good harvests and selling in poor ones; benefits: stable farm incomes, planning, investment, stable food prices for consumers. Problems: setting the band correctly (if too high, permanent surpluses); storage and wastage costs; perishable goods cannot be stored; a run of poor harvests empties the stock; political pressure; large funds needed; for exported crops, other countries' output matters. Evaluation (up to 4): more effective for storable goods (grains, metals) with a band near the long-run average price; judgement.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether direct provision by the state is the best way to ensure that everyone has access to clean drinking water.
parts.answer: For state provision: water networks are natural monopolies; clean water is a merit good with large external benefits (preventing disease); access for the poor and remote areas regardless of ability to pay; long-term infrastructure planning. Against: government failure – leaking pipes, poor maintenance, illegal connections, under-pricing leading to waste, weak incentives; budget constraints in developing countries. Alternatives: regulated private supply with obligations to serve all areas, public–private partnerships, subsidised connections for poor households, community-run filtration plants, regulation of water quality. Judgement: the state (or tightly regulated provider) is usually necessary, but success depends on governance, pricing and maintenance more than ownership.
parts.working: Higher-band answers need accurate, developed analysis (with a relevant diagram where useful) of both sides, applied to the context, and a reasoned judgement that answers the 'assess' question directly; one-sided or descriptive answers stay in the lower bands. Expect application of merit good/natural monopoly reasoning, analysis of government failure, at least one alternative compared, and a judgement on 'the best way'.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments
practice.stem: Invented data: the demand for cotton is Qd = 300 − P, where Qd is in thousand bales and P is the price in dollars per bale. Supply in any year is fixed by the harvest: 190 thousand bales in a good year and 110 thousand bales in a poor year. A buffer stock agency keeps the price between a floor of $130 and a ceiling of $170.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a year of good harvest, calculate the free-market price and the quantity the agency must buy to keep the price at the floor of $130. Calculate the cost to the agency.
parts.answer: Free-market price $110; agency buys 20 thousand bales; cost $2 600 thousand.
parts.working: M1: 300 − Q = 190 → P = 110; M1: at $130 consumers buy 170, so agency buys 190 − 170 = 20; A1: 20 × 130 = $2 600 thousand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a year of poor harvest, calculate the free-market price and the quantity the agency must sell to keep the price at the ceiling of $170.
parts.answer: Free-market price $190; agency sells 20 thousand bales.
parts.working: 1 mark: 300 − 110 = 190; 1 mark: consumers want 300 − 170 = 130, supply 110, so sell 20.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate farmers' total revenue in each year with and without the scheme.
parts.answer: Good year: $20 900 thousand without, $24 700 thousand with; poor year: $20 900 thousand without, $18 700 thousand with.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Using your answers, explain why a buffer stock scheme that stabilises price may not stabilise farmers' incomes.
parts.answer: Without the scheme, revenue is the same in both years because price moves in the opposite direction to the harvest (between these two points demand is unit elastic using the midpoint method: price and quantity both change by 80 on an average of 150); fixing price means revenue moves with quantity, so incomes now vary from 24 700 to 18 700.
parts.working: 1 mark: free-market price changes offset quantity changes; 1 mark: with stable price revenue varies with the harvest (data used).

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments
practice.stem: Invented data: a provincial government provides free textbooks costing Rs 3 000 per pupil to all 4 million pupils in its schools. A survey suggests that 25 % of families would have bought the books themselves if they were not free.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the scheme and the amount spent on textbooks for families who would have bought them anyway. Give your answers in Rs billion.
parts.answer: Total Rs 12 billion; Rs 3 billion on families who would have bought anyway.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this Rs 3 billion may be seen as a poor use of public money.
parts.answer: It does not change behaviour – these pupils would have had textbooks anyway – so it raises no extra consumption of the merit good; it is a transfer to (often better-off) families, with an opportunity cost elsewhere (e.g. teachers).
parts.working: 1 mark: no additional consumption; 1 mark: opportunity cost/benefits better-off families.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether the government should replace free textbooks for all with free textbooks only for low-income families.
parts.answer: Targeting: saves money (up to Rs 3 billion or more), concentrates help on those who would otherwise go without; but needs means-testing (costly, errors, stigma, low take-up), pupils without books may be missed, universal provision ensures every pupil has the same book on day one and keeps political support. Judgement depends on administrative capacity and how accurately poor families can be identified.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks: benefits of targeting; up to 2 marks: costs/problems of targeting; up to 2 marks: reasoned judgement.

topics.name: Basic economic ideas and resource allocation

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's economy is producing at a point inside its production possibility curve. What does this point show?
A all resources are fully and efficiently employed
B some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
C the combination cannot be reached with current resources
D the country has had an increase in productive capacity
parts.answer: B some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
