parts.working: A point inside the PPC means output could rise without giving up any other good, so resources are unemployed or misallocated. C describes a point outside the curve, not inside it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A flood destroys roads, bridges and factories in a country. Using a production possibility curve described in words, explain the effect on the country's productive capacity.
parts.answer: The PPC shifts inwards because the quantity of capital (a factor of production) has fallen.
parts.working: 1 mark: axes are two goods/services (e.g. agricultural goods and manufactured goods), not price and quantity. 1 mark: capital stock is destroyed, so the maximum output possible falls. 1 mark: the whole PPC shifts inwards (towards the origin); if mainly factories are lost the shift is larger on the manufactured goods axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this differs from the effect of a rise in unemployment caused by a fall in demand.
parts.answer: Unemployment moves the economy to a point inside an unchanged PPC.
parts.working: 1 mark: productive capacity is unchanged, so the PPC does not shift. 1 mark: actual output falls, shown by a movement from a point on the curve to a point inside it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which event would shift a country's production possibility curve outwards?
A a fall in the number of unemployed workers
B the discovery and development of new natural gas reserves
C a change in consumer tastes away from goods and towards services
D a decision to produce more capital goods and fewer consumer goods this year
parts.answer: B the discovery and development of new natural gas reserves
parts.working: New natural resources raise the economy's productive capacity, so the whole curve moves outwards. A moves the economy from a point inside the curve towards it (no shift); C and D are movements along the existing curve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a movement along a production possibility curve and a shift of the curve.
parts.answer: A movement along the curve is a reallocation of existing, fully employed resources from one good to another; a shift is a change in the economy's total productive capacity (quantity or quality of resources, technology).
parts.working: 1 mark: movement = reallocation of given resources between goods/change in combination produced; 1 mark: shift = change in productive capacity/potential output caused by a change in quantity or quality of resources or technology.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why an economy may be producing at a point inside its production possibility curve.
parts.answer: Any two of: unemployed labour; idle capital/factories working below capacity; inefficient use of resources (productive inefficiency), e.g. poor management or power cuts.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An economy moves along its production possibility curve from 60 units of capital goods and 300 units of consumer goods to 80 units of capital goods and 260 units of consumer goods. What is the opportunity cost of each extra unit of capital goods?
A 0.5 units of consumer goods
B 2 units of consumer goods
C 3.25 units of consumer goods
D 40 units of consumer goods
parts.answer: B 2 units of consumer goods
parts.working: Consumer goods given up = 300 − 260 = 40; extra capital goods = 80 − 60 = 20; 40 ÷ 20 = 2 units of consumer goods per unit. D is the total sacrifice, not the cost per unit; A inverts the ratio.

practice.stem:
The table shows the production possibilities of a farming region in Punjab that grows only wheat and cotton (invented data).
Combination: wheat (thousand tonnes), cotton (thousand bales)
A: 0, 500
B: 100, 470
C: 200, 420
D: 300, 340
E: 400, 220
F: 500, 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of one extra tonne of wheat when production moves from combination C to combination D.
parts.answer: 0.8 bales of cotton per tonne of wheat
parts.working: Cotton given up = 420 − 340 = 80 thousand bales (M1); ÷ 100 thousand tonnes of wheat = 0.8 bales per tonne (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of one extra tonne of wheat when production moves from combination E to combination F.
parts.answer: 2.2 bales of cotton per tonne of wheat
parts.working: 220 thousand bales ÷ 100 thousand tonnes = 2.2 bales per tonne (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answers to (a) and (b), explain why the production possibility curve for this region is concave (bowed outwards) from the origin.
parts.answer: Opportunity cost rises as more wheat is produced because resources are not equally suited to both crops.
parts.working: 1 mark: opportunity cost of wheat increases (0.8 → 2.2). 1 mark: land and labour best suited to cotton are moved into wheat last / factors are not perfectly mobile or equally productive in both uses. 1 mark: so each extra unit of wheat needs more cotton to be given up, making the slope steeper and the curve concave.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State whether the combination 200 thousand tonnes of wheat and 450 thousand bales of cotton can be produced. Give a reason.
parts.answer: No, it is unattainable.
parts.working: B1 not attainable; B1 at 200 thousand tonnes of wheat the maximum cotton output is 420 thousand bales, so 450 lies outside the PPC with current resources and technology.

parts.label: a
parts.text: With the help of a production possibility curve diagram, explain the effect of a new technology that raises productivity in the textile industry only, and consider whether such a change will always increase the economic welfare of the country.
parts.answer: The PPC pivots outwards along the textile axis only; welfare usually rises but not always.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): PPC shows maximum combinations of two goods (textiles and other goods) with given resources and technology; opportunity cost; correct axis labels. Analysis (3): the maximum output of textiles rises while the maximum of other goods is unchanged, so the curve pivots outwards from the other-goods intercept; at every point except that intercept the country can now produce more; the opportunity cost of textiles falls. Evaluation (2): welfare may not rise if the economy is inside its PPC (unemployment), if workers displaced by machines stay unemployed, if extra output creates pollution, or if textiles are mostly exported and the gains go to a few owners; a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A small island economy can produce either 400 tablet computers or 1000 tonnes of rice per month, or any combination on a straight-line production possibility curve between these two points (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of producing one tablet computer.
parts.answer: 2.5 tonnes of rice
parts.working: 1000 ÷ 400 = 2.5 tonnes of rice (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum quantity of rice the country can produce if it makes 150 tablet computers.
parts.answer: 625 tonnes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the straight-line shape of this production possibility curve assumes about the country's resources.
parts.answer: Resources are equally suited to both goods, so opportunity cost is constant.
parts.working: 1 mark: constant opportunity cost (same slope throughout). 1 mark: this assumes factors are equally productive in making tablets and rice / perfectly transferable, which is unlikely in reality.

practice.stem:
A provincial government can use its resources to treat hospital patients or to build roads. Its production possibilities for one year are (invented data):
Combination A: 0 million patients, 500 km of road
Combination B: 10 million patients, 480 km of road
Combination C: 20 million patients, 440 km of road
Combination D: 30 million patients, 360 km of road
Combination E: 40 million patients, 200 km of road

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost, in km of road, of treating the extra 10 million patients when the economy moves from combination C to combination D.
parts.answer: 80 km of road

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average opportunity cost per million patients of moving from combination A to combination E.
parts.answer: 12.5 km of road per million patients
parts.working: 500 km given up ÷ 40 million patients = 12.5 km (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the data, explain why the opportunity cost of treating patients increases as more patients are treated.
parts.answer: Each extra 10 million patients costs more road (20, 40, 80, 160 km) because resources are not equally suited to both uses; the resources moved last (e.g. road engineers, heavy machinery) are better at road building than health care.
parts.working: 1 mark: uses the data to show rising cost (20 → 40 → 80 → 160 km); 1 mark: explanation – resources are specialised/not perfectly substitutable between uses.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The province actually treats 25 million patients and builds 380 km of road. State whether this combination is on, inside or outside the production possibility curve, and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Inside the curve: with 25 million patients the province could build at least 400 km of road (midway between 440 and 360), so 380 km means resources are unemployed or used inefficiently.
parts.working: 1 mark: inside; 1 mark: justification using the data – maximum road at 25 million patients is about 400 km (higher still on a curve bowed outwards), so 380 km is below it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how unemployment and an outdated stock of capital equipment each affect an economy's position in relation to its production possibility curve, and consider which of the two problems would be easier for a government to correct.
parts.answer: Unemployment: the economy produces at a point inside its PPC; reducing it moves output towards the curve without any shift. An outdated capital stock: the PPC itself is closer to the origin than it could be; modernising it (investment, new technology) shifts the curve outwards but takes time and has an opportunity cost in consumer goods now. Judgement: cyclical unemployment can often be reduced quickly by raising demand, while renewing capital is slow; but structural unemployment may be as hard to fix as old capital.
parts.working: Marks: 3 knowledge and understanding, 3 analysis, 2 evaluation. Knowledge: point inside the PPC = unused resources; position of the PPC = productive capacity; correctly labelled axes (two goods, not P and Q). Analysis: unemployment → movement to the curve; new capital → outward shift; investment requires giving up consumer goods now (movement along the curve first). Evaluation: depends on the type of unemployment (cyclical vs structural); time lags; funding constraints; a reasoned conclusion.

practice.stem:
Invented data for two countries, average for 2015–2024:
Country X: investment as a share of GDP 32 %; average annual real GDP growth 6.1 %
Country Y: investment as a share of GDP 14 %; average annual real GDP growth 2.8 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the average growth rates of the two countries over the period.
parts.answer: Country X's average growth (6.1 %) was about 2.2 times that of Country Y (2.8 %), i.e. 3.3 percentage points higher.
parts.working: 1 mark: X grew faster. 1 mark: data manipulated, e.g. 3.3 percentage points higher or about 2.2 times as fast.

parts.label: b
parts.text: With the help of a production possibility curve described in words, explain how a decision to produce more capital goods now can affect a country's future output.
parts.answer: Choosing a point with more capital goods and fewer consumer goods now raises the capital stock, shifting the PPC outward in future.
parts.working: Axes labelled capital goods and consumer goods (1). Moving along the PPC towards capital goods means an opportunity cost of current consumer goods (1). Extra capital raises productive capacity (1). Future PPC shifts outwards further than for a country choosing more consumer goods, allowing more of both goods later (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether the data prove that Country Y should increase the share of output it devotes to investment.
parts.answer: Not proven: the data show an association, but growth also depends on other factors; a higher investment share has a current consumption cost.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): higher investment links to faster capacity growth (X); sacrifice of current consumption may harm living standards of poor households; return depends on type/quality of investment; growth also depends on labour skills, technology, demand, political stability; the data cover only two countries and averages, so correlation not causation. Evaluation (up to 2): a judgement, e.g. investment is likely to help but the data alone cannot prove it; it depends on whether Y has spare capacity or weak demand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether the production possibility curve is a useful way to explain the economic problem facing a low-income country.
parts.answer: Useful for showing scarcity, choice, opportunity cost and growth, but limited because it is a simplified two-good model.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks for analysis: PPC illustrates scarcity (finite resources), choice between combinations, opportunity cost (slope), unemployment (inside), growth (outward shift) and the trade-off between capital and consumer goods, which is key for a low-income country with low savings. Limitations: only two goods; assumes fixed resources and technology; does not show distribution of output, quality of life, or which point is best (a normative choice); points outside may be reached through trade or aid. Up to 4 marks for evaluation: a supported judgement, e.g. useful as a starting framework but policy decisions need further evidence on income distribution and markets. Level 3 (9–12): balanced, applied to low-income country, justified conclusion; Level 2 (5–8): some analysis, limited evaluation; Level 1 (1–4): descriptive.

practice.stem: Invented data for a country (US$ billion, at constant prices): potential output in 2024 was 500 and actual output was 470. In 2025 potential output grew by 5 % and actual output grew by 3 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output gap (potential minus actual output) as a percentage of potential output in 2024 and in 2025. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using a production possibility curve described in words, explain what happened to actual and potential growth between 2024 and 2025.
parts.answer: The PPC shifted outwards (potential growth 5 %) and the production point moved outwards (actual growth 3 %), but the point ended up further inside the new curve.
parts.working: 1 mark: outward shift of PPC shows potential growth. 1 mark: movement of the production point away from the origin shows actual growth. 1 mark: because actual grew less than potential, the gap between the point and the curve widened (more unused resources).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's production possibility curve shows manufactured goods on the horizontal axis and agricultural goods on the vertical axis. A new technology raises productivity in manufacturing only. Which statement is correct?
A The curve shifts outwards in parallel and opportunity costs are unchanged.
B The maximum output of agricultural goods rises and the opportunity cost of agricultural goods falls.
C The maximum output of manufactured goods rises and the opportunity cost of a manufactured good, measured in agricultural goods, falls.
D The maximum output of manufactured goods rises and the opportunity cost of a manufactured good, measured in agricultural goods, rises.
parts.answer: C The maximum output of manufactured goods rises and the opportunity cost of a manufactured good, measured in agricultural goods, falls.
parts.working: The curve pivots outwards along the manufactured-goods axis only; the agricultural maximum is unchanged. Each manufactured good now needs fewer resources, so fewer agricultural goods are given up per manufactured good. D reverses the direction; B wrongly moves the agricultural intercept; A ignores that only one industry changed.

practice.stem:
Two regions of a country each produce only wheat and machines, and each has a straight-line production possibility curve (invented data, per month):
North: either 60 tonnes of wheat or 30 machines, or any combination on the straight line between them
South: either 40 tonnes of wheat or 40 machines, or any combination on the straight line between them

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of producing one machine in each region.
parts.answer: North: 2 tonnes of wheat per machine; South: 1 tonne of wheat per machine.
parts.working: 1 mark each: North 60 ÷ 30 = 2; South 40 ÷ 40 = 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The two regions combine their production. State the maximum quantity of wheat and the maximum number of machines the combined economy can produce.
parts.answer: 100 tonnes of wheat or 70 machines.
parts.working: 1 mark: 60 + 40 = 100 tonnes of wheat; 1 mark: 30 + 40 = 70 machines.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum quantity of wheat the combined economy can produce if it makes 55 machines. Explain which region should make the machines.
parts.answer: 30 tonnes of wheat; South should make its 40 machines first because its opportunity cost is lower, and North makes the other 15.
parts.working: M1: South makes 40 machines (lower opportunity cost, 1 tonne each); M1: North makes 15 machines, giving up 15 × 2 = 30 tonnes; A1: North produces 60 − 30 = 30 tonnes of wheat, South none, total 30 tonnes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the combined production possibility curve is bowed outwards (concave to the origin) even though each region's own curve is a straight line.
parts.answer: As more machines are made, production moves from the low-cost region (South, 1 tonne) to the high-cost region (North, 2 tonnes), so the opportunity cost of machines rises and the combined curve has a kink that bows outwards.
parts.working: 1 mark: the two regions have different opportunity costs; 1 mark: extra machines must eventually come from the higher-cost region, so opportunity cost increases.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the best example of a free good?
A drinking water supplied by a city water board
B sunlight used by a family to dry washing on a roof
C a free textbook provided by the government to school pupils
D a public park in Islamabad with no entry charge
parts.answer: B sunlight used by a family to dry washing on a roof
parts.working: A free good has no opportunity cost: it is not scarce, and using it does not take resources from other uses. Sunlight is unlimited relative to demand. C and D have zero price to the user but use scarce resources, so they are economic goods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a public good.
parts.answer: A good that is non-rival and non-excludable.
parts.working: 1 mark non-rival: one person's consumption does not reduce the amount available to others. 1 mark non-excludable: people who do not pay cannot be stopped from benefiting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a private firm is unlikely to provide street lighting in a residential area of Lahore.
parts.answer: Because of the free-rider problem, the firm could not charge users and would make no revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark: street lighting is non-excludable, so non-payers cannot be prevented from using it. 1 mark: consumers have an incentive to be free riders and not reveal their willingness to pay. 1 mark: the firm cannot earn revenue to cover costs, so the market fails to provide it (missing market).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is meant by saying that a good is non-excludable?
A Once the good is provided, it is impossible or very costly to stop people who do not pay from benefiting.
B One person's use of the good does not reduce the amount available to others.
C The good is provided free of charge by the government.
D The good has no opportunity cost to society.
parts.answer: A Once the good is provided, it is impossible or very costly to stop people who do not pay from benefiting.
parts.working: Non-excludability is about being unable to prevent non-payers from benefiting. B describes non-rivalry, the most common confusion; C confuses who provides a good with its characteristics; D describes a free good.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the two characteristics that distinguish a private good from a public good.
parts.answer: A private good is rival (one person's consumption reduces what is available to others) and excludable (non-payers can be prevented from consuming it); a public good is non-rival and non-excludable.
parts.working: 1 mark: rivalry explained; 1 mark: excludability explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Classify each of the following as a private good, a public good or a free good, giving a reason in each case: (i) a cricket bat; (ii) a tsunami early-warning siren on a coastline; (iii) sea air at the beach.
parts.answer: (i) private good – rival and excludable; (ii) public good – everyone in range hears it (non-excludable) and one person hearing it does not reduce it for others (non-rival); (iii) free good – not scarce, so it has zero opportunity cost.
parts.working: 1 mark each for correct classification with a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A city holds a large fireworks display that can be seen from all over the city. Explain why the free-rider problem means a private firm would be unlikely to provide this display by charging people to watch it.
parts.answer: People can watch without paying because they cannot be excluded, so each person has an incentive to let others pay; the firm cannot collect enough revenue to cover its costs.
parts.working: 1 mark: non-excludable – viewers cannot be prevented from watching; 1 mark: so people do not reveal willingness to pay/free ride, and revenue is too low for a profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way in which a private firm might still finance such a display.
parts.answer: By selling sponsorship or advertising to businesses that want their brand seen by the large audience (or by charging for the best viewing seats close to the display).
parts.working: 1 mark: a valid method; 1 mark: explanation of why it avoids the free-rider problem.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A provincial government provides free lunches to all primary school pupils. How should these lunches be classified?
A a public good, because they are provided by the government
B a public good, because no price is charged
C a private good, because they are rival and excludable
D a free good, because they have no opportunity cost
parts.answer: C a private good, because they are rival and excludable
parts.working: One pupil's lunch cannot be eaten by another (rival) and people can be prevented from getting one (excludable), so it is a private good, whoever provides it; it may also be a merit good. A is the common error of linking public goods to who supplies them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why motorcycle helmets are classified as a merit good.
parts.answer: Riders underestimate the benefit of a helmet (protection from serious head injury), so in a free market fewer helmets are bought and worn than is in the riders' own interest.
parts.working: 1 mark: a merit good is one that would be under-consumed if left to the free market / benefits are greater than consumers realise. 1 mark: information failure – riders underestimate the risk of an accident or the severity of head injuries (or are over-confident about short journeys). 1 mark: so demand and consumption are below the level that best serves the rider (and society, e.g. lower hospital costs).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the government might make the wearing of helmets compulsory rather than subsidise their price.
parts.answer: A subsidy lowers the price, but riders who underestimate the benefit may still not buy or wear a helmet; a law changes behaviour directly.
parts.working: 1 mark reason (the cause of under-consumption is information failure, not mainly price / regulation has a low budget cost). 1 mark development, e.g. even a cheaper helmet may be left at home, while a law backed by fines makes every rider wear one; it also costs the government little compared with a subsidy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a merit good and a public good, and consider whether secondary education in Pakistan should be regarded as a merit good.
parts.answer: Public goods are defined by non-rivalry and non-excludability; merit goods by under-consumption due to information failure; education is usually a merit good, though this involves a value judgement.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): public good definition (non-rival, non-excludable, free-rider, missing market); merit good definition (under-consumed in free market, information failure, judged by government). Analysis (3): education is rival and excludable, so it is not a public good; households may underestimate future earnings and wider benefits, poor families face cost barriers or need children's labour; so consumption is below the level society desires. Evaluation (2): classification as merit good is partly a value judgement; for well-informed households demand may already be high; private schools show it can be supplied by the market; a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is best described as a quasi-public good?
A a lighthouse that warns ships of rocks
B a national defence system
C a city road that becomes congested at peak times
D a bottle of mineral water
parts.answer: C a city road that becomes congested at peak times
parts.working: A road is largely non-excludable but becomes rival when congested, so it has only some public-good characteristics. A and B are close to pure public goods; D is a private good (rival and excludable).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using alcohol as an example, explain the difference between a demerit good and a good that has negative externalities in consumption.
parts.answer: A demerit good is one whose harm to the consumer is underestimated (imperfect information), so it is over-consumed; e.g. drinkers underestimate damage to their own liver. A negative consumption externality is a cost to third parties, e.g. drunk-driving accidents or violence affecting others. Alcohol has both features, but the ideas are different: one is about the consumer's own judgement, the other about effects on people outside the transaction.
parts.working: 1 mark: demerit good definition (over-consumed because of information failure about private harm); 1 mark: example of private harm; 1 mark: negative externality = cost to third parties; 1 mark: example of external cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why deciding that a good is a demerit good involves a value judgement.
parts.answer: Someone (usually the government) decides that consumers' own choices are wrong and that they should consume less; this is a view about what ought to happen, not a testable fact.
parts.working: 1 mark: the government/society overrides individual choice; 1 mark: this is a normative judgement about what is good for people.

practice.stem:
A city council in Pakistan provides free public Wi-Fi in its parks. No password is needed (invented data):
Year 1: 20 000 daily users, average connection speed 25 Mbps
Year 3: 80 000 daily users, average connection speed 8 Mbps

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the number of daily users and in the average connection speed between Year 1 and Year 3.
parts.answer: Users: +300 %; speed: −68 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, explain why the free Wi-Fi is not a pure public good.
parts.answer: As more people use it, each user's speed falls sharply, so one person's use reduces the benefit available to others – the service is rival (at least when congested).
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies rivalry/congestion; 1 mark: uses the data (users ×4, speed down 68 %).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The council is considering requiring a password that is sold for a monthly fee. Explain how this would change the classification of the service.
parts.answer: It would make the service excludable: non-payers can be shut out, so with rivalry it becomes a private good that a firm could provide for profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: becomes excludable; 1 mark: rival and excludable = private good / market could supply it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A motorway between two cities charges drivers a toll at booths on every entrance. At night, when traffic is light, vehicles travel freely; during the morning rush hour it is heavily congested. Explain why the motorway is best described as a quasi-public good rather than a pure public good.
parts.answer: It is partly rival (congestion) and partly excludable (tolls), so it has some but not all characteristics of a public good.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition/idea of quasi-public good. 1 mark: at night one extra car does not reduce space for others (non-rival), but at rush hour extra users slow others down, so it becomes rival. 1 mark: toll booths mean non-payers can be excluded, so it is excludable. 1 mark: therefore it does not fully meet both conditions of a pure public good.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the government might still choose to finance the motorway from taxation.
parts.answer: Large external benefits/high fixed cost mean the market may under-provide it; tolls could reduce efficient use when the road is empty.
parts.working: 1 mark reason, 1 mark development (e.g. charging a toll when the road is empty discourages use that costs nothing extra; the economy-wide benefits of trade and travel are not captured by tolls).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether the classification of goods as merit goods or demerit goods is always based on objective evidence.
parts.answer: Not always: some classifications rest on strong evidence (tobacco harm), but many involve value judgements by governments.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 8): definitions of merit and demerit goods; role of information failure; evidence-based cases (smoking, vaccinations) where harm or benefit is measured scientifically; cases that are value judgements (alcohol, certain entertainment, arts, sugary foods) where the government's view replaces consumers' own preferences; paternalism; classification can vary between countries and over time; positive vs normative statements. Evaluation (up to 4): a weighed judgement, e.g. the evidence may be objective, but the decision that consumption is 'too high' or 'too low' is always partly normative. Level 3 (9–12) balanced with justified conclusion; Level 2 (5–8); Level 1 (1–4).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether the private sector could ever efficiently provide goods that are usually classified as public goods.
parts.answer: Arguments for: technology can make some goods excludable (toll roads with electronic tags, encrypted broadcasts), turning them into club/private goods; firms finance some 'public' goods indirectly (advertising-funded TV, sponsorship); assurance contracts or crowdfunding can overcome free riding in small communities. Arguments against: pure public goods such as national defence or flood defences remain non-excludable, so free riding prevents revenue; where exclusion is possible but marginal cost of an extra user is zero, charging excludes people who would benefit, so output is below the socially efficient level; profit-seeking firms may under-provide to poorer areas. Judgement: the private sector can provide quasi-public goods and some public goods with technology or indirect finance, but rarely at the efficient quantity for pure public goods; the answer depends on the good's characteristics and the possibility of exclusion.
parts.working: Higher-band answers need accurate, developed analysis (with a relevant diagram where useful) of both sides, applied to the context, and a reasoned judgement that answers the 'assess' question directly; one-sided or descriptive answers stay in the lower bands. Expect: definitions of non-rival and non-excludable; free-rider problem explained; examples where technology creates excludability; efficiency argument (zero marginal cost so any positive price is inefficient); conclusion distinguishing pure from quasi-public goods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the encryption of satellite television signals changed the classification of television broadcasts.
parts.answer: Before encryption anyone with a dish could watch (non-excludable, non-rival – a public good); encryption lets the broadcaster exclude people who do not pay for a decoder card, so broadcasts became excludable (a club/quasi-private good) and could be sold.
parts.working: 1 mark: earlier non-excludable; 1 mark: encryption creates excludability so a charge can be made.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a free online encyclopaedia, written by volunteers and funded by donations, is a public good.
parts.answer: For: one person reading an article does not reduce what others can read (non-rival, except at very high server load), and it is open to all (non-excludable in practice because the owners choose not to exclude). Against: exclusion is technically possible (logins, paywalls), so it is non-excludable by choice, not by nature; servers have a cost and heavy use can create congestion. Judgement: it has public-good characteristics and suffers free riding (few readers donate), but strictly it is a non-rival good that could be made excludable.
parts.working: 1 mark: non-rival explained; 1 mark: non-excludable in practice; 1 mark: but exclusion is technically possible / congestion; 1 mark: reasoned judgement (e.g. free riding shows public-good features).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a planned economy, how are most decisions about what to produce made?
A by consumers spending in markets
B by firms seeking the highest profit
C by the state through central planning
D by trade unions bargaining with employers
parts.answer: C by the state through central planning
parts.working: In a planned (command) economy the state owns most resources and decides what, how and for whom to produce. A and B describe the price mechanism in a market economy.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a market economy, what is the main signal that encourages firms to produce more of a good?
A a rise in the price of the good relative to its costs of production
B a production target set by a government ministry
C a fall in consumer demand for the good
D a rise in the costs of producing the good
parts.answer: A a rise in the price of the good relative to its costs of production
parts.working: A higher price relative to cost raises expected profit, which attracts resources into the industry. B describes a planned economy; C and D would reduce the incentive to produce.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the three fundamental questions that every economic system must answer.
parts.answer: What to produce; how to produce it; for whom to produce it.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the price mechanism answers the question 'for whom to produce?' in a market economy.
parts.answer: Goods go to those willing and able to pay the market price; people's purchasing power depends on their incomes from selling factors of production.
parts.working: 1 mark: allocated to those with willingness and ability to pay; 1 mark: depends on income/wealth earned from factor ownership.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a mixed economy.
parts.answer: An economy in which resources are allocated partly by the market (private sector, price mechanism) and partly by the government (public sector, planning, taxes and spending).
parts.working: 1 mark: both private and public sectors; 1 mark: allocation through both price mechanism and government decisions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the government in a mixed economy provides some goods, such as primary schooling, rather than leaving them to the private sector.
parts.answer: Education is a merit good: left to the market, it would be under-consumed because families underestimate its benefits or cannot afford it, so the state provides it to raise consumption (and to improve equity).
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies a reason (merit good/equity/public good where relevant); 1 mark: explains why the market would under-provide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by consumer sovereignty in a market economy.
parts.answer: Consumers decide what is produced: their spending ('money votes') raises the prices and profits of goods they want, so firms move resources into producing them.
parts.working: 1 mark: consumers determine what is produced; 1 mark: through spending/price signals affecting profits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why consumer sovereignty may be limited in practice.
parts.answer: Any one, explained: persuasive advertising shapes what consumers want; a monopoly can restrict choice and set prices; consumers lack information to make good choices; government regulation limits choices.
parts.working: 1 mark: valid reason; 1 mark: explanation of how it reduces consumers' control over production.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems that a planned economy may face in allocating resources.
parts.answer: e.g. information problems and weak incentives.
parts.working: 2 marks for each of two explained problems: (1) planners lack information about consumer preferences and costs, leading to shortages and surpluses; (2) weak profit/wage incentives reduce effort, innovation and quality; (3) bureaucracy and slow response to change; (4) limited consumer choice. 1 mark for identification, 1 for explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features of a mixed economy.
parts.answer: Both private and public sectors; prices allocate most goods but government intervenes.
parts.working: 1 mark each: private and public ownership exist together; market prices allocate many goods; the government provides public/merit goods, regulates markets or redistributes income.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a mixed economy is the best way to allocate a country's scarce resources.
parts.answer: Often yes, because it combines the incentives of markets with government correction of market failure, but the outcome depends on the balance and on government failure.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 8): the economic problem (what, how, for whom); market economy strengths (price signals, efficiency, choice, incentives) and weaknesses (public goods not provided, inequality, information failure, demerit goods); planned economy strengths (equity, coordination of large projects) and weaknesses (information, incentives); mixed economy aims to gain the advantages of both. Evaluation (up to 4): depends on the size and quality of the public sector, corruption and government failure, stage of development; 'best' depends on value judgements about equity vs efficiency; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which problem of a free market economy is a planned economy most likely to avoid?
A a lack of incentive to innovate
B the under-provision of public goods
C slow responses to changes in consumer demand
D shortages caused by prices that are set too low
parts.answer: B the under-provision of public goods
parts.working: A planning authority can decide to produce public goods that the market would not provide because of free riding. A, C and D are typical weaknesses of planned economies, not of markets.

practice.stem:
Invented data for three countries:
Country P: government spending 18 % of GDP; state-owned enterprises employ 4 % of workers
Country Q: government spending 38 % of GDP; state-owned enterprises employ 12 % of workers
Country R: government spending 52 % of GDP; state-owned enterprises employ 25 % of workers

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which country's economy is closest to a planned economy and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Country R: it has the highest government spending share (52 %) and the highest share of employment in state-owned enterprises (25 %).
parts.working: 1 mark: Country R; 1 mark: uses both indicators.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater Country Q's government spending share is than Country P's. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 2.11 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why all three countries can be described as mixed economies.
parts.answer: In each country both the state (spending 18–52 % of GDP, some state-owned enterprises) and the private sector (at least 75 % of workers are outside state-owned enterprises in every country, and private firms and households make most spending decisions) allocate resources.
parts.working: 1 mark: public sector present in all; 1 mark: private sector/market allocation also present in all.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Consider whether a larger government share of spending means that a country allocates its resources better.
parts.answer: Possibly better: more public goods and merit goods provided, more redistribution, correction of market failures. Possibly worse: government failure – weak incentives in state enterprises, inefficiency, political influence, higher taxes reducing incentives. Judgement: it depends on the quality of government and on what the spending is used for, not just its size.
parts.working: 1 mark: argument that more state involvement can improve allocation; 1 mark: argument that it can worsen allocation (government failure); 1 mark: development of either; 1 mark: reasoned judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A government sells its state-owned airline to private shareholders. Explain how the profit motive may change the way the airline allocates its resources.
parts.answer: Private owners aim for profit, so the airline is likely to cut unprofitable routes and surplus staff, raise fares on routes with inelastic demand, and invest where returns are highest; resources move towards what customers are willing to pay for and costs are controlled more tightly (productive efficiency).
parts.working: 1 mark: profit objective replaces political/social objectives; 1 mark each (up to 3) for developed changes: closing loss-making routes, cutting costs/overstaffing, pricing to demand, investment decisions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage of this change for people living in remote areas.
parts.answer: Loss-making routes to remote towns may be closed or fares raised, reducing access to travel and harming the regional economy – social benefits are ignored by a profit-seeking firm.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies route closure/higher fares; 1 mark: explains the external/social cost ignored by the market.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways, other than producing goods and services itself, in which the government in a mixed economy influences how resources are allocated.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: indirect taxes raise the price of goods such as tobacco and reduce resources used to make them; subsidies lower the price of goods such as fertiliser and attract resources into them; regulation/laws ban or limit certain goods or set standards; price controls (maximum or minimum prices) change quantities traded; transfer payments change who can afford goods.
parts.working: For each of two ways: 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for explaining how it changes the allocation of resources.

practice.stem:
Invented data for a country that moved from a planned economy to a market economy, starting in Year 1.
Year: real GDP index (Year 1 = 100), inflation rate (%), unemployment rate (%)
Year 1: 100, 4, 1
Year 2: 88, 300, 8
Year 3: 84, 95, 14
Year 4: 90, 30, 12
Year 5: 99, 12, 9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in real GDP between Year 1 and Year 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, explain why the move from a planned to a market economy might cause inflation and unemployment in the short run.
parts.answer: Price controls removed → prices jump to market levels; inefficient state firms close → workers lose jobs while new firms take time to grow.
parts.working: Inflation (2): removal of maximum prices lets prices rise to equilibrium where there were shortages; 300 % inflation in Year 2. Unemployment (2): subsidies to loss-making state enterprises end, so they cut jobs or close; labour is occupationally immobile and new private firms take time to develop; unemployment rose from 1 % to 14 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether the data suggest that the move to a market economy was a mistake.
parts.answer: Not necessarily: short-run costs were high, but by Year 5 growth had resumed and inflation fallen.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): Years 2–3 show large costs (inflation, unemployment, falling output); by Year 5 real GDP had recovered to 99 and inflation fell to 12 %, suggesting gains in efficiency; data say nothing about quality/choice of goods or distribution; unemployment still high at 9 %. Evaluation (up to 2): a judgement, e.g. too early to say; depends on the pace of reform and support for those who lost jobs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a market economy allocates resources, and consider whether the 'invisible hand' of the market always leads to an efficient outcome.
parts.answer: Explain: price signals, incentives and rationing; consumers' demand raises prices and profits, attracting resources (signalling and incentive functions); prices ration scarce goods; self-interest of buyers and sellers coordinates the economy without central direction. Consider: the market fails with public goods (not provided), merit and demerit goods (information failure), externalities (prices ignore third-party costs/benefits), monopoly power (output restricted) and immobile factors; efficiency also says nothing about fairness. Judgement: markets are often efficient for ordinary private goods in competitive conditions, but not always.
parts.working: Marks: 3 knowledge and understanding, 3 analysis, 2 evaluation. Knowledge: the three functions of the price mechanism. Analysis: chain from a change in demand to a change in price, profit and resource allocation (a demand and supply diagram helps). Evaluation: identifies conditions where markets fail and reaches a judgement on 'always'.

practice.stem:
Invented data for a country moving from central planning to a market system:
Under central planning the state set the price of bread at 20 currency units a loaf and planned output of 900 000 loaves a day. At that price consumers wanted to buy 1 200 000 loaves a day.
After market reforms the price rose to 35 currency units a loaf and 1 050 000 loaves a day were bought and sold.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the shortage under central planning and express it as a percentage of the quantity demanded.
parts.answer: Shortage 300 000 loaves a day, which is 25 % of quantity demanded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in total daily consumer spending on bread after the reform. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether consumers as a whole were better off after the market reform.
parts.answer: Better off: shortage and queues eliminated (quantity bought rose 16.7 %, from 900 000 to 1 050 000), so time costs fall; bread goes to those who value it most; firms have an incentive to raise output and quality. Worse off: price rose 75 % and spending more than doubled, hurting poor households for whom bread is a staple; if incomes did not rise, real incomes fell; some consumers who previously got cheap bread now buy less. Judgement: total welfare may rise (more traded, no queues), but distribution matters – poorer consumers may lose unless supported by transfers; the answer depends on what happened to incomes.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for arguments that consumers gained (with data); up to 2 marks for arguments that some lost (with data); up to 2 marks for a reasoned judgement (e.g. depends on income changes, distribution, time saved in queues).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess the view that the government, rather than the market, should allocate resources in the supply of electricity.
parts.answer: For government allocation: electricity networks are natural monopolies, so a private firm could restrict output and raise prices; electricity is essential, with equity concerns (access for rural/poor households); generation creates negative externalities (pollution) that markets ignore; long-term planning of capacity and grid investment may be easier for the state. For the market: private firms have profit incentives to cut costs, reduce line losses and collect bills; competition in generation can lower prices; state providers may suffer government failure – political pricing below cost, circular debt, overstaffing, weak maintenance and load-shedding. Middle way: regulated private supply, independent regulator, competitive generation with a state-owned or regulated grid, targeted subsidies for poor users. Judgement: neither pure option is best; it depends on the strength of regulation and of government institutions.
parts.working: Higher-band answers need accurate, developed analysis (with a relevant diagram where useful) of both sides, applied to the context, and a reasoned judgement that answers the 'assess' question directly; one-sided or descriptive answers stay in the lower bands. Expect analysis of natural monopoly, externalities and equity versus incentives and government failure, applied to electricity, with a supported conclusion (often a regulated mixed approach).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the factor of production that each of the following represents and the reward paid to it: (i) a plot of farmland in Sindh; (ii) a delivery van owned by a bakery; (iii) a nurse working in a hospital.
parts.answer: (i) land – rent; (ii) capital – interest; (iii) labour – wages
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct factor with its reward.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the role of the entrepreneur in a market economy.
parts.answer: The entrepreneur organises the other factors and takes the risk of business; the reward is profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: combines/organises land, labour and capital to produce goods. 1 mark: bears risk/uncertainty and receives profit (or loss).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is classified as capital in economics?
A money saved in a bank deposit account
B shares in a company bought by a household
C a sewing machine used in a garment factory
D a fishing lake owned by a farmer
parts.answer: C a sewing machine used in a garment factory
parts.working: Capital is a man-made aid to production, such as machinery. Money and shares (A, B) are financial assets, not real capital; the lake (D) is a natural resource, so land.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the reward to the factor of production enterprise?
A wages
B rent
C interest
D profit
parts.answer: D profit
parts.working: Entrepreneurs organise the other factors and take risks, and their reward is profit. Wages reward labour, rent rewards land, interest rewards capital.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between labour and enterprise as factors of production.
parts.answer: Labour is human effort, physical and mental, used in production in return for wages; enterprise is the organising of the other factors and taking of risk in return for profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: labour; 1 mark: enterprise (organisation and risk-bearing).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two characteristics of land as a factor of production.
parts.answer: Any two of: includes all natural resources (soil, minerals, fish, water); its total supply is largely fixed; it is geographically immobile; its reward is rent.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sialkot in Pakistan specialises in making sports goods such as footballs and cricket equipment. Explain two advantages to the region of this specialisation.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: workers become highly skilled through repetition, raising productivity and quality; specialist suppliers and services cluster nearby, lowering costs; a reputation for quality attracts export orders; firms can use specialised machinery at large scale.
parts.working: For each advantage: 1 mark for identification, 1 mark for explanation linked to output, cost or quality.

practice.stem: A call centre in Lahore has 12 workers. When every worker dealt with all types of customer query, each handled 30 queries a day. The centre then divided workers into a billing team and a technical team. The 12 workers now handle 468 queries a day in total (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the total number of queries handled after the change, and the new number of queries handled per worker.
parts.answer: 30 % increase; 39 queries per worker per day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one possible disadvantage of the change for the workers.
parts.answer: Any one: boredom/monotony from repetitive work; lower job satisfaction; narrower skills, making it harder to change job.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A furniture workshop in Chiniot employs 5 workers. When each worker made complete chairs, the workshop produced 20 chairs a day. After the work was divided into separate tasks (cutting, carving, joining, polishing), the same 5 workers produced 32 chairs a day (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in output per worker after the workshop introduced division of labour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why division of labour may have raised output per worker.
parts.answer: Workers become skilled at one task through repetition; time is saved by not switching tasks / tools; workers suited to tasks.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained reasons: practice improves skill and speed; less time lost moving between tasks and tools; workers can be matched to tasks they are best at; easier to use specialised machinery; training is shorter.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one disadvantage of division of labour for the workers.
parts.answer: Boredom from repetitive work (or loss of variety of skills / risk of unemployment if the task is automated).
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid disadvantage to workers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how specialisation and the division of labour can increase an economy's output, and consider whether a country should specialise in producing a narrow range of goods.
parts.answer: Specialisation raises productivity and output; but over-specialisation creates risks.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): meaning of specialisation (individuals, firms, regions, countries) and division of labour; need for exchange/money. Analysis (3): higher productivity through skill, time saving, use of machinery and economies of scale; lower unit costs; more output from given resources (PPC shifts outward / move to higher output). Evaluation (2): national specialisation increases dependence on world prices (e.g. a single crop or mineral), exposes the country to demand shocks and structural unemployment; diversification may reduce risk; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is the best example of an increase in a country's human capital?
A a hospital buying new X-ray machines
B a worker completing a two-year nursing qualification
C a rise in the number of people of working age
D an increase in the wages paid to nurses
parts.answer: B a worker completing a two-year nursing qualification
parts.working: Human capital is the skills, knowledge and health of workers; training raises it. A is physical capital; C increases the quantity of labour, not its quality; D is a reward, not a change in skills.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between occupational immobility and geographical immobility of labour.
parts.answer: Occupational immobility: workers cannot easily move between jobs because they lack the required skills or qualifications; geographical immobility: workers cannot easily move between places to take jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Many textile workers in a city have lost their jobs while software firms in another city report shortages of staff. Explain two reasons why the textile workers may be unable to fill these vacancies.
parts.answer: Occupational: textile skills do not transfer to software work and retraining takes time and money. Geographical: high housing costs in the other city, family ties, children's schooling, lack of information about vacancies, cost of moving.
parts.working: For each reason: 1 mark for identification, 1 mark for explanation in context (at least one should be occupational and one geographical for full marks, or two developed reasons of one type).

practice.stem: Invented data for a country in one year ($ billion): capital stock at the start of the year 1500; gross investment 120; depreciation (capital consumption) 90.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the country's net investment for the year and the percentage increase in its capital stock.
parts.answer: Net investment $30 billion; capital stock rises by 2 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why investment in capital goods involves an opportunity cost for the economy.
parts.answer: Resources used to make machines and buildings cannot be used to make consumer goods, so current consumption is given up in return for higher future output.
parts.working: 1 mark: resources diverted from consumer goods; 1 mark: current consumption sacrificed for future production.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what would happen to the capital stock if gross investment fell below depreciation.
parts.answer: It would fall (net investment negative).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the division of labour is limited by the size of the market.
parts.answer: Specialised workers each do one task and together produce large output; this only pays if enough units can be sold. In a small market (e.g. a village tailor's customers) demand is too small to keep specialist cutters, stitchers and finishers fully employed, so one worker does all tasks.
parts.working: 1 mark: division of labour raises output; 1 mark: output must be sold/specialists need full workloads; 1 mark: applied example or explanation that small demand makes specialisation unprofitable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how improvements in transport can increase specialisation in an economy.
parts.answer: Cheaper transport widens the market, so producers can sell to more customers and regions can specialise in what they produce best, trading for other goods.
parts.working: 1 mark: market size increases; 1 mark: allows greater specialisation by firms/regions.

practice.stem:
Two tailors work in the same workshop in Faisalabad. In a day (invented data):
Ali can make either 10 shirts or 5 pairs of trousers.
Bilal can make either 6 shirts or 6 pairs of trousers.
Each can divide the day between the two goods at a constant rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of one pair of trousers for each tailor.
parts.answer: Ali: 2 shirts; Bilal: 1 shirt.
parts.working: 1 mark each: Ali 10 ÷ 5 = 2; Bilal 6 ÷ 6 = 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which tailor should specialise in trousers.
parts.answer: Bilal, because his opportunity cost of trousers (1 shirt) is lower than Ali's (2 shirts). (Bilal also has the absolute advantage in trousers, 6 against 5, while Ali has both the absolute and the comparative advantage in shirts.)
parts.working: 1 mark: Bilal; 1 mark: comparative advantage/lower opportunity cost reasoning.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total daily output of shirts and trousers (i) if each tailor spends half the day on each good and (ii) if Ali makes only shirts and Bilal only trousers. State the gain from specialisation.
parts.answer: (i) 8 shirts and 5.5 trousers; (ii) 10 shirts and 6 trousers; gain = 2 shirts and 0.5 pairs of trousers.
parts.working: M1: Ali 5 shirts + 2.5 trousers, Bilal 3 shirts + 3 trousers → 8 and 5.5; M1: 10 and 6; A1: gain 2 shirts and 0.5 trousers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether enterprise is the most important factor of production for the economic development of a lower-income country.
parts.answer: For enterprise: entrepreneurs identify opportunities, combine land, labour and capital and take risks; without them other factors stay idle or used inefficiently; enterprise drives innovation, small-firm growth, exports and jobs. Against: entrepreneurs need capital (finance), skilled labour (human capital) and infrastructure; in many lower-income countries the binding constraint is lack of capital or education rather than lack of entrepreneurial spirit (large informal sector shows many entrepreneurs); land/natural resources can fund development; institutions (property rights, rule of law) determine whether enterprise is productive. Judgement: factors are complementary; enterprise is necessary but not sufficient, and the most important factor depends on which is scarcest in a given country.
parts.working: Higher-band answers need accurate, developed analysis (with a relevant diagram where useful) of both sides, applied to the context, and a reasoned judgement that answers the 'assess' question directly; one-sided or descriptive answers stay in the lower bands. Expect definitions of the four factors and their rewards, analysis of the role of enterprise, analysis of complementary factors (capital, human capital) and a judgement on 'most important' that considers the country's circumstances.

practice.stem: Invented data: a country's universities produce 20 000 IT graduates a year. A survey finds that 35 % of them emigrate within three years of graduating.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of the year's IT graduates who remain in the country.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the emigration of skilled workers affects the quality of the country's factors of production.
parts.answer: The country loses human capital (the most skilled labour), reducing average labour productivity and the capacity of IT firms to grow; the cost of training is lost; enterprise may also leave. Some offsetting: remittances can finance capital, and returning workers bring new skills.
parts.working: 1 mark: loss of human capital/quality of labour; 1 mark: lower productivity/output potential; 1 mark: development (lost training cost, fewer entrepreneurs, or offsetting remittances/return migration).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the government should restrict the emigration of skilled workers.
parts.answer: For restriction: keeps scarce skills at home, protects the return on public spending on education. Against: it restricts individual freedom; remittances support the balance of payments and household incomes; workers abroad gain experience and may return; restriction may discourage people from training at all. Better alternatives: improve pay and conditions, bonding schemes for publicly funded graduates. Judgement given.
parts.working: 1 mark: argument for; 1 mark: argument against; 1 mark: alternative policy or development; 1 mark: reasoned judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement is normative?
A Pakistan's inflation rate was higher in 2023 than in 2021.
B A rise in the price of petrol will reduce the quantity of petrol demanded.
C The government should spend more on primary schools than on motorways.
D Raising the minimum wage may increase unemployment among young workers.
parts.answer: C The government should spend more on primary schools than on motorways.
parts.working: C contains a value judgement ('should') and cannot be tested by evidence. D is positive: it is a testable prediction even though it uses 'may'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement is positive?
A The government should reduce the tax on petrol.
B The national minimum wage is unfair to small firms.
C A 10 % rise in the tax on petrol will reduce petrol consumption by 2 %.
D Reducing unemployment is more important than reducing inflation.
parts.answer: C A 10 % rise in the tax on petrol will reduce petrol consumption by 2 %.
parts.working: C is a statement about cause and effect that can be tested against evidence (it may turn out wrong, but it is still positive). A, B and D contain value judgements ('should', 'unfair', 'more important').

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a positive statement and a normative statement.
parts.answer: A positive statement is about what is, was or will be and can be tested against evidence; a normative statement contains a value judgement about what ought to be and cannot be tested.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write one positive statement and one normative statement about electricity load-shedding.
parts.answer: e.g. Positive: 'Load-shedding reduced factory output in the city by 5 % last year.' Normative: 'The government should end load-shedding for hospitals before anything else.'
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid statement; the positive one must be testable, the normative one must contain a value judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether each statement is positive or normative: (1) 'Sales of plastic bags in the city fell by 60 % in the year after the ban.' (2) 'The ban should be extended to the whole province.' (3) 'If the price of paper bags rises, shops will sell fewer of them.' (4) 'Shopkeepers deserve compensation for their losses from the ban.'
parts.answer: (1) positive; (2) normative; (3) positive; (4) normative.
parts.working: 1 mark each. (1) and (3) can be checked against evidence; (2) and (4) contain value judgements ('should', 'deserve').

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an economic model and why economists use simplifying assumptions when building one.
parts.answer: A model is a simplified representation of how part of the economy works, used to explain and predict (e.g. demand and supply). Assumptions remove less important detail so the key relationship can be identified and tested.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition of a model; 1 mark: purpose – explain/predict; 1 mark: assumptions simplify reality to isolate the key relationships.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one limitation of using economic models to predict behaviour.
parts.answer: Any one: assumptions may be unrealistic (e.g. people are not always rational); other factors change at the same time; behaviour changes over time.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An official forecasts: 'The new metro line will carry 400 000 passengers a day.' After a year it carries 250 000. Explain why the forecast was still a positive statement.
parts.answer: A positive statement is one that can be tested against facts; the forecast could be (and was) checked, and it turned out wrong. Being wrong does not make it normative.
parts.working: 1 mark: testable/refutable by evidence; 1 mark: being incorrect does not make it a value judgement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how value judgements can influence government policy even when economists agree on the facts.
parts.answer: Economists may agree on the effects of a policy (e.g. a fuel tax cuts pollution but hurts the poor), but deciding whether the benefit outweighs the cost depends on how much weight people give to the environment versus equity – a value judgement.
parts.working: 1 mark: agreement on positive analysis; 1 mark: choice depends on weights/priorities, which are normative.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify which of the following statements are positive and which are normative.
(1) The unemployment rate among graduates in the country rose from 9 % to 12 %.
(2) Income inequality in the country is unacceptably high.
(3) A tax on sugary drinks would reduce their consumption.
(4) Clean drinking water is more important than mobile phone coverage.
parts.answer: Positive: (1) and (3). Normative: (2) and (4).
parts.working: 2 marks for all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why economists make the assumption of ceteris paribus when building economic models.
parts.answer: To isolate the effect of one variable by holding all other factors constant.
parts.working: 1 mark: ceteris paribus means other things remain equal. 1 mark: in the real world many variables change at once and controlled experiments are not possible, so the assumption lets economists study one cause and effect at a time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why economics is described as a social science.
parts.answer: It studies human behaviour using scientific method but cannot run controlled experiments, and people do not behave consistently.
parts.working: 1 mark: it uses scientific method (theories, models, testing against data). 1 mark: it studies human behaviour in society, which is less predictable, and laboratory experiments are rarely possible.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An economist says, 'Ceteris paribus, a rise in the price of tea will reduce the quantity of tea demanded.' What does 'ceteris paribus' mean here?
A all other influences on the demand for tea are assumed to stay unchanged
B the market for tea is assumed to be in equilibrium
C consumers are assumed to have perfect information about tea
D price is assumed to be the only influence on demand in the real world
parts.answer: A all other influences on the demand for tea are assumed to stay unchanged
parts.working: Ceteris paribus means 'other things being equal': income, tastes, prices of related goods and so on are held constant so the effect of price alone can be analysed. D is the common misreading – economists do not claim other factors do not exist, only that they are held constant.

practice.stem: Extract (invented): A finance minister said, 'Our analysts estimate that a 20 % tax on sugary drinks would raise about Rs 40 billion a year. In a neighbouring country, sales of sugary drinks fell by 8 % in the first year of a similar tax.' A business leader replied, 'It is wrong for the state to tell people what to drink.' A health campaigner added, 'The tax should be doubled.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one positive statement and one normative statement in the extract.
parts.answer: Positive: e.g. 'sales of sugary drinks fell by 8 % in the first year' or 'a 20 % tax would raise about Rs 40 billion'. Normative: e.g. 'it is wrong for the state to tell people what to drink' or 'the tax should be doubled'.
parts.working: 1 mark each, quoted or closely paraphrased from the extract.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the normative statement you identified cannot be settled by collecting more data.
parts.answer: It depends on values (how far individual freedom should be limited, how health should be weighed against cost), so evidence can inform the debate but cannot prove one view correct.
parts.working: 1 mark: based on a value judgement; 1 mark: data cannot prove/disprove a view about what ought to be.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether economists should give normative advice to governments.
parts.answer: For: economists understand trade-offs and can make recommendations that are well informed; governments need clear advice. Against: their value judgements carry no special authority and may be presented as 'scientific'; better to set out positive consequences and let elected politicians decide. Judgement, e.g. advice is useful if values are made explicit.
parts.working: 1 mark: argument for; 1 mark: argument against; 1 mark: development; 1 mark: reasoned judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the example of a bakery, distinguish between the short run and the long run.
parts.answer: Short run: at least one factor is fixed – the bakery can hire more workers but cannot add ovens or a bigger building; long run: all factors are variable – it can build a larger bakery or add ovens.
parts.working: 1 mark each, with the bakery example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what economists mean by the very long run.
parts.answer: A period in which technology and the institutions in which firms operate can change, as well as all factors – e.g. a new automated baking technology is invented.
parts.working: 1 mark: technology/state of knowledge can change; 1 mark: example or explanation of why this differs from the long run.

practice.stem: Invented data from 40 rural districts: districts where more than 80 % of households own a mobile phone have average household incomes 35 % higher than districts where fewer than 50 % own one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the data do not prove that owning a mobile phone causes higher household income.
parts.answer: Correlation is not causation: richer households can afford more phones (causation may run the other way); a third factor such as education or living in a city may raise both; the data are for districts, not individual households.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: correlation ≠ causation; reverse causation; third/omitted variable; aggregation problem.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how an economist might test the hypothesis that mobile phones raise incomes.
parts.answer: Compare similar households before and after phones become available (e.g. when a new mobile tower is built), with a comparison group that did not get coverage, holding other factors constant.
parts.working: 1 mark: comparison over time/with a control group; 1 mark: holding other factors constant (ceteris paribus).

practice.stem: Invented data: an economist predicted that 'a 10 % rise in bus fares in the city will reduce bus journeys by 3 %, ceteris paribus'. During the following year the fare rose from Rs 50 to Rs 55, petrol prices rose sharply and a new metro line opened. Daily bus journeys fell from 2.0 million to 1.9 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual percentage changes in the bus fare and in the number of journeys.
parts.answer: Fare +10 %; journeys −5 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the outcome differed from the prediction even though the economist's model may have been correct.
parts.answer: The prediction assumed ceteris paribus; in reality other factors changed – the metro line attracted passengers from buses and the rise in fuel prices made cars dearer (which would have raised bus use). The net effect of these changes, not just the fare rise, determined journeys.
parts.working: 1 mark: ceteris paribus assumption; 1 mark: identifies a factor in the stem that reduced bus journeys (metro); 1 mark: explains that observed data mix several effects (or identifies the fuel price effect).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the economist's prediction was a positive or a normative statement.
parts.answer: Positive – it can be tested against evidence.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between positive and normative economics, and consider whether economists can ever be completely free of value judgements.
parts.answer: Explain: positive economics describes and predicts and can be tested; normative economics involves value judgements about what ought to be. Consider: value judgements enter even positive work – choice of what to study, which data to collect, which assumptions to make, what counts as a 'cost' or 'efficient'; measures such as GDP or the poverty line embody judgements. But positive claims can still be tested and economists can make their values explicit. Judgement: complete value-freedom is unlikely, but the distinction is still useful.
parts.working: Marks: 3 knowledge and understanding, 3 analysis, 2 evaluation. Knowledge: accurate definitions with examples. Analysis: how value judgements enter model choice, data and policy advice. Evaluation: whether the distinction is still useful and a judgement on 'ever completely'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess the usefulness of the ceteris paribus assumption when economists give advice on government policy.
parts.answer: Useful: isolates the effect of one variable (e.g. a tax on demand), allowing clear predictions; makes models manageable; allows policies to be compared on a like-for-like basis; experiments are impossible in economics, so it is the only way to think through single causes. Limitations: in reality many variables change at once, so forecasts are often wrong; policies themselves change other variables (a tax changes incomes, expectations, related markets); time lags; behavioural responses; reliance on it can lead to over-confident advice. Judgement: essential as a starting point but advice must allow for interactions, use evidence and be cautious.
parts.working: Higher-band answers need accurate, developed analysis (with a relevant diagram where useful) of both sides, applied to the context, and a reasoned judgement that answers the 'assess' question directly; one-sided or descriptive answers stay in the lower bands. Expect a clear definition, an applied example (e.g. predicting effect of an indirect tax), analysis of why other things do not stay equal, and a supported judgement on usefulness.

practice.stem: Extract (invented): Two economists study the same evidence about a proposed 25 % rise in a country's minimum wage. Both accept that it would raise the incomes of about 2 million low-paid workers and would reduce the employment of young workers by about 3 %. Economist A says, 'The government should not raise the minimum wage.' Economist B says, 'Protecting the low-paid matters more than a small loss of jobs.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one positive and one normative statement in the extract.
parts.answer: Positive: 'a 25 % rise in the minimum wage would reduce employment of young workers by about 3 %' or 'it would raise the incomes of about 2 million low-paid workers' (the evidence both accept). Normative: 'the government should not raise the minimum wage' or 'protecting the low-paid matters more than a small loss of jobs'.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider why two economists who accept the same evidence can reach different policy conclusions.
parts.answer: They give different weights to the outcomes – one values employment of the young, the other the incomes of the low-paid; different views on fairness and on the role of the state; different time horizons; different judgements about uncertainty in the estimates. Disagreement is therefore normative, not about facts.
parts.working: 1 mark: same positive analysis; up to 2 marks: different weights/values explained; 1 mark: conclusion that the disagreement is normative.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether economics can help a government decide whether to raise the minimum wage.
parts.answer: Helps: estimates of employment, income and price effects; identifies winners and losers; compares alternatives (tax credits, transfers); evidence from other countries. Limits: estimates uncertain, informal sector large; the final decision needs value judgements on fairness that economics cannot settle. Judgement: economics informs but cannot make the decision.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks: ways economics helps; up to 2 marks: limits; up to 2 marks: reasoned judgement.

practice.stem: A household in a country with 30 % annual inflation keeps Rs 100,000 in cash at home for one year. It earns no interest (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four functions of money.
parts.answer: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value, standard of deferred payment.
parts.working: 2 marks for all four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
