parts.text: Calculate the real value of the household's savings after one year, in Year 0 prices. Give your answer to the nearest rupee.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how very high inflation weakens two functions of money.
parts.answer: Store of value: money loses purchasing power. Standard of deferred payment / unit of account: future amounts and prices become unreliable.
parts.working: 2 marks each: store of value – each rupee buys less over time, so people switch to gold, property or foreign currency; unit of account – prices change so often that comparisons are hard; standard of deferred payment – lenders are repaid in money worth less, so they become unwilling to lend; medium of exchange – in extreme cases people turn to barter or foreign currency.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the function of money shown in each case: (i) a bookshop labels a book 'Rs 450'; (ii) a householder pays a plumber Rs 3 000 for a repair; (iii) a family keeps Rs 20 000 aside for Eid shopping in six months' time; (iv) a customer buys a refrigerator and agrees to pay for it in six monthly instalments.
parts.answer: (i) unit of account (measure of value); (ii) medium of exchange; (iii) store of value; (iv) standard of deferred payment.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the problem of the double coincidence of wants in a barter economy.
parts.answer: For a trade to happen, each person must want what the other has, at the same time and in the right quantities (a farmer with rice who wants shoes must find a shoemaker who wants rice); this makes trade slow and costly.
parts.working: 1 mark: both parties must want what the other offers; 1 mark: consequence – time/search costs, few trades.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how money solves this problem.
parts.answer: Money is accepted by everyone as a medium of exchange, so the farmer sells rice to anyone for money and uses the money to buy shoes from anyone; the two trades are separated.
parts.working: 1 mark: general acceptability/medium of exchange; 1 mark: one barter trade is split into two separate transactions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why durability and divisibility are important characteristics of money. Use fresh fish as an example of an item that would make poor money.
parts.answer: Durability: money must last so that it can be stored and reused – fresh fish rots within days, so it cannot act as a store of value. Divisibility: money must be split into small units so that items of different value can be bought – a fish cannot be divided into small exact amounts without losing value.
parts.working: 1 mark: durability explained; 1 mark: fish example for durability; 1 mark: divisibility explained; 1 mark: fish example for divisibility.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why bank deposits are counted as money.
parts.answer: Bank deposits are generally accepted as a means of payment (by debit card, cheque, online transfer, mobile banking) and can be used to settle debts, so they perform the functions of money.
parts.working: 1 mark: generally accepted means of payment; 1 mark: perform the functions (e.g. medium of exchange, store of value).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages of paying by bank transfer rather than with notes and coins.
parts.answer: Any two: safer (less risk of theft); convenient for large or distant payments; creates a record; no need to carry or count cash; faster.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Ali deposits Rs 500 000 in a savings account for one year at a nominal interest rate of 12 %. During the year the price level rises by 25 % (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the real value of Ali's savings at the end of the year, in prices at the start of the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the real rate of return on the savings, as a percentage. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what your answers suggest about how well money is acting as a store of value in this country.
parts.answer: Even with interest, savings lose about one-tenth of their purchasing power in a year, so money is a poor store of value; people may switch to land, gold or foreign currency.
parts.working: 1 mark: purchasing power falls; 1 mark: poor store of value / people move to other assets.

practice.stem: Invented data: in a country with hyperinflation the price level doubles every month. The price index is 100 in January and 3200 in June.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage rise in the price index between January and June.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why people in the country may start to use US dollars instead of the local currency.
parts.answer: The local currency loses value very quickly, so it fails as a store of value and unit of account (prices change daily); sellers become unwilling to accept it, so it fails as a medium of exchange; the dollar keeps its value, so people price and save in dollars (dollarisation).
parts.working: 1 mark: loss of store of value; 1 mark: loss of unit of account/medium of exchange function; 1 mark: dollar is stable/generally acceptable alternative.

practice.stem: A shopkeeper borrows Rs 1 000 000 from a relative and agrees to repay exactly Rs 1 000 000 after three years, with no interest. Prices rise by 10 % in each of the three years (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of the Rs 1 000 000 repayment in prices at the time the loan was taken. Give your answer to the nearest rupee.
parts.working: M1: price level after 3 years = 1.1³ = 1.331; A1: 1 000 000 ÷ 1.331 = Rs 751 315.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain who gains and who loses from unexpected inflation when money is used as a standard of deferred payment.
parts.answer: Borrowers gain because they repay money that buys less than the money borrowed; lenders lose because the real value of what they receive falls. If inflation is expected, lenders raise interest rates to protect themselves.
parts.working: 1 mark: borrowers gain; 1 mark: lenders lose, with reason (lower real value of repayment); 1 mark: expected vs unexpected inflation/interest-rate adjustment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain which characteristics of money gold possesses, and why gold is not used for everyday payments today.
parts.answer: Gold is durable, scarce (limited supply), homogeneous and generally recognised, and it has kept value over long periods. But it is not easily divisible into small amounts for daily purchases, it is heavy and risky to carry, its purity must be checked, and its price fluctuates, so it is a poor unit of account and medium of exchange for small transactions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two characteristics it has (max 2); 1 mark each for any two reasons why it is unsuitable for everyday payments (max 2).

practice.stem: In a barter economy every pair of goods has its own exchange ratio (for example, 1 goat = 4 bags of rice).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many different exchange ratios (prices) a barter economy with 5 goods needs, compared with an economy that uses money.
parts.answer: 10 exchange ratios in barter; 5 money prices.
parts.working: 1 mark: 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10 pairs of goods; 1 mark: one money price per good = 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how using money as a unit of account helps consumers make choices.
parts.answer: Every good has a price in the same unit, so consumers can compare values and costs directly (and work out opportunity cost) without remembering many exchange ratios.
parts.working: 1 mark: common measure of value; 1 mark: easy comparison/fewer prices to know.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the characteristics that an item needs in order to function well as money, and consider whether balances held in mobile phone wallets have these characteristics.
parts.answer: Acceptability, durability, portability, divisibility, limited supply, homogeneity; mobile wallets have most of them but depend on trust, technology and access.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): list and explain characteristics – generally acceptable, durable, portable, divisible, scarce/limited in supply, uniform/recognisable. Analysis (3): mobile wallet balances are easily divisible and portable, do not wear out, are units of the national currency so uniform and scarce; widely accepted where merchants have agreed. Evaluation (2): acceptability depends on network coverage, phone ownership and trust in the provider; not usable during power or network failures; may be part of broad rather than narrow money; justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Sana buys 0.5 units of a cryptocurrency when its price is $60 000 per unit. One month later its price is $36 000 per unit (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of Sana's holding at the start and at the end of the month, and the percentage change.
parts.answer: $30 000 at the start, $18 000 at the end: a fall of 40 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether this cryptocurrency functions well as money.
parts.answer: Store of value: poor – value fell 40 % in a month. Unit of account: few goods priced in it because its value changes so much. Medium of exchange: accepted by few sellers, transaction fees and slow confirmation. Some positives: durable, divisible, hard to counterfeit, portable, limited supply. Judgement: it has some characteristics of money but its volatility and low acceptability mean it does not function well as money; it behaves more like a speculative asset.
parts.working: 1 mark: store of value weakness with data; 1 mark: medium of exchange/unit of account weakness; 1 mark: characteristics it does have; 1 mark: reasoned judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the use of money makes specialisation and trade easier, and consider whether a modern economy could function efficiently without money.
parts.answer: Explain: money removes the need for a double coincidence of wants, lowers transaction costs, provides a common unit of account and allows saving and borrowing (deferred payment); so people can specialise in one job and buy everything else, raising productivity. Consider: without money, barter would limit specialisation; however, some trade could use credit records, digital ledgers or barter exchanges, and during hyperinflation economies use substitutes (foreign currency, cigarettes). Judgement: a modern, highly specialised economy needs some form of money, though its form can change.
parts.working: Marks: 3 knowledge and understanding, 3 analysis, 2 evaluation. Knowledge: functions of money and barter's problems. Analysis: chain from money → lower transaction costs → specialisation → higher output. Evaluation: possible alternatives to money and a supported judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether digital money (bank balances, cards and mobile wallets) meets the characteristics of good money better than notes and coins.
parts.answer: Digital money: highly divisible (exact amounts), portable (pay anywhere), durable (no wear), hard to counterfeit, convenient for large/distant payments, records reduce crime and tax evasion. Weaknesses: needs electricity, internet and phones; not accepted everywhere (small rural shops, informal sector); fraud and hacking; bank failures can threaten deposits; excludes the unbanked, the elderly and the poor; privacy concerns. Notes and coins: universally accepted, legal tender, no technology needed, private; but bulky for large sums, risk of theft, wear out, can be forged. Judgement: digital money meets most characteristics better, but general acceptability – the most important characteristic – depends on infrastructure and trust, so in many lower-income economies cash is still essential.
parts.working: Higher-band answers need accurate, developed analysis (with a relevant diagram where useful) of both sides, applied to the context, and a reasoned judgement that answers the 'assess' question directly; one-sided or descriptive answers stay in the lower bands. Expect the characteristics of money (acceptability, durability, divisibility, portability, scarcity/limited supply, homogeneity) applied to both forms, and a judgement that weighs which characteristics matter most in the context.

practice.stem: Invented data for a country: over five years inflation averaged 60 % a year. The share of bank deposits held in US dollars rose from 15 % to 45 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in the share of bank deposits held in US dollars, in percentage points.
parts.answer: 30 percentage points

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why high inflation would lead households to hold more of their deposits in US dollars.
parts.answer: Local-currency deposits lose purchasing power quickly (poor store of value), while dollar deposits keep their value and may gain as the local currency depreciates.
parts.working: 1 mark: loss of value of local currency; 1 mark: dollar acts as a better store of value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess the consequences of this change for the country's government and central bank.
parts.answer: Consequences: the central bank has less control over the money supply and interest rates (monetary policy weaker); seigniorage revenue falls; banks lending in dollars to borrowers who earn local currency face default risk if the currency depreciates; demand for dollars can worsen depreciation. Possible benefits: stops capital flight abroad (deposits remain in local banks), restores confidence and may reduce inflation if the government is forced into discipline. Judgement: mostly harmful for policy control, but a symptom rather than cause of the problem – the solution is to reduce inflation.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for developed consequences (at least one for the central bank's control of policy); up to 2 marks for evaluation/judgement.

practice.stem: Ayesha lives in Karachi. She has been offered a job at a bank paying Rs 65,000 a month. Instead, she chooses a two-year full-time diploma costing Rs 300,000 a year in fees (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the opportunity cost of Ayesha's decision.
parts.answer: The job at the bank (the next best alternative), including the income it would have paid.
parts.working: 1 mark: the next best alternative forgone – the bank job.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total economic cost to Ayesha of the two-year diploma (the fees plus the earnings she gives up).
parts.working: Earnings forgone 65,000 × 24 = Rs 1,560,000 (M1); plus fees 2 × 300,000 = Rs 600,000; total Rs 2,160,000 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Ayesha may still have made a rational choice.
parts.answer: She expects the future benefits (higher earnings, satisfaction) to exceed the opportunity cost.
parts.working: 1 mark: rational choice compares costs and benefits. 1 mark: the diploma may raise lifetime earnings or job satisfaction by more than Rs 2.16 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the basic economic problem.
parts.answer: Wants are unlimited but the resources available to satisfy them are limited (scarce), so choices have to be made.
parts.working: 1 mark: unlimited wants; 1 mark: limited/scarce resources requiring choice.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why opportunity cost arises from scarcity.
parts.answer: Because resources are scarce, using them for one purpose means they cannot be used for another; the next best alternative given up is the opportunity cost.
parts.working: 1 mark: resources have alternative uses; 1 mark: definition of opportunity cost as next best alternative forgone.

practice.stem: A farmer in Punjab has 10 hectares of land. He expects a profit of Rs 180 000 per hectare from sugarcane or Rs 150 000 per hectare from cotton. He decides to grow cotton on all 10 hectares (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost to the farmer of growing cotton on all 10 hectares.
parts.answer: Rs 1 800 000 of profit from sugarcane (the next best alternative).
parts.working: M1: next best alternative = sugarcane; A1: 10 × 180 000 = Rs 1 800 000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the farmer might still be acting rationally by choosing cotton.
parts.answer: Any two: sugarcane needs much more water, which may be scarce; sugar mills may pay late or below the expected price (risk); cotton harvest comes sooner, freeing land for a wheat crop; farmer has cotton-growing skills and equipment.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A provincial government has Rs 120 billion to spend on new projects. It can either build 400 km of rural road or 30 district hospitals, or any combination of the two at a constant rate (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the opportunity cost of building the 30 hospitals.
parts.answer: 400 km of road.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming a constant rate of exchange between the two projects, calculate the opportunity cost of one hospital. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 13.3 km of road

parts.label: c
parts.text: The government decides to build 15 hospitals. Calculate the length of road it can build with the rest of the budget.
parts.answer: 200 km
parts.working: Half the budget on hospitals leaves half for roads: 400 × 15/30 = 200 km (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a free good has no opportunity cost.
parts.answer: A free good is not scarce: there is enough to satisfy everyone's wants at zero price, so using it does not mean giving up any alternative.
parts.working: 1 mark: not scarce/supply exceeds demand at zero price; 1 mark: nothing is given up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why river water near a growing city may stop being a free good.
parts.answer: As population, industry and farming grow, demand for the water exceeds supply and pollution reduces usable supply, so the water becomes scarce: using it for one purpose (e.g. factories) means less for others (e.g. drinking, irrigation).
parts.working: 1 mark: rising demand/pollution makes it scarce; 1 mark: alternative uses now compete, so it has an opportunity cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the basic economic problem of scarcity exists in all economies, and consider whether scarcity is less of a problem for high-income countries than for low-income countries.
parts.answer: Wants are unlimited while resources are finite, so all economies must choose; richer countries face scarcity too, though basic needs are less affected.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): scarcity = unlimited wants vs limited resources; need for choice; opportunity cost; the three questions what/how/for whom. Analysis (3): resources (land, labour, capital, enterprise) are finite everywhere; as incomes rise new wants appear (health care, environment, leisure); even rich countries face trade-offs (e.g. health vs defence, ageing populations). Evaluation (2): in low-income countries scarcity affects basic needs (food, clean water), so its human cost is greater; in high-income countries it concerns more optional wants; absolute scarcity is universal but relative severity differs; justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Hamza has 6 free hours on Saturday. He can spend them studying for his economics examination or working in a shop for Rs 500 an hour. He chooses to study (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the money value of the opportunity cost of Hamza's decision to study for 6 hours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the true opportunity cost of Hamza's choice may not be measured fully in money.
parts.answer: The next best alternative may not be the paid work; it could be rest, time with family or sport, which has value but no money price; the job may also have given him experience. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative to the individual, which is subjective.
parts.working: 1 mark: next best alternative may be non-monetary; 1 mark: example; 1 mark: opportunity cost is subjective/value to the individual.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why government spending financed by borrowing still has an opportunity cost.
parts.answer: Borrowed money must be repaid with interest, so future taxes must rise or future spending fall; government borrowing uses savings that could have financed private investment (crowding out) and may raise interest rates; the real resources (workers, materials) used by the project cannot be used elsewhere now.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: future taxes/spending cuts; interest payments; crowding out of private investment; higher interest rates; real resources diverted now.

practice.stem: Invented data: in a country, renewable water available per person fell from 5 000 cubic metres a year in 1950 to 900 cubic metres in 2025. Agriculture uses about 90 % of the water withdrawn.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in water available per person between 1950 and 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how increasing water scarcity forces choices between agricultural and urban uses of water.
parts.answer: With less water per person, extra water for growing cities (drinking, industry) means less for irrigation and lower crop output, and vice versa; the opportunity cost of using water in one place rises; the government must decide on allocation (canal rotations, pricing).
parts.working: 1 mark: scarcity means one use reduces another; 1 mark: applied to agriculture vs cities; 1 mark: rising opportunity cost or need for an allocation mechanism.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether charging higher prices for irrigation water would be the best way to deal with this scarcity.
parts.answer: For: prices give farmers an incentive to save water (drip irrigation, less water-intensive crops) and allocate water to its highest-value uses; revenue can fund canal repairs. Against: demand may be price inelastic in the short run; small farmers' incomes fall; food prices rise; hard to meter water. Alternatives: investment in storage, lining canals, quotas. Judgement.
parts.working: 1 mark: argument for; 1 mark: argument against; 1 mark: alternative or development; 1 mark: reasoned judgement.

practice.stem: A garment factory has spare machine time this month. It can use it to make 2 000 shirts with a profit of Rs 150 each or 1 200 jackets with a profit of Rs 220 each, but not both (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total profit from each option and state the opportunity cost of producing jackets.
parts.answer: Shirts Rs 300 000; jackets Rs 264 000; the opportunity cost of producing jackets is the Rs 300 000 profit from shirts.
parts.working: 1 mark: 2 000 × 150 = 300 000 and 1 200 × 220 = 264 000; 1 mark: opportunity cost of jackets = Rs 300 000 shirt profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the firm might still choose to make jackets.
parts.answer: e.g. jackets keep an important customer who also places other orders; jacket demand is growing so future profit is higher; it builds skills for a new export market.
parts.working: 1 mark: valid reason; 1 mark: explanation (longer-term or non-financial benefit).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost, in rupees, of keeping Rs 200 000 in cash at home for one year instead of in a savings deposit paying 8 % interest.
parts.answer: Rs 16 000 of interest forgone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why people may still choose to hold cash despite this opportunity cost.
parts.answer: Cash is liquid and can be spent immediately for daily transactions and emergencies; some people do not trust or cannot reach banks, or want to avoid records.
parts.working: 1 mark: liquidity/convenience; 1 mark: development (emergencies, lack of access/trust).

practice.stem: A family has paid a non-refundable deposit of Rs 40 000 to book Hall A for a wedding. The full price of Hall A is Rs 200 000. They then find Hall B, which is equally suitable and costs Rs 140 000 in total, with nothing yet paid (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the further amount the family must pay for each hall from now on.
parts.answer: Hall A: Rs 160 000; Hall B: Rs 140 000.
parts.working: 1 mark: 200 000 − 40 000 = 160 000 for Hall A; 1 mark: Hall B 140 000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which hall the family should choose if the two halls are equally good, and why the deposit already paid should not affect the decision.
parts.answer: Hall B, because it costs Rs 20 000 less from now on. The Rs 40 000 deposit is a sunk cost: it cannot be recovered whichever hall they choose, so it is not part of the opportunity cost of either choice; only future costs and benefits matter.
parts.working: 1 mark: Hall B; 1 mark: deposit is sunk/unrecoverable; 1 mark: decisions depend only on costs that can still be avoided (opportunity cost of each choice).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the concept of opportunity cost can help a government decide how to spend its budget, and consider the difficulties of measuring opportunity cost in practice.
parts.answer: Explain: every rupee spent on one project is unavailable for others; comparing the benefits of the chosen project with the next best alternative helps allocate spending to the highest-value uses; a PPC illustrates the trade-off (e.g. defence vs education). Consider: benefits of many projects are hard to value in money (lives saved, education, environment); benefits arise far in the future and are uncertain; the next best alternative is not always clear; political pressures; distributional effects. Judgement: a useful framework even if estimates are imprecise.
parts.working: Marks: 3 knowledge and understanding, 3 analysis, 2 evaluation. Knowledge: definition of opportunity cost and scarcity. Analysis: application to government choices, possibly with a PPC. Evaluation: problems of measurement and a judgement on usefulness.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether 'free' public services, such as free university education, really have no cost to society.
parts.answer: They are free at the point of use but not free to society: real resources (lecturers, buildings, equipment) could have produced other goods – the opportunity cost; financed by taxes or borrowing, which reduce private spending or create future burdens; students also give up earnings while studying. Possible offsetting benefits: positive externalities (more productive workforce, innovation, lower crime), higher future tax revenue, more equal opportunity; so net cost may be low or even negative over time. Zero price may cause over-consumption (courses with low value, high drop-out) and rationing by entry requirements rather than price. Judgement: there is always an opportunity cost; the real question is whether social benefits exceed it.
parts.working: Higher-band answers need accurate, developed analysis (with a relevant diagram where useful) of both sides, applied to the context, and a reasoned judgement that answers the 'assess' question directly; one-sided or descriptive answers stay in the lower bands. Expect clear distinction between price and cost, opportunity cost of resources, financing, private opportunity cost of students, externalities/benefits, and a judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data for a country: GDP is $400 billion. Military spending is 4 % of GDP and education spending is 2 % of GDP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the government's current spending on the military and on education, in $ billion.
parts.answer: Military $16 billion; education $8 billion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government moves spending equal to 1 % of GDP from the military to education. Calculate the percentage increase in education spending.
parts.working: $4 billion extra ÷ $8 billion × 100 = 50 % (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether the opportunity cost of this switch is worth paying.
parts.answer: Gains: education is a merit good with large external benefits; human capital raises long-run growth and incomes; 50 % rise is large for schooling access. Costs: lower defence capacity – national security is a public good and the risk depends on the region; jobs and industries linked to defence may be lost; the extra education spending may be wasted if management is weak. Judgement: depends on security threats, how well the extra spending is used and the time horizon.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks: benefits; up to 2 marks: opportunity cost/risks; up to 2 marks: reasoned judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following acts as an automatic stabiliser in an economy?
A a progressive income tax system
B a one-off decision to build a new motorway
C a cut in the central bank's policy interest rate
D a new tariff on imported cars
parts.answer: A a progressive income tax system
parts.working: As incomes fall in a recession, people move into lower tax bands, so tax paid falls faster than income and disposable income is cushioned, with no new government decision needed. B is discretionary fiscal policy (a deliberate decision), C is monetary policy. D is a protectionist measure, not a stabiliser.

practice.stem:
Table 1: Tax revenue of Country P, 2025 (PKR billion; data invented for practice)
Income tax: 2900
Corporate (company) profits tax: 1100
General sales tax: 3400
Customs duties: 1200
Excise duties: 400

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a direct tax and an indirect tax, and identify the direct taxes in Table 1.
parts.answer: A direct tax is paid straight to the government by the person or firm on whom it falls, out of income or wealth; an indirect tax is levied on spending and can be passed on in the price. Direct taxes: income tax and corporate profits tax.
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct distinction (on income/wealth vs on spending, incidence can be shifted); 1 mark for identifying income tax and corporate profits tax.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate indirect taxes as a percentage of total tax revenue. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a general sales tax is likely to be regressive.
parts.answer: Poorer households spend a larger share of their income on taxed goods, so the tax paid takes a larger percentage of a low income than of a high income.
parts.working: 1 mark: regressive means the share of income paid in tax falls as income rises; 1 mark: low-income households spend (rather than save) most of their income, so sales tax paid is a higher % of their income.

practice.stem: A government in South-East Asia plans to cut the basic rate of income tax from 20 % to 17 % to support spending during a slowdown.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a progressive income tax.
parts.answer: A tax where the proportion of income paid in tax (the average rate) rises as income rises, because higher slices of income are taxed at higher marginal rates.
parts.working: 1 mark: average rate rises as income rises; 1 mark: higher marginal rates on higher bands of income (or an example).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a cut in income tax rates will increase aggregate demand.
parts.answer: Usually yes, because disposable income and consumption rise, but the effect may be small if households save the extra income, buy imports, or lack confidence.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for analysis: lower tax → higher disposable income (1) → higher consumption (1) → AD (C + I + G + X − M) shifts right (1); possible extra effect on incentives. Up to 1 mark for evaluation: the rise may be small if the extra income is saved (low confidence, debt repayment), spent on imports, or goes mainly to high earners with a low propensity to consume; or offset if spending is cut to pay for it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between automatic stabilisers and discretionary fiscal policy, and consider which is more useful in reducing the effects of a fall in aggregate demand.
parts.answer: Automatic stabilisers change tax revenue and spending without a decision as income changes; discretionary policy is a deliberate change. Stabilisers act quickly but only cushion; discretionary policy can be larger but suffers time lags.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: definitions of fiscal policy, automatic stabilisers (progressive taxes, unemployment benefits) and discretionary policy (deliberate changes in tax rates or spending); examples. Analysis: in a downturn, tax revenue falls and benefit spending rises automatically, supporting disposable income and AD; discretionary policy, e.g. extra infrastructure spending, shifts AD right by a chosen amount; AD/AS diagram. Evaluation: stabilisers work immediately and without political delay but only reduce, not reverse, a fall in AD; discretionary policy can be targeted and larger but has recognition, decision and implementation lags and may arrive too late; usefulness also depends on the size of the welfare system and the government's ability to borrow; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A government wants its tax system to follow the principle (canon) of certainty. Which statement describes this principle?
A Taxpayers know how much tax they must pay, and when and how to pay it.
B The cost of collecting the tax is small compared with the revenue it raises.
C People with higher incomes pay a larger proportion of their income in tax.
D The tax is collected at a time and in a way that suits the taxpayer.
parts.answer: A Taxpayers know how much tax they must pay, and when and how to pay it.
parts.working: Certainty means the amount, timing and method of payment are clear to the taxpayer. B describes economy (efficiency of collection), C describes equity based on ability to pay, and D describes convenience.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a country, the first PKR 600 000 of annual income is tax-free, the next PKR 600 000 is taxed at 5 % and all income above PKR 1 200 000 is taxed at 15 %. A worker earns PKR 1 800 000 a year. What are the worker's marginal and average rates of income tax?
A marginal rate 15 %, average rate 6.7 %
B marginal rate 6.7 %, average rate 15 %
C marginal rate 15 %, average rate 15 %
D marginal rate 5 %, average rate 6.7 %
parts.answer: A marginal rate 15 %, average rate 6.7 %
parts.working: Tax = 0 + 5 % × 600 000 + 15 % × 600 000 = 30 000 + 90 000 = PKR 120,000. Average rate = 120,000 ÷ 1 800 000 = 6.7 %. The marginal rate is the rate on the last rupee earned, 15 %. B reverses the two definitions.

practice.stem:
Table 2: Government finances of Country R (US$ million; data invented for practice)
Year 1: nominal GDP 52 000; government spending 10 400; tax revenue 8320
Year 2: nominal GDP 50 400; government spending 10 900; tax revenue 7860

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budget deficit as a percentage of GDP in Year 1 and in Year 2. Give your answers to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, explain how automatic stabilisers might account for the change in the budget deficit between Year 1 and Year 2.
parts.answer: GDP fell, so incomes, spending and profits fell; tax revenue fell automatically while spending on unemployment and welfare benefits rose automatically, so the deficit increased with no new policy decision.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies the fall in nominal GDP (52 000 to 50 400) as a sign of recession; 1 mark: lower incomes/spending/profits → lower revenue from income, sales and profits taxes (revenue fell 8320 → 7860); 1 mark: rising unemployment → more benefit payments, so spending rose (10 400 → 10 900); 1 mark: these changes happen without a government decision and cushion the fall in AD, so the rise in the deficit is partly cyclical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether expansionary fiscal policy is the best way to reduce unemployment during a recession.
parts.answer: Expansionary fiscal policy can raise AD and reduce cyclical unemployment, but its success depends on spare capacity, the multiplier, debt levels and time lags; it does little for structural unemployment, and monetary or supply-side policy may be better in some cases.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: higher government spending or lower taxes → higher AD → firms raise output and demand more labour; with a negative output gap there is little inflationary pressure (AD/AS diagram with AD shifting right on the flatter part of AS); spending can be targeted at regions or labour-intensive projects; comparison with monetary policy (interest rate cuts) and supply-side policies (training) is required by 'best'. Evaluation: works for cyclical (demand-deficient) unemployment but not structural or frictional; time lags; leakages to imports; a large existing debt may limit borrowing or raise interest rates; confidence may stay low; monetary policy may be faster but weak if interest rates are already near zero; a combination may be best; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a government could use fiscal policy to reduce demand-pull inflation, and consider whether doing so will harm economic growth.
parts.answer: Contractionary fiscal policy (higher taxes, lower spending) reduces AD and so the pressure on prices; it may slow growth in the short run, but stable prices can support long-run growth.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: demand-pull inflation is caused by AD rising faster than the economy's capacity; contractionary (deflationary) fiscal policy. Analysis: higher income tax or sales tax reduces disposable income and consumption; cuts in government spending reduce G directly; AD shifts left, reducing the price level rise (AD/AS diagram near full capacity). Evaluation: real output may fall and unemployment rise in the short run; cutting capital spending may reduce future LRAS; but if the economy is at full capacity the fall in output may be small, and lower inflation improves confidence, investment and competitiveness, helping long-run growth; judgement.

practice.stem:
Table 1: Public finances of Country N (invented data for practice), $ billion
Year 1: nominal GDP 400; budget deficit 16; national debt at end of year 240
Year 2: nominal GDP 440; budget deficit 14
Year 3: nominal GDP 490; budget deficit 12
Assume each year's deficit is financed only by new borrowing and no debt is repaid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the national debt at the end of Year 2 and at the end of Year 3.
parts.answer: Year 2: $254 billion; Year 3: $266 billion.
parts.working: Debt rises by each year's deficit: 240 + 14 = 254 (1); 254 + 12 = 266 (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the national debt as a percentage of nominal GDP at the end of Year 1 and at the end of Year 3. Give your answers to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the fall in the budget deficit from Year 1 to Year 3 shows that the government has made its fiscal policy more contractionary.
parts.answer: Not necessarily: the deficit may have fallen because of automatic stabilisers as nominal GDP grew, not because of deliberate tax rises or spending cuts; only a discretionary change shows a tighter fiscal stance.
parts.working: Up to 2 for analysis: a lower deficit could come from deliberate tax rises/spending cuts (contractionary, lower AD) OR from growth in nominal GDP (22.5 % over two years) raising tax revenue and cutting benefit spending automatically. Up to 2 for judgement: need data on tax rates and planned spending (the structural or cyclically adjusted position); inflation may also raise nominal revenue; the government is still running a deficit, so it is still adding to AD; conclusion that the data alone cannot show the fiscal stance.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A government's budget deficit fell from $40 billion last year to $25 billion this year. Assuming the government finances its deficit only by borrowing, which statement must be correct?
A The national debt fell this year.
B The national debt still rose this year, but by less than last year.
C Government spending fell this year.
D Tax revenue rose this year.
parts.answer: B The national debt still rose this year, but by less than last year.
parts.working: The national debt is the stock of past borrowing; any deficit adds to it, so a $25 billion deficit raises the debt by $25 billion, which is less than last year's $40 billion rise. A confuses a smaller deficit (flow) with a falling debt (stock); C and D are possible, but the deficit could fall through either, so neither must be true.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): A lower-middle-income country collects tax equal to only 9.5 % of its GDP of PKR 110 000 billion. Fewer than 4 % of adults file income-tax returns, and a large informal sector pays little tax. A lender has asked the government to raise the ratio to 12 % within three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the extra tax revenue the government would collect if the tax-to-GDP ratio rose from 9.5 % to 12 % with GDP unchanged.
parts.answer: PKR 2,750 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether widening the tax base is a better way to raise tax revenue than raising existing tax rates.
parts.answer: Widening the base is usually better for efficiency and fairness, but it is slower and harder to enforce; raising rates gives quicker revenue but may reduce incentives and encourage evasion. A judgement depends on administrative capacity and the size of the informal sector.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for analysis: widening the base (bringing traders, retailers, agricultural incomes and property into the net) raises revenue without higher rates, spreads the burden more fairly, and reduces distortions; raising rates on the few who already pay may reduce work and investment incentives, encourage evasion and avoidance, and can be regressive if it relies on sales tax; higher rates may raise revenue quickly. Up to 2 marks for evaluation: a broader base needs records, digital payments and political will, so it is slow; in the short run higher rates may be needed; overall judgement (e.g. a broader base is better for sustained revenue).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a government should always aim to balance its budget.
parts.answer: Not always: deficits can be justified in recessions or for productive investment, and surpluses during booms; but persistent deficits raise debt and interest costs, so a balanced budget over the economic cycle is a more sensible aim than a balanced budget every year.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: meaning of a balanced budget, deficit and surplus; benefits of balance: no rise in national debt, lower interest payments, confidence of lenders, avoids possible crowding out and future tax rises; costs: in a recession, cutting spending or raising taxes to balance the budget reduces AD further and deepens unemployment (AD/AS); deficits can finance infrastructure and education that raise future LRAS and tax revenue; a surplus in a boom can reduce demand-pull inflation. Evaluation: depends on the stage of the cycle, the size of existing debt, whether borrowing is in foreign currency, and what the borrowing pays for (investment vs current spending); conclusion that 'always' is too strong, balance over the cycle is more realistic.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): To reduce its budget deficit, a government has raised its general sales tax rate from 17 % to 18 %. An opposition party argues that it should have cut government spending instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A good has a price of PKR 1000 before tax. Calculate the percentage increase in its price when the sales tax rate rises from 17 % to 18 %, assuming the tax is fully passed on to consumers. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1: price with tax rises from PKR 1170 to PKR 1180. A1: 10 ÷ 1170 × 100 = 0.85 %. (Not 1 %: the base is the tax-inclusive price.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether raising the sales tax rate is a better way to reduce the budget deficit than cutting government spending.
parts.answer: A sales tax rise raises revenue quickly from a broad base but is regressive and adds to inflation; spending cuts avoid higher prices but can damage public services and growth. The better choice depends on what spending is cut and on the distribution of the burden.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for analysis: sales tax raises revenue from a wide base and is hard to avoid on formal-sector sales; it causes a one-off rise in the price level (cost-push) and falls more heavily on the poor (regressive); it reduces consumption and AD. Spending cuts reduce the deficit directly and do not raise prices, but cuts to health, education or infrastructure reduce future growth and welfare; both reduce AD in the short run. Up to 2 marks for evaluation: depends on whether essentials are exempt, on how efficient current spending is, on the state of the economy, and on PED of taxed goods; a justified judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The table shows the tax paid at three levels of annual income in a country (invented data).
Annual income ($): 10 000, 20 000, 40 000
Tax paid ($): 1 000, 1 800, 3 200
Which statement correctly describes this tax?
A It is progressive, because the amount of tax paid rises as income rises.
B It is proportional, because every income group pays some tax.
C It is regressive, because the average rate of tax falls as income rises.
D It is progressive, because the marginal rate of tax is higher than the average rate.
parts.answer: C It is regressive, because the average rate of tax falls as income rises.
parts.working: Average rates: 1 000/10 000 = 10 %, 1 800/20 000 = 9 %, 3 200/40 000 = 8 %. A falling average rate means the tax is regressive. A is the main distractor: a regressive tax can still take more money from the rich; what matters is the proportion of income. D is false: the marginal rates (800/10 000 = 8 %, 1 400/20 000 = 7 %) are below the average rates.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which policy is a supply-side policy?
A a reduction in the central bank's policy interest rate
B government subsidies for vocational training courses
C an increase in unemployment benefit payments
D a temporary cut in sales tax to boost spending
parts.answer: B government subsidies for vocational training courses
parts.working: Training raises the skills and productivity of the labour force, increasing the economy's productive capacity (LRAS). A and D mainly change aggregate demand (monetary and demand-side fiscal policy); C raises spending on benefits and may even weaken incentives to work.

practice.stem: A government in East Africa plans to double its spending on technical and vocational colleges over five years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define supply-side policy.
parts.answer: Government policy aimed at increasing the productive capacity (potential output) of the economy by improving the quantity and/or quality of factors of production or the efficiency of markets.
parts.working: 1 mark: increases productive capacity/potential output/LRAS; 1 mark: via quantity or quality of resources, or efficiency of markets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how increased government spending on technical education could affect the long-run aggregate supply of an economy.
parts.answer: Workers gain skills, so labour productivity rises; firms can produce more with the same inputs and costs fall; the economy's productive capacity rises, shifting LRAS to the right (and the PPC outwards), though only after a time lag.
parts.working: 1 mark: improves quality of labour/human capital; 1 mark: higher labour productivity/lower unit costs; 1 mark: increases potential output, LRAS shifts right (diagram description); 1 mark: time lag of several years before effects appear / also adds to AD in the short run.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between market-based and interventionist supply-side policies, and consider which type is likely to increase output more quickly.
parts.answer: Market-based policies rely on incentives and competition (tax cuts, deregulation, privatisation); interventionist policies use government spending and direct action (education, infrastructure, R&D grants). Speed depends on the specific policy; neither type is always faster.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: definition of supply-side policy; market-based examples and interventionist examples. Analysis: both aim to shift LRAS right; market-based policies change incentives to work, invest and compete; interventionist policies improve the quality and quantity of factors directly. Evaluation: deregulation or tax incentives can act within months, while education and large infrastructure projects take years; however, market-based policies depend on how firms and workers respond, which may be weak, and may increase inequality; interventionist spending also raises AD quickly; a judgement on which is faster in a given context.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A government's supply-side policies increase the productive capacity of the economy, while aggregate demand does not change. What is the most likely effect, shown on an AD/AS diagram?
A Real output rises and the general price level falls.
B Real output rises and the general price level rises.
C Real output falls and the general price level falls.
D Real output is unchanged and the general price level rises.
parts.answer: A Real output rises and the general price level falls.
parts.working: Supply-side policy shifts aggregate supply (LRAS) to the right; with AD unchanged, the new equilibrium has higher real output and a lower price level. B is the result of an increase in AD, the main distractor.

practice.stem: A government plans to cut the rate of tax on company profits from 29 % to 25 % and to remove the licences that new firms need before they can run road-transport services (invented data for practice).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define deregulation.
parts.answer: Removing or reducing government rules and restrictions on firms and markets, e.g. on entry into an industry.
parts.working: 1 mark for removing/reducing rules or controls; 1 mark for 'on firms or markets / entry / competition', or a relevant example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a lower rate of tax on company profits could increase long-run aggregate supply.
parts.answer: Firms keep more profit to invest in machinery and technology, raising productive capacity; the country becomes more attractive to foreign direct investment, adding to the capital stock and bringing new technology (also: stronger incentive for enterprise and risk-taking).
parts.working: For each of two ways: 1 mark for the way, 1 mark for the link to more/better resources and a rightward shift of LRAS. Ways: higher retained profits → more investment in capital; higher post-tax return → more FDI; incentive for entrepreneurs to start and expand firms; more funds for research and development.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is an interventionist supply-side policy rather than a market-based one?
A privatisation of a state-owned airline
B removing regulations that restrict entry into the telecommunications market
C a reduction in the top rate of income tax
D government investment in a new national rail network
parts.answer: D government investment in a new national rail network
parts.working: Interventionist supply-side policy uses direct government action or spending to raise productive capacity, such as infrastructure. A, B and C are market-based: they reduce the role of the state and rely on incentives and competition.

practice.stem:
Table 3: Output per worker in Country V (US$ per year, constant 2020 prices; data invented for practice)
2020: 5600
2025: 6100
The government plans to privatise its state-owned steel and electricity companies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in output per worker between 2020 and 2025. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether privatising state-owned enterprises is likely to raise productivity further.
parts.answer: Privatisation may raise productivity through the profit motive, competition and access to private capital, but gains are uncertain if a public monopoly simply becomes a private monopoly or if regulation is weak.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for analysis: profit motive and shareholder pressure → cost cutting and better management; access to private finance → investment in new technology; competition (if markets are opened) → efficiency; removes political interference. Up to 1 mark for evaluation: a private monopoly may lack incentive to improve; job losses may cut output in the short run; depends on regulation and on whether the market is contestable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether reducing labour-market regulations, such as limits on hiring and firing, is the most effective supply-side policy to reduce unemployment.
parts.answer: Labour-market deregulation can make firms more willing to hire and reduce frictional and some structural unemployment, but it may reduce job security and wages and does little where unemployment is caused by low skills or weak demand; training and education may be more effective for structural unemployment.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: flexible labour markets reduce the cost and risk of hiring, so firms take on more workers; quicker matching reduces frictional unemployment; lower non-wage costs increase competitiveness; compare with other supply-side policies: training and education (structural unemployment), better job-matching services, reducing benefit traps, geographic mobility (housing). Evaluation: deregulation may increase insecure work and inequality, reduce worker morale and productivity; does not help cyclical unemployment; effect depends on the type of unemployment, on how strict regulations were to begin with, and on the size of the informal sector (where rules are often not enforced anyway); justified conclusion on 'most effective'.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): After a new road link and an automated customs system were completed, the average time for an export container to clear the main port of a South Asian country fell from 6.5 days to 2.6 days. Exporters say the cost of handling a container fell from $420 to $315. The project cost the government $1.8 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in the average clearance time and the percentage fall in the handling cost per container.
parts.answer: Clearance time: 60 %; handling cost: 25 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this infrastructure project could shift the long-run aggregate supply curve.
parts.answer: Faster, cheaper movement of goods lowers firms' costs and raises the productivity of workers and capital, increasing the productive capacity of the economy, so LRAS shifts to the right.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower transport/handling costs or less time lost; 1 mark: higher productivity or more efficient use of resources; 1 mark: increase in productive capacity → LRAS shifts right.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the project will also affect aggregate demand.
parts.answer: Yes: the $1.8 billion of construction spending raises government spending (and incomes through the multiplier) in the short run, and lower export costs make exports more competitive so net exports rise; but the effect depends on how much of the spending leaks into imports and whether it was financed by cutting other spending.
parts.working: Up to 3 for analysis: G is a component of AD; construction creates jobs and income; cheaper exporting raises export volumes (X − M); imports of inputs may also be easier. Up to 1 for judgement: size of effect depends on import content, financing (higher taxes or other cuts would offset), and timing (AD effect immediate, supply effect later).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how reducing the power of trade unions could be used as a supply-side policy to increase long-run aggregate supply, and consider whether it is likely to benefit workers.
parts.answer: Weaker unions can make labour markets more flexible: wages adjust more easily, firms can change working practices and hire more, and costs fall, shifting LRAS right. Workers may gain from more jobs, but may lose bargaining power, pay and protection.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: supply-side policy (raising productive capacity/LRAS); market-based policy; role of trade unions (collective bargaining, wage above equilibrium, restrictive practices). Analysis: less union power → wages closer to equilibrium → more employment; fewer strikes and more flexible working → higher productivity and lower unit costs → LRAS shifts right, more output at lower price level. Evaluation: workers who find jobs gain, but existing workers may face lower pay, less job security and worse conditions; where employers have monopsony power, unions can raise both wages and employment, so weakening them may cut employment; effect depends on how strong unions were to begin with; judgement.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): Inflation in a South Asian economy has risen to 14 %, partly because of power shortages and congestion at its main port. The finance minister says supply-side reforms will 'bring prices down within a year'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why supply-side policies often take a long time to have an effect.
parts.answer: Building infrastructure, educating workers or changing behaviour in response to incentives takes years, so productive capacity rises only slowly.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies a slow process (training/education, construction, new firms entering); 1 mark: so the shift in LRAS happens after a long time lag.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether supply-side policies can reduce inflation in the short run.
parts.answer: Mostly not: their main effect on capacity comes in the long run, and extra government spending on infrastructure may even add to AD in the short run. Some measures, such as cutting import duties on inputs or removing supply bottlenecks, can reduce costs fairly quickly, so the effect depends on the policy and the cause of inflation.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for analysis: supply-side policy shifts LRAS/AS right, lowering the price level for a given AD (AD/AS diagram); this needs time (training, infrastructure); in the short run interventionist spending raises AD and may increase demand-pull inflation; tax cuts raise disposable income and AD; but some measures act quickly on costs, e.g. removing tariffs on imported inputs, clearing port bottlenecks, deregulating energy supply, which reduce cost-push pressure. Up to 2 marks for evaluation: depends on cause of inflation (cost-push vs demand-pull), type of policy, credibility; usually monetary/fiscal policy is needed in the short run; justified judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether supply-side policy is more effective than fiscal policy in achieving economic growth in a low-income country.
parts.answer: Supply-side policy is essential for sustained growth because it raises potential output, but in a low-income country it is slow and needs funds; fiscal policy can raise actual growth quickly where there is spare capacity, and much supply-side policy is itself funded through the budget. A combination is likely to be most effective.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: distinguish actual and potential growth; fiscal policy (higher G, lower taxes) raises AD and actual output where there is a negative output gap; supply-side policies (education, health, infrastructure, property rights, deregulation) shift LRAS right, raising potential growth without inflation; diagrams. Evaluation: in low-income countries, capacity constraints (power, skills, transport) limit the effect of extra demand, which may become inflation or imports; but supply-side policy is slow, costly and may depend on aid or borrowing; weak institutions and corruption may reduce the effect of both; overlap — infrastructure spending is both; judgement on 'more effective' with conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A government cuts the top rate of income tax so that high earners will work longer hours. Why might the hours worked by high earners fall instead?
A The income effect of higher take-home pay per hour outweighs the substitution effect, so they choose more leisure.
B The substitution effect makes leisure more expensive, so they choose more leisure.
C The tax cut reduces aggregate demand, so firms need fewer hours of work.
D The tax cut raises the marginal rate of tax paid on extra hours worked.
parts.answer: A The income effect of higher take-home pay per hour outweighs the substitution effect, so they choose more leisure.
parts.working: A tax cut raises the net wage. The substitution effect (leisure now costs more income) encourages more work, but the income effect (people can reach a target income with fewer hours) encourages more leisure. If the income effect is stronger, hours fall. B is wrong because the substitution effect leads to less leisure, not more.

practice.stem:
Table 2: Business regulation in Country T (invented data for practice)
Days needed to register a new company: 2023 21; 2025 7
New companies registered: 2023 12 400; 2025 15 500
Real GDP growth (%): 2023 3.1; 2025 3.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the number of new companies registered between 2023 and 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether reducing the time and paperwork needed to start a company is likely to raise the long-run growth rate of Country T.
parts.answer: It can raise growth by encouraging enterprise, competition and formal-sector investment, as the 25 % rise in registrations suggests, but many registrations may be existing informal firms becoming formal, growth rose only 0.3 points, and access to finance, power, skills and demand may matter more; the effect is positive but probably limited on its own.
parts.working: Up to 4 for analysis: lower start-up costs → more new firms, more competition, innovation, more efficient use of resources → LRAS shifts right → higher potential growth; formal firms can borrow and invest more; more tax revenue for public investment. Up to 2 for evaluation: data show only a small change in GDP growth and correlation is not causation; other constraints (finance, electricity, skills, demand) may bind; new firms may fail quickly; time lags; a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether supply-side policies can raise economic growth without conflicting with a government's other macroeconomic objectives.
parts.answer: Supply-side policies that shift LRAS right can raise growth while lowering inflation, reducing unemployment and improving competitiveness, so they often avoid the conflicts of demand-side policy; but some (tax cuts, infrastructure spending) worsen the budget, raise imports or increase inequality in the short run, and they take a long time to work.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: AD/AS diagram with LRAS shifting right → higher real output and lower price level, so growth and price stability together; training reduces structural unemployment; higher productivity improves export competitiveness and the current account; compare with expansionary AD policy where growth raises inflation and imports. Evaluation: interventionist policies cost money and may widen the budget deficit; tax cuts for high earners may increase inequality; deregulation may reduce job security; initial spending raises AD and may add to inflation before supply responds; effects take years; success depends on the type of policy and the state of the economy; justified conclusion (generally fewer conflicts in the long run, but not none).

practice.stem: A central bank in South America is concerned that inflation is well above its 3 % target.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two instruments of monetary policy.
parts.answer: Any two of: the central bank's policy interest rate; the money supply (e.g. open market operations, reserve requirements); quantitative easing; the exchange rate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct instruments.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how an increase in interest rates could reduce the rate of inflation.
parts.answer: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive, reduce disposable income of borrowers and may raise the exchange rate; consumption, investment and net exports fall, AD grows more slowly and demand-pull pressure on prices eases.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher cost of borrowing → less credit-financed consumption/investment; 1 mark: higher reward for saving / higher loan repayments reduce disposable income; 1 mark: possible appreciation → cheaper imports, fewer exports; 1 mark: AD falls/grows more slowly → less demand-pull inflation.

practice.stem:
Table 5: Car loans in Country M (data invented for practice)
Quarter 1: bank lending rate 12 %; car loans approved 48 000
Quarter 4: bank lending rate 16 %; car loans approved 39 600

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in the number of car loans approved between Quarter 1 and Quarter 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why higher interest rates reduce the number of car loans.
parts.answer: Higher interest rates raise monthly repayments, so a car bought on credit becomes more expensive and fewer households can afford or are willing to borrow.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher cost of borrowing/higher repayments; 1 mark: reduces affordability or willingness to buy on credit (or banks lend less to riskier borrowers).

practice.stem: A teacher in Faisalabad keeps Rs 500 000 in a savings account. After the central bank raises its policy rate, the bank raises its savings interest rate from 12 % to 15 % a year (invented data for practice).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in the annual interest the teacher receives.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how higher interest rates on savings may reduce consumer spending.
parts.answer: The reward for saving rises, so households save more of their income; the opportunity cost of spending now rises, so consumption falls and AD falls.
parts.working: 1: higher return/reward for saving; 1: opportunity cost of spending now is higher, so more income is saved (higher propensity to save); 1: consumption, a component of AD, falls.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two other components of aggregate demand that may fall when interest rates rise.
parts.answer: Investment and net exports.
parts.working: 1 each: investment (I); net exports (X − M), because higher rates may cause the currency to appreciate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between expansionary and contractionary monetary policy.
parts.answer: Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates or increases the money supply to raise AD; contractionary monetary policy raises interest rates or reduces the growth of the money supply to reduce AD.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description, including the direction of change in interest rates/money supply.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why lower interest rates may increase investment by firms.
parts.answer: Borrowing to buy capital goods becomes cheaper, so more projects become profitable; and the opportunity cost of using retained profits falls because those funds would earn less if saved (also: higher consumer demand raises expected sales).
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for the reason, 1 for explanation. Reasons: lower cost of borrowing → more projects have a return above the interest rate; lower opportunity cost of retained profit; existing loan repayments fall, leaving more funds; higher expected demand from consumers who borrow more.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A central bank raises its policy interest rate. Which effect is most likely?
A The country's currency depreciates.
B Household borrowing to buy cars and other durable goods falls.
C The interest cost of the government's debt falls.
D Households save a smaller proportion of their income.
parts.answer: B Household borrowing to buy cars and other durable goods falls.
parts.working: Higher interest rates raise the cost of loans, so credit-financed spending on durables falls, reducing consumption and AD. A is wrong: higher rates usually attract financial inflows and cause appreciation; D is wrong because saving becomes more rewarding.

practice.stem:
Table 4: Country K (data invented for practice)
January 2024: central bank policy rate 15 %; inflation rate 12 %
December 2024: central bank policy rate 22 %; inflation rate 29 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the approximation real interest rate = nominal interest rate − inflation rate, calculate the real interest rate in January 2024 and in December 2024.
parts.answer: January 2024: +3 %; December 2024: −7 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the increase in the policy rate may not have reduced inflation quickly.
parts.answer: Because inflation rose faster than the policy rate, the real interest rate actually fell (became negative), so borrowing became cheaper in real terms; in addition, monetary policy works with long time lags, and inflation caused by rising import and energy prices (cost-push) is not reduced much by higher interest rates.
parts.working: 1 mark: real rate fell from +3 % to −7 %, so policy was looser in real terms; 1 mark: time lags (12–24 months) before AD responds; 1 mark: if inflation is cost-push (energy, imports, currency depreciation) higher rates do little to the cause; 1 mark: other relevant reason, e.g. much spending is not financed by bank credit / large informal sector, or government borrowing continued to rise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a reduction in interest rates might increase aggregate demand, and consider why it might fail to do so during a severe recession.
parts.answer: Lower rates reduce the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving, raising consumption and investment, and may depreciate the currency, raising net exports; in a severe recession low confidence, high debt and banks' unwillingness to lend may weaken these effects.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: monetary policy; the components of AD; meaning of a cut in the policy rate. Analysis: cheaper credit → more spending on durables and housing; lower loan repayments raise disposable income; investment projects become profitable; lower rates may cause capital outflows → depreciation → exports rise, imports fall; AD shifts right (diagram). Evaluation: if consumers and firms are pessimistic they may not borrow; banks may ration credit; rates may already be close to zero; time lags; depends on how much spending is financed by credit; judgement.

practice.stem: Some central banks have bought large quantities of government bonds from banks and other financial institutions, a policy known as quantitative easing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by quantitative easing.
parts.answer: A policy in which the central bank creates new money (electronically) to buy financial assets, mainly government bonds, from banks and other financial institutions, to increase the money supply.
parts.working: 1 mark: central bank creates money / increases the money supply; 1 mark: by buying bonds or other financial assets from financial institutions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how quantitative easing might increase aggregate demand.
parts.answer: Bond purchases raise bond prices and lower long-term interest rates, and give banks more reserves to lend; cheaper and more available credit encourages consumer borrowing and business investment; higher asset prices make households feel wealthier, raising consumption; a possible depreciation raises net exports.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four linked points: higher bond prices → lower long-term interest rates; more bank reserves → more lending; lower borrowing costs → more C and I; wealth effect from higher asset prices → more C; lower interest rates → depreciation → higher net exports; C, I and (X − M) are components of AD.

practice.stem:
Table 3: Country Q (invented data for practice)
Central bank policy rate: March 12 %; September 16 %
Exchange rate (rupees per US$): March 280; September 266

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage appreciation of the rupee against the US dollar between March and September. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.working: Value of 1 rupee in US$ rises from 1/280 to 1/266 (1); (1/266 ÷ 1/280 − 1) × 100 = (280/266 − 1) × 100 = 5.3 % (1). (14/280 = 5.0 % is the fall in the rupee price of a dollar, not the appreciation of the rupee.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the appreciation could help to reduce inflation in Country Q.
parts.answer: Imported goods, fuel and raw materials become cheaper in rupees, lowering cost-push pressure and the CPI directly; exports become dearer abroad and imports cheaper, so net exports and AD fall, reducing demand-pull inflation; domestic firms face more competition and keep prices down.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four linked points: lower rupee price of imports; lower costs of imported inputs → less cost-push inflation; lower import prices enter the CPI directly; exports less competitive / imports more attractive → lower (X − M) → lower AD → less demand-pull inflation; competitive pressure on domestic prices.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why there are time lags between a change in interest rates and its effect on inflation, and consider whether these lags make monetary policy ineffective.
parts.answer: Households and firms take time to notice and react: existing loans may be at fixed rates, investment plans take months to change, and lower spending feeds slowly into prices. Lags make policy harder to time but not ineffective, especially if the central bank acts on forecasts and is credible.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: monetary policy; interest rate as instrument; recognition, decision and implementation lags. Analysis: fixed-rate loans and existing contracts delay the effect on borrowers; investment decisions are planned well ahead; lower AD reduces demand-pull pressure only gradually; wages and prices are often set by contracts; total lag often 12–24 months. Evaluation: lags can cause policy to act at the wrong point in the cycle and make inflation worse; but central banks use forecasts and inflation targets, and a credible bank can change expectations quickly; monetary policy usually has shorter decision lags than fiscal policy; judgement.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): A family in Lahore has a variable-rate loan of PKR 2 000 000 on which it pays interest only. The bank's lending rate rises from 18 % to 21 % after the central bank raises its policy rate to fight inflation caused mainly by higher prices of imported fuel and edible oil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in the family's annual interest payment and express it as a percentage of the original payment. Give the percentage to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Increase of PKR 60,000 a year, a 16.7 % rise

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether raising interest rates is an effective way to control inflation caused by rising import prices.
parts.answer: Only partly: higher rates may strengthen the currency and reduce second-round wage and price rises, but they do not lower world prices, and they reduce output and employment, squeezing households already hit by higher prices.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for analysis: inflation from import prices is cost-push (AS shifts left); higher interest rates reduce AD (consumption via higher repayments as in the data, investment), which limits second-round effects and inflation expectations; higher rates may attract capital inflows and appreciate the currency, reducing import prices; but they reduce output further, adding to the fall in real GDP (stagflation). Up to 2 marks for evaluation: depends on whether the import price rise is temporary, on how sensitive the exchange rate is to interest rates, on the share of households with variable-rate loans, and on the credibility of the central bank; justified judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether monetary policy is more effective than fiscal policy in reducing inflation.
parts.answer: Monetary policy is often more flexible and independent of politics, and works through several channels, but it has time lags and is weak against cost-push inflation; fiscal policy acts directly on AD but is slower to change and politically difficult. Effectiveness depends on the cause of inflation and the economy's circumstances.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: monetary policy: higher interest rates/reduced money supply → lower C, I and possibly net exports via appreciation → AD falls; independent central banks can act quickly and build credibility on inflation expectations. Fiscal policy: higher taxes, lower spending reduce AD directly and can be targeted; AD/AS diagram for demand-pull inflation. Evaluation: monetary policy affects all regions and sectors equally, may harm investment and raise government debt interest; works poorly where few people borrow from banks; fiscal tightening is politically unpopular, slow (budget timetable) and may cut useful public investment; neither works well against cost-push inflation; coordination matters; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A central bank cuts its policy interest rate while interest rates in other countries do not change. Through the exchange-rate channel, what is the most likely chain of effects?
A Financial capital flows out, the currency depreciates, exports become cheaper in foreign currencies and aggregate demand rises.
B Financial capital flows in, the currency appreciates, imports become cheaper and inflation falls.
C Financial capital flows out, the currency appreciates, exports become cheaper and aggregate demand rises.
D Financial capital flows out, the currency depreciates, import prices fall and inflation falls.
parts.answer: A Financial capital flows out, the currency depreciates, exports become cheaper in foreign currencies and aggregate demand rises.
parts.working: Lower domestic interest rates make deposits in the country less attractive, so 'hot money' flows out, reducing demand for the currency and causing depreciation.
