Exports become cheaper abroad and imports dearer, raising net exports and AD. B describes the effect of a rise in interest rates. D is wrong because depreciation raises import prices.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether raising interest rates is likely to be effective in reducing inflation in an economy where many households and small firms do not borrow from banks.
parts.answer: Effectiveness is reduced because the credit channel reaches few people, but higher rates can still work through large firms, mortgage and car borrowers, government borrowing costs, saving incentives, the exchange rate and expectations; if inflation is cost-push or caused by import prices, higher rates are less effective; other policies may be needed.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: transmission: higher rates → less borrowing for consumer durables and investment → lower AD → lower demand-pull inflation; exchange-rate channel → appreciation → cheaper imports; expectations channel with a credible central bank; saving channel. Evaluation: with a large informal sector and low financial inclusion, borrowing channel is weak; savers with bank deposits gain income and may spend more; inflation from food or fuel prices (cost-push) responds little; high rates raise government interest costs; time lags; fiscal discipline or supply-side measures may be needed; conclusion weighing which channels still work.

practice.stem:
Table 4: Country W (invented data for practice)
Central bank policy rate: Year 1 22 %; Year 2 12 %
Inflation rate: Year 1 25 %; Year 2 6 %
Bank lending to private firms ($ billion): Year 1 48; Year 2 51

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the approximation real interest rate = nominal interest rate − inflation rate, calculate the real policy rate in Year 1 and in Year 2, and the change between the two years.
parts.answer: Year 1: −3 %; Year 2: +6 %; the real rate rose by 9 percentage points.
parts.working: 22 − 25 = −3 % and 12 − 6 = 6 % (1); change = 6 − (−3) = +9 percentage points (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether the central bank's policy in Year 2 should be described as expansionary.
parts.answer: The nominal rate was cut by 10 points, which looks expansionary, but the real rate rose from −3 % to +6 %, so borrowing became more costly in real terms; policy is arguably tighter. Lending still rose by 6.25 %, so the outcome depends on expectations and on other conditions.
parts.working: Up to 4 for analysis: a nominal cut reduces loan repayments and signals easier policy; but borrowers and savers respond to the real rate; a positive real rate rewards saving and makes real debt burdens heavier, so in real terms policy tightened; lending rose from $48 bn to $51 bn (+6.25 %), which may reflect lower nominal repayments or other factors (growth, confidence). Up to 2 for evaluation: the stance should be judged against the neutral real rate and expected (not past) inflation; conclusion that 'expansionary' is misleading in real terms, but less contractionary than keeping the rate at 22 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is NOT one of a government's main macroeconomic policy objectives?
A low and stable inflation
B a low level of unemployment
C a fixed price for petrol
D sustainable economic growth
parts.answer: C a fixed price for petrol
parts.working: The main macroeconomic objectives are economic growth, low unemployment, stable prices (low inflation) and balance of payments stability (plus, often, income redistribution). A fixed petrol price is a microeconomic intervention in one market, not a macroeconomic objective.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two macroeconomic objectives of a government, other than low inflation.
parts.answer: Any two of: sustainable economic growth; low unemployment; a stable/sustainable balance of payments (current account); (also accepted: a fair distribution of income).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why governments usually aim for a low, positive rate of inflation rather than zero inflation.
parts.answer: A target of zero risks deflation, which can cause consumers to delay spending and raise the real value of debts; a little inflation lets real wages and relative prices adjust without cutting money wages; price indices may overstate inflation; positive inflation lets central banks keep real interest rates negative in a downturn.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four points: risk of falling into deflation; deflation → delayed spending → lower AD and higher unemployment; higher real burden of debt; allows real wage/relative price adjustment because money wages are sticky downwards; measurement bias (quality improvements); room for monetary policy (negative real rates); mild inflation is compatible with growth.

practice.stem:
Table 5: Country D (invented data for practice)
Consumer price index (base year = 100): 2024 180.0; 2025 194.4
Labour force (million): 2024 70.0; 2025 72.0
Unemployed (million): 2024 5.6; 2025 5.4
Government targets for 2025: inflation 5 % ± 1 percentage point; unemployment rate below 7.0 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the inflation rate in 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the unemployment rate in 2024 and in 2025.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State, with a reason, whether each target was met in 2025.
parts.answer: Neither was met: inflation of 8.0 % is above the 6 % top of the target range, and unemployment of 7.5 % is not below 7.0 %.
parts.working: 1 mark each: inflation target missed (8.0 % > 6 %); unemployment target missed (7.5 % > 7.0 %), though unemployment did fall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the main macroeconomic objectives of a government, and consider whether they can all be achieved at the same time.
parts.answer: The objectives are sustainable growth, low unemployment, low and stable inflation and a stable balance of payments. Demand-side policies often create conflicts (growth and low unemployment vs inflation and the current account), but supply-side improvements and favourable conditions can allow several to be met together for a time.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: each objective defined with a typical target (e.g. inflation 2–5 %, steady real GDP growth, low unemployment rate, sustainable current account). Analysis: higher AD → growth and lower unemployment but also higher inflation and more imports (conflict); contractionary policy reduces inflation but raises unemployment. Evaluation: conflicts are greatest near full capacity; with spare capacity, AD can rise without much inflation; supply-side growth (LRAS shifts right) can lower inflation and unemployment together; external shocks matter; judgement that all can be met only sometimes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by sustainable economic growth.
parts.answer: An increase in real output that can be maintained over time without using up resources or damaging the environment in a way that reduces the ability of future generations to meet their needs.
parts.working: 1: rising real GDP/productive capacity over time; 1: without harming future generations, e.g. by depleting resources or causing environmental damage (or without causing inflation/balance of payments problems that end it).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why governments aim to keep unemployment low.
parts.answer: Unemployment wastes resources, so output is below potential (economy inside its PPC); it lowers tax revenue and raises spending on benefits; it causes poverty, loss of skills and social problems.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 for the reason, 1 for explanation. Reasons: lost output/opportunity cost; fiscal cost (lower tax, higher benefits); poverty and inequality; loss of skills/hysteresis; social costs such as crime and ill health.

practice.stem:
Table 6: Targets and outcomes for Country H, 2025 (data invented for practice)
Real GDP growth: target at least 5 %; actual 6.1 %
Inflation: target 5–7 %; actual 11.4 %
Unemployment: target no more than 6 %; actual 5.2 %
Current account balance: target deficit no larger than 2 % of GDP; actual deficit 4.3 % of GDP

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which of the government's targets were met in 2025.
parts.answer: Economic growth (6.1 % ≥ 5 %) and unemployment (5.2 % ≤ 6 %) met; inflation and current account targets missed.
parts.working: 1 mark: growth target met; 1 mark: unemployment target met (and recognition that the other two were missed).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, explain one conflict between the government's macroeconomic objectives.
parts.answer: Fast growth and low unemployment came with high inflation and a large current account deficit: rising AD pushed the economy close to full capacity, so prices rose (demand-pull), and higher incomes increased spending on imports.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies a conflict from the data (growth/unemployment vs inflation, or growth vs current account); 1 mark: rising AD → output and employment rise; 1 mark: near capacity → demand-pull inflation (11.4 % vs 5–7 % target) or higher incomes → more imports; 1 mark: links to the data (current account −4.3 % vs −2 % limit) / higher inflation makes exports less competitive.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country imports most of the machinery and fuel it uses. Its government raises aggregate demand to achieve faster economic growth. Which other objective is most likely to become harder to achieve as a direct result?
A a sustainable current account position on the balance of payments
B a lower rate of unemployment
C a higher level of real GDP per head
D higher employment in the construction industry
parts.answer: A a sustainable current account position on the balance of payments
parts.working: Higher incomes and output raise spending on imports, especially machinery and fuel, so the current account tends to worsen. B, C and D usually improve when growth is faster, so they do not conflict with it.

practice.stem: In an invented low-income country, real GDP grew by 4.0 % in 2025 and the population grew by 2.5 %. The government's objective is 'rising living standards for all'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in real GDP per head in 2025. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.working: Index of real GDP per head = 1.040/1.025 = 1.01463 (1); change = 1.46 % (1). (The approximation 4.0 − 2.5 = 1.5 % gains 1 mark only.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the growth of real GDP per head is a better guide to changes in living standards than the growth of real GDP.
parts.answer: Real GDP may rise only because the population rises; output per person shows the average amount of goods and services available to each person.
parts.working: 1: real GDP growth may be shared among more people; 1: GDP per head measures average output/income per person.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether rapid economic growth is enough to meet the objective of 'rising living standards for all'.
parts.answer: Growth raises average incomes and tax revenue for public services, but 'for all' depends on how the gains are distributed; growth may also bring pollution, longer working hours or depletion of resources, so policies on inequality, health and education are also needed.
parts.working: Up to 2 for analysis: higher output and incomes, more jobs, more tax revenue for health and education. Up to 2 for evaluation: distribution of income (gains may go to a few); non-material aspects (environment, leisure, health); sustainability; informal economy; justified judgement that growth is necessary but not sufficient.

practice.stem:
Table 6: Current account of Country F, 2025 (invented data for practice), $ billion
Exports of goods: 32
Imports of goods: 54
Trade in services (net): −3
Primary income (net): −5
Secondary income, mainly workers' remittances (net): +27
Nominal GDP: 375

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current account balance in 2025 and express it as a percentage of nominal GDP. Give the percentage to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Deficit of $3 billion; −0.8 % of GDP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a government may aim to avoid a large and persistent current account deficit.
parts.answer: A persistent deficit must be financed by borrowing from abroad, running down foreign currency reserves or selling assets; this can lead to a falling exchange rate and imported inflation, higher interest payments abroad, and a loss of confidence; it may also show that domestic firms are uncompetitive, costing output and jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four points: financed by capital inflows/borrowing/reserves; reserves may run out → crisis or IMF loan; pressure for depreciation → imported inflation; rising foreign debt and interest payments (primary income outflows); signals lack of competitiveness → lower domestic output and jobs; deficit financed by short-term 'hot money' is unstable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why a central bank may set its inflation target as a range, such as 5–7 %, rather than as a single figure.
parts.answer: Inflation cannot be controlled exactly because of shocks and time lags, so a range allows flexibility without the bank being seen to fail at every small deviation, which keeps the target credible.
parts.working: 1: inflation is affected by shocks/lags and cannot be hit exactly; 1: a range allows flexibility and protects credibility (avoids over-reacting to small changes).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a fall in unemployment might lead to a worsening of the current account of the balance of payments.
parts.answer: More people in work means higher incomes and spending, some of which goes on imports; firms may divert output from exports to the home market; a tighter labour market raises wages and costs, so exports become less price-competitive.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four linked points: higher employment → higher disposable income; higher consumption → more imports (marginal propensity to import); goods diverted to the home market → fewer exports; rising wages/costs → higher prices → exports less competitive; current account deficit widens.

practice.stem: Country G (invented data for practice): nominal GDP was $840 billion in 2024 and $945 billion in 2025. The GDP deflator was 100 in 2024 and 108 in 2025. The government's growth objective is real GDP growth of at least 5 % a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the growth rate of real GDP in 2025. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the growth rate of nominal GDP in 2025.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the government measures its growth objective in real terms rather than nominal terms, and state whether the objective was met.
parts.answer: Nominal GDP growth includes price rises, which do not represent more goods and services; real GDP removes inflation and shows the change in output. Real growth was 4.2 %, so the 5 % objective was not met even though nominal GDP grew by 12.5 %.
parts.working: 1: nominal growth includes inflation; 1: real growth measures change in the volume of output; 1: objective not met (4.2 % < 5 %).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether keeping inflation low should be a government's most important macroeconomic objective.
parts.answer: Low inflation supports confidence, investment and competitiveness and protects the poor, so it is a strong candidate; but in a recession or with high unemployment, growth and employment may matter more, and the priority depends on the country's current problems.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: the four main objectives; benefits of low and stable inflation: protects real incomes and savings (especially of those on fixed incomes), reduces uncertainty, encourages investment, keeps exports competitive, avoids menu and shoe-leather costs; conflicts between objectives (e.g. low inflation vs low unemployment in the short run); costs of unemployment and low growth. Evaluation: the priority depends on circumstances: with inflation at 25 %, controlling it comes first; with deflation risk or high unemployment, growth and jobs matter more; low inflation can be seen as a means to sustainable growth rather than a rival; central bank inflation targets show many governments give it priority; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a government should give priority to reducing unemployment rather than to reducing a current account deficit.
parts.answer: Unemployment has direct human and output costs, so it often deserves priority, but a large deficit financed by short-term borrowing can trigger a currency crisis that raises unemployment later; the priority depends on the size of each problem, how the deficit is financed and the type of unemployment.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: costs of unemployment (lost output, poverty, lower tax revenue, higher benefit spending, loss of skills); costs of a current account deficit (falling reserves, depreciation, imported inflation, debt); conflict: expansionary policy to cut unemployment raises imports and widens the deficit; contractionary policy or expenditure-reducing measures cut the deficit by reducing incomes and jobs. Evaluation: deficit may be sustainable if financed by FDI or offset by remittances; deficits from importing capital goods may raise future output; long-term unemployment is hard to reverse; supply-side policy may help both; priority depends on circumstances; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether economic growth should be the main macroeconomic objective of a government in a low-income country.
parts.answer: Growth is vital in a low-income country because it raises incomes, jobs and tax revenue for health and education, but rapid growth may bring inflation, a current account deficit, inequality and environmental damage; stable prices and sustainability support growth itself, so growth should be a main but not the only objective.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: growth → higher real GDP per head, poverty reduction, more employment, more government revenue; growth is needed to absorb a fast-growing labour force. Conflicts: demand-led growth → inflation (hurts the poor most) and higher imports → current account deficit. Evaluation: quality of growth matters (inclusive, sustainable); high inflation and balance of payments crises can halt growth, so macro stability is a precondition; distribution and environmental costs; judgement on priority in context.

practice.stem:
Table 7: Selected data, 2025 (invented data for practice), %
Real GDP growth: Country A 5.5; Country B 2.1
Inflation rate: Country A 9.0; Country B 2.4
Unemployment rate: Country A 6.5; Country B 4.8
Current account balance (% of GDP): Country A −4.2; Country B +1.1
The 'misery index' is the inflation rate plus the unemployment rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the misery index for each country.
parts.answer: Country A: 15.5; Country B: 7.2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess, using the data, which country achieved its macroeconomic objectives more successfully in 2025.
parts.answer: Country B did better on inflation, unemployment and the current account (misery index 7.2 vs 15.5), while Country A grew much faster; overall B seems more successful, unless A's higher growth reflects catch-up investment that will raise future living standards; the answer depends on the weight given to each objective and on what each country's targets were.
parts.working: Up to 4 for analysis using the data: B lower inflation (2.4 vs 9.0) and unemployment (4.8 vs 6.5), current account surplus (+1.1 % vs −4.2 %); A faster growth (5.5 vs 2.1 %); misery index ignores growth and the balance of payments. Up to 2 for evaluation: one year only; stage of development (a low-income country may need faster growth); A's deficit may be financing investment; targets may differ; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In Keynes's liquidity preference theory, which motive for holding money is most sensitive to changes in the rate of interest?
A the speculative motive
B the transactions motive
C the precautionary motive
D the store of value motive
parts.answer: A the speculative motive
parts.working: Speculative balances are held instead of bonds; when interest rates are high, bonds are attractive and the opportunity cost of holding money is high, so speculative demand falls. Transactions demand (B) depends mainly on income.

practice.stem: A central bank in South Asia has raised its policy rate three times this year and has also lent emergency funds to a small commercial bank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between narrow money and broad money.
parts.answer: Narrow money is money that can be spent immediately: notes and coins (plus banks' reserves at the central bank or sight deposits, depending on the measure); broad money also includes less liquid bank and savings deposits that can be turned into spending power.
parts.working: 1 mark: narrow = notes, coins/highly liquid; 1 mark: broad = narrow money plus time/savings deposits (less liquid).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two functions of a central bank.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g.: carries out monetary policy (sets the policy interest rate, controls the money supply) to meet an inflation target; acts as lender of last resort to commercial banks in a crisis; is banker to the government (manages its accounts and borrowing); supervises and regulates banks; issues notes and coins; manages foreign exchange reserves and the exchange rate.
parts.working: For each of two functions: 1 mark for identification, 1 mark for explaining what it involves or why it matters.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): In an East African country, the number of people using mobile-phone wallets has risen from 9 million to 31 million in six years. Market traders, taxi drivers and utility companies now accept wallet payments, and the share of payments made in cash has fallen from 70 % to 40 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two characteristics of money that a digital wallet balance must have if it is to function as money.
parts.answer: For example: general acceptability — shops and people must be willing to accept it in payment; divisibility — it can be used for small and large amounts; durability/security — balances cannot be destroyed or easily forged; portability — payments can be made anywhere; limited supply/stable value so it holds purchasing power.
parts.working: For each of two characteristics: 1 mark for naming it, 1 mark for applying it to digital wallet balances.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a shift from cash to digital payments could affect commercial banks' ability to create credit.
parts.answer: Less cash is withdrawn and held outside the banking system, so the cash leakage falls; more deposits stay with banks and are available as reserves, so the credit multiplier and banks' ability to lend increase (subject to demand for loans and regulation).
parts.working: 1 mark: less cash held by the public/smaller cash leakage; 1 mark: more deposits/reserves stay in banks; 1 mark: larger credit (bank) multiplier → more lending possible.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item is included in a measure of broad money but not in a measure of narrow money?
A notes and coins in circulation with the public
B commercial banks' reserve balances held at the central bank
C savings (time) deposits held by households in commercial banks
D cheques written by customers but not yet cleared
parts.answer: C savings (time) deposits held by households in commercial banks
parts.working: Broad money adds bank deposits, including less liquid time/savings deposits, to narrow money. Notes and coins (A) and banks' reserves at the central bank (B) are part of narrow money (the monetary base); a cheque (D) is only an instruction to transfer a deposit, not money itself.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the transactions and precautionary motives for holding money.
parts.answer: Transactions motive: money held to pay for day-to-day purchases between receiving income; precautionary motive: money held to meet unexpected expenses or emergencies.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how each of these motives is likely to change when national income rises.
parts.answer: Both rise: higher incomes mean more spending, so more money is needed for transactions, and people hold larger reserves for emergencies in proportion to their spending.
parts.working: 1 mark: transactions demand rises with income/spending; 1 mark: precautionary demand rises with income.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Commercial banks keep 8 % of deposits as reserves and lend the rest. A customer deposits $40 million of new cash. Assuming no cash leaks out of the banking system, what is the maximum total increase in bank deposits?
A $500 million
B $460 million
C $320 million
D $43.2 million
parts.answer: A $500 million
parts.working: Credit multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.08 = 12.5, so maximum deposits = 12.5 × $40 million = $500 million. B ($460 million) is the maximum increase in new loans, which excludes the original deposit.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): A customer deposits PKR 10 million of cash in Bank A. All banks keep 10 % of every deposit as reserves and lend out the rest, and all loans are redeposited in the banking system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the new loans made in each of the first three rounds of lending, starting with Bank A.
parts.answer: Round 1: PKR 9.0 million; round 2: PKR 8.1 million; round 3: PKR 7.29 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum total increase in bank deposits that could result from the original deposit.
parts.answer: PKR 100 million
parts.working: Credit multiplier 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10; 10 × 10 = PKR 100 million (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the actual increase in deposits is likely to be smaller than this.
parts.answer: For example: borrowers hold part of the loans as cash (cash leakage), so it does not return to banks; banks may keep reserves above the minimum during uncertain times; there may be too few creditworthy borrowers or weak demand for loans; capital requirements may limit lending.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for identification, 1 mark for explaining how it reduces redeposits or lending.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which commercial banks' ability to create credit is limited.
parts.answer: Banks can create deposits by lending a multiple of their reserves, but their ability is limited by reserve and capital requirements, cash leakages, the demand for loans, the supply of creditworthy borrowers, central bank policy and confidence. The extent of the limit varies over the economic cycle.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: functions of commercial banks; process of credit creation and the credit multiplier (1 ÷ reserve ratio) with a numerical example; liquidity vs profitability conflict; limits: required reserve/liquidity ratios, capital adequacy rules, cash leakage, banks' own prudence, demand for loans, interest rates set by the central bank, competition from non-bank lenders. Evaluation: in booms limits are weak and credit may expand rapidly (asset bubbles); in recessions demand for loans and bank confidence are the main limits even with ample reserves; financial innovation and digital payments reduce cash leakage; the multiplier model oversimplifies modern banking; justified judgement on 'extent'.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): in an economy the money supply (M) is $200 billion, the velocity of circulation (V) is 5 and the volume of transactions (T) is 1 000 billion units of output, where MV = PT.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average price level (P).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The money supply rises by 10 %. Calculate the new price level if V and T are unchanged, and the new price level if V falls to 4.5 at the same time.
parts.answer: 1.1 if V is unchanged; 0.99 if V falls to 4.5.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why monetarists argue that V and T are broadly constant in the short run, and why Keynesians disagree.
parts.answer: Monetarists: V depends on slowly changing payment habits and institutions; T (real output) is determined by supply-side factors and tends towards full employment; so changes in M mainly change P. Keynesians: V is unstable – extra money may be held idle (speculative demand, liquidity trap) so V falls; when there is spare capacity, higher spending raises T (output) rather than P.
parts.working: 1 mark: monetarist view of V; 1 mark: monetarist view of T; 1 mark: Keynesian view of V; 1 mark: Keynesian view of T (spare capacity).

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): the assets of a commercial bank, as a percentage of total assets: cash in its vaults 5 %; balances at the central bank 3 %; short-term government bills 12 %; advances (loans) to customers 70 %; long-term investments 10 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the bank's assets held in liquid form (cash, balances at the central bank and short-term bills).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the conflict between liquidity and profitability that a commercial bank faces.
parts.answer: Liquid assets (cash, central bank balances, bills) can meet customer withdrawals quickly but earn little or no interest; advances (loans) earn high interest but cannot be turned into cash quickly and carry default risk. Holding more liquid assets reduces the risk of a run but lowers profit; lending more raises profit but increases liquidity and solvency risk.
parts.working: 1 mark: liquid assets earn low returns; 1 mark: loans are profitable but illiquid/risky; 1 mark: need to meet withdrawals/confidence; 1 mark: trade-off explained.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a rise in the bank's reserve requirement would affect its ability to create credit.
parts.answer: The bank must hold a larger share of deposits as reserves, so it has less to lend; the credit multiplier (1 ÷ reserve ratio) falls, reducing deposit creation.
parts.working: 1 mark: less excess reserves to lend; 1 mark: smaller credit multiplier.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
According to the quantity theory of money (MV = PT), the money supply rises by 8 %, the velocity of circulation is unchanged and the number of transactions rises by 3 %. By approximately how much does the price level change?
A a rise of 4.9 %
B a rise of 8.0 %
C a rise of 11.2 %
D a fall of 2.7 %
parts.answer: A a rise of 4.9 %
parts.working: P = MV ÷ T, so P changes by 1.08 ÷ 1.03 − 1 = 4.9 % (roughly 8 % − 3 %). B assumes T is fixed, as in the strict monetarist version, but here T rises.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): In an economy the demand for money is given by Md = 600 − 40r, where Md is in $ billion and r is the rate of interest in per cent. The money supply is fixed by the central bank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium rate of interest when the money supply is $360 billion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The central bank increases the money supply to $400 billion. Calculate the new equilibrium rate of interest.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a liquidity trap and why, in a liquidity trap, a further increase in the money supply would not reduce the rate of interest.
parts.answer: At a very low interest rate people expect bond prices to fall (interest rates to rise), so they are willing to hold any extra money rather than buy bonds; the demand for money becomes perfectly elastic, so extra money supply is simply held and the interest rate does not fall.
parts.working: 1 mark: very low interest rate where demand for money becomes perfectly elastic (horizontal); 1 mark: expectation that bond prices will fall/interest rates rise, so speculative demand absorbs extra money; 1 mark: shifting the money supply curve right leaves the interest rate unchanged, so monetary policy cannot stimulate investment this way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that controlling the money supply is the most effective way to control inflation.
parts.answer: Monetarists argue, using the quantity theory, that inflation is caused by excess money growth and is best controlled by limiting it; Keynesians argue that velocity and output are not stable, that money supply is hard to control, and that inflation has other causes (cost-push, demand from fiscal policy). Money supply control can be effective in some cases (hyperinflation, monetary financing of deficits) but is rarely the most effective tool on its own.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: MV = PT; monetarist assumptions (V and T fixed or stable) → P rises proportionately with M; transmission through interest rates and spending; Keynesian view — V varies, T can rise when there is spare capacity, money demand sensitive to interest rates; difficulty of controlling money supply when banks create credit; central banks now usually target interest rates; alternatives: interest rate policy, fiscal policy, supply-side policy, exchange rate policy. Evaluation: depends on the cause of inflation (excess money creation vs cost-push from oil or depreciation), on whether the economy is near full capacity, on central bank credibility; evidence that money and inflation are closely linked in the long run and in hyperinflations, weaker in the short run; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A banking system has total deposits of $500 million and reserves of $60 million. The required reserve ratio is 10 %. If banks lend out all their excess reserves and all loans are redeposited, what is the maximum further increase in bank deposits?
A $10 million
B $60 million
C $100 million
D $600 million
parts.answer: C $100 million
parts.working: Required reserves = 10 % × 500 = $50 million, so excess reserves = $10 million. The credit multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10, so deposits can rise by 10 × 10 = $100 million. A is only the first round of lending; D wrongly multiplies all reserves (60 × 10) and ignores the deposits already supported.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that the loanable funds theory gives a better explanation of how the rate of interest is determined than the liquidity preference theory.
parts.answer: Loanable funds: interest rate is the price that balances the supply of savings (plus new credit) with the demand for borrowing for investment; a rise in thriftiness lowers interest; links to real factors (productivity of capital, time preference). Liquidity preference (Keynes): interest is the reward for parting with liquidity; set where money demand (transactions, precautionary, speculative) equals money supply fixed by the central bank; explains how monetary policy changes rates and the liquidity trap. Evaluation: loanable funds suits the long run and real factors; liquidity preference suits the short run and the central bank's role in setting policy rates; in practice central banks set a policy rate and banks create money endogenously, so neither theory is complete; risk premia and global capital flows also matter. Conclusion: depends on time period and institutional setting; the two can be seen as complementary.
parts.working: Top band: accurate definitions, a correct, fully explained diagram where relevant, developed chains of analysis on more than one side, and evaluation that weighs the arguments and reaches a justified conclusion that answers the question; mid band: sound but partly developed analysis with limited evaluation; low band: descriptive points or assertion. Expect: both theories explained with diagrams described in words (supply/demand for loanable funds; money demand curve and vertical money supply), what shifts each curve, and an evaluated judgement on 'better'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would show potential economic growth rather than only actual economic growth?
A an outward shift of the economy's long-run aggregate supply curve
B a movement from a point inside the production possibility curve to a point on it
C an increase in aggregate demand when there is a large negative output gap
D a fall in unemployment caused by higher consumer spending
parts.answer: A an outward shift of the economy's long-run aggregate supply curve
parts.working: Potential growth is an increase in productive capacity, shown by an outward shift of LRAS (or of the PPC). B, C and D show actual growth from using existing spare capacity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between actual and potential economic growth.
parts.answer: Actual growth is an increase in real output (real GDP) produced; potential growth is an increase in the economy's productive capacity — the maximum output it could produce.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct definition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two causes of potential economic growth.
parts.answer: For example: investment in capital goods increases the capital stock; improvements in technology raise productivity; education and training improve the quality of labour; a larger labour force (population growth, migration, higher participation); discovery of natural resources.
parts.working: For each of two causes: 1 mark for identification, 1 mark for explaining how it increases productive capacity (LRAS shifts right).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two possible costs of rapid economic growth.
parts.answer: Any two of: environmental damage and pollution; depletion of non-renewable resources; demand-pull inflation; current account deficit as imports rise; greater income inequality; congestion and stress; opportunity cost of investment (less consumption now).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how economic growth could increase income inequality.
parts.answer: Growth may be concentrated in sectors such as finance, technology or mining that employ skilled workers and owners of capital, whose incomes rise fastest; unskilled or rural workers gain little, and returns to capital may rise faster than wages, so the gap widens.
parts.working: 1 mark: gains concentrated in certain sectors/regions; 1 mark: skilled workers and owners of capital gain most; 1 mark: unskilled/rural/informal workers gain little, so the Gini coefficient rises.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by sustainable economic growth.
parts.answer: Growth in real output that can be maintained over time without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their needs – it does not depend on running down natural resources or causing irreversible environmental damage.
parts.working: 1 mark: growth that can be maintained in the long run; 1 mark: without depleting resources/harming future generations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of how rapid growth can run down a country's natural capital.
parts.answer: Any two: deforestation for timber or farmland; over-extraction of groundwater for irrigation; over-fishing; soil degradation; air and river pollution from industry.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how an increase in the quantity and quality of a country's capital stock can lead to economic growth.
parts.answer: More capital (machines, infrastructure) per worker raises labour productivity; better-quality capital embodies new technology; together they increase the productive capacity of the economy, shifting the LRAS curve to the right (PPC outwards), so potential output and, if demand rises too, actual output grow.
parts.working: 1 mark: more capital per worker raises productivity; 1 mark: new technology/quality; 1 mark: increase in productive capacity; 1 mark: LRAS shifts right/potential growth.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): Country G's nominal GDP was 50 000 billion in 2024 and 56 100 billion in 2025 (in local currency). The GDP deflator was 100 in 2024 and 108 in 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate real GDP in 2025 at 2024 prices and the rate of real economic growth between 2024 and 2025. Give real GDP to one decimal place and the growth rate to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Real GDP 2025 = 51,944.4 billion; real growth = 3.89 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why real GDP is a better measure of economic growth than nominal GDP.
parts.answer: Nominal GDP rises when prices rise even if output does not; real GDP removes the effect of inflation, so it shows the change in the volume of goods and services produced.
parts.working: 1 mark: nominal GDP includes inflation (here nominal rose 12.2 %); 1 mark: real GDP measures change in output/volume.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): In 2025 a South Asian country's real GDP grew by 4.2 % and its population grew by 2.4 %. Much of the growth came from farming that depends on pumping groundwater, and from clearing forest for new farmland.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the growth rate of real GDP per head in 2025. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1: 1.042 ÷ 1.024 = 1.01758; A1: growth of real GDP per head = 1.76 % (approximately 4.2 % − 2.4 %).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the country's present rate of economic growth may not be sustainable.
parts.answer: For example: growth based on rapid use of non-renewable resources such as groundwater and forests reduces future capacity; pollution and environmental damage lower future productivity and health; growth driven by borrowing or a consumer boom may cause inflation and current account deficits; rapid population growth puts pressure on land and water.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for identification, 1 mark for explaining why it threatens future growth (meeting present needs without compromising future generations).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that investment in human capital is the most important cause of long-run economic growth.
parts.answer: Human capital raises productivity, adaptability and innovation and is central to growth, but its effect depends on physical capital, technology, institutions and demand for skilled labour; it is one of several key causes, and the most important cause varies by country.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: meaning of human capital (education, training, health); effects on labour productivity, innovation and ability to use technology; LRAS shifts right/PPC outwards; compare with physical capital investment, technological progress, natural resources, labour force growth, institutions and property rights. Evaluation: returns to education depend on quality, not years of schooling; skilled workers may emigrate (brain drain); without capital and infrastructure skills are underused; time lags are long; endogenous growth view gives human capital a central role; justified conclusion with reference to country type.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's real GDP grows at a constant 3 % a year. Approximately how many years will it take for real GDP to double?
A 10 years
B 23 years
C 33 years
D 50 years
parts.answer: B 23 years
parts.working: Doubling time = ln 2 ÷ ln 1.03 ≈ 23.4 years (the 'rule of 70': 70 ÷ 3 ≈ 23). C (100 ÷ 3) ignores compounding; A and D are far too short and too long.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): Country X and Country Y each have GDP per head of $1 500 today. Real GDP per head grows at 2 % a year in Country X and at 6 % a year in Country Y.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate GDP per head after 15 years for each country. Give your answers to the nearest dollar.
parts.answer: Country X: $2 019; Country Y: $3 595.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why small differences in annual growth rates matter so much over long periods.
parts.answer: Growth compounds: each year's growth is on a larger base, so the gap widens over time – here a 4-point difference in growth rates leads to Y's GDP per head being about 78 % higher than X's after 15 years.
parts.working: 1 mark: compounding; 1 mark: use of the data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a higher GDP per head may not mean higher living standards for most people.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: income may be unequally distributed; growth may come from pollution-intensive industries harming health; longer working hours/less leisure; spending on defence rather than consumption; prices differ (PPP); informal sector not measured.
parts.working: For each: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem:
Data (invented for practice), $ billion:
Year 1: GDP 200; value of forest and mineral depletion 6; estimated cost of pollution damage 10
Year 2: GDP 210; value of forest and mineral depletion 8; estimated cost of pollution damage 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the 'green' GDP (GDP minus the cost of depletion and pollution damage) for each year and the growth rate of green GDP. Give the growth rate to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Year 1: $184 billion; Year 2: $190 billion; green GDP growth 3.26 % (compared with 5 % for GDP).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why conventional GDP growth may overstate sustainable growth.
parts.answer: GDP counts output from using up natural resources as income without deducting the loss of natural capital; spending to clean up pollution is added to GDP; future costs (health, climate) are ignored; so measured growth includes some unsustainable output.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three developed points.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): A Southeast Asian country's real GDP is US$300 billion. The government targets real growth of 5 % a year while cutting carbon emissions from electricity by 30 % by 2035. Coal still provides 60 % of its electricity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the country's real GDP after four years if it grows at 5 % a year. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.answer: US$364.65 billion
parts.working: M1: 300 × 1.05⁴; A1: 364.65 (not 300 × 1.20 = 360, which ignores compounding).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a carbon tax on electricity generators could affect the country's long-run aggregate supply.
parts.answer: In the short run it raises generators' costs, shifting AS left; in the long run it encourages investment in renewable energy and energy efficiency and reduces the pollution damage to health and farmland, which may protect or increase LRAS.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher costs of production in the short run (AS shifts left); 1 mark: incentive to invest in cleaner technology/renewables; 1 mark: reduced pollution protects health, productivity and natural capital, so long-run capacity is maintained or rises.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the government can achieve both rapid economic growth and environmental sustainability.
parts.answer: Possibly, if growth comes from cleaner technology, renewables and efficient resource use (green growth); but in the short run there is often a trade-off because coal is cheap and clean energy needs heavy investment.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for analysis: trade-off — fossil-fuel growth increases emissions; green investment raises costs now; but innovation and renewables can decouple growth from emissions and create jobs. Up to 1 mark for a judgement depending on finance, technology and time scale.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether policies to achieve sustainable economic growth must reduce the rate of economic growth.
parts.answer: In the short run, sustainability policies such as carbon taxes, regulations and resource conservation can raise costs and slow growth; but in the long run they protect natural capital and health and can create new industries, so sustainable growth need not be slower and may be faster over a long period.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: meaning of sustainable growth; policies: environmental taxes, tradable permits, regulation, subsidies for renewables, investment in human capital and technology; short-run effects — higher costs, AS shifts left, lower output in polluting sectors; long-run — less depletion, fewer climate and health costs, innovation and green industries shift LRAS right; measurement issues (GDP ignores environmental depletion). Evaluation: depends on the time period, on the policy design (market-based vs command), on whether clean technology is affordable, on international coordination, and on a country's stage of development; low-income countries may face sharper trade-offs; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that technological progress, rather than the accumulation of capital, is the key to sustained long-run economic growth.
parts.answer: Capital accumulation: more machines and infrastructure per worker raise productivity and shift LRAS right; important for low-income countries with little capital; but diminishing returns to capital mean growth from investment alone slows; requires saving (opportunity cost of consumption). Technological progress: raises total factor productivity, offsets diminishing returns, can reduce resource use per unit of output (supporting sustainability); depends on R&D, education, institutions, openness. Evaluation: the two are linked – new technology is often embodied in new capital; human capital needed to use it; for catching-up economies, capital and adopting existing technology both matter; for advanced economies, innovation is the main source; sustainability considerations strengthen the case for technology. Conclusion justified.
parts.working: Top band: accurate definitions, a correct, fully explained diagram where relevant, developed chains of analysis on more than one side, and evaluation that weighs the arguments and reaches a justified conclusion that answers the question; mid band: sound but partly developed analysis with limited evaluation; low band: descriptive points or assertion. Expect: LRAS/PPC diagrams described, diminishing returns explained, clear distinction between capital deepening and productivity growth, application to developing vs developed economies, and a supported judgement.

practice.stem:
Data (invented for practice): a simple growth model gives: growth rate (%) = investment as % of GDP ÷ capital–output ratio, where the capital–output ratio is the number of dollars of new capital needed to produce one extra dollar of output a year.
Country A: investment 24 % of GDP; capital–output ratio 4
Country B: investment 30 % of GDP; capital–output ratio 6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the formula, calculate the predicted growth rate for each country.
parts.answer: Country A: 6 %; Country B: 5 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Country B grows more slowly despite investing a larger share of its GDP.
parts.answer: Its capital–output ratio is higher, so each dollar of investment adds less output: investment may be in low-productivity projects (prestige buildings, state firms), poorly maintained, affected by corruption or by shortages of skilled workers and power.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher capital–output ratio = less output per unit of investment; 2 marks: reasons for low productivity of investment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether raising the investment share of GDP is the best way for Country B to raise its growth rate.
parts.answer: For: more investment raises capacity (LRAS), and with an unchanged ratio, raising investment to 36 % would give 6 % growth. Against: the problem is efficiency of investment, not its quantity; higher investment requires more saving or foreign borrowing (opportunity cost of consumption, debt); diminishing returns. Alternatives: improve the efficiency of investment (governance, competition, better project selection), education and training, technology adoption, reducing energy shortages. Judgement: improving the productivity of investment may give more growth for less sacrifice; the formula is a simplification (Harrod–Domar) that ignores technology and human capital.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks: analysis for raising investment; up to 3 marks: limitations and alternatives; up to 2 marks: justified conclusion that comments on the simplifying assumptions of the formula.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an open economy with a government, the marginal propensity to save is 0.1, the marginal rate of tax is 0.15 and the marginal propensity to import is 0.25 (all measured as fractions of national income). Government spending rises by $30 billion. What is the final increase in national income?
A $60 billion
B $120 billion
C $300 billion
D $40 billion
parts.answer: A $60 billion
parts.working: Multiplier = 1 ÷ (MPS + MRT + MPM) = 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2; increase in income = 2 × $30 billion = $60 billion. C uses only the MPS (multiplier 10), ignoring taxes and imports.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between injections and withdrawals in the circular flow of income of an open economy with a government sector.
parts.answer: Injections are additions of spending to the circular flow that do not come from domestic households' income: investment, government spending and exports. Withdrawals (leakages) are parts of income not passed on as spending on domestic output: saving, taxation and imports.
parts.working: 1 mark: injections named (I, G, X); 1 mark: withdrawals named (S, T, M); 1 mark: explanation — injections add to spending on domestic output, withdrawals remove income from the flow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what happens to national income when injections are greater than withdrawals.
parts.answer: Spending on domestic output exceeds the income leaking out, so firms see stocks fall and raise output; incomes rise, and as income rises withdrawals rise too, until withdrawals equal injections at a new, higher equilibrium income.
parts.working: 1 mark: total spending/demand exceeds output, stocks fall; 1 mark: output and income rise (multiplier process); 1 mark: withdrawals rise with income until W = J at a new equilibrium.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a withdrawal (leakage) from the circular flow of income?
A spending by foreign residents on the country's exports
B government spending on new hospitals
C spending by households on imported goods
D spending by firms on new machinery
parts.answer: C spending by households on imported goods
parts.working: Spending on imports flows out of the domestic circular flow, so it is a withdrawal. A, B and D are injections (exports, government spending and investment).

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the three withdrawals from the circular flow of income in an open economy with a government, and explain how each is likely to change when national income rises.
parts.answer: Saving, taxation and imports. All rise when income rises: households save more out of higher income; income tax and spending taxes yield more revenue; households and firms buy more imported goods.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies all three; 1 mark each for explaining how saving, taxation and imports change with income.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps
practice.stem: Data (invented for practice), in $ billion for one period: national income 1200; saving 120; taxation 180; imports 60; investment 90; government spending 150; exports 90.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate total injections and total withdrawals in the period.
parts.answer: Injections = 330 billion; withdrawals = 360 billion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain what is likely to happen to national income in the next period.
parts.answer: National income will fall, because withdrawals (360) exceed injections (330), so spending on domestic output is less than income/output; firms cut production until withdrawals fall to equal injections.
parts.working: 1 mark: income falls; 1 mark: because W > J, so aggregate demand is less than output.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the role of the financial sector in linking saving and investment in the circular flow.
parts.answer: Households' savings are deposited with banks and other financial institutions, which lend them to firms for investment; if the financial sector channels saving into investment efficiently, the saving withdrawal is offset by an investment injection; the interest rate helps balance them.
parts.working: 1 mark: savings held by banks/financial institutions; 1 mark: lent to firms (and government) for investment; 1 mark: links withdrawal (S) to injection (I); if saving is not lent on, income falls.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps
practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): When national income in a country rose by $400 billion, households' spending on domestically produced goods rose by $240 billion. The government now plans to spend an extra $12 billion on rural roads.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the marginal propensity to consume domestically produced goods.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of the multiplier and the eventual increase in national income caused by the extra government spending.
parts.answer: Multiplier 2.5; national income rises by $30 billion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the actual increase in national income may be smaller than this.
parts.answer: For example: the government may borrow to finance the spending, raising interest rates and crowding out private investment; if the economy is near full capacity, prices rise rather than output; time lags mean the full effect takes years; withdrawals (e.g. saving) may rise if confidence is low; extra spending may go to imports.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for identification, 1 mark for explaining how it reduces the final rise in real income.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether an economy with a high marginal propensity to import should rely on increasing exports, rather than increasing government spending, to raise its national income.
parts.answer: A high marginal propensity to import reduces the multiplier for any injection, so it does not by itself favour exports over government spending; but exports bring foreign currency and improve the current account, while government spending leaks heavily into imports. Exports depend on world demand and competitiveness, which the government cannot easily control, so a mix is likely to be best.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: open-economy circular flow; both exports and government spending are injections with the same multiplier; high MPM → small multiplier → limited effect of either; extra government spending with a high MPM worsens the current account; export-led growth earns foreign exchange, may attract investment and economies of scale; methods to raise exports (depreciation, supply-side policy, trade agreements). Evaluation: exports depend on trading partners' growth, exchange rates and protectionism; government spending can be targeted at domestic labour-intensive projects with low import content; spending on infrastructure may raise export capacity too; debt constraints; justified conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an economy, households spend 60 % of each extra dollar of income on domestically produced goods. Government spending rises by $40 billion. What is the eventual increase in national income?
A $16 billion
B $40 billion
C $66.7 billion
D $100 billion
parts.answer: D $100 billion
parts.working: The marginal propensity to withdraw is 1 − 0.6 = 0.4, so the multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5 and national income rises by 2.5 × 40 = $100 billion. C wrongly divides by 0.6 (40 ÷ 0.6); A multiplies by 0.4.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps
practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): in an economy, total planned withdrawals W = 0.25Y − 30 and total planned injections J = 120, where Y is national income and all values are in $ billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium level of national income.
parts.answer: $600 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Injections rise by $20 billion. Calculate the new equilibrium national income and the value of the multiplier.
parts.answer: $680 billion; multiplier 4.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Full-employment national income is $700 billion. Starting from the original equilibrium, calculate the increase in injections needed to reach it, and explain what kind of output gap exists at the original equilibrium.
parts.answer: Increase of $25 billion needed; there is a negative (deflationary) output gap of $100 billion – actual income is below full-employment income, so there is unemployment and spare capacity.
parts.working: 1 mark: (700 − 600) × 0.25 = 25 (or 100 ÷ 4); 1 mark: negative/deflationary gap; 1 mark: explanation – spare capacity/unemployment.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps
practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): at the end of Year 1, a country's potential output index was 100 and actual output index was 99 (an output gap of −1 % of potential). During Year 2, potential output grew by 3.5 % and actual output grew by 1.5 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output gap at the end of Year 2 as a percentage of potential output. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two likely consequences of the change in the output gap between Year 1 and Year 2.
parts.answer: The negative gap widened from −1 % to about −2.9 %: cyclical unemployment rises as firms need fewer workers; inflationary pressure falls (disinflation, possibly deflation) because of spare capacity; firms delay investment; tax revenues fall and benefit spending rises, widening the budget deficit.
parts.working: For each of two consequences: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation linked to the wider gap.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an economy, investment is $120 billion, government spending is $200 billion and exports are $180 billion; these do not depend on income. Saving, taxes and imports are 15 %, 20 % and 15 % of national income respectively. Exports then rise by $50 billion. What is the new equilibrium level of national income?
A $1100 billion
B $1050 billion
C $1000 billion
D $1333 billion
parts.answer: A $1100 billion
parts.working: Equilibrium where injections = withdrawals: 500 = 0.5Y, so Y = 1000. After exports rise, 550 = 0.5Y, so Y = 1100. B adds only the $50 billion rise in exports and ignores the multiplier of 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps
practice.stem:
Table 11: Real GDP of Country D ($ billion; data invented for practice)
Year 1: actual 820; potential 850
Year 2: actual 860; potential 870
Year 3: actual 905; potential 890
Year 4: actual 930; potential 910

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output gap as a percentage of potential output for each year. Give your answers to two decimal places.
parts.working: Output gap = (actual − potential) ÷ potential × 100. Year 1: (820 − 850) ÷ 850 × 100 = −3.53 %; Year 2: (860 − 870) ÷ 870 × 100 = −1.15 %; Year 3: (905 − 890) ÷ 890 × 100 = 1.69 %; Year 4: (930 − 910) ÷ 910 × 100 = 2.20 %. 3 marks all four correct; 2 marks for three; 1 mark for correct method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the first year in which there was an inflationary (positive) output gap and explain why inflation might rise in that year.
parts.answer: Year 3: actual output exceeded potential output, so firms were working beyond normal capacity; labour and resource shortages push up wages and costs and demand exceeds supply, so prices rise (demand-pull).
parts.working: 1 mark: Year 3; 1 mark: explanation — output above capacity → shortages, overtime, rising wages/costs → inflation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it is difficult for a government to measure the output gap accurately.
parts.answer: Potential output cannot be observed directly; it must be estimated from trends in productivity, the labour force and capital, which change with technology and shocks; GDP data are revised and the informal economy is not fully measured, so the estimated gap may even have the wrong sign.
parts.working: 1 mark: potential output is not observable/estimated; 1 mark: depends on assumptions about productivity, labour force, natural rate of unemployment; 1 mark: data revisions/informal sector/time lags in data.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that, because of the multiplier, an increase in government spending will always be an effective way to end a recession.
parts.answer: The multiplier means extra government spending raises national income by more than the initial injection, which can help end a recession with spare capacity; but the size of the multiplier may be small in an open economy with high taxes and imports, and crowding out, time lags, debt and confidence can weaken the effect. 'Always' is too strong.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: circular flow, injections and withdrawals; multiplier = 1 ÷ (MPS + MRT + MPM), numerical illustration; AD shifts right, closing a negative output gap; accelerator effects may add investment. Evaluation: a small multiplier in very open economies (high MPM) or with high tax rates; crowding out of private investment if borrowing raises interest rates; Ricardian equivalence (households save for expected future taxes); time lags in planning projects; quality of spending (productive vs wasteful); debt sustainability and lender confidence; effectiveness greater in a deep recession with low interest rates; justified conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether policy-makers should respond differently to a negative output gap caused by a fall in aggregate demand and one caused by an adverse supply shock.
parts.answer: Demand-caused gap: AD shifts left, output and inflation both fall; expansionary fiscal or monetary policy can close the gap with little inflation cost; multiplier effects; risk of time lags and debt. Supply shock (e.g. oil or energy price rise): SRAS shifts left, output falls while inflation rises (stagflation); stimulating AD closes the output gap but adds to inflation and may de-anchor expectations; tightening fights inflation but deepens the recession; supply-side responses (energy diversification, targeted support) work slowly. Also: a permanent supply shock may lower potential output, so the measured gap is smaller than it looks; output gaps are hard to estimate in real time. Judgement: the cause matters for the policy mix – demand management suits demand shocks, while supply shocks need a cautious, targeted response that protects credibility; but in practice causes overlap and accurate measurement is difficult.
parts.working: Top band: accurate definitions, a correct, fully explained diagram where relevant, developed chains of analysis on more than one side, and evaluation that weighs the arguments and reaches a justified conclusion that answers the question; mid band: sound but partly developed analysis with limited evaluation; low band: descriptive points or assertion. Expect AD/AS diagrams described for both cases, analysis of the policy trade-offs, consideration of measurement problems and expectations, and a justified conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps
practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): a government increases spending on road building by $50 billion. In every round, households spend 60 % of any extra income on domestically produced goods; the rest is saved, taxed or spent on imports.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in spending in each of the first four rounds, and the total increase in income after four rounds.
parts.answer: Rounds: $50 bn, $30 bn, $18 bn, $10.8 bn; total after four rounds $108.8 bn.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the final increase in national income and the percentage of it reached after four rounds. Give the percentage to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate the usefulness of the multiplier when a government is deciding how much to increase its spending.
parts.answer: Useful: shows that the final rise in income is a multiple of the injection, so a smaller injection may be needed; helps estimate the effect on unemployment and tax revenue. Limits: the size of the multiplier is uncertain (MPC, import propensity and tax rates change, confidence effects); time lags – each round takes time, so the full effect may arrive when the economy has already recovered; crowding out if interest rates rise or the economy is near full capacity (prices rather than output rise); Ricardian-type saving responses. Judgement: a useful guide to direction and rough size but not a precise forecast.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks: usefulness; up to 2 marks: limitations; up to 2 marks: justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a country, the working-age population is 140 million, the labour force is 84 million and 78.12 million people are employed. What are the unemployment rate and the labour force participation rate?
A unemployment rate 7.0 %, participation rate 60.0 %
B unemployment rate 4.2 %, participation rate 60.0 %
C unemployment rate 7.0 %, participation rate 55.8 %
D unemployment rate 4.2 %, participation rate 55.8 %
parts.answer: A unemployment rate 7.0 %, participation rate 60.0 %
parts.working: Unemployed = 84 − 78.12 = 5.88 million; unemployment rate = 5.88 ÷ 84 × 100 = 7.0 % (of the labour force, not the working-age population, which gives 4.2 % in B). Participation rate = 84 ÷ 140 × 100 = 60.0 %.

practice.stem: A textile region in a South Asian country has lost many jobs as factories move to automated production, while technology firms in the capital report shortages of programmers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between frictional unemployment and structural unemployment.
parts.answer: Frictional unemployment is short-term unemployment while people move between jobs or search for their first job; structural unemployment is longer-term unemployment caused by a mismatch between the skills or location of workers and the available jobs, after changes in the structure of the economy (e.g. decline of an industry).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the natural rate of unemployment and one factor that could reduce it.
parts.answer: The natural rate is the level of unemployment that exists when the labour market is in equilibrium, with no demand-deficient unemployment — made up of frictional and structural unemployment; it can be reduced by, for example, better job-matching information, training and retraining schemes, or improved geographical mobility.
parts.working: 1 mark: unemployment at labour market equilibrium/when AD is at full employment level/no cyclical unemployment; 1 mark: consists of frictional + structural (voluntary) unemployment; 1 mark: one valid supply-side factor that reduces it, with brief reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between the labour force survey method and the claimant count method of measuring unemployment.
parts.answer: Labour force survey: a sample of households is asked whether people are without work, actively seeking and available for work (international definition); claimant count: the number of people receiving unemployment-related benefits. The survey includes those not entitled to benefits; the claimant count is cheaper and quicker but depends on benefit rules and excludes many unemployed people.
parts.working: 1 mark: survey method; 1 mark: claimant count; 1 mark each for up to two valid differences or comparative points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by demand-deficient (cyclical) unemployment.
parts.answer: Unemployment caused by a fall in aggregate demand, e.g. in a recession: firms produce less and need fewer workers.
parts.working: 1 mark: caused by insufficient AD; 1 mark: linked to the economic cycle/derived demand for labour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one policy that could reduce demand-deficient unemployment.
parts.answer: Expansionary fiscal policy (more government spending or lower taxes) or lower interest rates raises AD, so firms increase output and hire more workers.
parts.working: 1 mark: policy; 1 mark: explanation via AD and derived demand.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): a country's working-age population is 120 million. The labour force participation rate is 55 % and the unemployment rate is 7 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the size of the labour force, the number unemployed and the number employed, in millions.
parts.answer: Labour force 66 million; unemployed 4.62 million; employed 61.38 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the employment rate (employed as a percentage of the working-age population). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether reducing structural unemployment should be a higher priority for a government than reducing demand-deficient (cyclical) unemployment.
parts.answer: Structural unemployment is long-lasting and lowers potential output, so reducing it raises the natural rate of employment permanently; cyclical unemployment is temporary but can be large in a recession and can turn into structural unemployment through hysteresis. The priority depends on which type dominates at the time.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: causes of each type (mismatch of skills/location from structural change, automation, globalisation vs deficient AD in a downturn); costs: lost output, lower tax revenue, higher benefit spending, social costs, deskilling; policies: supply-side (training, mobility, information) for structural vs fiscal and monetary expansion for cyclical; diagrams (labour market or AD/AS). Evaluation: in a deep recession cyclical unemployment is the main problem and quick to fix with demand policies; structural policies are slow and costly; but persistent structural unemployment harms growth and inequality; hysteresis links the two; context of countries with large informal sectors; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would reduce a country's measured unemployment rate even if no new jobs were created?
A Unemployed workers become discouraged, stop looking for work and leave the labour force.
B More school-leavers start looking for work.
C The state pension age is raised, so more older people remain in the labour force seeking work.
D Labour productivity falls.
parts.answer: A Unemployed workers become discouraged, stop looking for work and leave the labour force.
parts.working: The unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force. Discouraged workers leave both the count of unemployed and the labour force, so the rate falls without any job creation. B and C add job seekers, raising the rate; D does not directly change the count.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between voluntary and involuntary unemployment.
parts.answer: Voluntary: people choose not to accept jobs available at the current wage (e.g. searching for a better job, or benefits make work not worthwhile); involuntary: people are willing to work at the current wage but cannot find a job.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a high replacement ratio of unemployment benefits can increase voluntary unemployment.
parts.answer: The replacement ratio is benefit income as a proportion of income in work; when it is high, the gain from taking a job is small (especially after travel costs and tax), so some people stay unemployed longer or search longer, raising voluntary/frictional unemployment and the natural rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition of replacement ratio; 1 mark: small financial gain from work; 1 mark: longer search/higher natural rate.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): in a country, the unemployment rate is 11.2 % for people aged 15–24 and 4.8 % for people aged 25–54.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times higher the unemployment rate for 15–24 year-olds is than for 25–54 year-olds. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 2.33 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain three reasons why unemployment is usually higher among young people.
parts.answer: Any three: lack of experience/skills, so employers prefer older workers; frictional unemployment as they search for a first job and change jobs often; skills mismatch between education and jobs; minimum wage may exceed their productivity; 'last in, first out' in a downturn.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why long spells of youth unemployment may raise the natural rate of unemployment in the future (hysteresis).
parts.answer: Young people out of work lose skills and work habits and do not gain experience; employers see long gaps on CVs as a bad signal; some become discouraged; so they remain less employable even when demand recovers, raising structural unemployment and the natural rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: loss of skills/experience; 1 mark: employer perceptions/discouragement; 1 mark: links to higher natural rate even after recovery.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): a country has 2 million unemployed people. If employed, each would produce output worth $9 000 a year on average.
