Each unemployed person receives $1 200 a year in benefits, and the government would have collected tax equal to 20 % of the value of the lost output.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of output lost each year because of unemployment, in $ billion.
parts.answer: $18 billion
parts.working: 2 million × $9 000 = $18 billion (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total yearly cost to the government budget of unemployment benefits plus lost tax revenue.
parts.answer: $6 billion
parts.working: M1: benefits 2 million × 1 200 = $2.4 bn; lost tax 20 % × 18 = $3.6 bn; A1: total $6 bn.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two costs of unemployment that are not included in these figures.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: loss of skills and human capital (hysteresis); poverty, ill-health and stress for families; crime and social unrest; greater inequality; lower investment because firms expect weak demand.
parts.working: For each: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem:
Table 12: Inflation and unemployment in Country E (data invented for practice)
Year 1: inflation 4.1 %; unemployment 8.2 %
Year 2: inflation 5.3 %; unemployment 6.9 %
Year 3: inflation 6.8 %; unemployment 5.6 %
Year 4: inflation 9.5 %; unemployment 5.4 %
Year 5: inflation 12.0 %; unemployment 5.5 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between inflation and unemployment shown in the data.
parts.answer: From Year 1 to Year 3 higher inflation is associated with lower unemployment (an inverse relationship, as in the short-run Phillips curve); from Year 3 to Year 5 inflation keeps rising sharply while unemployment stays at about 5.5 %.
parts.working: 1 mark: inverse relationship in Years 1–3 (inflation 4.1 → 6.8 %, unemployment 8.2 → 5.6 %); 1 mark: in Years 3–5 unemployment stops falling/stays around 5.4–5.6 % while inflation rises to 12.0 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the expectations-augmented Phillips curve, explain the pattern in Years 3 to 5.
parts.answer: Unemployment has reached the natural rate (about 5.5 %). Workers now expect higher inflation and demand higher money wages, so the short-run Phillips curve shifts up; further rises in AD only increase inflation, and unemployment returns to the natural rate — the long-run Phillips curve is vertical.
parts.working: 1 mark: natural rate of unemployment around 5.5 %; 1 mark: inflation expectations adjust upwards/workers bargain for higher money wages; 1 mark: short-run Phillips curve shifts upwards; 1 mark: long-run Phillips curve vertical at the natural rate — no lasting trade-off.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that there is a trade-off between unemployment and inflation in the long run.
parts.answer: The original Phillips curve suggested a stable trade-off, but the expectations-augmented view argues that in the long run unemployment returns to the natural rate whatever the inflation rate, so there is no long-run trade-off; however, hysteresis, very low inflation and wage rigidity mean the long-run curve may not be perfectly vertical.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: original Phillips curve (inverse relationship, demand-pull explanation); expectations-augmented Phillips curve: short-run trade-off, adaptive expectations, shifting short-run curves, vertical long-run Phillips curve at the natural rate (NAIRU); rational expectations view (no trade-off even in the short run if policy is anticipated); stagflation evidence in the 1970s. Evaluation: hysteresis — long recessions raise the natural rate; at very low inflation, downward wage rigidity may create a trade-off; flattening of the Phillips curve in recent decades; supply shocks shift curves; implications for policy (supply-side policy to lower the natural rate); justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that technological change will inevitably increase unemployment in the long run.
parts.answer: For: automation and artificial intelligence replace routine manual and clerical jobs; structural unemployment where workers' skills do not match new jobs; occupational and geographical immobility; regions dependent on declining industries; in lower-income countries, labour-intensive manufacturing may shrink. Against: technology raises productivity, lowers costs and prices, raises real incomes and creates demand for new goods and services and new occupations; historically employment has risen despite major technological change (the 'lump of labour' fallacy); complements as well as substitutes for labour; long-run unemployment depends on the natural rate, which depends on labour-market flexibility and training. Evaluation: transition costs can be large and long-lasting for some groups; outcome depends on the speed of change, education and retraining, social safety nets and labour-market policies; 'inevitably' is too strong.
parts.working: Top band: accurate definitions, a correct, fully explained diagram where relevant, developed chains of analysis on more than one side, and evaluation that weighs the arguments and reaches a justified conclusion that answers the question; mid band: sound but partly developed analysis with limited evaluation; low band: descriptive points or assertion. Expect: types of unemployment (structural, frictional) explained, LRAS/productivity analysis, labour demand as derived demand, historical/real-world awareness, and a justified conclusion on 'inevitably'.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): at the start of a year a country had 3.0 million unemployed people and a labour force of 40.0 million. During the year 1.2 million people became unemployed, 0.9 million unemployed people found jobs and 0.2 million unemployed people stopped looking for work and left the labour force. At the end of the year the labour force was 40.2 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of unemployed people at the end of the year.
parts.answer: 3.1 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the unemployment rate at the start and at the end of the year. Give the end-of-year rate to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Start 7.5 %; end 7.71 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why looking at the flows into and out of unemployment gives more information than looking at the unemployment rate alone.
parts.answer: The stock changed only slightly, but 1.2 million people became unemployed and 1.1 million left unemployment; high flows with short spells suggest frictional unemployment in a dynamic labour market, while low flows with a stable stock suggest long-term (structural) unemployment; flows also show how many leave the labour force (discouraged workers) rather than find jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark: large flows hidden by small change in stock; 1 mark: duration/type of unemployment; 1 mark: outflows to inactivity vs jobs.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate whether a stable unemployment rate means that a country's labour market is working well.
parts.answer: Possibly well: stable rate near the natural rate, steady flows into jobs, low long-term unemployment. Possibly not: stable rate may hide rising long-term unemployment, discouraged workers leaving the labour force, underemployment (part-time or informal work), falling participation, regional or youth differences; a stable but high rate signals structural problems. Judgement: need further data on duration, participation and underemployment before concluding.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks: why stability may be good; up to 2 marks: what it may hide; up to 2 marks: justified conclusion.

practice.stem:
Data (invented for practice): a country's labour force is 30 million in both years.
Year 1: unemployment rate 9 %; 20 % of the unemployed had been out of work for more than 12 months
Year 5: unemployment rate 7 %; 38 % of the unemployed had been out of work for more than 12 months

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of long-term unemployed people in Year 1 and in Year 5, and the percentage change. Give the percentage to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Year 1: 540 000; Year 5: 798 000; an increase of 47.8 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rise in long-term unemployment may mean that the natural rate of unemployment has increased.
parts.answer: Long-term unemployed lose skills and motivation and face employer discrimination, so they no longer compete effectively for jobs; they do not restrain wage demands, so inflation can rise at a higher unemployment rate (higher NAIRU); this is hysteresis – a temporary downturn has a lasting effect.
parts.working: 1 mark: loss of employability; 1 mark: less downward pressure on wages/NAIRU; 1 mark: hysteresis explained.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate the policies a government could use to reduce long-term unemployment.
parts.answer: Supply-side: retraining and education matched to vacancies; job-search support and subsidised employment (wage subsidies for hiring the long-term unemployed); relocation help; reforms to benefits so work pays. Demand-side: keeping AD high helps, but long-term unemployed may not be hired without other support. Evaluation: costs and time lags; deadweight (subsidies paid for people who would be hired anyway); effectiveness depends on cause (skills mismatch vs regional decline); the evidence that the overall rate fell suggests AD is not the main problem. Judgement: targeted active labour-market policies are likely to be most effective.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks: analysis of supply-side/active policies; up to 2 marks: role and limits of demand-side policy; up to 3 marks: evaluation and justified conclusion using the data.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an open economy with a government, the marginal propensity to save is 0.1, the marginal tax rate is 0.15 and the marginal propensity to import is 0.25. Government spending rises by $20bn. By how much will national income eventually rise?
A $20bn
B $40bn
C $80bn
D $200bn
parts.answer: B $40bn
parts.working: Multiplier = 1 ÷ (MPS + MPT + MPM) = 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2. ΔY = 2 × 20 = $40bn. D uses only the MPS (1 ÷ 0.1 = 10), ignoring taxes and imports.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy
practice.stem: Invented data: an economy's actual real GDP is $480bn and its potential real GDP is $520bn. The marginal propensity to withdraw (MPS + MPT + MPM) is 0.4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output gap and state whether it is positive or negative.
parts.answer: $40bn; negative
parts.working: 1 480 − 520 = −40: negative output gap of $40bn.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of the multiplier.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the increase in government spending needed to close the output gap.
parts.answer: $16bn

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain one reason why the increase you calculated in (c) might not close the output gap.
parts.answer: e.g. the multiplier is estimated and may be smaller (higher leakages to imports or saving); crowding out; time lags; private spending may fall because of low confidence; potential output is estimated inaccurately.
parts.working: 1 reason; 1 explained.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by quantitative easing and how it may increase aggregate demand.
parts.answer: The central bank creates money electronically to buy government bonds and other assets from banks and financial institutions. This raises bond prices, lowers long-term interest rates, increases banks' reserves and wealth, encouraging lending, borrowing, consumption and investment.
parts.working: 1 central bank creates new money; 1 buys bonds/financial assets; 1 lowers long-term interest rates/raises asset prices; 1 more borrowing and spending → AD rises.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one risk of using quantitative easing.
parts.answer: e.g. inflation if too much money is created; asset-price bubbles that increase wealth inequality; banks may hoard reserves so little effect; currency depreciation.
parts.working: 1 risk; 1 explained.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy
practice.stem: Invented data: in one year a government spends Rs 9.2 trillion and receives Rs 7.4 trillion in tax revenue. GDP is Rs 106 trillion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budget deficit in Rs trillion and as a percentage of GDP, to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Rs 1.8 trillion; 1.7% of GDP

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the budget deficit is likely to change automatically if the economy enters a recession.
parts.answer: It will increase: lower incomes and spending reduce tax revenue, and spending on transfer payments rises, without any change in policy.
parts.working: 1 tax revenue falls; 1 government spending on benefits/transfers rises; 1 so the deficit increases (cyclical deficit).

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy
practice.stem: Invented data. The central bank cuts its policy rate from 10% to 7%, and banks pass the full cut on to borrowers. A household has a variable-rate loan of Rs 5,000,000 on which it pays interest only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the household's annual interest payments before and after the cut, and the amount saved each year.
parts.answer: Rs 500,000 → Rs 350,000; saving Rs 150,000 a year

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a cut in interest rates is transmitted to aggregate demand.
parts.answer: Lower interest payments raise disposable income of borrowers (as in (a)); borrowing for consumer durables and investment becomes cheaper; saving is less attractive; asset prices rise (wealth effect); the currency may depreciate, raising net exports. C, I and (X − M) rise, so AD rises.
parts.working: 1 each for up to four channels, linked to components of AD.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between market-based and interventionist supply-side policies, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: Market-based: reduce government involvement so markets work better, e.g. privatisation, deregulation, lower income tax, reform of trade unions. Interventionist: the government acts directly to improve supply, e.g. spending on education/training, infrastructure, research subsidies.
parts.working: 1 each definition; 1 each example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a market-based supply-side policy might increase income inequality.
parts.answer: e.g. cutting the top rate of income tax or welfare benefits mainly benefits high earners and/or reduces the incomes of the poor.
parts.working: 1 policy; 1 effect on distribution.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two types of time lag that reduce the effectiveness of macroeconomic policy.
parts.answer: Recognition lag: data take time to collect and reveal the problem. Implementation (decision) lag: time to agree and introduce the policy. Effect lag: time before the policy changes spending and output.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for each of two lags.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the implementation lag is usually shorter for monetary policy than for fiscal policy.
parts.answer: An independent central bank can change interest rates at its next meeting, whereas tax and spending changes need a budget and approval by parliament.
parts.working: 1 central bank decides quickly; 1 fiscal changes need legislative approval.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an economy with high inflation and rising unemployment is difficult to manage with demand-side policy alone.
parts.answer: Tightening AD reduces inflation but worsens unemployment; expanding AD reduces unemployment but adds to inflation; the problem may come from a supply shock, which demand policy cannot remove.
parts.working: 1 contractionary effect; 1 expansionary effect; 1 conflict; 1 supply-side cause.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how combining tight monetary policy with supply-side policy could help.
parts.answer: Tight monetary policy controls inflation in the short run; supply-side policy shifts LRAS right, raising output and employment without adding to inflation over time.
parts.working: 1 role of each policy; 1 combined effect.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which situation is a cut in interest rates least likely to raise aggregate demand?
A Interest rates are already close to zero and households and firms expect prices to fall.
B Firms have strong business confidence and many profitable projects.
C Households have large variable-rate mortgages.
D The exchange rate is floating and exports are price elastic.
parts.answer: A Interest rates are already close to zero and households and firms expect prices to fall.
parts.working: Near-zero rates with deflationary expectations is a liquidity trap: people hold extra money rather than spend it, and real interest rates stay high, so monetary policy has little effect. B, C and D are conditions in which a rate cut works strongly (investment, disposable income, depreciation).

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text:
According to the Laffer curve, which statement is correct?
A Any cut in the income tax rate will raise tax revenue.
B Tax revenue is highest when the tax rate is 100%.
C If the tax rate is above the revenue-maximising rate, a cut in the rate can increase tax revenue.
D Tax revenue rises at a constant rate as the tax rate rises.
parts.answer: C If the tax rate is above the revenue-maximising rate, a cut in the rate can increase tax revenue.
parts.working: The Laffer curve shows revenue rising and then falling as the rate rises, because high rates discourage work and encourage avoidance. Only above the revenue-maximising rate does a cut raise revenue. A is the common misreading: below that rate a cut reduces revenue.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two supply-side policies that could reduce the natural rate of unemployment.
parts.answer: Any two: training and education (reduce skills mismatch/structural unemployment); better job-matching information and job centres (reduce frictional unemployment); reform of benefits to strengthen incentives to work; relocation grants or housing reforms to raise geographical mobility; reducing trade union power/labour market flexibility.
parts.working: Up to 2 each: policy identified + how it reduces frictional or structural unemployment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider why the effects of these policies may take a long time to appear.
parts.answer: Training and education take years to raise skills; workers must find and move to new jobs; firms need time to adjust; policies must be funded and implemented; benefit reforms may face resistance.
parts.working: 1 time lag reason; 1 explained; 1 judgement (e.g. effect depends on the type of unemployment and policy design).

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy
practice.stem:
Invented data for Country M over one year:
Central bank policy rate: 12% → 15%
Inflation rate: 14% → 9%
Real GDP growth: 4.0% → 1.5%
The currency appreciated by 6% against the US dollar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the approximation real interest rate = nominal rate − inflation, calculate the real interest rate at the start and at the end of the period.
parts.answer: Start: -2%; end: 6%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a rise in interest rates can reduce the rate of inflation.
parts.answer: Higher borrowing costs and saving incentive reduce consumption and investment → AD falls; appreciation of the currency makes imports cheaper and exports dearer, lowering imported inflation and AD.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for two channels identified (spending/borrowing, exchange rate, asset prices/expectations); 1 for explanation linking to lower AD or lower costs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the data show that monetary policy was effective.
parts.answer: Inflation fell sharply (14% → 9%) and the currency appreciated, consistent with the policy working; but growth slowed from 4% to 1.5%, inflation remained above most targets, and other factors (falling world prices) may explain the fall.
parts.working: 1 evidence of success; 1 cost/limitation (lower growth, still high inflation); 1 other factors/time lags, judgement.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how progressive income taxes and unemployment benefits act as automatic stabilisers.
parts.answer: In a downturn incomes fall, so tax revenue falls more than proportionately and benefit payments rise automatically, cushioning disposable income and AD; in a boom tax revenue rises and benefits fall, restraining AD. No new decision is needed.
parts.working: 1 recession: tax revenue falls; 1 benefit spending rises → supports AD; 1 boom: opposite effect dampens AD; 1 automatic, without discretionary changes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether automatic stabilisers are likely to be effective in an economy with a large informal sector.
parts.answer: Less effective: few workers pay income tax or receive unemployment benefits, so revenue and transfers change little with the cycle; the stabilising effect is weak, so discretionary policy is needed. But indirect taxes still vary with spending and cash-transfer programmes may help.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): narrow tax base, low benefit coverage, small size of government; Consideration (1+): sales taxes, targeted transfers, judgement.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a cut in interest rates may affect the exchange rate and the current account of the balance of payments.
parts.answer: Lower rates reduce returns on deposits in the currency → hot money outflows → lower demand for the currency → depreciation; exports become cheaper and imports dearer, which may improve the current account (if Marshall–Lerner holds), but higher domestic spending also raises imports.
parts.working: 1 capital outflow/less demand for currency; 1 depreciation; 1 exports more price competitive, imports dearer; 1 net effect on current account depends on elasticities/higher income raising imports.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider why the effect of the interest rate cut on the current account may be small.
parts.answer: Demand for exports and imports may be price inelastic in the short run (J-curve); higher incomes from cheaper borrowing raise imports; other countries may also cut rates; exchange rates are affected by many other factors.
parts.working: 1 reason; 1 explained; 1 judgement/second reason.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which situation is an increase in government spending most likely to cause a large rise in real output?
A a large negative output gap, a high marginal propensity to consume and a low marginal propensity to import
B the economy is at full employment with a high marginal propensity to consume
C a large negative output gap and a very high marginal propensity to import
D households expect future tax rises to pay for the spending and save the extra income
parts.answer: A a large negative output gap, a high marginal propensity to consume and a low marginal propensity to import
parts.working: Spare capacity means extra demand raises output rather than prices, and low withdrawals give a large multiplier. B leads mainly to inflation; C leaks into imports; D describes Ricardian equivalence, which weakens the effect.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy
practice.stem: Invented model of a Laffer curve. The tax base is B = 2,000(1 − t) and tax revenue is R = t × B, where t is the tax rate (as a decimal) and R and B are in $bn.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate tax revenue at tax rates of 0.6 and 0.5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate tax revenue at tax rates of 0.3 and 0.25.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answers, explain why some economists support cutting tax rates and others oppose it.
parts.answer: Above the revenue-maximising rate (0.5), cutting the rate raises revenue and improves incentives (from 0.6 to 0.5 revenue rises by 20); below it, cuts lose revenue (0.3 to 0.25 loses 45). The disagreement is about where the economy actually is on the Laffer curve.
parts.working: 1 revenue rises at high rates; 1 revenue falls at low rates; 1 incentive effect; 1 uncertainty about position.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy
practice.stem: Invented data. A government increases spending by $20bn, financed by borrowing. Interest rates rise and private investment falls by $8bn. The multiplier is 2.5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the final change in national income with and without crowding out.
parts.answer: Without crowding out $50bn; with crowding out $30bn

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how government borrowing can crowd out private investment.
parts.answer: To sell more bonds the government must offer higher yields; interest rates rise across the economy; firms' cost of borrowing rises, so some investment projects become unprofitable.
parts.working: 1 more borrowing/bond supply; 1 interest rates rise; 1 private investment falls.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider when crowding out is likely to be small.
parts.answer: When there is a large output gap and spare savings (weak private demand), when the central bank keeps interest rates low, or when the spending raises business confidence or productivity (crowding in).
parts.working: Up to 2 conditions; 1 judgement.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a country with a fixed exchange rate and free movement of financial capital may be unable to use monetary policy to boost aggregate demand.
parts.answer: If the central bank cuts interest rates, capital flows out, putting downward pressure on the currency; to keep the peg it must buy its own currency with reserves, which shrinks the money supply and pushes rates back up; so interest rates must stay in line with the anchor country.
parts.working: 1 rate cut → outflows; 1 pressure on the peg; 1 intervention reverses the cut; 1 conclusion: monetary independence lost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether fiscal policy is likely to be more effective in this situation.
parts.answer: Yes: with interest rates fixed by the peg, extra government spending does not raise rates or cause appreciation, so crowding out is small; but fiscal policy is limited by debt levels and import leakages. Judgement.
parts.working: Up to 2 analysis; up to 2 evaluation.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy
practice.stem: Invented data. Commercial banks hold $50bn of reserves at the central bank. The central bank raises the minimum reserve ratio from 10% to 12.5%. Assume banks lend as much as they are allowed and all money is held as bank deposits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the credit multiplier and the maximum level of bank deposits at each reserve ratio.
parts.answer: 10%: multiplier 10, deposits $500bn; 12.5%: multiplier 8, deposits $400bn
parts.working: M1 multiplier = 1 ÷ reserve ratio; A1 10 and 500; A1 8 and 400.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in maximum deposits.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the actual fall in the money supply may be much smaller than calculated.
parts.answer: Banks may already hold excess reserves above the minimum; demand for loans may be weak anyway; people hold cash outside banks; banks may raise reserves from the central bank or abroad.
parts.working: 1 each for up to three points.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which situation is an increase in government spending financed by borrowing most likely to be offset by crowding out?
A The economy is near full capacity and private investment is very sensitive to interest rates.
B The economy has high unemployment and spare capacity.
C The marginal propensity to consume is high.
D The marginal propensity to import is low.
parts.answer: A The economy is near full capacity and private investment is very sensitive to interest rates.
parts.working: Government borrowing raises demand for loanable funds; with little spare capacity and interest-sensitive investment, higher interest rates (and real resource limits) displace private spending. B, C and D all make fiscal expansion more effective, not less.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy
practice.stem: The quantity theory of money: MV = PT. In an invented economy the money supply M is $400bn, the velocity of circulation V is 5 and the volume of transactions T is 1,000 billion units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average price level P.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The money supply rises by 10% while V and T are unchanged. Calculate the new price level and the percentage change.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Instead, the money supply rises by 10% while the volume of transactions rises by 4%. Calculate the percentage change in the price level, to one decimal place.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why monetarists assume that V and T are roughly constant in the short run, and one criticism of this assumption.
parts.answer: V depends on slowly changing payment habits and institutions; T is fixed at full-employment output (determined by supply-side factors). Critics: V changes, for example when people hoard money in recessions or with new payment technology, and output is not at full employment, so more money can raise T rather than P.
parts.working: 1 V determined by habits/institutions; 1 T determined by real factors/full employment; 1 valid criticism (unstable velocity, spare capacity, Keynesian view).

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether supply-side policies are more effective than demand-side policies in achieving sustained economic growth.
parts.answer: Supply-side policies raise productive capacity (LRAS), allowing non-inflationary sustained growth, but are slow, costly and uncertain. Demand-side policies act faster to close negative output gaps but cannot raise capacity and risk inflation or debt if used alone. Supply-side policies are more effective for sustained growth, with demand management needed for stability.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: AD/AS diagrams — AD shift (actual growth, inflation near capacity), LRAS shift (potential growth); market-based supply-side policies (tax cuts, deregulation, privatisation, labour market reform) and interventionist ones (education, infrastructure, R&D); fiscal and monetary demand management. Evaluation: time lags; cost to the budget; effectiveness depends on country (infrastructure gaps, governance); some policies (infrastructure spending) work on both sides; demand needed to use new capacity; inequality from market-based reforms. Judgement on 'more effective' for 'sustained' growth.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of monetary policy in controlling inflation in an economy that relies heavily on imported fuel and food.
parts.answer: Monetary policy reduces demand-pull inflation and can strengthen the currency to lower import prices, but much inflation in such an economy is cost-push from world prices and exchange-rate shocks; controlling it through interest rates requires large output losses. Effectiveness depends on the cause of inflation, credibility, transmission and fiscal discipline.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: transmission mechanism (interest rates → consumption, investment, exchange rate, expectations); AD/AS diagram; appreciation lowers import costs (SRAS shifts right). Evaluation: imported cost-push inflation (world oil and food prices) not caused by domestic demand; small formal credit market weakens transmission; fiscal dominance (large deficits financed by borrowing); central bank independence and credibility; time lags; conflict with growth and debt servicing; alternatives (supply-side, targeted subsidies, exchange-rate policy). Conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether an increase in government spending is an effective way to reduce unemployment during a recession.
parts.answer: Higher G raises AD with a multiplier effect, increasing output and cyclical employment; effectiveness depends on the size of the multiplier, spare capacity, crowding out, time lags, financing and the type of unemployment (it does little for structural unemployment).
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: AD/AS diagram with negative output gap; multiplier (k = 1/MPW) and derived demand for labour; reduces cyclical unemployment. Evaluation: size of multiplier (leakages to imports); crowding out (less likely in deep recession); time lags in planning projects; debt and future taxes, Ricardian equivalence; type of spending (infrastructure vs transfers); structural and frictional unemployment need supply-side policies; compare with monetary policy, especially if rates near zero. Conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy
practice.stem: Invented data. A government is choosing between raising its spending by $10bn and cutting income tax by $10bn. Households spend 0.8 of any increase in disposable income on consumption in the first round. The marginal propensity to withdraw from national income is 0.5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the eventual change in national income from the increase in government spending.
parts.working: M1 multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2. A1 10 × 2 = $20bn.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the eventual change in national income from the income tax cut.
parts.working: M1 initial rise in consumption = 0.8 × 10 = $8bn (the rest is saved or spent on imports, treated as already part of the withdrawals). A1 8 × 2 = $16bn.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the tax cut has a smaller effect than the same increase in government spending.
parts.answer: All of the extra government spending is an injection into the circular flow in the first round, whereas part of a tax cut is withdrawn before it is spent.
parts.working: 1 G adds directly to AD; 1 only part (MPC) of the tax cut is spent in the first round.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Consider one reason why the tax cut might have an even smaller effect than calculated.
parts.answer: e.g. households expect future tax rises to repay borrowing and save the tax cut (Ricardian equivalence); low confidence; much spending goes on imports; benefit mostly to high earners with low MPC.
parts.working: 1 reason; 1 explained.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A government raises its spending by $10bn. The multiplier is 2.5 and the government receives 20% of any increase in national income as tax. Once the multiplier process is complete, by how much has the budget deficit increased?
A $0, because the spending pays for itself
B $2.5bn
C $5bn
D $10bn
parts.answer: C $5bn
parts.working: National income rises by 2.5 × 10 = $25bn, so tax revenue rises by 0.2 × 25 = $5bn. The deficit rises by 10 − 5 = $5bn. D ignores the extra tax revenue; A assumes the extra tax equals the spending.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy
practice.stem: Invented data for a central bank. Year 1: policy rate 22%, inflation 25%. Year 2: policy rate 28%, expected inflation 20%. Exact real interest rate = (1 + nominal rate) ÷ (1 + inflation rate) − 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the exact formula, calculate the real interest rate in Year 1 and in Year 2, to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why monetary policy did little to reduce inflation in Year 1 even though the nominal interest rate was very high.
parts.answer: The real rate was negative: borrowers repaid less in real terms than they borrowed and savers lost purchasing power, so there was little incentive to cut spending or to save.
parts.working: 1 negative real rate; 1 no incentive to save; 1 borrowing still attractive.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why raising the real interest rate in Year 2 might still take time to reduce inflation.
parts.answer: Time lags (fixed-rate loans, planned investment); or inflation is caused by import prices/cost-push which interest rates affect only indirectly; or expectations adjust slowly.
parts.working: 1 reason; 1 explanation.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether monetary policy is more effective than fiscal policy in reducing a high rate of demand-pull inflation.
parts.answer: Monetary policy can be changed quickly by an independent central bank and works through several channels (borrowing, saving, exchange rate, expectations); fiscal tightening acts directly on AD but is politically difficult and slow. Effectiveness depends on credit use, debt levels, openness, credibility and the lags of each. Judgement.
parts.working: Knowledge, understanding and analysis (up to 14): demand-pull inflation with AD/AS; monetary transmission mechanism; contractionary fiscal policy and the multiplier; time lags; side effects on growth, exchange rate and investment. Evaluation (up to 6): size of interest-rate sensitivity; informal economy and low credit use; fiscal credibility and politics; combination of policies; reasoned conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether privatisation and deregulation are effective supply-side policies for a developing economy.
parts.answer: They can raise efficiency through competition and profit incentives, attract investment and reduce fiscal burdens of loss-making state firms; but private monopolies may exploit consumers, weak regulators allow abuse, essential services may become unaffordable, and job losses occur. Effectiveness depends on regulation, competition and governance. Judgement.
parts.working: Knowledge, understanding and analysis (up to 14): meaning of privatisation and deregulation; productive and dynamic efficiency; LRAS shift; effect on government finances; examples (telecoms, airlines, power). Evaluation (up to 6): natural monopoly and need for regulation; equity; sale price and corruption; short v long run; comparison with interventionist policies; conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Effectiveness of fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy
practice.stem: Invented data. During a recession a government increased its spending by $15bn. Economists estimated the marginal propensity to withdraw at 0.4. One year later, real national income was found to be $21bn higher than it would otherwise have been.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the predicted increase in national income using the multiplier, and the actual multiplier implied by the data.
parts.answer: Predicted $37.5bn; actual multiplier 1.4

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the actual increase in national income was smaller than predicted.
parts.answer: Crowding out through higher interest rates; households saved more because of uncertainty or expected tax rises; more spending leaked into imports; time lags (not all effects within a year); some spending raised prices rather than output.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for each of two developed reasons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether the fiscal stimulus was effective.
parts.answer: It did raise GDP by $21bn and probably saved jobs during a recession, but the effect was smaller than planned and added to government debt; full effects may come later; the counterfactual is unknown. Judgement using the data.
parts.working: Analysis up to 5; evaluation up to 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An economy is on its short-run Phillips curve. Aggregate demand rises. What is likely to happen in the short run?
A Unemployment falls and inflation rises.
B Unemployment rises and inflation rises.
C Unemployment falls and inflation falls.
D Unemployment and inflation are both unchanged.
parts.answer: A Unemployment falls and inflation rises.
parts.working: Higher AD raises output and employment but also bids up prices and wages, so the economy moves up and to the left along the short-run Phillips curve. B describes a shift (e.g. a supply shock), not a movement along the curve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four main macroeconomic objectives of a government.
parts.answer: Low and stable inflation; low unemployment; sustained economic growth; a sustainable current account position (balance of payments stability). Also accepted: fair distribution of income.
parts.working: 2 marks for four correct; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why using contractionary fiscal policy to reduce inflation may conflict with the objective of low unemployment.
parts.answer: Higher taxes or lower government spending reduce AD; firms sell less and need fewer workers (derived demand), so cyclical unemployment rises while inflation falls.
parts.working: 1 contractionary fiscal policy reduces AD; 1 lower inflation; 1 lower output → higher unemployment (movement along SRPC).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the natural rate of unemployment.
parts.answer: The rate of unemployment when the labour market is in equilibrium and inflation is stable: it consists of frictional and structural unemployment, with no cyclical unemployment.
parts.working: 1 equilibrium/stable inflation (NAIRU idea); 1 voluntary, frictional and structural unemployment only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two factors that determine the natural rate of unemployment.
parts.answer: Any two: occupational and geographical mobility of labour; level and availability of unemployment benefits; information about vacancies; trade union power and minimum wages; skills mismatch from structural change.
parts.working: Up to 2 each: factor identified + explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A central bank raises interest rates to reduce inflation. Which other objective is this most likely to conflict with in the short run?
A economic growth
B price stability
C a smaller current account deficit
D a stronger exchange rate
parts.answer: A economic growth
parts.working: Higher interest rates reduce consumption and investment, slowing growth. B is the aim of the policy; C and D are usually helped (lower imports; financial inflows).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why most governments aim for low and stable inflation rather than zero inflation.
parts.answer: Zero inflation risks slipping into deflation, which delays spending and raises real debt burdens; a little inflation allows real wages to adjust without nominal wage cuts and lets real interest rates go below zero; measured inflation overstates true inflation because of quality improvements.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for each of two developed reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why stability of inflation matters as well as its level.
parts.answer: Unpredictable inflation creates uncertainty, discouraging investment and long-term contracts, and redistributes income arbitrarily.
parts.working: 1 uncertainty; 1 effect.

practice.stem:
Invented data for a country.
Real GDP growth: actual 1.2%, target 4%
Inflation: actual 11%, target 5–7%
Unemployment: actual 8%, target 6%
Current account balance: actual −3.5% of GDP, target no worse than −2% of GDP

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which of the government's targets are being missed.
parts.answer: All four are missed: growth (1.2% v 4%), inflation (11% v 5–7%), unemployment (8% v 6%) and the current account (−3.5% v no worse than −2%).
parts.working: 2 for all four; 1 for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why using only interest rates is unlikely to achieve all of these targets at once.
parts.answer: Raising rates would help inflation and the current account but slow growth and raise unemployment; cutting rates would do the reverse. One instrument cannot hit several independent targets, so a mix of policies (e.g. supply-side) is needed.
parts.working: 1 effect of higher rates; 1 effect of lower rates; 1 conflict; 1 need for more instruments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how rapid economic growth may conflict with environmental sustainability.
parts.answer: More output uses more energy and raw materials, raising pollution and carbon emissions and depleting non-renewable resources; the costs fall on future generations (external costs).
parts.working: 1 resource use; 1 pollution/emissions; 1 depletion; 1 future costs/externalities.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one policy that could reduce this conflict.
parts.answer: e.g. a carbon tax or subsidies for renewable energy, which change relative prices and encourage cleaner production while output grows.
parts.working: 1 policy; 1 explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a conflict between macroeconomic objectives.
parts.answer: When a policy that helps achieve one objective makes another objective harder to achieve.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, with an example, how expansionary fiscal policy may help to achieve two objectives at the same time.
parts.answer: In a recession with spare capacity, higher government spending raises AD, so real output grows and unemployment falls together; inflation need not rise much because of the output gap.
parts.working: 1 context (spare capacity); 1 growth; 1 lower unemployment.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes the monetarist view of the long-run Phillips curve?
A It slopes downwards, giving a permanent trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
B It is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment, so trying to keep unemployment below that rate leads to accelerating inflation.
C It is horizontal, so unemployment can be cut without any inflation.
D It slopes upwards, so higher inflation always causes higher unemployment.
parts.answer: B It is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment, so trying to keep unemployment below that rate leads to accelerating inflation.
parts.working: When expectations adjust, workers demand higher money wages and unemployment returns to the natural rate at a higher inflation rate; the long-run curve is vertical. A describes only the short-run trade-off.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one period in the data that supports the existence of a short-run Phillips curve and one period that does not.
parts.answer: Supports: 2021 to 2023 (unemployment fell from 5.5% to 4.0% while inflation rose from 3.5% to 9.0%); also accept 2019–2020, 2020–2021 or 2024–2025. Does not support: 2023 to 2024 (unemployment and inflation both rose: 4.0% → 5.5% and 9.0% → 10.5%); also accept 2025–2026 (both fell).
parts.working: 1 supporting period with data; 1 non-supporting period with data; 1 explanation of the inverse relationship.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the short-run relationship between inflation and unemployment might break down.
parts.answer: Supply shocks (e.g. higher oil prices) shift SRAS left causing stagflation; inflation expectations rise so workers demand higher wages and the short-run Phillips curve shifts upward; changes in the natural rate.
parts.working: Up to 2 for supply shock explained; up to 2 for expectations shifting the curve (or another valid reason).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using a long-run Phillips curve, why monetarists believe that expansionary demand-side policy cannot permanently reduce unemployment below the natural rate.
parts.answer: Expansion moves the economy up the short-run curve: unemployment falls and inflation rises. Workers then expect higher inflation and demand higher money wages; real wages return to equilibrium and unemployment returns to the natural rate at a higher inflation rate. The long-run curve is vertical at the natural rate.
parts.working: 1 short-run movement along SRPC; 1 adaptive expectations/higher wage demands; 1 SRPC shifts up, unemployment returns to natural rate; 1 vertical LRPC → only higher inflation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider the implications of this view for a government that wants to reduce unemployment.
parts.answer: It should use supply-side policies to lower the natural rate rather than demand expansion; but Keynesians argue demand policy can reduce cyclical unemployment when there is a negative output gap, and expectations may adjust slowly.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): supply-side measures; risk of accelerating inflation; credibility of low-inflation policy. Consideration (1+): Keynesian view/hysteresis/slow adjustment; judgement.

practice.stem: Invented data. In an emerging economy, real GDP growth rose from 3% to 6% in two years, while the current account deficit rose from 1.5% to 4.7% of GDP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why rapid economic growth may cause the current account deficit to increase.
parts.answer: Higher incomes raise consumer spending, much of which goes on imports (high MPM); investment needs imported machinery and fuel; domestic producers may switch sales from export to home market; inflation may reduce competitiveness.
parts.working: 1 rising incomes; 1 higher imports (consumer goods, capital goods, energy); 1 further link (diverted exports, inflation, reduced competitiveness).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider which policies could reduce the conflict between growth and the current account.
parts.answer: Supply-side policies to raise productivity and export capacity, import substitution in energy, and policies to attract FDI into export industries allow growth without such a large deficit; demand restraint (higher interest rates, contractionary fiscal policy) reduces the deficit but at the cost of growth.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): expenditure-switching and supply-side measures explained; expenditure-reducing policies as trade-off. Consideration (1+): time lags, cost, retaliation, dependence on imported oil; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how supply-side policies can reduce the conflict between economic growth and low inflation.
parts.answer: They increase productive capacity (LRAS shifts right) and productivity, so real output can grow without AD outrunning capacity; unit costs fall, reducing cost pressures. Growth can therefore occur with stable or lower prices.
parts.working: 1 supply-side policy example (training, infrastructure, deregulation); 1 LRAS/productive capacity rises; 1 real output increases; 1 price level stable or lower (diagram may be used).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why supply-side policies may fail to remove this conflict.
parts.answer: e.g. long time lags, so in the short run demand-led growth still causes inflation; high cost to the budget; uncertain effectiveness; may be undermined by external cost shocks.
parts.working: 1 reason; 1 explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a depreciation of the currency intended to reduce a current account deficit may conflict with the objective of low inflation.
parts.answer: Depreciation makes imports dearer in domestic currency (imported fuel, food, raw materials) → cost-push inflation; exports become cheaper, so net exports and AD rise → demand-pull pressure; workers may demand higher wages.
parts.working: 1 imports more expensive; 1 higher costs → SRAS left → cost-push; 1 higher net exports raise AD → demand-pull; 1 second-round wage effects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether this conflict is likely to be serious for an economy that imports most of its energy.
parts.answer: Likely serious: energy demand is price inelastic, so the import bill rises and prices of transport and electricity increase throughout the economy; the current account may even worsen in the short run (J-curve). It is less serious if the central bank is credible, there is spare capacity, or world energy prices are falling.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): inelastic energy imports; wide pass-through; J-curve and Marshall–Lerner condition. Consideration (1+): credibility, spare capacity, offsetting policies; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sharp rise in world oil prices is most likely to cause which change for an oil-importing economy?
A the short-run Phillips curve shifts upwards, so inflation and unemployment rise together
B a movement down the short-run Phillips curve to lower inflation and higher unemployment
C a movement up the short-run Phillips curve to higher inflation and lower unemployment
D the long-run Phillips curve shifts to the left
parts.answer: A the short-run Phillips curve shifts upwards, so inflation and unemployment rise together
parts.working: A supply shock raises costs and inflation at every level of unemployment while reducing output, so the SRPC shifts up (stagflation). B and C describe demand changes.

practice.stem:
Invented data for a country:
Year A: inflation 9.5%, unemployment 6.0%
Year B: inflation 4.0%, unemployment 8.5%
Year C: inflation 12.0%, unemployment 5.0%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the misery index (inflation rate + unemployment rate) for each year.
parts.answer: Year A 15.5; Year B 12.5; Year C 17.0
parts.working: 2 all correct; 1 two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether the data are consistent with a short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
parts.answer: Yes: in Year C inflation is highest and unemployment lowest; in Year B inflation is lowest and unemployment highest, as the short-run Phillips curve predicts.
parts.working: 1 identifies inverse relationship; 2 data used for two years.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one limitation of the misery index as a measure of macroeconomic performance.
parts.answer: It gives equal weight to inflation and unemployment, ignores growth and the balance of payments, and ignores the distribution of costs.
parts.working: 1 limitation; 1 explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how keeping a fixed exchange rate can conflict with the objective of low unemployment.
parts.answer: To defend the peg against downward pressure, the central bank may raise interest rates or the government cut spending; this reduces AD and raises unemployment; it also cannot devalue to improve competitiveness.
parts.working: 1 pressure on peg; 1 higher rates/tight policy; 1 lower AD and jobs; 1 loss of exchange rate adjustment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a government should give up a fixed exchange rate to reduce unemployment.
parts.answer: Floating would free monetary policy and allow depreciation to boost exports; but the peg may give price stability and credibility, and a sudden fall could cause inflation and raise foreign-currency debt burdens. Judgement.
parts.working: Up to 2 analysis; up to 2 evaluation.

practice.stem: Invented data. Over two years a country's real GDP growth rose from 4% to 7% while its inflation rate rose from 5% to 12%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why rapid growth of real GDP above its trend rate can lead to rising inflation.
parts.answer: Growth above trend means AD is growing faster than productive capacity, closing the output gap; shortages of labour and materials push up wages and costs; firms raise prices (demand-pull and cost-push).
parts.working: 1 AD > potential; 1 positive output gap; 1 shortages; 1 rising prices.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a government should accept higher inflation to keep growth high.
parts.answer: Some inflation may be acceptable if it is temporary and growth reduces poverty and unemployment; but rising inflation erodes real incomes, damages competitiveness, may become entrenched and later need a costly recession to cure. Judgement.
parts.working: Up to 2 analysis; up to 2 evaluation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a long recession can raise the natural rate of unemployment (hysteresis).
parts.answer: Workers who are unemployed for a long time lose skills and motivation and are seen as less employable; they stop searching; so they become structurally unemployed even when demand recovers.
parts.working: 1 loss of skills; 1 discouraged workers/employers' view; 1 higher natural rate persists.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether hysteresis means a government should use expansionary demand-side policy quickly at the start of a recession.
parts.answer: Yes in part: acting early keeps workers in jobs, so skills are not lost and the natural rate does not rise; but time lags may mean the stimulus arrives late, it adds to government debt, and if the fall in output is caused by a supply shock it may mainly raise inflation. Retraining (supply-side) may also be needed. Judgement.
parts.working: Up to 2 analysis (early action prevents long-term unemployment and loss of skills); up to 2 evaluation (lags, debt, cause of recession, need for supply-side measures, judgement).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a government that faces an election may prefer high growth to low inflation.
parts.answer: Voters notice rising incomes and jobs quickly, while the inflation caused by expansion appears later (time lag), so a government may boost demand before an election and tighten afterwards — a political business cycle.
parts.working: 1 visible benefits of growth; 1 lag before inflation; 1 timing around elections; 1 political business cycle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether making the central bank independent removes this problem.
parts.answer: It removes control of interest rates from politicians, improving credibility; but governments can still use fiscal policy before elections, appoint central bank leaders, or pressure the bank. Judgement.
parts.working: Up to 2 analysis; up to 2 evaluation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an invented economy the short-run Phillips curve is: inflation (%) = 12 − 1.5 × unemployment (%). The central bank's inflation target is 3%. What unemployment rate is consistent with meeting the target in the short run?
A 2%
B 4%
C 6%
D 9%
parts.working: 3 = 12 − 1.5U → 1.5U = 9 → U = 6%. D (9%) forgets to divide by 1.5; B uses 12 ÷ 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a government can achieve low inflation and low unemployment at the same time.
parts.answer: In the short run demand-side policy faces a trade-off (short-run Phillips curve), but both can be achieved if unemployment is at or above a low natural rate and inflation expectations are anchored; supply-side policies that lower the natural rate and raise productivity make both possible; supply shocks make it harder.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: short-run Phillips curve and AD/AS; demand-pull trade-off; long-run vertical Phillips curve; natural rate; supply-side policies shifting LRAS right and the LRPC left; credibility of an independent central bank anchoring expectations. Evaluation: supply shocks (oil, food, exchange rate) create stagflation; time lags of supply-side policies; hysteresis; evidence of periods with low inflation and low unemployment (e.g. flattened Phillips curves); country context. Conclusion on 'can'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that economic growth should be the most important macroeconomic objective for a low-income country.
parts.answer: Growth raises incomes, creates jobs, funds public services and reduces poverty, so it is often a priority; but without price stability, external balance and fair distribution, growth may be unsustainable (boom–bust, inflation, debt crises) or fail to reach the poor; environmental sustainability also matters. Growth is necessary but not sufficient; priority depends on current conditions.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: benefits of growth (real GDP per head, employment, tax revenue, poverty reduction); links to other objectives — growth may raise inflation and the current account deficit; trickle-down vs inclusive growth. Evaluation: high inflation hurts the poor most; balance-of-payments crises and IMF programmes can stop growth; unequal distribution; environmental costs; population growth means GDP growth may not raise GDP per head; quality of growth. Conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether reducing a large budget deficit is compatible with achieving economic growth and low unemployment.
parts.answer: Short run: cutting spending or raising taxes reduces AD, growth and employment (multiplier). Long run: lower borrowing may reduce interest rates, crowding in, restore confidence and avoid debt crises, supporting growth. Compatibility depends on the state of the economy, the method of deficit reduction and the response of monetary policy.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: contractionary fiscal policy and AD/AS; multiplier; cyclical vs structural deficits; crowding out/crowding in; debt sustainability and interest costs. Evaluation: timing (in recession vs boom); composition (cutting investment harms long-run growth; cutting wasteful subsidies or broadening the tax base may not); expansionary fiscal contraction debate; accompanying monetary easing or depreciation; credibility with lenders; distributional effects. Conclusion on 'compatible'.

practice.stem:
In an invented economy the expectations-augmented Phillips curve is:
actual inflation (%) = expected inflation (%) + 10 − 2 × unemployment (%)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the inflation rate when unemployment is 4% and expected inflation is 3%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Workers now expect inflation to be the rate you calculated in (a). The government keeps unemployment at 4%. Calculate the new inflation rate.
parts.working: M1 expected inflation = 5. A1 5 + 10 − 8 = 7%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate of unemployment at which actual inflation equals expected inflation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain what these results show about the trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
parts.answer: Holding unemployment below 5% (the natural rate) gives ever-rising inflation (5%, then 7%, ...) as expectations adjust; the trade-off exists only in the short run, and the long-run Phillips curve is vertical at 5%.
parts.working: 1 inflation accelerates when U is held below the natural rate; 1 because expectations adjust upward each period; 1 so no permanent trade-off/vertical LRPC at 5%.

practice.stem: Invented model. Inflation each year is given by: inflation this year = inflation last year − 0.5 × (unemployment rate − 6). Inflation was 10% last year and the government wants it to fall to 4%. All rates are in %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: If the central bank keeps unemployment at 8%, calculate how many years it takes for inflation to fall from 10% to 4%.
parts.answer: 6 years
parts.working: M1 inflation falls by 0.5 × (8 − 6) = 1 point a year. A1 6 ÷ 1 = 6 years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sacrifice ratio (total percentage-point-years of unemployment above 6% ÷ the fall in inflation in percentage points).
parts.working: M1 2 × 6 = 12 point-years. A1 12 ÷ 6 = 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Instead the central bank keeps unemployment at 10%. Calculate the number of years needed and the sacrifice ratio.
parts.answer: 3 years; sacrifice ratio 2
parts.working: M1 inflation falls by 2 points a year → 3 years. A1 excess 4 × 3 = 12 point-years; ratio 2.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain what your answers suggest about choosing between a gradual and a rapid reduction in inflation.
parts.answer: In this model the total cost in unemployment is the same; the choice is between a smaller rise in unemployment for longer and a sharp, short recession. In practice credibility (faster change in expectations) or hysteresis could make one approach cheaper.
parts.working: 1 same total cost; 1 trade-off between depth and length / role of expectations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that conflicts between macroeconomic objectives are unavoidable in the short run but disappear in the long run.
parts.answer: Short run: demand changes create trade-offs (Phillips curve, growth v current account, inflation v growth). Long run: monetarists argue the LRPC is vertical so there is no lasting inflation–unemployment trade-off; supply-side growth can raise output without inflation. But some conflicts persist (growth v environment, growth v current account with high MPM, inequality) and hysteresis means short-run choices affect the long run. Judgement.
parts.working: Knowledge, understanding and analysis (up to 14): objectives listed; short-run Phillips curve and AD/AS conflicts; long-run Phillips curve and natural rate; supply-side policies; examples of persistent conflicts. Evaluation (up to 6): role of expectations; hysteresis; structural features of economies; policy mix; reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether giving an independent central bank an inflation target helps a government to achieve all of its macroeconomic objectives.
parts.answer: Independence and a target improve credibility, anchor expectations and reduce the sacrifice ratio, supporting stable growth and investment; it removes the political business cycle. But the bank may raise rates in a supply shock, hurting growth and jobs; it ignores the current account and inequality; fiscal policy may pull in the opposite direction. Judgement.
parts.working: Knowledge, understanding and analysis (up to 14): meaning of central bank independence and inflation targeting; expectations and credibility; effects on growth, unemployment, the exchange rate and the current account. Evaluation (up to 6): supply shocks; coordination with fiscal policy; developing-country issues (fiscal dominance, imported inflation); conclusion.

practice.stem:
Invented data for a country that tightened fiscal and monetary policy:
Year 1: inflation 24%, unemployment 6.0%, real GDP growth 5.5%, budget deficit 7.5% of GDP
Year 2: inflation 18%, unemployment 7.2%, growth 1.0%, deficit 6.0%
Year 3: inflation 11%, unemployment 8.1%, growth −0.4%, deficit 4.8%
Year 4: inflation 7%, unemployment 7.6%, growth 2.3%, deficit 4.1%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fall in inflation between Year 1 and Year 4, and the largest rise in unemployment compared with Year 1, in percentage points.
parts.answer: Inflation fell by 17 points; unemployment rose by up to 2.1 points (Year 3)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one conflict between objectives shown in the data.
parts.answer: Between low inflation and low unemployment/growth: tight policy cut inflation from 24% to 7% but unemployment rose to 8.1% and growth fell to −0.4%.
parts.working: 1 conflict named; 2 data used.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why unemployment fell in Year 4 even though inflation continued to fall.
parts.answer: As expectations of inflation fell, the short-run Phillips curve shifted down, so lower inflation became consistent with lower unemployment; recovery in growth (2.3%) and possible supply-side improvements also helped.
parts.working: 1 expectations; 1 SRPC shifts; 1 recovery/supply-side.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate whether reducing inflation was worth the costs shown in the data.
parts.answer: Benefits: inflation down 17 points, more stable environment, smaller budget deficit (7.5% → 4.1%). Costs: a recession, higher unemployment and lost output in Years 2–3. The costs seem temporary; long-run gains depend on whether low inflation persists. Judgement.
parts.working: Analysis up to 5 with the data; evaluation up to 3.

practice.stem: Invented data. A central bank's inflation target is 5% ± 1 percentage point. It forecasts inflation of 8% next year if its policy rate is unchanged, with unemployment at 6%. It estimates that each 1 percentage point rise in the policy rate lowers next year's inflation by 0.6 percentage points and raises unemployment by 0.3 percentage points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rise in the policy rate needed to bring inflation down to 5% next year, and the resulting unemployment rate.
parts.answer: 5 percentage points; unemployment 7.5%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rise in the policy rate needed to bring inflation down to 6%, the top of the target band, to two decimal places, and the resulting unemployment rate.
parts.answer: 3.33 percentage points; unemployment 7.0%

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether the central bank should aim for the middle or the top of its target band.
parts.answer: Top of band: smaller rate rise, 0.5 point less unemployment, still within target; middle: stronger credibility and anchors expectations, reducing future costs. Depends on cause of inflation (supply shock may be temporary), reliability of estimates and lags. Judgement.
parts.working: Up to 2 analysis using results; up to 2 evaluation.
